instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Jesse. How you doing today?
Client: Not too good. Doctor Grande?
Counselor: Not so good.
Client: Nah. I just got into a. I got into a fight with my parents.
Counselor: What's been going on?
Client: Well, I. I've been doing heroin for a few months now, and I didn't think my parents knew, but I guess they. They found a needle in my room and, I mean, they knew what I was doing, and they. They told me that I have to start shaping up and I need to stop doing any kind of drugs because they said. They said the next time that they find any kind of drugs, then that's it, they're going to kick me out of the house.
Counselor: All right. So they're at the point where anything else happens and they discover it, and you're out in the street. Right. What are your feelings about being out in the street?
Client: I don't want to be out there. I don't know. I don't know who would be. I mean, it would be hard just to kind of stop cold turkey. I know a couple of buddies that did that, and it's not good when you get junk sick. And, I mean, I'm kind of stuck because. I don't know. I don't want to be out on the streets, but it's just going to be so hard, so hard to give it up.
Counselor: So there are conflicting feelings here. You don't want to be out in the street, but you don't want to give up the heroin at the same time.
SPK_3: Right. Right.
Client: I just. I mean, I don't want to give it up, but I mean, I kind of know I have to. I mean, I'm a young guy. I couldn't make it outside of my parents house, and I definitely don't want to be on the streets.
Counselor: You want to stop to avoid the consequences, what could happen, right. But to this point, you haven't been able to.
Client: I mean, I guess at this point, I really haven't had, like, something that would make me, like, I've been doing it for a while, and, I mean, it's been pretty great, but I, you know, I never really had any kind of, like, problem with it. And nothing too bad has happened. So this is kind of the first time I've been like, something's hit me where it's like, oh, man, I really gotta stop it.
Counselor: So this is the first consequence or potential consequence that's motivated you since you started using? How strong is the craving to use?
Client: I mean, when I first started, it was. I mean, it was pretty freaking great. I mean, the rush that you get from it. It's. It's just mind numbing. It's. It's just amazing. But I've. I've noticed recently that, like, the rush isn't as intense anymore, and it's even, like, it's even kind of started to backfire a little bit where, like, actually, I'll feel a little sick without using it. And that, I mean, that kind of scares me. But the crazies are definitely still there.
Counselor: All right, so when you try to cut back, have you tried to cut back?
Client: I had before, but, I mean, there was no reason to, so I didn't try very hard.
Counselor: But when you did try, did you have the feeling where you were getting sick?
Client: I did, yeah. It wasn't as bad as any of my buddies, but I definitely. I mean, I didn't feel well.
Counselor: Have your parents given you any options in terms of, like, do they understand that you're. It seems like you're a little dependent on.
Client: Yeah, I mean, they, they do. I definitely, like, I don't hold anything against my parents. Like, actually, I have a pretty good relationship with them. I know what I'm doing isn't good for me. And they said that they would completely support me. They told me that they have a place picked out where I can go and that they'd be willing to pay for it and everything. But they said if I don't meet them halfway, then it's just. That's it. They're done.
Counselor: All right, so they have a solution, in a sense, for what's going on, right? Like, it's like a detox.
SPK_3: It is.
Counselor: Okay, detox. So they have a. They have a solution to help get you off the heroin, but there's still. There's still part of you that doesn't want to go that route.
Client: I mean, I, you know, I think. I think I'm starting to come to terms, and it's. That. That it's time to stop. And it might be good that maybe I'm stopping so early. I know. I know my friends have been doing it for a lot longer than I have, but I just. I don't know if the detox is going to work. I mean, it's hard for me to focus on, like, anything until sometimes. Until I get my next fix.
Counselor: All right, so there's a few problems here. So one is, can you. Can you commit to going to detox? And the second is, even if you successfully complete that, when you come back out, you can avoid the heroin.
Client: Right. It's tough right now because, actually, my dealer lives in my neighborhood. I mean, he's, I mean, he's just, like, a few. A few houses down. My girlfriend lives in our community, too, and, like, he's. He's on the way to her house, so, like, I'll. I'll kind of just maybe pick it up on my way, throw him. Throw it in my book bag, and then get. Hang out with my girlfriend a bit, and then maybe on my way back home, I'll shoot up the buddy, so.
Counselor: Right, so really, you're running into him as you walk to your girlfriend's house, right?
Client: Yeah, yeah.
Counselor: And he's there, and the temptations is great. And.
Client: I mean, it's like, that house is kind of, that's where I shoot up a lot. So it's like, whenever in his house. Right, right. So it's like, whenever. Whenever I'm coming up to his house, I'm like, I start getting excited. You know, I started anticipating how. How great it's gonna feel the next time, and it's. I don't know. It's, like, stuck with me. I get excited when it's his house.
Counselor: So you have a feeling. So let's explore this. As you're walking up to the. Well, as you're getting ready to pass this house on your way to your girlfriend, you divert to kind of go to his house, and you have this feeling of excitement. What's the thought that's going through your mind?
Client: I kind of. I just can't wait for the next hit. Now I got past this house since my parents are giving me the ultimatum, and now it's kind of mixed. Cause I'm like, oh, man, if I go do that and somehow they find out, like, it's kind of all over for me. But on the other hand, I'm thinking about how great it's gonna be. I'm just kind of, like, I'm planning in my mind how much I'm going to do and, like, what kind of plans we'll have for the rest of the night.
Counselor: Okay, so you have a. You have a few things going on. Do you think, like, is your plan right now to go into the detox?
Client: It is. Yeah. It's. Yeah. I mean, my. My definite plan is to go in the detox. And if the detox works, like, I mean, I think I could be done with it, but it's just, I don't, I don't know if the detox can work. And, I mean, I've never. I only tried to cut back that one time. I mean, I don't know how good I'll be at it. You know, let's.
Counselor: Let's presume for a second that the detox would be successful and. And you wouldn't be. You wouldn't be on heroin coming out of detox. Right, right. You're worried at that point that you'll go right back?
Client: I don't know if I'll go right back. Like, I think if I can get off it, if the detox actually works like they say I do, I think I can stay off it. I think, like, my. I think my cravings will still always be there. But now that. It's, like, now that I've come to the realization of some of the stuff that I can lose if I get caught, I mean, if I can get off it for good, I don't. I don't think I'd go back. It might be hard, like, if I run into my buddy or something.
Counselor: That's the point of worry. Right.
SPK_3: Right.
Counselor: So there's. There is a concern that you'll. You could. You could go back if you run into them.
Client: Right.
Counselor: But if you could stay away from him, you think you'd increase your chances of being successful?
Client: Well, I mean, yeah, definitely. I won't. Like, there's so many, like, experiences in this house that kind of feed into the anticipation and the cravings. I mean, if that doesn't happen, you know, probably hope.
Counselor: When are your plans in terms of going into detox?
Client: Pretty soon, I think. I'm supposed to go on Monday, after the weekend, so, like, three days.
Counselor: Okay. So it actually sounds like what your parents have put in place, you believe will work. Right. You have confidence it'll work and that your worry is what worry you have is when you get out, can you avoid. Can you avoid your friend?
Client: Right.
Counselor: You don't buy from anybody else other than your friend.
Client: No. No.
Counselor: So that's really becomes the. Maybe one of your key goals here, since you're sound like you're committed to the detox part. Right. I'm reading that incorrectly. That seems to be something you're.
Client: No. Yeah. If it works, then I can try.
Counselor: So it's preparing for life after detox.
Client: Right.
Counselor:
output: And avoiding. Well, you've heard the phrase people, places, things with the addictions or substance use. So in this case, you need to avoid, it would seem, your friend and where he lives, which is unfortunately not far from you and in between, like, his house is in between your house and your girlfriend.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Okay, so you said that when you're at work, you really worry that you're gonna say something stupid?
Client: Yeah, that's something that's always on my mind.
Counselor: What would be so bad about that if you did say something stupid at work?
Client: Because people would think I was weird.
Counselor: Then what would be so bad if people. People at work thought you were weird?
Client: They wouldn't want to be friends with me.
Counselor: And what would be so bad about that if people at work didn't want to be friends with you?
Client: Well, I just have no one to talk to at work.
Counselor: Then what would be so bad about having no one to talk to at work?
Client: I mean, the shoots can go on the whole day, so I'd just be by myself the whole time.
Counselor: And what would be so bad about being by yourself, you know, for a whole day?
Client: I don't know. I guess I should be used to it now. I spend a lot of my time by myself.
Counselor: Oh, that must be tough. What does that mean to you? That you spend a lot of time on your own?
Client: Dunno. I guess it's just like I spend so much time by myself that it's kind of like I'm nothing even worth being friends with.
Counselor: So it sounds like deep down that you think that you're not worth being friends with. That's quite a negative belief. I mean, how much would you say that you believe that out of a hundred? If 100 is where you believe it totally. And zero is where you don't believe it at all?
Client: I guess like 9500.
Counselor: When did you start believing that?
Client: I think it was probably at school. Yeah, I think at school.
Counselor: And what was it about school that made you start to believe that you weren't worth being friends with?
Client: Just like quite a lot of things. Like I wouldn't have anyone sit at lunch or people's birthdays and stuff. I wasn't invited and you know, like I was the last one picked for teams and stuff like that.
Counselor: And what is it now that makes you think that that's still true?
Client: I mean, it's kind of similar at work, obviously. Difference is that it's work, not school. But you know, people go for drinks and stuff after work or after a shoot, and I just kind of excluded a lot of the time.
Counselor: That sounds tough. Is there anything that makes you think that it's not true that you are worth being friends with?
Client: I guess my friends and family would say that I am. Like, I try to make a lot of time for my friends and stuff.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like deep down you have this thought that you're not worth being friends with. And that started at school when you had trouble making friends at school and that you weren't always picked for teams and that now at work it feels like the same thing is happening, that you're not always invited out for drinks with people and that sometimes you feel that you're excluded from their social groups. But then that's not the whole story. That on the other hand, you are close to family and you do have friends who would say that it's not true that you are worth being friends with. In CBT, we do a thing called thought challenging where when we have these negative thoughts, sometimes we actually put them up to scrutiny. We weigh up the evidence for and against them. I like to think of it as putting the thought on trial. Could we do that now where we just actually try and weigh up the evidence for and against that thought a bit more?
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Okay. So if I just put two columns here, so for and against. And it sounds like the evidence for this thought that makes you think that it is true is difficulty at school, making friends, being picked for teams, and difficulty at work, feeling excluded sometimes from groups.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But actually in this other column we have that you are close with your family and that you have some close friends. Okay. Now moving back to this first column, is there anything else that makes you think it's true that you're not worth being friends with?
Client: Just like, I kind of don't go to a lot of stuff. People have, like gatherings and things and a lot of the time I just. I don't go and rather just stay at home.
Counselor: Don't go to parties. What kind of parties are we talking? Like big parties, small parties, mainly big ones.
Client: If there's a lot of people there, I just find it really. It kind of makes me really anxious. So a lot of the time I just prefer not even to be in that situation in the first place.
Counselor: Okay. So you don't go to larger parties and events. Okay. Is there anything else that maybe thinks that it's makes you think that it's not true that actually you are worth being friends with?
Client: I mean, I guess my friends would say that I was. I do have close friends and, you know, when it's like their stuff that's important to them, I always make sure that I think about that. And even if I find it stressful, I'll always make sure that I can kind of put them first.
Counselor: Okay. So your friends would say that you are worth being friends with and it sounds like you put your friends first.
Client: Yeah, I do. Make sure I try and do that.
Counselor: In what kind of ways do you put your friends first?
Client: I guess when it's birthdays or, you know, something important to them, I'll always make sure that I'm there and that I put a lot of thought into presence and stuff like that.
Counselor: Can you give me an example of a time that you've done that?
Client: It was my friend's birthday a few weeks ago and we did like a big surprise at hers and I made a cake and stuff like that.
Counselor:
output: So you actually helped to organize events for your friends?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Carly. How you doing today?
Client: Doing okay.
Counselor: You doing okay?
Client: I guess, yeah.
Counselor: Not sure.
Client: I don't know, just the same.
Counselor: Yeah, still a little down.
Client: Yeah, I've been sleeping a lot. Going to work is a struggle. I don't really ever want to go. Just I haven't been eating much, so I think I've lost like ten pounds since past, like four months or so.
Counselor: Past four months?
Client: Um, just the guy. I don't know, I just haven't really been doing anything.
Counselor: You still been working?
Client: Well, yeah, yeah.
Counselor: But not much else?
Client: No, I usually just go to work and go home.
Counselor: Tell me what happens after you arrive at home, like after work?
Client: Um, well, my fiance tries to talk to me and really I just kind of want to go to sleep for just. I don't know. I tried, I tried reading the other day. Cause I used to like that and it's just, I think I got like into two pages and put the book down and decided to go to bed.
Counselor: What were you thinking when you put the book down?
Client: Just that I wasn't really happy doing it. I didn't really get any enjoyment out of it.
Counselor: I. And before you were depressed, which is, I guess about eight months now, you did enjoy reading?
Client: Mm hmm. Oh, yeah, all the time.
Counselor: So what would you have thought if you had to put a book down back then?
Client: Oh, I used to fall asleep reading. I would be up till like two in the morning just reading a book.
Counselor: Something you look forward to?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But not now?
Client: No, I just didn't really get any. I just wanted to try it and then I put it back down and was like.
Counselor: Were there other things that you used to enjoy doing that you don't feel motivated or comfortable to do now?
Client: Yeah, I used to be a runner and then I tried going for a run the other morning with my dog and I. I think we walked a block and that was pretty much it. I just couldn't wait for it to be over.
Counselor: Alright, so it wasn't a pleasant experience. Was there any part of it you connected with when you were running, like when you first started?
Client: Not really. I mean, it was a change to be outdoors and I realized I hadn't really seen the sun in a while, so. But other than that, I just, I had the intention of going out to run. I had my running shoes on and my dog was really excited. And then by the time I got out there, I was like, yeah, we're gonna walk. And then I thought about walking like our normal route. And by the time I got to the corner, I was like, yeah, we're gonna turn around and walk back.
Counselor: So what was the feeling like when you returned to your home after planning to run and then kind of walking and coming back?
Client: Kind of a mix of, like, relief just because it was over, and then, I guess more sadness because I didn't do anything. I didn't do what I had intended to do.
Counselor: Sadness, maybe disappointment.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So I've seen you a few times now, and based on those conversations, and, of course, what you said today, it seems like you have, for a variety of reasons, given up on the activities that you used to enjoy, you're not motivated toward them anymore.
Client: Yeah, I guess you could say that.
Counselor: And that's a common symptom of depression. I think we've talked about this a little bit before. So it's tough when you're depressed to find joy, satisfaction, happiness in activities that you once enjoyed. So we've been working with the cognitive piece. Right, like we did last time, we talked about the automatic thoughts that come up and kind of how that leads to some of the feelings of sadness and what we can do with the self talk. I'd like to talk about a different technique today that approaches the problem from a different angle. We'll continue to work the cognitive angle, but I want to add a new angle. And the technique is called behavioral activation. The theory behind it is that if you engage, if you schedule and engage in activities that you once enjoyed, even if you kind of have to fight your way through it a little bit, like with the running, that will connect to your mood. Right. Remember, we believe in cognitive therapy, that affect and behavior and cognition are all connected. So what you're thinking affects your behavior and your mood and what you do. Your behavior affects your thinking and your mood. Does that kind of make sense based on what we talked about?
Client: It does, yeah.
Counselor: So you mentioned the reading was one thing you like to do. That's tough to do. Now you try unsuccessfully with the reading and I the running. Anything else you could think of that maybe we could plan for you to do, even if it's just a short time, even if it's a little bit uncomfortable, that we could plan to do? That would be an activity that you used to enjoy?
Client: Well, my fiance and I used to go out with two other couples, and we used to go out once or twice a week, and even if it's just each other's houses, but we haven't really seen them in a while. They've tried to schedule things, but I've kind of come up with reasons of not feeling well or to kind of just stay home.
Counselor: So they're trying to initiate meeting, going out, doing something, and you're. You're kind of pushing them off.
Client: Yeah, I just. I haven't really wanted to see anybody lately.
Counselor: All right, so that's. So we have reading, running, and then going out with these two other couples. Anything else you can think of that you used to really enjoy before that you can't quite motivate yourself to do now?
Client: I mean, I used to like going for, like, just walks and shopping with my fiance. Like, I. We used to spend a lot of time together, and lately it's just kind of. I come home, say hello, we eat dinner, and then I kind of do my own thing.
Counselor: So spending time with your fiance outside the house in some manner? Shopping was one example. Any other activities like movies or going out to eat?
Client: Yeah, I would kind of put those in with the things that we would do outside together. We would try to switch it up every now and then.
Counselor: Okay, so that's distinct from what you did with the couples because that's just you and your fiance?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So let's do this. What kind of books do you like to read?
Client: I like a lot of fiction. I do a lot of reading for school, so I usually enjoy those books too. Mystery novels.
Counselor: Mystery novels. Okay, let's center on mystery novels. How long would it take you to read, say, a chapter of a mystery.
Client: Novel, roughly, depending on the size of the chapter, probably a couple minutes normally.
Counselor: So not long at all.
Client: No.
Counselor: So you could get a lot of reading done in, say, ten minutes, like something worthwhile. And how often would it. How often would you, what was the duration of a run? Like when you would go run? How long would it take?
Client: Probably, like a half hour.
Counselor: Half hour.
Client: Half hour to 45 minutes. Yeah. I used to do long distance running, so.
Counselor: Okay, and how often would you do that?
Client: Three or four times a week.
Counselor: Three or four times a week? Half hour, 40 minutes. And you mentioned you went out with the couple once or twice a week. How often would you go out with your fiance?
Client: I would say we try to do something every day, like, even if it was just going for a walk together, like around the park or walking the dog together.
Counselor: Okay. So I'd like to make collaboratively with you a schedule that involves those four activities, but I want to make it realistic. You tried a couple times, you weren't successful. So we don't want to be too ambitious, but I want to try to plan a schedule. You can get the habit of doing these activities again. So let's start with the kind of, I guess the simplest in terms of logistics, which would be probably the reading. Would it be possible, say, five nights out of seven, to read for ten or 15 minutes? Like, I know you're going to have to force your way through it a little bit, but I think it's something.
Client: I could try to do.
Counselor: So you're going to have automatic thoughts that come up, right. Like, just like you did before, and you're going to be tempted to give up. I want you to try to push through, say, this at least ten minutes. So focus on that as you go into it. It's a behavioral exercise, of course. It has a cognitive component to kind of think, you know, I just have to make this ten minutes.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: And again, you might not really enjoy it the same way it did before. We kind of know that, but over time, that may change.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: All right, so does five nights a week seem reasonable? That's 50 minutes a week.
Client: Yeah, that seems fine.
Counselor: Okay, then let's move to the running, because you just recently tried that. You run with your dog. You said, yeah, okay, how about that? Twice a week. Would that be possible?
Client: Yeah, I can try to do that.
Counselor: What days of the week you think you could do it?
Client: Probably the weekends. So probably like Saturday or Friday night or Saturday morning.
Counselor: Okay, so Saturday morning and Friday night, would you run Friday night and then again Saturday morning?
Client: No, I guess not. So probably I'd see maybe Wednesday night and Saturday morning.
Counselor: Okay, so Wednesday night and Saturday morning run for, say, a minimum of a half hour.
Client: I can try for that, yeah.
Counselor: Again, remember, you're gonna have these automatic thoughts, likely that will be telling you that you should stop, but you have to kind of talk your way through that or do the best you can.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Right. The adaptive response maybe being something like, in the end, this will help me. It's tough now, but this will help me. Okay, so let's look now toward the more social aspects. Logistically, moving up the ladder here to the most complex. It sounds like going out with their fiance would be the next. At the next level.
Client: Yeah, he's. I don't know if he's kind of just been mad at me lately or if he just thinks I need to be alone, but we've kind of been getting some distance there, so I think that would, out of everything, that would be the relationship I'd want to work on the most.
Counselor: Focus on. All right, so maybe you're running Wednesdays and Saturday mornings. Could you go out and do something to fiance twice a week.
Client: Yeah, I think we could manage that.
Counselor: Cause sometimes you said you just walk around, like, the neighborhood, so it's not even. Doesn't have to be necessarily, like, a lot of time. It's just something.
Client: Mm hmm.
Counselor: All right. What do you think you can do to motivate yourself to do that?
Client: I don't know. I guess just having, like, him maybe remind me or suggest it.
Counselor: So you could tell him that this is something that you're planning to do and you might need a little push to. To do it.
Client: Yeah, pretty much.
Counselor: Or to maintain it.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So you might get outside the same thing when you run. You might want to come right back in.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right. And then moving to the most complex, but also the one with the highest social engagement, going out with the two couples now, once or twice a week, you'd mentioned before. How about we shoot for. How do we shoot for now? Once every couple weeks?
Client: I think I could handle that.
Counselor: Like, maybe a Saturday night or a Friday night.
Client: Yeah, I think that could work.
Counselor: What can you see being an obstacle there? Like, what might help you be motivated to continue that?
Client: Just having to actually go to their houses or go somewhere because they don't really live close to us. They're not far. But just the fact that we would have to get in the car, drive over there, and I would actually have to, like, look relatively nice. I can't just go and pajamas.
Counselor: So for this to work, that is for you to do it, you really have to schedule at their house. You can't have them come to you.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So that's one thing we know. You have to. You have to make some time and drive over there, or maybe if your fiance drives, whichever. But you have to.
Client: We physically have to go over.
Counselor: So once you're there. So it might be tough, like, to get in the car and make the drive over once you're there, how do you think it would feel?
Client: I don't know if it's like the run, I probably just want to turn around and come back.
Counselor: Do these couples know that you're down?
Client: I think they've noticed, and I think that's probably why they've kind of started to back off with asking us to do things. So I think they've noticed it, but they don't know, like, any. They don't know what's really going on.
Counselor: Are those relationships you're worried about losing because they're backing off?
Client: Yeah. Yeah. I. I mean, they're our closest friends, so I think we've known each other for a really long time.
Counselor:
output: And could you see this behavior being one that brings you closer together with them? Like restore some of that?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Okay, Marsha, so how can I help you today?
Client: Well, I'm working full time. I'm a part time student. I've just gotten engaged, and I live at home. There's just so much stress in my life. I have everything happening all at once. Just to top it all off, I failed an exam, a really big exam, and I just feel like I can't do anything anymore. I can't do anything right. I've just got so much stress, and I feel like such a disappointment, such a failure. And I've embarrassed my family by failing. I just don't know what to do anymore. I guess I've come here today to tell you, like, I want to leave uni, and I guess that's why I've come here to you today.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like a whole lot of stuff's on top of you at the moment.
Client: Yeah, just so much. Just all parting on. Yeah.
Counselor: So you're working full time, plus part time study. Part time study. And then you've got your wedding preparation.
Client: Yeah, just got engaged, and weddings just a month away now, so, yeah, so I've just got so much happening. Work is really, really demanding and. Yeah, just fail this exam. It's just. Yeah, don't know what to do all too much.
Counselor: So imagine you've been sweating on this for a while, and it's all been swirling around in your head.
Client: Just been building up and building up and so much pressure with everything. And I'm living at home, so my parents, you know, a lot of pressure, need to do everything right. And. Yeah, by failing this, I feel like I've just embarrassed and disappointed them, and I just don't feel like I'm good enough, you know, to go on studying.
Counselor: Okay. And have they said much to you about failing your exam?
Client: They haven't said much. I was really scared to tell them, actually, because I knew they'd just be so disappointed and just embarrassed by the fact that I did fail. Yeah. I've never failed anything before. And so, yeah, really hard.
Counselor: Yeah. So it's new and you don't like it at all?
Client: Not at all, no. And I think leaving uni will just be the way out, just so I don't have to go through it again.
Counselor: Right. Okay. Well, I'm glad you've come to counselling, because it's good for us to get an outsider's opinion when we've got so much on our plate and we're confused as to what to do and our emotions can get in the way. And you've just said earlier that a whole lot of stuff's on your plate at the moment. Okay. So I'm glad you've come here. Here at the clinic, we use the ABC model, which is a cognitive behavioural therapy model. So, Marsha, some counsellors have put together a list of beliefs that we often use and we don't realise that we're using those beliefs and they tend to be faulty ones. Here's the list. Here, have a look through that to see if there are any beliefs that you might be operating on at the moment.
Client: I think number two.
Counselor: Okay, read that one out for me.
Client: That it's necessary to have a high degree of order uncertainty in order to be happy and perform well.
Counselor: Yeah, yeah, you mentioned that earlier.
Client: Number four, that it's necessary to be competent and successful in all those things which are attempted.
Counselor: Yeah, that's an expectation from your family.
Client: Yeah, possibly. Number eight, that life should be entirely pleasant and enjoyable and that any frustration, discomfort or pain would be unbearable.
Counselor: Which one of those stands out the most for you at the moment?
Client: Um, probably number four.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor:
output: How would you put that in your own words?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Maria. How are you doing today?
Client: I'm doing well. How are you?
Counselor: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. How things been going?
Client: Um, okay. I've been having some trouble with some friends and stuff. I just. I think just people just don't get me. I just don't think people get me.
Counselor: They don't understand it. Your friends don't understand you?
Client: No, they just don't. And right now, I just, you know, I just don't want to be friends with anybody right now because they just don't understand me. And I don't know. I think I'm just not gonna have friends for a while.
Counselor: That seems like a fairly large shift from kind of your position before on having friends, you seem to really like spending time with them. Has something happened that led to this?
Client: Well, you know, I just said some things, and now it's just gotten out of hand, and I just think I need to break from this friendship group for a little bit.
Counselor: You seem upset about this.
Client: Yeah, I mean, we were just talking about some things, and, you know, I was just telling them that, you know, I play tennis and I enjoy tennis, and I was just maybe went on a little bit about how I play tennis.
Counselor: Tell me about that.
Client: Well, it's a little embarrassing. I just. I was exaggerating about how I play tennis, and they were telling me how they had wanted to go to the US Open, and they want to go every year because they love it. And I've never been really. But I wanted to. I wanted to be part of the conversation a little bit. So I told them that I had studied under a famous tennis player and that they were really impressed with that. And so I just kept talking about that and all the stuff that I learned and told them that I was really good at tennis.
Counselor: And in reality.
Client: I maybe played a couple of times, so. And I've never met that person, let alone studied under them. And I really don't know how I got to the point where I was elaborating the story. And so they want to have some lessons. They want to learn what I learned under this person. And, you know, they started talking back, getting together, and at that moment, I kind of got caught up and I said, sure. And, yeah, we'll schedule it, like, Saturday mornings. We'll get together and we'll just kind of hit together and play some sets. And I don't know. I don't know what to do. It's just really embarrassing now because they're gonna know that I really don't know how to play tennis. You know, I could maybe have faked it a little bit, but now they think I had professional training, so.
Counselor: So it's gonna be very obvious to them that you weren't being completely honest if you have to play tennis with them.
Client: Right. And they're just gonna know and then they might question some other things.
Counselor: I've said things that are not tennis related.
Client: Yeah. So.
Counselor: Do you feel that in your relationship with these friends that you have not been honest? Frequently? A few times. Like, how would you categorize this is.
Client: Really hard to admit. It's just stupid. I just. It's stupid. It's just something I do. Sometimes I get kind of caught up or I'm feeling left out of a situation and they're all talking about a topic and I want to fit in. So I might say a couple of things that make it sound like I know what I'm talking about or that I can relate to the topic when I can't.
Counselor: Alright, so in social situations, when you're feeling isolated from the conversation or maybe detached from the people, you create a story that helps reintegrate you back into that conversation.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. You know, it's hard. I feel stupid just standing there, like, having no idea. Like, when they talk about traveling and seeing different cities and stuff, I haven't really been outside of my small town, you know, gone to Florida, went to Disney World and went to Epcot. So, you know, when they're talking about going to Paris and, you know, seeing the Eiffel Tower and seeing Notre Dame, or they're talking about going to Rome and, you know, I just. I can't. I can't really. I don't really have anything to say. I don't really have that kind of a life, and it's not very exciting. So sometimes I might say stuff about that and it's a lot of little things, you know, that I just. I find myself saying things that aren't true and trying to just go along with what they're talking about when I don't even know what they're saying, you know, and they talk about fashion or they talk about just different things, and I don't know what to do in that situation. And I'm just finding myself just making things up and saying things that I think that they want to hear and I don't even know if they believe it. You know, I kind of got the feeling this time that they were kind of calling me out because they were. They were getting an idea of what I had been doing, and it was really embarrassing. I feel like I just want to run away from the situation, and I don't want to talk to anybody, and I just want to break off friendships.
Counselor: So a possible solution to what you consider the inevitable embarrassment if you have to play tennis with them is to just not see them, just not return their calls.
Client: Right. I just. I don't want them to know what, you know, that I have a really boring life and that I don't. I'm not as smart as they are, and I'm not as successful, and I just. I don't want them to know and that I'm kind of like a loser compared to all of their exciting things that they do and say. I just don't match up.
Counselor:
output: You feel you can't keep up with them on really so many levels. You talked about travel and fashion and, of course, now the athletics area with the tennis. So is a sense of being inadequate when you're with them or.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: So these daggy little sheets we use for cognitive behavioral therapy or strategies. Counselor: Okay, so what have you written in there?

Counselor: Okay.
Client: That's the one.
Counselor: Do you want to write that in and see? Are there any other feelings that really resonate with you? I mean, that's enough. But is there anything other sort of feeling you have when you're
Client: scared?
Counselor: Okay, so pop that one in there. Anything else?
Client: Embarrassed.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: All right.
Counselor: Do you want to pop that one in there as well? This is great. You've really sort of clicked with it. All right, so now why are we doing all this? Because what I'm going to ask you now is to imagine what the little voice in your head, you know, that little self talk is saying when you're feeling anxious. So what are you feeling anxious about? What's the sort of story in your head that's going on there?
Client: All right, I'm. How's it. What happens? I'm thinking I'm gonna get lost.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Yeah. So I'm anxious because I think I'm gonna get lost.

Client: Yeah.

Client: Happens.

Client: Um, yeah, I reckon I start blushing and, you know, going red.

Client: Panic that I'll go red. Blush.

Client: I do.
Counselor:
output: So this is sort of really useful. We've been able to sort of tease out your situation, the feelings. And really, what's that little voice in your head that's going on? instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Maury. How you doing today?
Client: I'm doing all right.
Counselor: You doing all right?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I know last time you were here, you were discussing some relational issues. You want to continue with that?
Client: Yeah, yeah. I mean, you know, it kind of came up again. You know, every time my wife yells at me, you know, I feel like a failure, you know, like I told you last time, I just. I just feel like I can't do anything right, you know? Like everything I try to do is met with arguing and yelling, and I just feel like there's nothing I can do right.
Counselor: So no matter what you do, it's not going to end up the way you want?
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: So it's frustrating.
Client: Yeah, it definitely is.
Counselor: How is what's going on impacted your relationship with your wife?
Client: I mean, it's rocky, you know, because I feel like I can't do anything right. She doesn't understand that. And then, you know, we don't get along ever because we're just always yelling and I'm always feeling bad, and then it just keeps going like that.
Counselor: So when you. You mentioned you feel like a failure when she. When she yells at you?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Can you think back to maybe the last time, one of the last times you guys argued and try to remember that thought? We've talked about automatic thoughts before. Remember that thought that comes in that moment when she starts. She starts yelling at you?
Client: I mean, she'll yell at me. I mean, I feel, you know, frustrated. Like, why are you yelling at me right now? And. I don't know. I mean, as I was thinking about, like we were talking about it, and as I was thinking about it more this week, kind of felt like, you know, kind of like what happened with my dad, you know? I guess I kind of felt that same way when I was younger. You know, like, if my dad would yell at me or when he would yell at me, I kind of feel that same way. And it feels like the same thing. Yeah. It's kind of the first. I guess kind of the first thought that comes to mind.
Counselor: The first thought is I've been through something like this before, I guess.
Client: Yeah. I mean, I'm not really thinking those exact words, but that's definitely what it feels like, you know? Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. Like, it's like just a sense that this isn't brand new.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And the feeling you're connecting with it is the same feeling you had when your dad. Yahweh. Yeah.
Client: Yeah, pretty much, yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. So, in a sense, these arguments are taking you back to another point in time.
Client: I guess so, in a way, that's distressing.
Counselor: Yeah, it is.
Client: I mean, it feels, you know, pretty crappy.
Counselor: Now, in these arguments, she yells at you. You mentioned before that you do some yelling of your own, you know, in the midst of all that. Right. How would you rate it in terms of, like, any physical violence? Nothing like that.
Client: No, it's just words. I mean, we're just, you know, just yelling.
Counselor: And what level, like, what level of yelling would you say? How severe compared to what you've experienced in the past?
Client: Yeah, I don't know. I mean, it's like, you know, sometimes it can get up to, like, the eight or nines, you know, but just, I guess generally it's, you know, down. Closer to a seven on scale, like one to ten. Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: So sometimes it's seven. That would be pretty bad.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But some other times it's not.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So do you feel like your reaction is being frustrated is disproportionate to what's really going on or you feel like it's money?
Client: I don't know what else to do. You know? I mean, it's just. It's kind of my reaction, my gut reaction to it, you know? I think I'm justified in it because, you know, she just doesn't understand how much she yells at me, you know, and how much that hurts me. You know? I do feel justified. I mean, but it just. It just keeps going, though. And I feel justified, though. I don't know.
Counselor: Let's talk for a moment about, if you're okay with it, about your father and his yelling. You've discussed this with me a little bit before. In the past few sessions. I remember you saying that most. It was in the afternoon. Most of the yelling was when you were both home.
Client: Yeah, I mean, it was. I mean, mostly when I get home from school. I mean, I wasn't, you know, I was in high school, and then after that, you know, I went to college. And so I wasn't really home much during college, but, you know, I guess it'd be after I got home from high school. You know, I'd get home and he'd get home from work and, you know, just kind of be aggravated, whatever, just start yelling and. Yeah, usually when I got back from school, yeah.
Counselor: So he would get back from work, you would get back from school. And how long would that last? How long would the period where you were kind of vulnerable to being yelled at last?
Client: I don't know. I mean, sometimes about an hour, you know, and he'd be yelling because he's, you know, frustrated from work and he's frustrated from the drive home and whatever else, you know? And at some point, he would usually start drinking, you know, so maybe about an hour or so, you know, where that was. Like, you knew you were gonna get it.
Counselor: So kind of every day you could predict that between when you. Or between when he came home after you were already home from school and when he started drinking, you were gonna. He was gonna find something to yacht you about.
Client: Yeah, yeah, yeah. And, I mean, there were some days, like, I knew when he came home, he came home the same time every day. I knew I could get out of the house, you know? Cause at some point, I had a car, my friends had cars, you know, whatever.
Counselor: You had more freedom.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. You know, at some point, I had a job, so sometimes I'd work after school and stuff, so I knew I'd be able to leave the house at times, you know, like when I knew he was gonna start yelling and stuff. But, I mean, there was a period of time probably like my senior year of high school that I just didn't, you know, I just came home and, you know, it was gonna happen, you know, that's the way it happened.
Counselor: Even though you were able to escape it.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Right. You could have stayed out long enough for him to start drinking. Yeah.
Client: Instead you stayed in the house.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: I mean, it was pretty much my whole senior year come home. I knew what was gonna happen, and I just took it. You know, I just. I knew he was gonna yell. I just took it that.
Counselor: Was there ever a period when you first got your freedom that you tried, like.
Client: Oh, yeah, yeah, I did. And. I don't know. I don't know why I didn't just keep doing that. It probably would have been easier, but. I don't know. The whole senior year, I just started. I was just back there at the house when he came home from work.
Counselor: So in that period, were you. Were you. There's times when you did leave, what did he do instead of yell at you?
Client: I guess he had to yell at somebody else. I mean, my. My sister, my brother were home. I guess he probably yelled at them. I don't know. I mean, it felt good to not be there, but I guess he probably yelled at them, which just sucks. I mean, you know, I guess somebody had. Whoever was there was gonna take it, you know?
Counselor: Somebody was gonna get you out there.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. I mean, I guess it was them when I wasn't there. I don't know.
Counselor: And how do you think you took it. When you were there, how well did you respond?
Client: I just got used to it, you know, I knew what was gonna happen. I knew he was gonna yell. I knew that it was gonna make me upset. I knew that just those repeated times, just like now, you know, I'm gonna feel like a failure, which ultimately I did. You know, maybe I probably just became numb to it, you know, it happens so often and same thing every day. Probably just became numb to it and just kind of stopped caring and kind of stopped, I don't know, believing in myself or something, you know?
Counselor: Like you've just given up.
Client: Yeah, probably. That's probably. I don't know. Probably. Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: And how many years total did this experience go on? Do you endure the yelling?
Client: I mean, it would have been while I was in middle school and most of high school. I mean, I told you at some point I was able to leave, but probably all of middle school, most of high school, and I left, and then some, you know, for the rest of the senior year, I would be there. So, I don't know, quite a few years, I guess.
Counselor: A long time to suffer.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: And now if we move back forward in time, you're in a relationship where you're getting yelled at a bit. Right. And that's sometimes quite a bit, and that's causing you distress.
Client: It's like the same thing. You're yelling a little bit and. Yeah.
Counselor: So you feel like you're back in the same place.
Client: Yeah, I mean, it does. Yeah. I mean, obviously, you know, she's. She's not doing anything like he was, you know, like drinking or anything like that, but it does. I mean, it's like the same thing that happened is happening again.
Counselor: So that's. In your opinion, that's the consequence of what happened to you. Like, all this yelling that you endured before in some way is significantly contributing to what you're going through now.
Client: Maybe. I mean, I guess it could, you know, because it is the same thing. So maybe it's.
Counselor: There could be some connection.
Client: Maybe. Yeah.
Counselor: I mean, maybe not 100% explain it, but it explains part of it.
Client: Yeah, it definitely could. I definitely could.
Counselor: So your functioning has been affected a bit. I mean, to the point where you're here with me now, we're talking about it, and you're frustrated, and it does sound painful. Now, I'm curious. You mentioned you had a younger sister and a younger brother, and they grew up in the same house. How are they doing?
Client: Well, my sister, she's three years younger than I am. She's doing great. I mean, she graduated from college, like, top of her class kind of thing, you know? And she's about to get married, too. That's cool. Got a really great guy, you know. She's doing great. She lives next town over for me. I get to see her a lot. Yeah, she's great, though. My brother, he's five years younger than I am. He's doing pretty good, too. He's just about to graduate from college. I think he gets really good grades, too, from what I hear, from what he tells me. I don't get to see him as much as I do her because she's in college, but I think he's doing really well, too. You know, they both. Yeah, they both do some really good stuff. They have really good goals and stuff like that.
Counselor: You seem like you have a good relationship with them. You're proud of them. Yeah, definitely.
Client: I'm definitely proud of them. I think they're doing some really good stuff, you know, really trying to make something of themselves. Yeah.
Counselor: So, you know, I wonder. They're doing pretty well. You're doing okay, but you're having a rough time right now. How would things have been if you had taken that? I know it's difficult to predict, but if you had taken that opportunity to not be there, if you had, like you said, you had a car, your friends had cars, you could have avoided. You could have avoided the situation directly between your dad and you.
Client: Yeah, I mean, yeah, I guess I could have. I don't know. I mean. I mean, I took the yelling and stuff, so, you know, it's obviously affecting me now.
Counselor: You took the brunt of the abuse.
Client: Yeah, I guess I did. I mean, you know, I bring it up to them sometimes and they're like, yeah, I mean, dad yelled sometimes, but, you know, it wasn't that bad. Definitely a different experience from what I had. You know, they don't see it like I do, you know? I don't know. Maybe things would have been worse for them.
Counselor: So, in a sense, your father verbally abused you. Nothing makes that right. But in a sense, you, because you were there and you were the target. And. Could ride it out, you shielded them from that abuse.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I mean, you mentioned it would have been somebody else, right?
Client: Yeah. Yeah, it probably would have been them. Probably was them when I wasn't there, you know? Yeah, I don't know.
SPK_3: I guess you're probably right.
Client: I mean, they are doing pretty well, you know, I think probably they're doing better than I am, I guess.
Counselor: You know, probably no small part because of your protecting them.
Client: Right.
Counselor: I mean, you were in an impossible situation, and you made the choice to stay there.
Client: I guess I did. Right.
Counselor: There was some negative consequences for you, which we'll try to work through, but some really positive consequences for your siblings.
Client: Yeah. Yeah, I guess so. I mean, they, you know, I feel like a failure most of the time, but, I mean, they don't. They're doing good stuff, you know? Shoot, I guess you're right. I mean, that could have been it. I guess I'd love to ask them, like, what, you know, like, what they think would have happened if, you know, the yelling would have been more or something towards them, you know?
Counselor: And maybe you'll find out that when you weren't there, that is what would happen.
Client: Maybe.
Counselor: So you feel like a failure, but at the same time, you're happy for them and proud of all their accomplishments.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor:
output: It seems like you were a part of that success.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Jeff. How you doing today?
Client: I'm alright. Thanks for actually seeing me today. Sure.
Counselor: How have you been? I know last time I spoke with you, you were having some difficulties at work.
Client: I'm still having difficulties at work and that's why I'm glad I have a session today because it hasn't stopped. The frustration and anger is just, it's there ten times more than normal.
Counselor: You're really frustrated. Way more than normal, way more angry.
Client: Yes, it's, there seems to be a lot that's going on and I continually don't get the help that I need, not only not from my coworker, but also my supervisor. So it just feels so that everything is my responsibility and I have to make it happen. And if I don't make it happen, it's not going to happen. And then it's just, it's all on me and I don't feel as though that it's fair. But I also don't want us to not succeed. So I don't know how to navigate those two field.
Counselor: So the weight of the work assignments is really on you. You're feeling that pressure. You want to do right by your employer and there's an emotional toll this is taken on you. Has it reached a point where you've talked to your, it's a coworker supervisor you mentioned?
Client: Yes. So I talked to my supervisor about my coworker actually assisting me with some of the projects that we have going on. And my supervisor keeps on saying, oh, they're helping out and they're doing what they're supposed to do, but they're not doing what they're supposed to do because I end up doing their work. Because, say, for example, last week we actually had to turn in this huge report that we were working on for over a month. Literally, my coworker came to me on Monday and said I didn't do my portion of the report. And I was just like, we had a month to work on a lot of time. And so I spent the next three days doing everything for their part of the report. Luckily, I had already finished my part of the report and then combined it and actually turned it into my supervisor. Of course we get the, oh, this is a wonderful, great job that you guys did. And I'm just like you guys, as.
Counselor: If you both contributed equally.
Client: Correct? Correct.
Counselor: So in three days, you made up for a month's worth of work.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So I could see how that could be. It's very stressful.
Client: Very, very taxing. Very, very taxing.
Counselor: And this wasn't an isolated incident?
Client: Oh, no. This has been going on for probably three or four months now.
Counselor: So this is almost the expectation when you get to work.
Client: Correct? Correct. I think that you hit the nail on the head. It's expected of me and nobody actually sees it as an expectation anymore.
Counselor: It's just what you do. It's just what I do. So you can know that going into work the next day, you go in, whenever that is, that there's always this probability, this chance that you could have work just thrown on you that wasn't budgeted for, you weren't planning on.
Client: Correct. And sometimes that work actually comes out from my supervisor, but it's mostly coming from my coworker. Like, I know they're not going to do their portion, so I just automatically start doing it anyway because, you know.
Counselor: You kind of have to.
Client: I know it's going to fall on my lap either today, tomorrow, next week. So I would rather be preemptive and actually start it then so that I'm not rushing like I was, like last week to finish a month's worth of work and three days worth of time. So I'm not as stressed.
Counselor: So you've tried to address this in the framework, in the context of your work. You've talked to the supervisor, to the co worker?
Client: I talked to the supervisor, I'm afraid. Well, I can't really talk to the coworker because I don't feel as though that's my position. However, I have expressed my frustration, my anger, my disappointment with my supervisor. And my supervisor keeps on saying, oh, I'll fix it, or, oh, it doesn't seem as though that they haven't done their piece of the work because I do all of it and it's turned in. So I have. But there doesn't seem to be anything happening outside of that.
Counselor: What kind of options, in terms of your job do you feel like you have now?
Client: I don't feel as though that I have any options. That's the thing. I think that either if I can, if I don't do the work and we fail, we're going to lose some of these big projects that we're working with, which then is going to impact our entire office. And if it impacts our entire office, like somebody might be let go. And because I am the newest person in our office, I feel as though that's going to be me. So I need to protect my job by doing not only my work, but my coworkers work and sometimes my supervisors work.
Counselor: So you're really figuratively fighting for survival?

Client: Yeah.

Client: Yeah.

Client: Yeah.

Client: Well, I can, you know, keep. Stay in the mindset that I have that extra money and spend what I think is that extra money, digging into the money I paid for my rent, my food, my gas, my insurance, and me, who's somebody without all that.
Counselor: So you could fail to pay expenses that need to be paid.
Client: And they helped me go to my full time job that I still have. I don't have another expense. Right. And how would this. How would that connect to losing your job?

Counselor: So it'd be. So the ticket would be so expensive, you would lose your.

Client: I'd lose my insurance.
Counselor: And then by losing your insurance, you lose your transportation altogether because you can't drive that insurance. And then you lose your job.
Client: Mm hmm. I mean, it's either go to work with an uninsured car, and then I can get pulled over and go to jail for driving with no insurance multiple times.
Counselor: No, that's serious. Yeah. You wouldn't want to do that.
Client: I wouldn't go to jail.
Counselor: So there's two. You have two kind of causal change. One is losing your job. And now even just the idea you can end up incarcerated.
Client: Yes. I mean, which I definitely lose my.
Counselor: Job if I'm in jail, I would imagine.
Client: And so that would have. So then I wouldn't even have, like, any money to help me through jail. Like, to. For the commissary and stuff.
Counselor: Because you would have no income.
Client: I would have no income. And then when I get out of jail, I'm. No one's gonna hire me.
Counselor: Because you have a criminal record.

Counselor: Which makes it challenging to find employment in some instances. That's understandable that you'd be upset about that. I doubt many people would be happy about losing additional income, but you move from there, from losing additional income, which is what has actually happened to this possibility that you could be in jail or lose your job because of this. So I remember maybe last week. Week before, you're talking about the. The letter that you received from. It was like a late notice. It wasn't. Turned out wasn't.

Client: Yeah. That it was, you know, it wasn't me. And, you know, that was a relief. But this is something that's solid. I don't have my part time job anymore.
Counselor: You've lost real income.
Client: I mean, this isn't a mistake. This isn't a. We fired the wrong person. You know, this is real. So there's real concerns here.
Counselor: I.
Client: Unlike last time, where I was lucky.
Counselor: So this. This situation, you see, is different than the first situation because the first situation was more. You were perceiving something was wrong that wasn't wrong because you weren't the intended recipient of the letter.
Client: Yeah.

Counselor: You struggled.

Counselor: But you've had other jobs that didn't work out before and that didn't affect you getting that job.
Client: That's true.
Counselor: So the worst case scenario, I guess what I'm getting at the worst case scenario is, in your case, ending up in jail or losing your full time job, which you've had for a while.
