Counselor: Does that make sense? Yeah, but you don't do the same thing for the positive side. You don't look at how something could work out. Well, would you say it's fair assessment?
Client: Yeah. Yeah, no, that's. That's pretty accurate.
Counselor: But still, you're worried about this.
Client: I mean, yeah, I am worried. I'm not gonna be thrilled about it, but I suppose I don't have to go to when I'm gonna go to jail or I'm gonna lose my full time job.
Counselor: I think there's a lot of intervening factors that could occur before going to jail or losing your job. There's other things that you could do.
Client: I suppose I could get a family member to drive me or take the bus if I lost my insurance and lost my car.
Counselor: So, alternate forms of transportation. Yeah. There's adapting your spending back to where it was before.
Client: That's true.
Counselor: Part of your fear was that you wouldn't be able to adapt your spending. Right. But that's something you would have control over.
Client: I guess. I can keep, you know, better track of how much I do spend and, you know, keep track of my bank accounts and exactly how much money I have in them.
Counselor: So, having talked through this a little bit. Right. What I'm going to refer to, or is referred to as catastrophizing. Remember we talked about that when we reviewed the cognitive distortions.
Client: That sounds familiar. Yeah.
Counselor: Where a negative is taken and just making way more negative than it is at the moment. Right. Kind of knowing that, that tends to be what you do. It's what we call an error in thinking that you tend to make. Does that lower your anxiety about the situation? Does it change it in some way?
Client: I mean, knowing that I'm thinking about it wrong makes me feel a little better.
Counselor: I would say you're thinking about it in a way that's less than useful.
Client: Okay. That actually makes me feel better. Knowing that, you know, these things can happen, but it might not. There's other things that can happen before them.
Counselor: Yeah. I mean, I would even say probably not.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So one way, potentially, and there's a few things we can review over the next few sessions. One way to address catastrophizing, in addition to the adaptive responses which we've talked about before, would be to find some sort of peace with the worst outcome, meaning you kind of take away the power of that anxiety over you. When you can accept worst possible outcomes doesn't mean you look forward to them or you think they're likely, or you dwell on them and ponder them. But I mean, obviously, being in jail, even though it's an extremely low probability event in your circumstance, being in jail would be survivable. Being unemployed would be survivable.
Client: People weaker than me have gone through jail.
Counselor: I guess a lot of people have been to jail. A lot of people lost their jobs. And while it's certainly a struggle, to use your word, right, I mean, that would be more than a struggle. It'd be quite unpleasant. It's at the point where you can accept that that could happen and that you would survive, that you could find some peace with the catastrophizing. Again, we'll have other routes. We'll attack these cognitive distortions from a few different angles. But one of the angles is reaching a point where you could accept that those things could happen. They're unlikely. They could happen, and you would survive.
Client: Okay.
Counselor:
output: I mean, one thing you've shown throughout your. I mean, based on what you described to me, is that you're a survivor. You find a way to make it work.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Alisa, how are you doing today?
Client: I'm doing well, thank you.
Counselor: Doing well.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: What's going on?
Client: I have family coming into town and I have to go to the airport to pick them up.
Counselor: So you have family flying in?
Client: Yes. That's something that I get very anxious about, having to cross the bridge. I have to cross the Ben Franklin bridge and then get over the bridge that goes to the airport by the stadium. I think that's the Girard point bridge. Yeah. That's two levels there. I have to do that both ways.
Counselor: Going and coming both ways. You have to cross four times?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So what kind of feeling is this bringing up for you?
Client: I get very anxious even just thinking about it right now.
Counselor: So you're anxious right here with me?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So I want to try to scale this. We talked about this before with cognitive therapy. So let's say that ten is really the most anxious you're felt about crossing bridges, and one is no anxiety. Where would you be right now?
Client: Right now, probably an eight. Yeah.
Counselor: I don't love anxiety.
Client: Yes. It's worse when I'm at that point on that day, but right now, I think just knowing that I have to do that. Yes.
Counselor: And what's it on that day?
Client: A ten.
Counselor: It reaches a ten, definitely.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: All right. So. But even now, how far away is the. Until they.
Client: Oh, it's a week.
Counselor: So even now, a week out, it's. Nate, this is really hurting.
Client: Yes. I don't like that at all.
Counselor: So for your job and local travel, you don't really have to cross any.
Client: Ten minutes to work every day. And banks. So 20 minutes, shopping centers and everything is just within the vicinity. I don't have to cross any bridges.
Counselor: So no bridges?
Client: No, not at all. I probably planned it that way, too.
Counselor: That worked out well.
Client: That worked out very well.
Counselor: All right. But coming up, pick up the family you will be crossing. So let's look at this at each stage. So, I mean, you're clearly anxious now, as you mentioned. But let's go to, let's try to move forward a week to the day that they'll be flying, what time they fly in.
Client: It's going to be a 04:00 flight. In the afternoon.
Counselor: In the afternoon. So about what time would you have to leave to?
Client: I would have to leave probably at 03:00 because it's only about 20 minutes to the airport. Really?
Counselor: Really.
Client: But I would like to leave earlier. They'll probably take them time. By the time they land and go through, you know, getting their luggages, they probably won't even come out till maybe 430, but I'd like to make sure I'm there at around 334 o'clock.
Counselor: All right, so let's go to that day. Let's go to that day and to that afternoon. So you're still at home. And let's say we're about 15 minutes before you have to get in the car. Car. What are you thinking then?
Client: I have to do this. I have to get up and go. They need me to be there this week. It's my parents coming in and they're elderly, so I don't want them to be stuck at the airport. There's no one else that actually can go pick them up. So I have to get up and go and pick them up.
Counselor: That's what's going through your mind?
Client: That's what's going through my mind. So, you know, there's nobody else that can do this. I mean, it's cheaper than there's no. I probably can't even afford to get a taxi for them because you'd have to cross that's from Philly to. Into New Jersey. So that's going to be very expensive. I can't afford that. When all I'd have to do is pay $5 for the tow and maybe gas up my car for $10 or something. But, um, I. Yeah, I'll be thinking about, I have to do this.
Counselor: I have to do it.
Client: I can do it. Something that I can save money that way. And I don't want to leave them stranded. Definitely someone else can. I mean, they'd be lost. They're not familiar with the airport. And Philly airport is crazy to me.
Counselor: Yeah, it's a big place. A lot going on. So. So you're sitting at home in 15 minutes before getting the cardinal and you're thinking, I have to do this. But your reasons are positive. Like you save money and protect your parents from having to be there alone. So when does the anxiety come in?
Client: Just the thought of the bridge, it's just. I could drive off the bridge. I can fall off. Usually what I do is try to stay in the middle lane. I can't do more than 40 miles an hour. And I just. I'm shaking. I have the radio on and windows down because I can't swim. So if for any reason I'm to fall off, I mean, that's it for me. I even have a little metal one of those. I think it's an instrument that you use in the house for, I don't know, plier or something. Something real hard that I can hit the ground with. It sits right there on my door, on the side of my door. So I'm already, I planned, I have that. I planned ahead of time. I know what I'm going to do as soon as I approach the bridge, but I still feel anxious.
Counselor: So you're anxious before you leave and you're starting to think about the bridge at that point. You already think about it. How about when you get in your car, you start driving toward the bridge?
Client: I say a prayer. I am still anxious. I turn on the radio and the closer I get to, especially the toll point, and I know it's at me. And you see those lights flashing. Last exit before the, you know, the.
Counselor: Toll, you know you're going over once.
Client: Yeah, there's no turning back. There's no turning back.
Counselor: So before that, when you can still exit, what's your anxiety level?
Client: Before, when I can still exit?
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: It'S probably still high. It's probably at a nine or so.
Counselor: It's still high, but it's not maxed out yet. But it's pretty bad.
Client: Yeah, I think it's pretty bad at that point.
Counselor: And how about when you cross through the.
Client: That's when it's at a ten.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Yes, yes.
Counselor: So your specific fear as you start to cross, this is the Ben Franklin would be the first bridge. Right. You can go across. Is that your car will go off the bridge?
Client: Yes, definitely.
Counselor: And when does that, so that's a ten anxiety. When does that anxiety start to go away?
Client: As soon as I'm getting close to getting off the bridge, I'm now leaving a little sigh of the, there's a little release there. And I know that I've been able to manage those two, three minutes of cross. I don't know how many minutes it takes actually crossing the bridge. I start feeling a little bit of relief, but then again, I know I have to take that exit and there's another one coming right up, so starts all over again.
Counselor: All right, so then you cross the second bridge, the Gerard point bridge, you go to the airport. Does your anxiety drop, any of those points?
Client: Oh, as soon as I'm descending from the Gerard Point bridge, there's less, you know, it's almost reduced. I come, you know, really low.
Counselor: It's almost gone.
Client: Yes. It's almost gone. Yes.
Counselor: And when do you start thinking about that? You're going to have to cross them again?
Client: As soon as I'm exit, I'm getting back on 95 going north. And I know, here we go again. And cars are zooming by and you.
Counselor: Know, because you're not going very quickly.
Client: No, no, I'm that person. The middle lane doing 40 miles an hour. Yes.
Counselor: All right. So you're doing everything you can to keep your car on the bridge, but you're still feeling anxiety, like you're going to go off the bridge.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: The whole time. Until you start really descending.
Client: Exactly.
Counselor: And then you feel like you made it.
Client: Especially when there are those big trucks.
Counselor: Tractor trailers coming because the air.
Client: Yes, yes. Or if it's also in bad weather or at night, it's worst because on the bridge, especially the top one, you kind of see the sky and there's nothing else you see. So it's like you're gonna fall off. Yes.
Counselor: So in the lower level it's not as bad.
Client: On the lower, lower level, coming back it's not as bad because you're kind of like protected here and there. So it's not as bad, but going it's definitely worse. Yes.
Counselor: Are you aware of any time a car would have gone off the bridge?
Client: I hear on the news once in a while you'll hear something happen, or sometimes in movies you see things happen. I think it's possible.
Counselor: It's possible?
Client: Yes.
Counselor:
output: You think it's a high risk?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Okay, so you said that when you're at work, you really worry that you're gonna say something stupid?
Client: Yeah, that's something that's always on my mind.
Counselor: What would be so bad about that if you did say something stupid at work?
Client: Because people would think I was weird.
Counselor: Then what would be so bad if people. People at work thought you were weird?
Client: They wouldn't want to be friends with me.
Counselor: And what would be so bad about that if people at work didn't want to be friends with you?
Client: Well, I just have no one to talk to at work.
Counselor: Then what would be so bad about having no one to talk to at work?
Client: I mean, the shoots can go on the whole day, so I'd just be by myself the whole time.
Counselor: And what would be so bad about being by yourself, you know, for a whole day?
Client: I don't know. I guess I should be used to it now. I spend a lot of my time by myself.
Counselor: Oh, that must be tough. What does that mean to you? That you spend a lot of time on your own?
Client: Dunno. I guess it's just like I spend so much time by myself that it's kind of like I'm nothing even worth being friends with.
Counselor: So it sounds like deep down that you think that you're not worth being friends with. That's quite a negative belief. I mean, how much would you say that you believe that out of a hundred? If 100 is where you believe it totally. And zero is where you don't believe it at all?
Client: I guess like 9500.
Counselor: When did you start believing that?
Client: I think it was probably at school. Yeah, I think at school.
Counselor: And what was it about school that made you start to believe that you weren't worth being friends with?
Client: Just like quite a lot of things. Like I wouldn't have anyone sit at lunch or people's birthdays and stuff. I wasn't invited and you know, like I was the last one picked for teams and stuff like that.
Counselor: And what is it now that makes you think that that's still true?
Client: I mean, it's kind of similar at work, obviously. Difference is that it's work, not school. But you know, people go for drinks and stuff after work or after a shoot, and I just kind of excluded a lot of the time.
Counselor: That sounds tough. Is there anything that makes you think that it's not true that you are worth being friends with?
Client: I guess my friends and family would say that I am. Like, I try to make a lot of time for my friends and stuff.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like deep down you have this thought that you're not worth being friends with. And that started at school when you had trouble making friends at school and that you weren't always picked for teams and that now at work it feels like the same thing is happening, that you're not always invited out for drinks with people and that sometimes you feel that you're excluded from their social groups. But then that's not the whole story. That on the other hand, you are close to family and you do have friends who would say that it's not true that you are worth being friends with. In CBT, we do a thing called thought challenging where when we have these negative thoughts, sometimes we actually put them up to scrutiny. We weigh up the evidence for and against them. I like to think of it as putting the thought on trial. Could we do that now where we just actually try and weigh up the evidence for and against that thought a bit more?
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Okay. So if I just put two columns here, so for and against. And it sounds like the evidence for this thought that makes you think that it is true is difficulty at school, making friends, being picked for teams, and difficulty at work, feeling excluded sometimes from groups.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But actually in this other column we have that you are close with your family and that you have some close friends. Okay. Now moving back to this first column, is there anything else that makes you think it's true that you're not worth being friends with?
Client: Just like, I kind of don't go to a lot of stuff. People have, like gatherings and things and a lot of the time I just. I don't go and rather just stay at home.
Counselor: Don't go to parties. What kind of parties are we talking? Like big parties, small parties, mainly big ones.
Client: If there's a lot of people there, I just find it really. It kind of makes me really anxious. So a lot of the time I just prefer not even to be in that situation in the first place.
Counselor: Okay. So you don't go to larger parties and events. Okay. Is there anything else that maybe thinks that it's makes you think that it's not true that actually you are worth being friends with?
Client: I mean, I guess my friends would say that I was. I do have close friends and, you know, when it's like their stuff that's important to them, I always make sure that I think about that. And even if I find it stressful, I'll always make sure that I can kind of put them first.
Counselor: Okay. So your friends would say that you are worth being friends with and it sounds like you put your friends first.
Client: Yeah, I do. Make sure I try and do that.
Counselor: In what kind of ways do you put your friends first?
Client: I guess when it's birthdays or, you know, something important to them, I'll always make sure that I'm there and that I put a lot of thought into presence and stuff like that.
Counselor: Can you give me an example of a time that you've done that?
Client: It was my friend's birthday a few weeks ago and we did like a big surprise at hers and I made a cake and stuff like that.
Counselor: So you actually helped to organize events for your friends?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor:
output: Is there anything that you do that you wouldn't do if you weren't a good friend?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: So, hello, Michael. Welcome back.
Client: Thank you. Hi.
Counselor: So, for this session, I'm just going to briefly discuss what we went over in our last session, including the goals that we set for you, and then we can kind of discuss how those went for you. Does that sound good?
Client: Okay,
Counselor: so what we discussed in the last session is we went over what your diet and lifestyle are like, and we discussed those goals for you, with your overall goal being to become more plant based and just healthier. And the specific goals that we set for this week were to swap out your usual breakfast of yogurt with nuts and berries for a plant based smoothie five out of seven days this week. And your second goal was to track your food intake using myfitnesspal every day this week with the goal of keeping your sugar intake to under 50 grams per day. So, starting with that first goal of swapping out your breakfast five out of seven days this week for a plant based smoothie. How did that go?
Client: I would say I had moderate success in that I had smoothies three out of, so far, six days of this week. I started the week on Sunday and now it's Friday. So a couple things that got in the way of reaching the goal. One is that I basically forgot the goal. It wasn't in the forefront of my mind. I was more focused on making smoothies for mom and not making sure I had them. And then secondly, I'm out of town from this morning until tomorrow afternoon. And so I essentially lost like a day or two mornings where I would normally be at home and be able to make a smoothie for myself. So I can try to make up for one of the smoothies tomorrow when I get home, but really need to make it more of a habit and have it in a forefront of my mind.
Counselor: So you talk a lot. You mentioned a few times that making that in the forefront of your mind. And the first thing you said was that the reason you didn't complete the goal was that you just forgot about it. So would it be alright with you if we maybe discussed some ways to increase your memory of the goal?
Client: Sure.
Counselor: All right. So what do you think you could do to remember to make this goal happen, to get up to those five smoothies?
Client: Well, a couple things. One is I have a daily, I have an app on my computer that I used to put down task items into the to do list, basically, and I review that every day. So, you know, if I have a separate diet related category for my to Dos, I could enter it there and have it there. I could put a reminder on my fridge and then also doing the meal tracking that I was doing with my fitness pal would of course make it evident that I'm not doing it. But that was a lot of work this week. I would not want to put in that much work. And then finally, I think once it gets going so it's on automatic, you're making a habit, then that in and of itself reminds me.
Counselor: So you mentioned some really good ideas. So you talked about you have this reminder app on your computer. I think that that's a great way. If it's something that you're already checking every day, then you should definitely consider adding in this reminder to make the smoothies there. And you also mentioned putting a reminder on your fridge. So insofar as continuing with this goal, if we were to rewrite it, what would you say?
Client: You mean like perhaps including items to help you reach the goal?
Counselor: Yes.
Client: And then sub to do items? In a sense, yeah. So I think that would be helpful. Listing specific actions which I'm going to take to try to help me reach this other action I'm trying to do. That would be helpful. And I think what we've talked about using my to do app is probably the best because since I go back and forth between two places during the week, I have to maintain, you know, a list of each place on the fridge. I don't necessarily pay attention to that every day. I think because I'm using my computer every day and I use this to do that every day. That's a natural place to start.
Counselor: Okay, so I'm just going to write it down so I can send it to you in an email what our modified version of the smooth equal will be. So what you were saying was would you like to maintain the five out of seven days or would you like to increase it or decrease it?
Client: I would like to. I think it should be at least five and maybe even seven out of seven. Let's start with five, though for now, I always prefer to start small and not confuse things too much. So many things to remember. So two and five out of seven. And also because using myfitnesspal this week, it became evident that I'm not getting enough protein, at least according to what my fitness panel thinks I should be getting. So the smoothies are a good way to add protein to my diet.
Counselor: Okay, so then perhaps we can structure the goal of saying that. So five out of seven days in the next week, you will make a plant based smoothie with. How would you be adding the protein?
Client: Protein powder, most likely.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: And, you know, there'd be some soy milk or plant based milk, which you have some protein in, but most of it's going to come from protein powder.
Counselor:
output: So making the smoothie five out of seven days for the next week with the plant based protein powder and or a serving of a high protein plant based milk. And you would be doing that by setting the reminder for yourself within your computer app and writing a reminder on the fridge. How does that sound?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, Aspen. How you doing today?
Client: I'm doing well, thank you. How about yourself?
Counselor: I'm doing all right, thanks for asking. I had met you last time for our first session, and we talked a little bit about kind of your circumstances, what brought you here. And I was hoping today we could get into trying to really figure out how we can help you. Any thoughts on your current situation? Anything changed?
Client: Nothing's really changed. I mean, I'm amazing at my job. My boss just really is someone that I hold, you know, in higher regards than others I work with especially. We went to. We went to the same college. College, of course. And he suggested I come into counseling and he's way off. Way off. So I'm just gonna, you know, let him know.
Counselor: So, as I understand it, you came into counseling because he requested it.
Client: That was what initiated it. But now it's. I need to prove him wrong.
Counselor: Alright, so at first it was because he told you it would be a good idea, but now you kind of see it as an opportunity to prove your point.
Client: Yeah, have a little bit of fun with it. Prove my point.
Counselor: What would you. What would you like to prove through this?
Client: That I'm not the one in the wrong. You know, I. I'm extremely good at my job. I mean, I am the best employee that they have ever had. Not just currently, just. I mean, just ever. I make no errors. So how can I be wrong when it comes to these circumstances with my coworkers?
Counselor: Right. So your co workers have made some criticisms about you and that led to your boss suggesting this.
Client: I would call them criticisms because it's really hard to criticize me. So I would say they take it personally that I'm better than them, you know? So I feel that it's important for me to be able to work for this particular company. It needs to be the best company. And so I need the other employees to at least be at my level. Well, I mean, that's. That's really hard for them to come to my level, but at least be above average. At least.
Counselor: All right, so you have an expectation of them to become at least close to you in terms of your skill.
Client: I mean, it's pretty hard to not make any errors when it comes to accounting with the numbers, with the amount of numbers and the volume of accounts that we have, it's hard to be as good as I am with it, as far as no errors. But yes, I expect a higher standard from the coworkers.
Counselor: And you don't feel like they're performing at that level now?
Client: No, not at all.
Counselor: And evidently you made some different comments to them which maybe they took the wrong way.
Client: I just pointed out the facts of the situation.
Counselor: What type of facts did you, when.
Client: They make mistakes and, you know, how they should be better at certain tasks. I mean, they didn't attend the same, you know, type of college as far as, you know, Ivy League as myself. However, they do have a college education so, you know, that alone would, you know, just kind of go to speak to them having some sort of ability in that area.
Counselor: So you've kind of, in a way you've expressed your disappointment with them.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: To them?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And what are some of the observations or comments they made regarding you?
Client: Oh, they told me my ego is too big, that I'm cocky. That's one. Yeah. I'm just overall, like, I don't know how you can be too confident when your ability is at that level. I mean, I am the best employee they've ever had overall. You know, I was the best student at my college. I received numerous awards from the president of the college alone. I received numerous calls from the college and other companies as well, trying to recruit me to work for them. You know, so I don't think there's, it's impossible to be overly confident, but they, you know, they consider it cocky and arrogant. Get arrogant a lot.
Counselor: The comment arrogant. So you feel they're just really, are they misunderstanding you?
Client: I think they take it as a personal attack.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Like I'm can, like I'm that concerned with them personally. Like it affect, like I'm talking about them as a person instead of just their performance at work because I'm really not concerned with them as far as like existence outside the realm of performance at work.
Counselor: Alright. So your commentary to them has nothing to do with their value as a person, more with their performance as an employee. And you feel they're misconstruing your observations about their performance?
Client: Very much so.
Counselor: They're taking it personally.
Client: Taking it personally and trying as best they can to push it back on me as I'm the one who's wrong, but I'm obviously not.
Counselor: Alright, so you're not wrong in this and you're frustrated by their reactions.
Client: I mean, I'm okay with it, you know, I mean it's, I don't really take anything they say to heart because they're not at the level to really be able to criticize me. You know, I can take criticism, you know, from constructive criticism, from someone who would, you know, be at my level or above, however, they are not. So it's really nothing. It really doesn't affect me. It does interfere with my job as far as my employer is concerned.
Counselor: Right. That's what led to you. That's what led to him recommending you come here initially. So you don't feel that they're at a level where they can really criticize you. It doesn't really bother you if they have criticism in the first place, but you can appreciate how getting along with them would be better for you as an employee.
Client: I mean. I mean, overall, I like this company. You know, I like working for it. I've been friends with my boss. I mean, we went to the same college, you know, so we have that in common. You know, he is an extraordinary person as far as his abilities, you know, I would say as in the level realm as myself. So, you know, I hold his, you know, opinion, you know, in some sort of regards above the others, so.
Counselor:
output: Okay, so to the extent that they communicate negative sentiment to him about you, that that affects you?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Victoria. How you doing today?
Client: Pretty good.
Counselor: Very good. How has the anxiety been around the germs?
Client: I still catch myself, like, double, almost like double touching. Like going to touch it and then reeling back. So I'm starting to notice it, but I still, I still have that anxiety. I still don't want to touch it.
Counselor: When you pretty much touch anything you might think has germs on it.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What are some things that you've touched in the last, between the last session and this session that have distressed you?
Client: Well, I had to go to the store, which is always a nightmare for me because I don't even like touching my credit card because it's been in so many machines and there's so much dirt and junk that gets in there and then the counters and all the. I keep thinking about the food that's there, and I, you know, if I pick it up off the shelf, how many people have picked it up with their nasty hands or kids picked it up with nasty hands and then put it back, and it's like, I need to eat. But shopping's a nightmare for me.
Counselor: So really, in a, like, a supermarket, everything can be containing germs. Have germs on it?
Client: Yeah, everything does.
Counselor: Everything does. And that's what you're thinking about as you're walking through and shopping. We talked about last time, exposure and response prevention, and I explained kind of the general idea. But you remember that conversation. Yeah, I remember. I indicated that we might try some experiments right in session to see how, see if we can move kind of forward and treating your, kind of your fear and obsession with germs and really the anxiety it's causing for you, it's like getting in the way of your life.
Client: It is. It really is.
Counselor: So I was wondering, is there anything in here, in this office, as you look around, that you would look at and think, I don't want to touch that because it could have germs on it.
Client: I'm really not liking the covers on this chair because, I mean, I can't. I mean, at least what I'm sitting in now, my clothes are protecting me from the rest of the chair.
Counselor: Mm hmm.
Client: But, I mean, I have no sleeves on, so I don't like touching the armrests and the covers.
Counselor: So even thinking about, like, your arms touching the back of the chair, and.
Client: I'm not liking it, I really feel like I should probably go wash my arms.
Counselor: So what would happen if you put your hands right on the arm covers? What was your usual reaction to that?
Client: To go wash my arms until I feel like it's gone. Until all the dirt is gone.
Counselor: And how long would that take you to be sure?
Client: I mean, something like this, probably. I'd probably be in there for a good 510 minutes. Just washing.
Counselor: 510 minutes. How many times a day would you end up washing your hands?
Client: Okay. I don't. I don't keep track anymore. It makes me upset. How many?
Counselor: It says that it's that many. That is distressing. And I know that this will be uncomfortable, but I would like you to try to. If you can feel comfortable with it, put your hands on the. On the arms of the chairs. On the chair. Let's see what I'm doing. It's like. Try to stay like that. So tell me what's going through your mind?
Client: I can just. I feel the chair, and I. I don't like it. And I just. I feel almost like I can feel everybody who's ever touched it. And just what have they been doing? And what did they touch before they touched this? They probably didn't wash their hands before they touched this, and it's just really making me comfortable.
Counselor: Okay, so you're anxious now?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Is it tolerable?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So once you remember, we talked about scaling before. So, like, ten being a tremendous amount of anxiety, one being hardly any anxiety. Where. Where are you now as you sit here with your hands?
Client: What am I going to say about six or seven?
Counselor: Six or seven?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Are you feeling an urge to go wash your hands?
Client: Yes. Yes, I am.
Counselor: Yes. This is a six or seven. I want you to sit with it for a few seconds, process that, you know, feeling. Right. That you're touching everybody that's ever been in the chair. Right. So consider that thought.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: So what's the ultimate fear? Like, what's gonna happen if you don't go wash your hands now?
Client: I'm gonna get sick.
Counselor: You're gonna get sick that someone who's.
Client: Been in this chair was sick or touched something gross that can make you sick. And I'm gonna get sick, and I'm gonna die, and I don't want to die.
Counselor: Do you feel yourself getting sick?
Client: I feel like it's harder to breathe, I guess. Like, my chest is kind of just tight. Yeah.
Counselor:
output: You can still breathe, though.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Carly. How you doing today?
Client: I'm good. How about you?
Counselor: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. How did you do this week?
Client: Better. Well, last time we talked about that postpone gratification. Yeah, that, and I think you wanted ten minutes for me to put it off.
Counselor: Ten minutes, yeah.
Client: So I did better. I think I ended up only doing, like, a joint a half instead of two. I was able to put it off for, I think, the ten minutes a couple times. And then I. There was, I think, one or two days where I went out for a walk because I was tired of staring at the clock, waiting for the ten minutes to pass. So I got up, went for a walk, and then I passed one of my friends, so I ended up walking with her. And I actually didn't get back to my house for, like, an hour, so I kind of put it off for, like, an hour because then I came home and took a couple hits.
Counselor: All right, so it sounds like. It sounds like you were able to maintain waiting ten minutes to smoke marijuana, at least in most cases. It was rough.
Client: It was rough, yeah.
Counselor: So it was difficult for you, but in most cases, you're able to hold off the ten minutes, and it sounds like there was a few instances where you're able to hold it off longer because something else kind of.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Came up.
Client: Yeah, I found I actually, like, talked to a couple people on the phone. Before I knew it, like, a half hour had gone by.
Counselor: So another activity presented itself. And you forgot about the marijuana?
Client: Kind of, yeah. Yeah, I guess I just wasn't thinking about it.
Counselor: So has your. Have your feelings about marijuana changed since we last talked?
Client: No, not really.
Counselor: Tell me about that.
Client: I mean, it's. I don't see it as a problem. It's legal in a lot of states now, and, I mean, it's not that bad for you. It doesn't really endanger me much.
Counselor: So you still. You still believe you should have the right to smoke marijuana?
Client: Yeah, I mean, I'm not hurting anybody.
Counselor: Else, but at the same time, you want to go back to work, and if I remember right, you're the person that you could go work for. I guess you know them, right?
Client: Yeah, it's my uncle.
Counselor: Your uncle. And you need to be clean for, what was it, about two months?
Client: Yeah, I think two to three months.
Counselor: So you have kind of opposing forces here, right? You have your enjoyment of marijuana, and then you. That's something you, like. You don't want to give up, and you believe you should have a right to do that, but then there's that job.
Client: Yeah. I mean, my parents are pretty cool with it. Like, they know, but, I mean, I'm at the point now where they kind of want me to move on and move out. But I don't know. I mean, I just. It'd be nice to have that job. Like, it's a really good job, but at the same time, like, I don't see why I have to sacrifice something that I like.
Counselor: So it doesn't seem fair to you, but she recognizes the reality of your situation. Yeah, it really does come down, in your instance, to marijuana use or employment.
Client: Yeah, it's pretty accurate.
Counselor: Okay, so you're not happy about that choice?
Client: Not at all.
Counselor: Yeah. And kind of what we did with the postponed gratification was just. I mean, I really just ask you to wait ten minutes, and you were able to do that and more. Although it was difficult.
Client: It was difficult.
Counselor: It was difficult for you. So I asked you to track the number of times you smoked marijuana. Did you. Were you able to track that over the last week?
Client: Yeah, for the most part.
Counselor: Do you remember how many times that was?
Client: I think. I think I did, like, 15.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Between 15 and 20.
Counselor: Between 15 and 20. And how many times did something kind of get in the way? Did something else come up in that ten minute span that distracted you or that you enjoyed?
Client: Like, almost closer to 20 times, I guess. Otherwise I probably would have kept going, smoked more. I mean, there were a couple times where, like, somebody would call me or somebody would text me, and that kind of distracted me, so I was able to put it off for a little bit.
Counselor:
output: So you can see in that ten minutes, things can happen. Things can happen that can help you to avoid the marijuana. Sometimes nothing does, and after the ten minutes you use it, and sometimes something does kind of get in the way with the marijuana, like, distract you or you have another activity that you enjoy and then you didn't use. So with that in mind, you found the experience rough. But was it tolerable?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hey, Carly. How are you doing today?
Client: I'm good. How are you?
Counselor: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. What's been going on this last week?
Client: I've just been feeling kind of in a rut. I mean, I've been looking for a job and haven't really gotten anywhere. And then I had a drink the other night, and I just felt like me not having a job and me going out and having that drink, it wasn't deserved. And I just felt like such a loser because that was the time that I should have been at work if I had a job, and instead I was at the bar drinking. So I had one drink, and then it led to another. Cause then I just felt worse and I figured I had one, so.
Counselor: All right, so how much did you drink in total?
Client: I think I lost track after four or five.
Counselor: How long had it been since you had a drink before that?
Client: I did really well. It was, I think, like three weeks.
Counselor: Three weeks?
Client: Three weeks or so.
Counselor: Oh, so you did really well and then you had one drink and that just made you feel like you weren't successful?
Client: I felt like a loser.
Counselor: Felt like a loser. And you feel that kind of led to drinking some more? So you had a rough time with things?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. How about now?
Client: I mean, now I just kind of. I don't know, I'm afraid to go back. Like, I'm afraid to go out with, like, some friends. They invite me out to dinner, but I know there's alcohol and.
Counselor: Is that where you were when you had that first drink? Was that with friends?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right, so there's a few things going on. We've talked in the past, right, about separating the behavior from the person. Right. So behavior is what we do, not who we are. You remember those discussions? And correct me if I'm wrong, but it sounds like I'm going to use some different words than you used. But it sounds like when you had that first drink, you're kind of ashamed that you had a drink and you had it during the time when you would have been working.
Client: Yeah, that's pretty accurate.
Counselor: That's pretty accurate. So, taking yourself back to that moment, right. We had that first. That first drink, like, you finished that first drink. What was your thought at that moment?
Client: Just, like, shameful. Like, I did really, really well, and then here I was, and I had just finished a drink, and I knew I wanted another one.
Counselor: Okay, so shameful is kind of like the feeling, but the thought is I did really, really well. Right. So that's what you're thinking was, I did really, really well. And what was that the end of the thought? Or was that. Was there more before you had that next drink?
Client: I guess just I was doing well, and then I had a drink, and I just felt like an awful person. So figured what was the. The hurt and having more.
Counselor: So the sequence would have been you had the drink, you felt shameful. At the same time, you're thinking that you were doing really well, and then just really, as you said before, you just felt like a loser. And then you decided, might as well just have the second drink. So another thought might be that, like, I might as well, just might as well just have a second drink.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. So you can see how there's some thoughts and some feelings at work. Right. As you finished that first drink, was it fairly quick? Were those thoughts and feelings fairly occur fairly quickly after the drink?
Client: Yeah, I would say as I was finishing and then finished.
Counselor: Right away, you regretted it. And in that regret, as you thought about it, thought, might as well just continue drinking now because you kind of blew it.
Client: Yeah, I already messed up. I might as well keep going.
Counselor: Okay. And that's a common cycle to fall into. And you had three weeks where you hadn't had a drink prior to that. So let's look at this. Let's try to separate the behavior from the self a little bit. If you had a friend who was in the same predicament, who had a history of using alcohol and then had three weeks without any alcohol use, and then their behavior was to have a drink, what would you think of them?
Client: I would think that they had a rough day or something must have happened where? I mean, it's just one drink.
Counselor: Okay. They had a rough day. One drink. And what would you think of their behavior? How would you categorize that behavior?
Client: I guess just they made a mistake.
Counselor: So not ideal, depending on their point of view. Maybe a little irresponsible.
Client: Yeah, I think irresponsible would be irresponsible.
Counselor: But you wouldn't necessarily characterize them as a bad person. No, but their behavior was a bit irresponsible, you know, in terms of, like, the recovery plan, which would be to not drink. But when you apply that same examination to your own situation, how do you characterize yourself after you had that first drink?
Client: It was my mistake. It was in it. It makes me a worse person for doing it.
Counselor: So you see how you're being a little. Well, it'd be quite a bit rougher on yourself. Like, your evaluation of yourself is. Is fairly harsh. You mentioned loser earlier and ashamed. Whereas you wouldn't necessarily evaluate someone else that way. How would you evaluate your behavior? How would you judge your behavior of taking that first drink?
Client: Shameful. I mean, irresponsible, bad overall.
Counselor: So bad, irresponsible, shameful. Is there a way to separate that behavior in terms of your thinking, in terms of the way you evaluate it from yourself? Like, are you into behavior together, enmeshed, or can you be separated?
Client: Um, I think we could be separated, but it. It feels like we're, like I am.
Counselor:
output: That behavior in that moment, it's very congruent for you.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: So one of the things that we know is that sometimes people who have difficulty with anxiety and things like that have also had some bad experiences in their lives. So I'm going to ask you some questions about some of your difficult experiences that you may have had. And I'm just going to ask sort of yes or no questions. I only need sort of headlines. I don't need a lot of detail about the things that happened right now, but I'm just going to ask you those questions. And if anything about this interview starts to make you uncomfortable, you can take a break. If I ask a question you don't want to answer, you can just say, pass, and I'll just move on. So it's really up to you what you share, but I do want to ask you these questions. Is that okay?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. So have you ever been physically hurt by anyone, any. Either as a child or an adult? You know, hit.
Client: Yeah, my. I had a boyfriend a couple years ago, and he. He would hit me sometimes, but we're not together anymore, so.
Counselor: Mm hmm. Was there other kinds of physical abuse? You know, did he do more than hit you? Was there anything.
Client: No, he would just slap me sometimes. Usually when he was like, if he'd had a really hard day at work and maybe he would be drinking or something. He wouldn't slap me when he got home, but I got out of that, so that's good.
Counselor: Well, it's good that you recognize that that was really not acceptable behavior and that you didn't want that in your relationship. And it's great that you were able to get away from that. That's really good self care, that you were able to make that decision and, you know, and make a different choice and create more safety for your. Yourself. That's really good.
Client: Thanks.
Counselor: What about sexually? Has anybody ever, you know, when you were a child or as an adult, touched you against your will, anything like that?
Client: Yeah. I don't really want to talk about it, though, but, yeah, when I was. When I was little.
Counselor: How little? Just vaguely ten. Okay. Okay. And was it a family member or a stranger or.
Client: It was. It was a family member, but I don't really like talking about it.
Counselor: Okay. You don't have to. Okay, great. Thank you for telling me that much. That's really all I need for right now. Although it may be important for you to talk about that later, at some point you can wait until you're ready.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Okay. As a child, you know, sometimes parents aren't very available, don't provide basic food, clothing, shelter, that kind of thing. Did you ever have that experience of being neglected? Hmm? What's going on, Tricia?
Client: I don't like all these questions.
Counselor: Yeah? Starting to get uncomfortable, huh? You feel that somewhere in your body, you're feeling that in your. Your body? Yeah. Sometimes these questions can bring up very difficult things. I know. Sorry. When you're feeling like this, what helps you?
Client: My cat.
Counselor: Hmm. Tell me about your cat.
Client: She's a jerk. She's a jerk? Yeah. She's not very friendly. Um, she's friendly to me, though, when I'm really upset. She, uh, she'll, like, cuddle with me on the bed and stuff, so she knows when I'm really upset. But it's great that she knows. Yeah.
Counselor: That's pretty amazing.
Client: She's just kind of a jerk. She'll bite and scratch it, whoever she wants to. She wants to be snuggled until she doesn't want to be snuggled.
Counselor: What's her name?
Client: Persephone.
Counselor: Persephone. That's a great name for a cat.
Client: She came with it, and I decided to just leave it.
Counselor: Wow. I like it a lot.
Client: Great.
Counselor: It's wonderful to have a cat named Persephone who's good at helping you when your feelings are difficult. That's really good. That's, you know, that's a blessing there. Can we go on with the interview now?
Client: Yeah, I guess.
Counselor: Okay. About continuing. Okay. I'm going to ask you some different questions. I want to ask you a little bit about your living situation. So what kind of housing do you live in?
Client: I have an apartment.
Counselor: Mm hmm. And how long have you lived there?
Client: Almost a year.
Counselor: So not that long. And who do you live with?
Client: Just the cat.
Counselor: Just per second. Okay. Do you feel safe where you live?
Client: Safer than when I was homeless.
Counselor: Mm hmm. Safer, but maybe not entirely safe.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. What makes you not feel that safe where you live?
Client: I've kind of a. Have a landlord situation. Mm.
Counselor: Difficult relationship with your landlord?
Client: You could say that.
Counselor: Can you tell me about it?
Client: I don't. I don't make a lot of money, and my hours got cut at work recently, and he said he was going to evict me, and I really didn't want to be homeless again, so he said if I had sex with him that I wouldn't have to pay my rent.
Counselor: Wow. That's really hard. It makes sense. So you agreed to that I didn't.
Client: Want to be homeless again.
Counselor: That's right. And in order to survive, anyone is going to do what they have to do. Right.
Client: But it sounds like that's what I keep telling myself.
Counselor: Mm hmm. But it's also upsetting you a lot.
Client: I just keep thinking, like, what if somebody finds out? And now I told you so, obviously people are gonna find out.
Counselor: Well, what do you mean people?
Client: Well, I mean, don't you have to tell people when stuff like that happens?
Counselor: No, actually, what you and I discuss is between us, and you'll get to decide what you want to do about that situation so we can talk about it. But you get to decide. I only have to disclose if you're going to kill yourself or someone else to somebody else. Those are, you know, or if you're abusing an elder. Those are the circumstances under which I have to let other people know. So this is something that's just for you and I to talk about. And as part of, you know, our work together, we can decide what's the best way to take care of yourself going forward. So it's entirely up to you what we do from here. And I totally appreciate the courage it took to let me know that that was happening. And I'm happy to be with you as you sort out what's really the best path for you going forward for your own well being. We'll work on that together. Does that make sense to you?
Client: Kind of. No one's ever said it to me like that before, so I thought you had to tell people. But no. If not, but no.
Counselor: And I should tell you that. Remember how I said earlier in the interview that people who've had adverse experiences like sexual abuse in their past or physical abuse in their past, that sometimes that's connected to what happens going forward?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Well, it's not. It's really common for girls who've experienced sexual abuse later in life to end up using or being in a position where they end up using that for survival purposes. So what you're experiencing is actually probably a lot more common than you think. But just like you didn't want to talk about it, you know, the reason you don't know that other people are doing that is because they don't have often talk about it. So that way you think you're the only one in the world who ever ended up in this position. But in reality, lots of girls who've experienced sexual abuse grow up and it changes something that then they end up putting themselves, they end up in situations. Now, obviously you didn't create this situation. Your landlord is the one who is proposing to use his position of power to get you to do something that isn't what you want to do. And you're not responsible for his doing that. You're not. You're just doing what you've learned to do to help you survive. And we can work together for you to figure out what other options you have and what else you can do. Do.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Does that make sense?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Good. Thanks. Thanks for being so open. So are you ready to continue with the rest of the interview?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. You're doing a really good job. A really good job, a lot of hard stuff. And you're letting me in and that'll help us to be able to, you know, figure out together what you need to do to, you know, help with your anxiety and to make your life work better for you.
Client: Okay?
Counselor: Okay. So now I'm going to ask you some questions about your. So we've come to the end of all the questions and thanks for hanging in with me. I know it was a lot of questions, but I feel like, you know, I've gotten to know you a lot by asking these questions. So actually you've done a really good job of helping me to sort of begin to piece together the puzzle of what we're going to work on together. So that's really good. So now that the interview is over, the next step will be we'll make an appointment before you go, you know, for you to come back. But I just want to ask you now, how are you doing? How are you feeling?
Client: Well, I'm not shaking anymore, so that's good. I think I'll be okay.
Counselor: All right. So if after this interview you go about your life and you start to have difficult feelings, what are some things that you already know that you can do to help yourself with those feelings?
Client: Well, I. I play the guitar, so I think sometimes that helps a little bit. And, you know, and then there's Persephone, the mean cat. Yeah.
Counselor: Yes. Uh huh.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And is there anyone in your life that you could call if you were having a hard time?
Client: Yeah, actually my best friend, she knows about all my anxiety and everything, so. So sometimes I'll call her and just say, hey, I really need to not, you know, be here or whatever. And she lets me come over.
Counselor: So that's great. So you have some ways to take care of yourself. I just want to make sure that the stuff we opened up in this interview doesn't end up interfering too much in your regular life. So thanks very much, Tricia, and I'll see you next week.
Client: Thank you.
Counselor:
output: Take care of.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, mister Urban. It's nice to see you again. From our previous session, I know you spoke about the relationship you and your wife were going through. In the bad terms, she got left off. So I want to ask you, what would make you cheat on your wife?
Client: You know, I've been asked that question every day for the past two, three weeks. And the only thing I can respond with is what would make a wife cheat on her husband? I mean, it's petty. I know it's petty. But I loved her. And finding out that more than once she was with somebody else, that took something from me that I couldn't get back. And for months I was dealing with. What could I have done? What was it? What did I do? Because it has to have been me. She's too nice a person for that, right? She's too smart a person for that, right? And then weeks of me finally understanding that it wasn't me. A decision that you make is a decision that you make. So when Susie, my administrative assistant, came into the picture, I had a decision that I had to make. I have to take it off and spend time with Susie. Or keep it on and spend many a night alone. So why? You figure it out.
Counselor: So do you think that you did it for revenge? Were you trying to get back at your wife?
Client: I guess. I mean, what else could it be? Yeah, maybe I am that petty. But it's just. It's not love anymore.
Counselor: So why are you still in a marriage, mister Urban? If it's not love, if it's not for love, why do you feel that you must stay in America?
Client: Because that's the type of household I was brought up in.
Counselor: Explain that to me.
Client: My dad always told me that you take care of your business and your girl is your business. You never leave her. You take care of her no matter what. That's what you do. So when I got older, I asked him, what do you mean you never leave her? He said, divorce is not an option. That's pretty much how it is in my household.
Counselor: So are you saying because of how you were raised up is why you're still in the marriage?
Client: It's the only thing that makes sense.
Counselor: Are you happy?
Client: Do I seem happy?
Counselor: Have you spoken to your wife about this?
Client: No. So everything that I feel, everything that I am is stuck on the inside. This is actually the first time I've actually talked about any of her.
Counselor: Okay, mister Ermen, so let's try this exercise. I'm gonna pull out chairs, so pretend that that this is your wife here. Why are we here and express your feelings.
Client: Why do I have to do this?
Counselor: Because you never spoke about it. Right? So express your feelings. Let it out, and see how you would tell her what you're feeling inside. Do you feel uncomfortable?
Client: I felt uncomfortable since the moment I found out that you just didn't love me anymore. I felt uncomfortable every single night I've been in the guest room because I just couldn't take being with you. I felt uncomfortable since the very moment I felt like it was okay because of what you did to me. To take off my wedding band, to forget my vows, to forget you, to try and be something that I'm not. Every night that I was with Susie, I imagined that I was with you, but not who you are now. I imagine that I was with the woman that I first met, woman that I first loved. But you're not the same person anymore. I haven't been the same person over a year. Every day that I wake up and I see your face, I have to imagine that you are that same person because that's the. The only thing that keeps me around. That and the fact that I just don't think I can make. And it's not because I love you so much anymore, because it's not you that I love. It's not because of anything religious. It's because I don't want to deal with my family.
Counselor: I know that was hard to do. Mister Urban, are you doing all right? Are you feeling okay?
Client: I'm fine.
Counselor: Okay. So I want you to realize, like, can you not see that your belief is causing this pain inside your depression and your unhappiness?
Client: It makes sense, if that's what you're saying. The question is, how am I supposed to deal with, like, right now? I know I've got the option of staying with her and dealing with this every day for as long as I stay with her and deal with this or just leaving, and then I have to deal with everything else around me. How am I supposed to get past that? That's my question. And I don't know. I don't even know if that's really the right way to go.
Counselor: What is everything else?
Client: My family, the judgments. What? I'm gonna have to deal with my brother, who, by the way, is married, and he's not dealing with infidelity, but he's dealing with the same depression I am. The love isn't there anymore. We don't get divorced. Not in my household.

Client: That I was thinking this way? My dad would probably disown you.

Client: Especially when I seen that he dealt with the same thing. My family doesn't do well with marriages because I haven't met a single person in my lineage that has a happy marriage.
Counselor:
output: Do you see your family often, Mister Urban?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.

Counselor: That's great. That's awesome. And I think that's part of your goals that you've already achieved.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. So I'm really glad that we were able to talk last week because that really helped me to kind of plan ahead.
Counselor: Yeah, that's good. That's good. So let's talk about a little bit more of the schoolwork and the anxiety that you experienced during that time. So what stop is it really? It's a point for you to reflect.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: So from the time you start experiencing the anxiety, you stop. You put everything down, put all the papers, push them aside, and you just take a deep breath, breath in, and you breathe out. You could do it a few times and really reflect on what you want to achieve and how your feelings are impacting the way that you accomplish those goals. So you need to complete your assignment, but being anxious, you get worked up, and you cannot finish those assignments. So what this activity does is help you to relax. You can practice breathing techniques. You could put your arms on the, like, put your arms under your legs, or you could practice just stretching. Whenever you feel worked out, you could do it to the back, and that really helps to calm the nerves in the body and help you to relax a little bit. And then you can really gain your focus and come back to look at whatever you were doing, whatever assignment that you were trying to complete. So you could do this exercise as often as you feel any type of anxiety coming on. And I think that would really help to, like, relax.
Client: Yeah, I think it's gonna help.
Counselor: Breathing exercise, especially the stretching, will get you, when you get worked up to, you know, like, take out all the tension in your body.
Client: Yeah, yeah.
Counselor: So another thing we could touch on now that we've talked about an activity or something you can do to relieve anxiety, another thing I see that's been affecting you is the expectations from your family.
Client: Yeah. I mean, they really want me to do well, but whenever I feel like I'm, like, I don't pass my classes, I just fail one of the tests, and I just feel like I'm a failure. And I don't want to be a failure. I don't want to do that to my parents.
Counselor: I know that's a big expectation for you, to have that placed on you and knowing that if you fail that you will bring disappointment to your family.
Client: And, like, if I fail the school, that I'm just gonna fail for my life. I don't know what to do.
Counselor: So do you think that's positive thinking? Do you think that is true?
Client: I mean, I'm not going to fail my life, but I just feel like, you know, I'm a failure because I cannot even finish school.
Counselor: So let's try to restructure that thinking because I think probably that thinking is 40, so probably to think of it in another way. Okay, how about you try thinking about times that you've been successful?
Client: Hmm? Yeah, actually I, well, until last semester I did pretty well in my classes. And so far it's just this last semester I just have a lot of things to do. But so far I did pretty well and I'm pretty involved in school and I am involved in student council, so I do a lot of activities and you know, I work too, so. And people, people like me, I think so, yeah.
Counselor: So that's good. You have a lot of things here that you should be positive about, especially being part of an organization, being part of student council. It shows that you're responsible and you're capable of handling your task. So what really is taking the best of you is like the last semester and I being overwhelmed with the papers that are coming to you. So I think thinking positive about being capable and using positive self talk and telling yourself that you're able to complete your assignments, you have done this before and you've been reliable and responsible. So using those things, at least try using them throughout the day to motivate you to keep up the good work and believe in yourself that you can complete your assignments. And you know, just take the focus of the negative thinking and think positive about yourself and think positive that you will complete your assignments because you've done it before and you're capable of doing it again. So I think that would work for you. Probably using that as a tool.
Client: Yeah, yeah.
Counselor: And we also mentioned about quitting. I think that's one of your top goals you already discussed.
Client: Yeah, I wanted to stop thinking.
Counselor: Yeah. So I think stopping can be dangerous sometimes. I'll more likely influence you to think of it as minimizing your drinking and dealing with all the soft goals. And then I think that would really help you. And another way to do that is I found this agency that started a clinic that I have researched as we talked about the last time, and they're starting a session next Saturday at twelve.
Client: How does that look for you to schedule next Saturday? I think, I think at twelve I think I can make it. Yeah.
Counselor: So we have the intake form, so what we could do, we could fill that out and I could call and make the appointments for you. And it is a, it is a five session, it's within a group. So you have other people who also struggle in dependency. So you get to meet with others and talk about your feelings and probably that would help you to cope with it and find ways to deal with that. How is that?
Client: Yeah, I like that.
Counselor: So good. I glad that we're making some steps. So what we've discussed overall, just to do a recap, we talked about the, the school, like reaching out to your professors and you said that worked for you. We talked about the techniques, the coping skills. You could do some breathing techniques or exercise and stretching and also the clinic dependency clinic that's setting up. So I think we on a good start.
Client: Yeah, I'm excited to start the therapy and I'll definitely try the stop method that you're telling me about.
Counselor: That's good. All right.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Nice meeting you again.
Client: See you next week. Okay, bye. Hi, Janice. Hi. Welcome back.
Counselor: Thank you.
Client: It's really good to see you again. I'm really glad that you're able to come back this time.
Counselor: Yeah, I really want to do this and I thought about it and I think that in order to reach my goals I need to participate and do something about it. And I'm glad that you going to help me.
Client: Okay. I'm here to help you. I'm really glad that you're able to really make your time and come.

Client: So today what we're going to do is you shared with me last time how you are feeling anxious about not being able to finish school because of your alcohol dependency. Am I correct?

Client: Okay. So how was that for the last, last week after we met? Yeah.
Counselor:
output: I've been drinking a lot because I've accumulated a lot of papers. I work full time and I really don't have the time to do my assignment.
