instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, Jordan. How you doing today?
Client: Could have been better.
Counselor: Could be better.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What's going on?
Client: Um, well, you know, I have two jobs.
Counselor: Mm hmm.
Client: And I lost one of them.
Counselor: You lost your job? Yes. Which one did you lose?
Client: I lost one at the grocery store.
Counselor: That was your part time?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I'm sorry to hear that.
Client: Me too. And I'm just. It's all I think about now.
Counselor: And when did this happen?
Client: It happened about two, three days ago.
Counselor: Two, three days ago?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So if I remember right, you took that job not too long ago to kind of supplement your income.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So certainly that would be upsetting, but I know that's not a major part of your income.
Client: It's not, but, I mean, I'm still very worried about it.
Counselor: Tell me about the worry.
Client: I mean, I worry that, you know, I'm. Now I only had so much money, and now I have less than that. I mean, without my money, you know, God knows how many things can happen.
Counselor: So before you had the job, you were paying all your bills. You want some extra income, you've lost that extra income. And I can certainly understand how that would be disturbing. But as I understand that you were doing okay before with your full time job.
Client: I was doing okay, but, I mean, I got comfortable with that extra income, and so now my fear is that I've gotten too comfortable with it, and now that it's not there anymore, it's going to affect the fact I'm not going to be able to pay for food or my rent.
Counselor: Okay, so you adjusted to the new income level with the full time and the part time job together, and you're worried you can't adjust back?
Client: I'm worried that, I mean, things are just gonna get worse from here. I mean, it's a big deal, losing your job. Even if it was part time, I've gotten comfortable from having so much money, from the money I had to. Now that's, you know, been divided and, I mean, God knows how many things, like I said, God knows how many things can happen.
Counselor: Well, what. What can happen? So you have that income, your income is reduced now to just your full time job. What can happen from this point on?
Client: Well, I can, you know, keep. Stay in the mindset that I have that extra money and spend what I think is that extra money, digging into the money I paid for my rent, my food, my gas, my insurance, and me, who's somebody without all that.
Counselor: So you could fail to pay expenses that need to be paid.
Client: And they helped me go to my full time job that I still have. So, I mean, if I can't, if I spend the money that was from my insurance because I thought I had extra, then I'm not gonna have insurance on my cardinal. I can get pulled over, lose my license, not going to be able to get to work, and then I'll get fired there too.
Counselor: All right, so the kind of chain of causality you're seeing is that without that part time income, you might not adapt with your expense management. You might fail to pay, for example, your car insurance. You could get pulled over for something the police officer could see, don't have insurance, give you a ticket, which is just money. I don't have another expense. Right. And how would this. How would that connect to losing your job?
Client: Because I wouldn't be able to get to work.
Counselor: So it'd be. So the ticket would be so expensive, you would lose your.
Client: Well, the ticket would be expensive, so I wouldn't be able to try to pay the next month's insurance. So I just wouldn't have insurance on my car. So I.
Counselor: So you'd lose your insurance?
Client: I'd lose my insurance.
Counselor: And then by losing your insurance, you lose your transportation altogether because you can't drive that insurance. And then you lose your job.
Client: Mm hmm. I mean, it's either go to work with an uninsured car, and then I can get pulled over and go to jail for driving with no insurance multiple times.
Counselor: No, that's serious. Yeah. You wouldn't want to do that.
Client: I wouldn't go to jail.
Counselor: So there's two. You have two kind of causal change. One is losing your job. And now even just the idea you can end up incarcerated.
Client: Yes. I mean, which I definitely lose my.
Counselor: Job if I'm in jail, I would imagine.
Client: And so that would have. So then I wouldn't even have, like, any money to help me through jail. Like, to. For the commissary and stuff.
Counselor: Because you would have no income.
Client: I would have no income. And then when I get out of jail, I'm. No one's gonna hire me.
Counselor: Because you have a criminal record.
Client: Exactly.
Counselor: Which makes it challenging to find employment in some instances. So what's happened is kind of in your mind, and we've talked about how thoughts work and beliefs work, is you, in reality, you've lost this part time job. And as I said, that's certainly. That's understandable that you'd be upset about that. I doubt many people would be happy about losing additional income, but you move from there, from losing additional income, which is what has actually happened to this possibility that you could be in jail or lose your job because of this. So I remember maybe last week. Week before, you're talking about the. The letter that you received from. It was like a late notice. It wasn't. Turned out wasn't.
Client: Yeah, it was sent to me, but it was somebody else's credit card mistake. Yeah.
Counselor: Do you remember the conclusions you drew from when you believe that was actually for you, that late notice, that my.
Client: Credit score was gonna go down, that I would. I'd be stuck in that apartment, and then I'd go into depression. I wouldn't be able to do anything.
Counselor: Yeah. So you ended up in that scenario. You end up in a situation where you just couldn't function at all. And you moved there from a letter that you believe was addressed to you, saying you were one month or six days late or something on a credit card, which, of course, you don't want to be late on a credit card, but you move from there to being so depressed you couldn't work, couldn't function, I think, is how you put it. Couldn't function. Do you see, kind of, given how we've talked about cognitive behavioral strategies and concepts, do you see a pattern that's emerged over the last few times I've seen you?
Client: I mean, I've seen that, you know, sometimes I can. I can think the worst, and then. And I know it didn't happen last time, but that was, you know, a stroke of good luck.
Counselor: That it wasn't you.
Client: Yeah. That it was, you know, it wasn't me. And, you know, that was a relief. But this is something that's solid. I don't have my part time job anymore.
Counselor: You've lost real income.
Client: I mean, this isn't a mistake. This isn't a. We fired the wrong person. You know, this is real. So there's real concerns here.
Counselor: I.
Client: Unlike last time, where I was lucky.
Counselor: So this. This situation, you see, is different than the first situation because the first situation was more. You were perceiving something was wrong that wasn't wrong because you weren't the intended recipient of the letter.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But in this situation, it's different because it's real. You really lost your income.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And, of course, keeping in mind that this job, again, only a few months old, and you survived well before that, is it reason to believe you could survive well again, that you could adapt to this lost income?
Client: Well, I suppose there is, but I'm concerned about whether I'm not, whether I won't adapt.
Counselor: Well, let's look at this in terms of probabilities, right. You've had several jobs throughout your career. You've had some of them worked out. You've lost other ones. You're still paying your bills. So in terms of probabilities, how many times have you, how many times have you ended up in jail or losing your full time job?
Client: I mean, they haven't happened yet.
Counselor: It hasn't happened.
Client: Not yet. But I mean, I, I struggled a little bit when I lost a part time job or when I was younger and I had those little jobs.
Counselor: So you had to adapt.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And it was painful.
Client: I did struggle, yeah.
Counselor: You struggled.
Client: Yeah. I mean, but I'm older now. These are, you know, even though grocery stores, not a serious job. It was income.
Counselor: Sure. Yeah. And again, to lose income would be disappointing for just about anybody. Are there any upsides to not having that job?
Client: I suppose I have more time to focus on my full time job because, I mean, that is really intensive.
Counselor: Is there a possibility that you could find another part time job just as you found that one?
Client: I mean, because will somebody else take me because I was fired from that job? I mean, that's my concern, is that.
Counselor: Nobody, they're going to find out.
Client: Yeah. And then they're going to go, oh, she was fired, you know. No, we don't. We don't want her.
Counselor: But you've had other jobs that didn't work out before and that didn't affect you getting that job.
Client: That's true.
Counselor: So the worst case scenario, I guess what I'm getting at the worst case scenario is, in your case, ending up in jail or losing your full time job, which you've had for a while.
Client: Yeah, I really don't want to lose my job.
Counselor: And it seems like they like you there.
Client: I hope they do.
Counselor: Right? Yeah. So those scenarios, I guess, are possible, but they seem, based on what you're saying, is pretty unlikely. So I wonder how useful it is to invest a lot of energy in kind of tracking that causal chain to jail or prison or to unemployment when that's really not the most likely outcome. Sorry to interrupt you, but do you invest as much energy in tracking the positives or the probable outcomes?
Client: No, not even close. I know that I don't think about the positive things. I mean, I don't get fired and then go, what's good about this?
Counselor: Or get a letter in the mail and say, what's, you know, although I can see there's not much upside to that, although it turned out that was an error, so. But this has still been a theme that I've seen over the last eight to ten weeks, where you really have, you really emphasize the negative, possible, even unlikely outcomes, kind of expanding the negative as you move through. Like a causal chain.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Does that make sense? Yeah, but you don't do the same thing for the positive side. You don't look at how something could work out. Well, would you say it's fair assessment?
Client: Yeah. Yeah, no, that's. That's pretty accurate.
Counselor:
output: But still, you're worried about this.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, Hazel. How you doing?
Client: I'm all right. I'm a little bit stressed out right now.
Counselor: A little stressed? What's going on?
Client: Well, as you know, I'm in a graduate program right now, and I'm just really coming to the. Near the end of my program, and I'm just finding it increasingly difficult. I'm just really stressed with how things have been going.
Counselor: Okay. Now, we've talked about some different struggles you've had as you balance work and school and everything. What specifically is bothering you now? It seems like you're a little more distressed today.
Client: Well, I don't really know. Just I. As I have told you before, I take school really seriously, and I really strive to do well in school and well on my assignments, and I just feel like I'm not performing as well as I need to.
Counselor: Now, what kind of grades you've been getting lately?
Client: Well, I've been getting A's, but.
Counselor: Anything else? No, just a's. Okay. That's usually considered pretty good, right?
Client: Yeah. I just feel like it's getting harder to get the a's.
Counselor: Okay. So you're working harder to get the same grade?
Client: Right. It used to be so easy for me to do what my teachers expect and to get good grades. Now I feel like it's really a struggle and I'm not doing as well as I need to. Constantly worried about not doing as well.
Counselor: Have you been getting any feedback from professors or your classmates about your performance?
Client: My teachers all seem to think I'm doing well. I seem to get good feedback on my assignments, but I feel like. I feel like I. Just to make sure I'm doing well, I really focus on, like, the details, like, making sure that the instructions are really clear, like, I'm doing everything, like, perfectly as the instructor wants, because I'm really afraid that, you know, if I'm not really clear on what the assignment is, then maybe I won't do it the right way.
Counselor: All right, so before, when you got A's, you were working hard to do a good job, but not to the level of precision in terms of, like, the detail of the assignment that you are now. You're trying to get more information about the assignments. You're working harder to get the same grade that you used to get before.
Client: Right? Like, I find myself, like, emailing the teacher, like, almost, like, obsessively, like, trying to clarify the assignment and to make sure do they think I'm doing well in class and whatnot.
Counselor: So when you're having this feeling that I guess it's a feeling of anxiety or stress.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What's going through your mind? What are you thinking about?
Client: Well, I guess I'm just feeling that, you know, I've worked really hard this whole program, and I don't want to mess it up now or, you know, because if I don't get these grades, then I feel like, what was the use? If I met, then I'm going to be ruining all this hard work that I've done, this whole program. If I kind of. If I don't maintain that level of, you know, like you said, precision, I feel like. Like that I've let myself down or that I'm a failure because I'm. I just slacked off at the end of the program, and it's so close to being done.
Counselor: So what grade would you have to receive for you to feel like you have failed?
Client: Probably less than an a. Anything other than an a.
Counselor: And right below an a is an a minus.
Client: I mean, I guess I would be okay with that, but I wouldn't be really happy with it.
Counselor: How about a b?
Client: I wouldn't be that excited about that.
Counselor: A b.
Client: I wouldn't be happy with that.
Counselor: No, that would be worse. Okay, so an a, you can tolerate an a minus. You're not exactly sure, but you think you could.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But a b plus and a b, to me, like.
Client: Like a a minus, I would maybe be okay with. But, like, below that, like, to me, like, a b is a b, whether it's, like, a b minus, a b, a b plus, it's all a b, and that's not an a.
Counselor: So what would it mean to you if you received a bde that I.
Client: Didn'T try hard enough? That there's something else I could have done to do better? That I was, like, slacking or I didn't read the directions right or I didn't have enough responses or make my paper long enough. I just didn't do enough.
Counselor: That you didn't try hard enough. That you didn't do enough. What would it mean if that were true?
Client: If I didn't try hard enough? That I was lazy.
Counselor: You were lazy?
Client: Yeah. Then I could have tried harder, and I didn't. So why didn't I try? Maybe I didn't care. I was lazy. Kind of like, what's the use? If you're not gonna try your best, then why try it all?
Counselor: Okay. And we've talked before about automatic thoughts and cognitive distortions, right? In other sessions. And one of the cognitive distortions is this idea that an unuseful type of thinking and error in thinking is when you think of everything in terms of, like, black or white, all or nothing. So it sounds like you have a little tolerance for, like, an a minus, so you're not completely there. Generally, it's kind of an a of some type or you're not interested. Right. It would get down to you didn't try hard enough, and if that were true, then you would be lazy.
Client: Right.
Counselor: Which, you know, having seen you in these last few sessions is clear to me. You're not lazy, but that's the thought you're having.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Now, it seems that earlier, in your earlier years in the program, the A's were not effortless for you, but you didn't have to work as hard for them.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What do you think has changed?
Client: I'm not quite sure. Like, it didn't stress me out as much in the beginning of the program, I really like school, but now I feel like I almost dread it because it's anxiety producing for me because I'm constantly worried.
Counselor: You mentioned part of it was you're getting close to the end. Right. So is there anything else?
Client: Well, the only thing I can think of is we have the same students throughout our program, but I guess this semester there's a new student in the program. And now that you mention it, it seems like she's kind of really stressing me out.
Counselor: How so?
Client: Well, see, throughout the program, I kind of considered myself, like, to be the student who got the best grades. And there's this award at the end of the program for doing really well. And I kind of made it a goal of mine to get this award at the end because I felt like that would show that I really tried hard. Program really meant a lot to me. It would show people who viewed it that I really busted my butt and did a good job in this program. And for the whole program so far, that was me. I was kind of the front runner, I guess, for this award. And this semester there's a new student and then come to find out, like, she had a 4.0 in her other program. So.
Counselor: So if I'm reading you right, you. You really didn't have any competition for this award that you were aware of, right? And now you feel like you really do, right?
Client: Like, I feel like the pressure's on. Like, I felt like I tried so hard this whole program, and now, like, this new person comes in and she might win it over me. So I really need to go above and beyond to make sure that I'm still on track. So when that's the word.
Counselor: And paradoxically, that's caused you to be more anxious and more stressed. And you're performing well. You're still getting the A's, but you're working harder to get the A's right.
Client: And it's causing me a lot of anxiety with school, where it's not as enjoyable for me as it once was.
Counselor: So what would it mean if you couldn't get the award? If you didn't win the. What's the name of the news? What's the first name of the new student? Joyce. Joyce. Okay. What if Joyce won this award and you didn't? What'd that mean?
Client: I guess part of me feels like, then why did I do the program? If, you know, part of me feels like, if you're not gonna be the best, why try? So if she got the award over me, then it's kind of like, why did I work so hard this whole time? Like, I could have been slacking this whole time and just skated by. So why did I bust my butt if it was all for nothing? I don't have anything to show for it.
Counselor: So it's all for nothing if you don't win the award?
Client: I mean, I guess it's not the only thing that matters, but part of me feels that way sometimes, that I have these. These thoughts that if I don't try my hardest and do well and win this award, then why did I try so hard the rest of the time? Like, it negates all the positive things that this. You know, kind of like the end result. Like, if you tried hard the whole race, and then you lose, you know, at the end.
Counselor: Right. But you're not really losing the whole race because you would still graduate.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Right. You're. You're just not getting an award, which you would like and which would be great and certainly an accomplishment. But the reason you came to the program was to get the degree, right.
Client: I didn't even know about the award until probably, like, the second year anyway. So that wasn't the reason I entered. But.
Counselor: But it's now. It's now taken on some importance for you. Winning this award has been a real goal. So with the new student, Joyce, coming in, they have this increased competition, and it's causing anxiety. It's causing you to work harder for the same grade. All right. So, as we talked before, you have a tendency to be. I mean, this is a compliment. A little perfectionistic. Right?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I don't think it's necessarily a bad thing if it's taken too far. It can be right. It can be not useful. You ever hear the phrase perfect is the enemy of good?
Client: No.
Counselor: Does that make sense, what that might mean?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. So this desire to be perfect or to win the award is potentially causing you not even to perform well. Right?
SPK_3: Right.
Counselor: You're still getting the a's, but it's causing the anxiety and you're working hard.
Client: Right. And I'm not even. I feel like when I read, like, I'm so stressed with it, I'm reading the right thing and memorizing every word that I'm not retaining all the information. So it could. And it's starting to, like, impact school.
Counselor: So is there any way that you cannot win the award and still walk away having accomplished worthy goals? Or does it have to be the award or none of this was worth it?
Client: I mean, it kind of sounds silly when you're reflecting it back to me, how you know, that I have to earn the awards. Like, I think that it makes sense, you know, that wasn't my goal going into it. You know, why does it matter so much to me that there's different degrees of success? I think, as you've said before, that it's not all about the award. And I think I would be happy with just, you know, getting the degree and all the stuff that I've learned, and I would feel like it was if I didn't get the award, rather, I would have feel like it was still a worthwhile journey, but in the moment, sometimes it's really upsetting at the thought of not getting the award. But that's a possibility.
Counselor: The award validates all the hard work you've done, right?
Client: Exactly.
Counselor: And in your mind, losing the award invalidates all the hard work you've done, right. But in reality, there's probably a between ground there, a shade of gray where you're still an excellent student, you still graduate, you just don't have an extra plaque to hang on the wall. Whatever the award is, that's really all you'd be missing, right? Would this award have any impact on employment?
Client: I don't think so. I don't think in the long term many people would know about it besides me or if I put it, you know, on a resume or something, but I don't think it would make that much of a difference.
Counselor: And you didn't even know about it when you first came in.
Client: You were already working hard right at the beginning. I didn't even know about it.
Counselor: So in a sense, and of course, we can't do this, but in a sense, if you could forget about the award, you'd probably win it.
Client: Right.
Counselor: Right. Because you were already doing so well. What is the thought of this potential failure not wearing the word that's holding you back?
SPK_3: Right.
Client: It makes me paranoid to make mistakes or to try and take risks or to really, you know, do well because I'm so worried about judgment, like, from my teachers, if I'm doing well or not.
Counselor: Yeah. There's no. There's no tolerance for any type of mistake.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So now that this award's out there, you really feel like you can't make any type of mistake or you just go right to a catastrophe.
Client: Right. Like I'm walking on eggshells and I'm just expecting my grades to tank if I. If I kind of, like, deviate from that line.
Counselor: So for you to feel better about this one way, I guess, right. Would be to not have to not place so much value in winning.
Client: It's really hard.
Counselor: Yeah. You really want that. And it would be great. And that's okay. Right. We talked about the adaptive responses before, right. What are. What's the automatic thought you have when you're sitting there and trying to get every assignment right and you're kind of vaguely thinking about not losing or not winning this award? What's the automatic thought that comes to mind?
Client: If I'm. You mean if I'm. When I'm just doing the work.
Counselor:
output: Yeah. When you're doing your work and you sense that anxiety. Come on. Right. As you start maybe vaguely thinking about winning or losing this award. I guess losing it really what's going through your mind right at that moment?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Ann. How you doing today?
Client: Good.
Counselor: Doing well?
Client: Yeah, I guess so. I've been working still on the fear of leaving the home for extended periods of time, like vacation, and it's been a little harder recently because I have this planned trip with a friend of mine coming up in a few months, and that's kind of been weighing on my mind.
Counselor: Where's the trip to Georgia, and how long will you be there?
Client: She wants to go, like, six days, but, yeah, I'm not sure. With work and school and everything, I can make the full six days, and plus, I'm a little nervous to go that long.
Counselor: So that's a long time for you.
Client: It is, yes.
Counselor: So when did you discover this trip.
Client: Was going to be actually last? Just a few days ago. She messaged me and said, hey, you want to go with me? And we'll go golfing and swimming? I love golfing. Like, you know, I want to go, but I just have these, just, you know, a little nervous about leaving.
Counselor: A little nervous. So when she made that call just a couple days ago, what was the first thought you had?
Client: God, I can't go that long. That was my first thought, that's too long. But then it was like, wow, this would be great. I want to go down there golfing so bad and get away from the cold weather. So, I mean, my immediate thought was, no, not that long, but, yes, I want to go.
Counselor: All right, so you had two kind of conflicting thoughts, right. So one. One is, I could never go that long. Six days, way too long. And the other one is, that would be enjoyable. You enjoy that?
Client: Absolutely, yeah.
Counselor: So which way are you leaning right now?
Client: I want to go to go, but maybe not for six days. Maybe just like a long weekend.
Counselor: Three, four days.
Client: Two would be ideal, but two would probably be idea, but two or three days. Yeah.
Counselor: So what do you think is causing this worry about being gone more than two days?
Client: I don't know. I mean, I've always, as a late teenager in my twenties, I've always had just nervous to leave home. As much as I love being home, I love to travel, too, and do different things. It's just, I guess I'm just afraid something to happen when I'm not around.
Counselor: So you're afraid something will happen to your house or.
Client: Well, I have pets, so I worry about them. My parents are getting older, so I worry about them mainly, like, my immediate family, mainly, I guess, my dad, because he's had a history of heart attacks, and then my pets, that's just worry something will happen. I won't be there.
Counselor: And how about when you were younger, you said this problem's been out for a while.
Client: It's the same thing.
Counselor: The same thing. So mostly family and now some pets.
Client: Well, I had pets then, too.
Counselor: You had pets then, too? Okay, so that's really what's bothering you here, is that you'll be away, and that's when something will happen and it'll be something bad. What about coming back? Like, you can come back?
Client: Yeah, like, I'm ready to come back, but then I'm missing home. Like, I want to go back to my family and everything's okay, but I miss, you know, where I just left because it's away from home. I know it sounds really conflicting and weird, but, you know, I like to get away. I enjoy being away from this small town.
Counselor: So, yes, you have feelings that are fighting one another.
Client: Absolutely.
Counselor: And right now, the feeling, the thought, anyway, of, you know, I would like to go on a trip is winning, but the fear thought is kind of dragging you down. So what's the sensation? Anxiety.
Client: Yeah. I get anxious. Yeah. My heart gets. Feels like it's heavy. My chest heavy. And I just. All these thoughts go through my mind, like, you know, I know my parents. Somebody can watch my pets, but they may not take care of them like I would. I don't know, it's just. I mean, you know, they've always. They'll take care of them. I know, but they'll miss me and they might tear my house up. I don't know. All these thoughts go through my mind that seem crazy to me.
Counselor: So it seems like an endless stream of worries.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Surrounding family and the pets and what might happen. So really, that's. That's it. Right. It's what might happen. It's the uncertainty.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So has anything ever happened?
Client: No. No.
Counselor: So, so far, all this worrying, anxiety really hasn't paid any dividends.
Client: No.
Counselor: Do you end up going on the trips anyway?
Client: Yes. And now that I'm older, when I was younger, I probably wouldn't like an overnight, but now that I'm older. Yes, I do. I just say I got to live my life and it'll be okay. I just try to tell myself they're in good hands. If something happens, somebody will call me. But then I feel like, oh, but I'm going to be hours away. I'm a plane ride away. And then I get thinking about that, but I do go.
Counselor: But you didn't in the past.
Client: No.
Counselor: So something changed. What changed?
Client: I don't know. I really I don't know. I don't know what what made a difference. Maybe I just feel more and, I don't know, say in control. But now that I'm living on my own, so that's what I wouldn't go is when I lived at home with my parents still, which seems weird because somebody was always there to look after my animals and. But now that I'm living on my own, maybe I just feel yden more responsible that I have to go do these things. I really don't know what changed.
Counselor: All right. So you're not sure what changed. But you used to not go. Now you do go. So when you're down there or wherever you're going, the trip, you're feeling better, like you're enjoying yourself, but you're also worried at the same time.
Client: Not too. Once I get there, I'm usually okay. Maybe the first night I get a little worried. And then maybe when I'm getting ready to come home, I'm, like, a little anxious. I'm ready to get home to make sure everything's okay.
Counselor: And the rest of the time I'm usually okay.
Client: I want to get some alcohol involved, so it kind of limits my anxiety. But once I get into, like, playing the golf and all that, I really do allow myself to enjoy it. It's just. It seems like it's going and coming. That's all.
Counselor: Right. So the problem really isn't when you're there leading up to the problem is now leading up to. Right.
Client: Exactly.
Counselor: And maybe just the first half day or day when you're there. Maybe the last half day or day.
Client: You'Re there, it's like a plane. Like, I don't have a problem riding, like, flying out, but it's the thinking, like, while I'm waiting for the plane, like, what if a terrorist is on there? What if we crash? I'll think about all that before. But once I'm there and on the plane, it's like, right. Take off. I'm fine. I'm completely fine. I'm not anxious. It's leading up to the actual event that makes me anxious.
Counselor: It's just anticipation. So that's the worst part. So the period between now and when you leave is going to be the worst part?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: But you'll probably still go.
Client: Probably. But I'll have changed my mind probably a dozen times before I actually say, yes, I'm going.
Counselor: And when you do go, you have a good time. And the probability of something happening that you're worried about based on the history seems low.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor:
output: Something could happen, certainly, but it hasn't so far. All right, so there's a few angles here. So what happens if you go down there and a bad scenario or worst case scenario does happen?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, mister Urban. It's nice to see you again. From our previous session, I know you spoke about the relationship you and your wife were going through. In the bad terms, she got left off. So I want to ask you, what would make you cheat on your wife?
Client: You know, I've been asked that question every day for the past two, three weeks. And the only thing I can respond with is what would make a wife cheat on her husband? I mean, it's petty. I know it's petty. But I loved her. And finding out that more than once she was with somebody else, that took something from me that I couldn't get back. And for months I was dealing with. What could I have done? What was it? What did I do? Because it has to have been me. She's too nice a person for that, right? She's too smart a person for that, right? And then weeks of me finally understanding that it wasn't me. A decision that you make is a decision that you make. So when Susie, my administrative assistant, came into the picture, I had a decision that I had to make. I have to take it off and spend time with Susie. Or keep it on and spend many a night alone. So why? You figure it out.
Counselor: So do you think that you did it for revenge? Were you trying to get back at your wife?
Client: I guess. I mean, what else could it be? Yeah, maybe I am that petty. But it's just. It's not love anymore.
Counselor: So why are you still in a marriage, mister Urban? If it's not love, if it's not for love, why do you feel that you must stay in America?
Client: Because that's the type of household I was brought up in.
Counselor: Explain that to me.
Client: My dad always told me that you take care of your business and your girl is your business. You never leave her. You take care of her no matter what. That's what you do. So when I got older, I asked him, what do you mean you never leave her? He said, divorce is not an option. That's pretty much how it is in my household.
Counselor: So are you saying because of how you were raised up is why you're still in the marriage?
Client: It's the only thing that makes sense.
Counselor: Are you happy?
Client: Do I seem happy?
Counselor: Have you spoken to your wife about this?
Client: No. So everything that I feel, everything that I am is stuck on the inside. This is actually the first time I've actually talked about any of her.
Counselor: Okay, mister Ermen, so let's try this exercise. I'm gonna pull out chairs, so pretend that that this is your wife here. Why are we here and express your feelings.
Client: Why do I have to do this?
Counselor: Because you never spoke about it. Right? So express your feelings. Let it out, and see how you would tell her what you're feeling inside. Do you feel uncomfortable?
Client: I felt uncomfortable since the moment I found out that you just didn't love me anymore. I felt uncomfortable every single night I've been in the guest room because I just couldn't take being with you. I felt uncomfortable since the very moment I felt like it was okay because of what you did to me. To take off my wedding band, to forget my vows, to forget you, to try and be something that I'm not. Every night that I was with Susie, I imagined that I was with you, but not who you are now. I imagine that I was with the woman that I first met, woman that I first loved. But you're not the same person anymore. I haven't been the same person over a year. Every day that I wake up and I see your face, I have to imagine that you are that same person because that's the. The only thing that keeps me around. That and the fact that I just don't think I can make. And it's not because I love you so much anymore, because it's not you that I love. It's not because of anything religious. It's because I don't want to deal with my family.
Counselor: I know that was hard to do. Mister Urban, are you doing all right? Are you feeling okay?
Client: I'm fine.
Counselor:
output: Okay. So I want you to realize, like, can you not see that your belief is causing this pain inside your depression and your unhappiness?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Danielle. How are you doing today?
Client: I'm good, how are you?
Counselor: I'm good, thanks for asking. What's been going on?
Client: Well, last time we spoke, you know, I just got a promotion.
Counselor: It's great news.
Client: Yeah, great news. I'm really, really excited about the opportunity and the career advancement, but sure. I just really, it just hit me that I'm going to be having to give presentations and really kind of be a team leader and kind of be the face of a group of individuals and it's kind of making me a little shaky.
Counselor: Well, shaky. Are you a big fan of public speaking?
Client: Not. I wouldn't say a big fan, no, it's been bearable. But the thought of having to do it continuously, it's definitely a little frightening for me.
Counselor: That's frightening for you. How often would you have to, do you say continuously? How often would it be in this new job?
Client: In this new job, I would actually have to meet with them every weekly. Weekly.
Counselor: How many people on the team that you now supervise?
Client: There are ten people. Yeah.
Counselor: All right, so you have ten people that you, you're gonna have to speak to?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Right. And how long is the talk each week?
Client: Normally? Average is about like half an hour.
Counselor: Half an hour. Have you ever had to do it in the past or anything like it?
Client: I've done something like this for school, but definitely not for 30 minutes. Not for half an hour.
Counselor: Alright, so the length of time is a major stressor. How about the number of people, like ten?
Client: Is that, that's, that's a, I mean, when I did it for school, it was a group of us, so it was less anxiety. But to be doing it by myself for, you know, and all attention on me, that's. Yeah. And ten people, that's a lot of people looking up to me and, you know.
Counselor: All right, so the number of people being ten, that stresses you a bit. Little anxiety there, a good amount of anxiety and then the duration.
Client: Yeah, absolutely.
Counselor: So ten people for a minute. That wouldn't.
Client: That's not too bad.
Counselor: You can handle that?
Client: I could handle that.
Counselor: Or a half hour with like one.
Client: Person, I can definitely handle 100 one's not too bad.
Counselor: 100 one's not too bad.
Client: 100 one's not too bad. But the thought of ten people staring at me, hanging on my every word for that long, that's, that's definitely puts me out there in terms of anxiety.
Counselor: All right, so there's a lot of anxiety there and that's painful for you. Let's do this. I know that you mentioned that you're taking over for somebody but they still work there?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: How long do you have before you need to start taking over that responsibility?
Client: I have about six weeks.
Counselor: About six weeks. So you have six weeks to become reasonably comfortable with speaking in front of ten people for a half hour once a week. So what I'd like to do is I'd like to develop some steps that you can take at work. So I know you do a lot of different things at work and you mentioned that you're good with people individually, so I'm going to create some steps that you can actually conduct at work, you know, collaboratively with you. I want you to be a big part of this, and I want to rank them from the least anxiety provoking to the most anxiety provoking. And let's use about five levels. Five steps. So I'm going to develop together with you five steps. So the fifth one will be the hardest. And I'm going to take a wild guess and say that would be speaking in front of all ten people for a half hour.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So that's the most stressful it can get.
Client: Yeah, definitely.
Counselor: That's the most stressful part of your job now. Or what your job will be when you take that over. All right, so let's make that. If you agree, we'll make that kind of a five out of five. So five is the maximum level of anxiety.
Client: I can agree to that, yeah.
Counselor: So let me think of some other ways you can approach this. You said you're really good one on one. How about with two people? Like, if you're in a room with two people and talk to them, that's.
Client: Not, that's not too bad.
Counselor: That's not too bad. That's definitely not a five out of five.
Client: No, it's definitely not a five out of five.
Counselor: So let's make that one of the steps. How about speaking to two of the people for around 15 minutes? Make that one of the steps. And how about another step would be speaking to four people for 15 minutes?
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Right. Which of those two would be. Would be scarier?
Client: The four people.
Counselor: Four people.
Client: For 15 minutes.
Counselor: For 15 minutes. All right. And then if we were to say four people for a half hour, what would that rank?
Client: I would definitely say that's like a four and a half or four.
Counselor: So that's. That's higher up than the. So, so far, if we rank these in terms of anxiety from the least anxiety provoking a couple people, 15 minutes, you think you could do that?
Client: That's manageable.
Counselor: Double that number of people of four for the same amount of time. That would be the next level up. Taking those four people and talking to them for a half hour, maybe one more level up.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So where would all ten people for 15 minutes rank? Would that be more anxiety provoking than four for a half hour?
Client: Definitely. Because of the duration? Yeah.
Counselor: But not as anxiety provoking as ten people for a half an hour.
Client: No, not. No, I think that would definitely be my.
Counselor: That's still the top.
Client: Yeah, that's at the top.
Counselor: So nothing I've introduced is a step anxiety provoking as all ten for a half hour?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So if that's a five, then a four would be ten people for 15 minutes, three would be the four people for a half hour, two would be the four people for 15 minutes, and the one would be two people for 15 minutes. And I can write all this out for you.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: All right.
Client: That's great.
Counselor: Would you agree that's an accurate ranking from the most stressful, most anxiety provoking down to.
Client: Yeah, I would absolutely agree to that.
Counselor: And you'd agree that the first step, the least things I. Provoking the two people, 15 minutes, that's not a huge deal for you?
Client: No.
Counselor: You think you could handle that?
Client: I could handle that.
Counselor: So what my hope is, is that you move into each step, you conduct that step, you take part in that behavior enough times to where, even though it's a little anxiety provoking in the beginning, you do enough times to where that anxiety comes down. So you have six weeks to get through, really four of the steps, because the final step will be all ten people. So you have six weeks to get through these four steps. So for this, let's use this first step for this next week, because I'll see you again in a week and meet with two people. And you probably want to vary it like two different people.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Okay. Each time, if you didn't, they also might wonder what you're doing if you meet the same people over there. Right. So. But, you know, make it productive. Make it part of your job. Make it something that's necessary for your job. Like, you can see an opportunity where you have to talk. Remember, it's about 15 minutes. It ends up being ten or 20, you know, about 15 minutes. And meet with them a few times this week. And I'm hoping that through this week, you'll notice that your anxiety decreases. So right after the meeting, if you could just take a quick second and note kind of how stressed you were at the beginning, maybe scale one to ten or ten being really anxious and how stressed you were at the end and any thoughts you might be having in terms of, like, what you were thinking while it was going on or what you. What you're thinking afterwards, like, maybe you're. You're going to think, well, I held that pretty well.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Or maybe you're thinking, that was still a little stressful.
Client: Okay.
Counselor:
output: Or somewhere in between.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Okay, Marsha, so how can I help you today?
Client: Well, I'm working full time. I'm a part time student. I've just gotten engaged, and I live at home. There's just so much stress in my life. I have everything happening all at once. Just to top it all off, I failed an exam, a really big exam, and I just feel like I can't do anything anymore. I can't do anything right. I've just got so much stress, and I feel like such a disappointment, such a failure. And I've embarrassed my family by failing. I just don't know what to do anymore. I guess I've come here today to tell you, like, I want to leave uni, and I guess that's why I've come here to you today.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like a whole lot of stuff's on top of you at the moment.
Client: Yeah, just so much. Just all parting on. Yeah.
Counselor: So you're working full time, plus part time study. Part time study. And then you've got your wedding preparation.
Client: Yeah, just got engaged, and weddings just a month away now, so, yeah, so I've just got so much happening. Work is really, really demanding and. Yeah, just fail this exam. It's just. Yeah, don't know what to do all too much.
Counselor: So imagine you've been sweating on this for a while, and it's all been swirling around in your head.
Client: Just been building up and building up and so much pressure with everything. And I'm living at home, so my parents, you know, a lot of pressure, need to do everything right. And. Yeah, by failing this, I feel like I've just embarrassed and disappointed them, and I just don't feel like I'm good enough, you know, to go on studying.
Counselor: Okay. And have they said much to you about failing your exam?
Client: They haven't said much. I was really scared to tell them, actually, because I knew they'd just be so disappointed and just embarrassed by the fact that I did fail. Yeah. I've never failed anything before. And so, yeah, really hard.
Counselor: Yeah. So it's new and you don't like it at all?
Client: Not at all, no. And I think leaving uni will just be the way out, just so I don't have to go through it again.
Counselor:
output: Right. Okay. Well, I'm glad you've come to counselling, because it's good for us to get an outsider's opinion when we've got so much on our plate and we're confused as to what to do and our emotions can get in the way. And you've just said earlier that a whole lot of stuff's on your plate at the moment. Okay. So I'm glad you've come here. Here at the clinic, we use the ABC model, which is a cognitive behavioural therapy model. So, Marsha, some counsellors have put together a list of beliefs that we often use and we don't realise that we're using those beliefs and they tend to be faulty ones. Here's the list. Here, have a look through that to see if there are any beliefs that you might be operating on at the moment.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Okay. Ali, welcome back to our session today.
Client: Hi.
Counselor: Hi. How are you? How are you doing today?
Client: I'm fine, thank you.
Counselor: Good. Have you gotten up to anything interesting today or this week?
Client: Well, yeah, I want to talk specifically about a situation that I had with a home.
Counselor: Okay, that sounds great. So I'm just going to put a pin in that for a sec. We'll put that on our agenda. Before that, let's just talk, do a bit of a check in. Would you say that your mood today, I know we're working on some depression and anxiety, some lower mood. Would you say that your mood is about the same as last week? Better or worse than last week?
Client: A little bit better.
Counselor: A little bit better?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.

Counselor: Hello, Liz. How you doing today?
Client: I'm okay. How are you?
Counselor: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. How things been going?
Client: They've been all right.
Counselor: Last time we were talking, it sounds like you're still having some difficulty with the quizzes. Is that still the case?
Client: Yeah, I still panic when I take them.
Counselor: You still panic. Can you tell me about the process of taking the quizzes? I know we've touched on this a little bit before.
Client: Okay, so I'm going to class. I'm fine. I sit down to take the test. I'm fine. The test is in front of me. Question one. I'm not going to get that answer.
Counselor: So you're looking down. So you take these quizzes in class?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Like a paper, pencil. Okay. With other students around?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: All right. Is the. Is having other students around distracting to you?
Client: No, it's happened in previous online classes. It's the same.
Counselor: So it's. You're pretty sure it's the quiz itself and not some external. Okay. So it's paper and pencil. You're seated, you're in the room. Rooms relatively distraction free.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. Everybody's quiet.
Counselor: And you're looking down at, really the first item on the.
Client: Mm hmm.
Counselor: On the quiz. And what's happening? What's happening? Then as you look down, you read that first item. What's happening at a thought. We'll start a thought level. What's happening with your thinking?
Client: I'm thinking. I'm reading the question, and I'm thinking, oh, my God, there's. Okay, there's four. Okay. So it's got to be. It's got to be one of them. And I am not going to pick the right one. I'm going to think I picked the right one, and it's going to be the one that my second choice is, and I am not going to pick the right one.
Counselor: Okay, so your thought is that you're going to get. You're going to select the wrong response and therefore get that quiz item wrong. How about behavior? Like, do you notice anything physically going on as you're thinking about that quiz item and how you're gonna get it wrong?
Client: I'd say my palms are probably sweaty. Like, I'm probably a little tense.
Counselor: A little tense.
Client: Yeah. That's really it.
Counselor: All right. So what it could be is that this thought of I'm gonna get this item wrong is leading to these uncomfortable feelings, the physical feelings. So what happens when you answer item one like, you don't know if you have it right or wrong immediately? Right because it's a paper and pencil. So you answer item one, and you move on to item two. What happens then?
Client: It starts all over again. I'm already, like, well, I already got the first one wrong, and now I'm. My chances are higher of getting this one wrong.
Counselor: So you feel like it because you. Because you thought that you got the first one wrong, that your chances of getting the second one wrong actually increase?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Like, I get one wrong the whole test, it's all gonna be wrong.
Counselor: Have you ever had a quiz that you've taken where you were confident that you got the first item right?
Client: I'm sure I have. I can't remember any.
Counselor: But eventually you're going to come to one item that you're going to have these doubts about?
Client: Yes. Inevitably it happens.
Counselor: There's going to be one that's maybe a little more difficult or difficult for you. So it seems like what you're saying is that when you reach that item where you have that thought from that point on, the next item is. Is more difficult because you're having a similar thought. Does that pattern continue throughout the test?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So explain to me what, like, let's just go with the example of the first item, like, just to keep it more simple. So you have the first item, and that didn't work out for you, that thought? Right. The second one, your thought was, I have even a greater chance of missing a. So what happens after you respond to that second item?
Client: It just compounds. I just start. I feel worse and worse as the quiz, as I continue.
Counselor: That's awful. So it's an awful feeling for me. Right. So by the time you get to.
Client: Item five or six, I'm convinced it's over. I've gotten a zero. If it's the. Yeah, if I start at the first, I've gotten a zero. I've gotten a bad grade.
Counselor: So that's what's on your mind. And how about those physical symptoms? Are they the same, different or new symptoms?
Client: If it, like. If it's. If it, like, starts early at the beginning of the test, my heart's, like, pounding at this point, but I still have the sweaty palms. I'm still, like, tensing.
Counselor: So it really just gets mentally and physically more unpleasant for you the whole time. So when you're saying panic, the panic's really occurring a few items in after you have the first one that you thought you missed. And this has been happening for a while, as you described, right?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Well, how about your grades? How have you actually been doing on the quizzes?
Client: I've been a pretty solid b student, so. And I feel. I wish I did better. I wish I got a's, but, I mean, these are fine. But when I take those quizzes, it's not. It doesn't. I don't know how it translates.
Counselor: How about your study habits? You consider yourself effective at studying?
Client: I've tried. I've taken a workshops on studying. I've. I. I think I'm pretty effective at studying. I've found what doesn't work. So I try to study by reading the chapters, taking outlines, reviewing flashcards, which has, I think, the best results, but.
Counselor: Okay, so your study habits are good, right. And your quiz scores are good, but you're still having these distressing thoughts and these uncomfortable physical sensations when you take the quizzes.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Is that about right?
Client: Yeah, that's absolutely right.
Counselor: So really you don't necessarily need your performance to change. You just. You just need your thoughts and feelings and behaviors to change.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So how you. How you're reacting to the quizzes maybe?
Client: Yeah, because I get b is, like I said, so, yeah.
Counselor: And b is good.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So. All right, so I want to take you back to the moment when you're looking at the first item. Let's go back to that for a second. Okay. So you're taking a quiz and you're having those thoughts surrounding that first item, which I'm not mistaken, the automatic thought. We talked about this, right? With the cognitive behavioral therapy. The automatic thought is that I'm not going to get this one right or something to that effect. What does that mean to you?
Client: It means once I don't get that right, I'm not going to get anything else right.
Counselor: All right. So what that thought means to you is that you're going to miss that item and then you're going to miss all the rest of the items. So you're going to fail the whole quiz.
Client: The whole thing, yeah.
Counselor: So looking at that, let's call that an intermediate belief, right. It's more of a rule or an expectation. Right. What does that mean to you?
Client: It just gets worse. If I fail the quiz, then I'm like, oh, my God, I'm gonna fail the final, I'm gonna fail the course and that's going to affect my GPA.
Counselor: So it just keeps stacking. So other beliefs. So you're going to fail the course and we're going to fail the final rather than you can fail the course. So if you failed the course, what would that mean to you then?
Client: I'm not going to graduate.
Counselor: You're not going to graduate. So we move from fail in the quiz if we just look at the meaning, right. To fail in the final, to fail in the course, and now to not graduating. So if you didn't graduate, what would that mean to you?
Client: I can't. I can't be a teacher. I can't do what I want to do.
Counselor: So your chosen vocation to be a teacher would be not possible.
Client: Right.
Counselor: Right. So we go a step further and say, what would it mean to you if you couldn't be a teacher?
Client: I don't know who I'd be at that point. That's what I always saw as my career. So I don't know what my future would look like at that point without that.
Counselor: So if you were to phrase it and kind of think back as we to the CBT techniques and I kind of conceptualization we've covered, if you're to phrase that as an I am statement, right. What would you. What would you be if you couldn't be a teacher? What would that make you?
Client: I am a person who didn't make it. I'm a person that failed.
Counselor: Like we said earlier, I'm a person that didn't make it. I'm a person who failed. So in a way you're saying I'm a failure, right? Is that close?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So remember we talked before about core beliefs and how these core beliefs drive these intermediate beliefs which combine with situations like, in your case, taking a quiz to form these automatic thoughts. So one of your core beliefs may be that you're a failure. You may believe that. Does that seem like something that you've said to yourself before or thought before.
Client: About it like that? Until we did the step up to it now. But I can relate to that because a lot of times I do feel like, oh, I'm not going to be able to do this because it's me. I won't be able to do it.
Counselor: Not because it's challenging or difficult, but something to do with you. So that's where kind of you're personalizing.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So you're saying to yourself at a variety of levels, I'm going to be unsuccessful, I'm going to fail. Does that make sense?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you think that's what's happening?
Client: It must be because, like I said, I study, I get good grades. I've been tested years ago. I don't have ADHD. Anything intrinsic that would prohibit me.
Counselor: So you're able to focus and concentrate.
Client: Well, yes, I can do all of that, but when it comes to it, I'm like, I can't do it.
Counselor: So somewhere. Somewhere is this discord belief, and it's possible that it has something to do with you believing that you are a failure. Unsuccessful.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: How do you think your, say, friends or family would interpret that? Like, if. I'm not suggesting, telling them that, but if they were to somehow know that, that you believed you were a failure, how would they react?
Client: I don't think they would see the connection. I think they would be like, well, you do well in school. I don't understand.
Counselor: So they wouldn't believe that you're a failure?
Client: No.
Counselor: You may believe it.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: And similarly, if you had a classmate that was in the same situation and, you know, struggled with these disturbing thoughts and feelings and behaviors during quizzes, how would you evaluate them?
Client: I guess I'd say the same thing that my family would say. Like, you're look at the evidence, you're not a failure.
Counselor: You'd say, look at the evidence and you'd evaluate that they weren't a failure.
Client: Right.
Counselor: But with yourself, you're being a little more harsh.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Which isn't uncommon. So there's a few levels in which I think we can go after this, what I'll call a problem. But really it's a series of thoughts and beliefs. Okay. The first is that the kind at the ground level, and that's when you are taking the quiz and you have that automatic thought that says, I'm going to miss this item.
Client: I'm not going to get it right.
Counselor: I'm not going to get it right. That's your thought. I'm not going to get it right. In these situations, I like to encourage clients to apply what's called an adaptive response or self talk. If you're in a quiz in a quiet classroom, it wouldn't literally be self talking.
Client: Right? Right.
Counselor: But it's a thought that you're consciously applying. So the other thought, that's automatic.
Client: Right.
Counselor: That just pops in your head. Right.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: This one would be one that you deliberately think and make myself. So what could you think to yourself that would be a counter to that automatic thought that you're having, that you're gonna get that item wrong?

Counselor: Okay. So just looking at the probabilities based on your past performance, even though I'm thinking I'm going to get it wrong, chances are I'm going to get it right.
Client: Right. Somehow I still have a b. So.
Counselor: So you are getting most of them right.
Client: Right. So I have a good chance.
Counselor: So I like that adaptive response. Right. Do you think that makes sense for you? Yeah, I think you did well there. So the next time you're taking a quiz, I want you to apply that adaptive response. Now, this takes work, right. So this automatic thought is going to come upon you, and before you know it, you're gonna have that feeling. Right. The physical symptoms you discussed. The sweaty palms. Right. And the feeling of, I think you mentioned.
Client: Intense. Yeah.
Counselor: So don't let it discourage you. Those symptoms come on so quickly.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Right. There is an intervening thought, and you've identified it. So you will have an opportunity most likely to apply that automatic thought at some point. But the first few times, it might be a little rough.
Client: Yeah. Touch and go.

Client: Right. It's more than one.

Client: That was what initiated it. But now it's. I need to prove him wrong.

Counselor: Right. So your co workers have made some criticisms about you and that led to your boss suggesting this.
Client: I would call them criticisms because it's really hard to criticize me. So I would say they take it personally that I'm better than them, you know? So I feel that it's important for me to be able to work for this particular company. It needs to be the best company. And so I need the other employees to at least be at my level. Well, I mean, that's. That's really hard for them to come to my level, but at least be above average. At least.
Counselor: All right, so you have an expectation of them to become at least close to you in terms of your skill.
Client: I mean, it's pretty hard to not make any errors when it comes to accounting with the numbers, with the amount of numbers and the volume of accounts that we have, it's hard to be as good as I am with it, as far as no errors. But yes, I expect a higher standard from the coworkers.
Counselor: And you don't feel like they're performing at that level now?
Client: No, not at all.
Counselor: And evidently you made some different comments to them which maybe they took the wrong way.
Client: I just pointed out the facts of the situation.
Counselor: What type of facts did you, when.
Client: They make mistakes and, you know, how they should be better at certain tasks. I mean, they didn't attend the same, you know, type of college as far as, you know, Ivy League as myself. However, they do have a college education so, you know, that alone would, you know, just kind of go to speak to them having some sort of ability in that area.
Counselor: So you've kind of, in a way you've expressed your disappointment with them.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: To them?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And what are some of the observations or comments they made regarding you?
Client: Oh, they told me my ego is too big, that I'm cocky. That's one. Yeah. I'm just overall, like, I don't know how you can be too confident when your ability is at that level. I mean, I am the best employee they've ever had overall. You know, I was the best student at my college. I received numerous awards from the president of the college alone. I received numerous calls from the college and other companies as well, trying to recruit me to work for them. You know, so I don't think there's, it's impossible to be overly confident, but they, you know, they consider it cocky and arrogant. Get arrogant a lot.
Counselor: The comment arrogant. So you feel they're just really, are they misunderstanding you?
Client: I think they take it as a personal attack.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Like I'm can, like I'm that concerned with them personally. Like it affect, like I'm talking about them as a person instead of just their performance at work because I'm really not concerned with them as far as like existence outside the realm of performance at work.
Counselor: Alright. So your commentary to them has nothing to do with their value as a person, more with their performance as an employee. And you feel they're misconstruing your observations about their performance?
Client: Very much so.
Counselor: They're taking it personally.
Client: Taking it personally and trying as best they can to push it back on me as I'm the one who's wrong, but I'm obviously not.
Counselor: Alright, so you're not wrong in this and you're frustrated by their reactions.
Client: I mean, I'm okay with it, you know, I mean it's, I don't really take anything they say to heart because they're not at the level to really be able to criticize me. You know, I can take criticism, you know, from constructive criticism, from someone who would, you know, be at my level or above, however, they are not. So it's really nothing. It really doesn't affect me. It does interfere with my job as far as my employer is concerned.
Counselor: Right. That's what led to you. That's what led to him recommending you come here initially. So you don't feel that they're at a level where they can really criticize you. It doesn't really bother you if they have criticism in the first place, but you can appreciate how getting along with them would be better for you as an employee.
Client: I mean. I mean, overall, I like this company. You know, I like working for it. I've been friends with my boss. I mean, we went to the same college, you know, so we have that in common. You know, he is an extraordinary person as far as his abilities, you know, I would say as in the level realm as myself. So, you know, I hold his, you know, opinion, you know, in some sort of regards above the others, so.
Counselor: Okay, so to the extent that they communicate negative sentiment to him about you, that that affects you?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And so what do you think, if anything, what do you think needs to be fixed here?
Client: Well, I think it's on their area and, you know, on their side. They didn't take what I said the wrong way.
Counselor: Okay. So if they had accurately interpreted your comments, that would fix the problem?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Do you think that's realistic.
Client: If they worked at it, possibly.
Counselor: How long have you worked there?
Client: It's been about 15 years.
Counselor: 15 years. And how long has this been something that you've been aware of them not feeling so great about your comments to them?
Client: Well, every now and then, this is. We've hit a peak here recently because a lot of the people that I work with feel here recently more. So they've been taken in the wrong way, more prevalent than in the past. In the past, they would, you know, I'd hear, you know, certain comments, but I understood, you know, comments just directed at me, and I just understood that, you know, it was just, you know, envious because I was able to give them. I was at a level where I was able to critique their work. So it never got to a point where I had someone like my boss say anything to me. So this is really the first time that has gotten to that point.
Counselor: So you've noticed things like this in the past, but now it's become more urgent to address it.
Client: It's become more urgent to prove that I'm not wrong in this fact that it is. You know, if this were the case, then, you know, it would have been, you know, it would have been continuous, not just, oh, don't come to a head. So, I mean, that just proves my point even more, that it is their issue and not mine.
Counselor: All right, so if you could somehow prove that they're in the wrong, would that help you?
Client: I mean, it's kind of. To me, it's obvious they are in the wrong because the numbers speak for themselves. It's the fact of the matter. So if. But I guess that if there was something that could change between the relationships that I have with them, then at least would be a little bit better of a flow. So maybe we could get up to the level, you know, that this company is deserving of.
Counselor: Okay, so there's like two. There's two things operating. There's your desire for them to improve and make the company better. And then they're discontent with withdeze your comments to them. So you'd like the company to improve. And you feel that means that you need to be able to voice your opinion to them in an honest way. But everybody needs to get along too. And that's at least to some extent, and that's not happening because they're upset. So do you think there's any steps you could take that could reduce the tension in those relationships?
Client: I need to figure out a way to present the information at a level that they would understand. So drop it down to their level, but also kind of sugarcoat it so they're not, you know, taking it the wrong way.
Counselor: All right, so you need to deliver the same message in a more polite, less threatening package.
Client: I mean, you could say that, yeah.
Counselor: Do you have any ideas how that might look?
Client: I mean, I could start with not comparing their work to mine because that's just unfair. I mean, at no point in time are they ever going to reach that. That level of quality with their work. So that could be a place to start.
Counselor: Okay, so just refraining from drawing that comparison. That could help.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Do you think there could be a benefit in just taking a break from offering any comments to them, any observations, just to let things cool down a bit?
Client: I mean, I could see where you would say, you know, refer that as cool down.
Counselor: Just in an effort to restore the peace. You could still, of course, be aware of different shortcomings in their performance. It might just be helpful to not share that for a while. Just as an idea. Does that seem like an idea that might work. Yeah.
Client: Just keep to myself a little bit more. I mean, that's not very hard around.
Counselor: Them keeping to yourself.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Do you think you would be okay with the. With doing that? Because you wouldn't really be able to offer those. Those helpful comments like, about performance.
Client: If. Well, really, it would, in fact, prove my point behind it all. It would prove that I was right, that it's not me, that it is them taking it the wrong way. You know, because, in fact, if it was, you know, if it wasn't them taking it the wrong way, then I would just say that that would, you know, it would continue. As far as trying to point out, I mean, really, I think it comes down to an issue of being jealous and seeing themselves as less than, so needing to bring. To try to bring me down to make themselves feel better. So if they don't have that to do that, it would prove my point behind this whole thing.
Counselor:
output: Yes. You feel like they're just trying to. They're just trying to tear you down to make up for their own inadequacy.
