instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Leigh. How you doing today?
Client: I'm good.
Counselor: You're doing good?
Client: Yeah. Okay. I guess you guessed. Yeah. Um. Well, I guess I'll tell you, but I, I'm kind of embarrassed to tell you, but, so, like, I'm in college, and all my friends are dating, and I'm just really, like, nervous to just tell you, but, like, I really haven't dated before, and I'm really nervous and scared to date, and I just I just don't know how to do it, and I don't know. I'm just nervous.
Counselor: So, nervousness and some anxiety around dating. You said you'd never really dated before.
Client: No, not really. I mean, I just was never, you know, that was never enforced in my family. I was never allowed to really do that. So just the thought of it is, like, like, scary, scary for you? Yeah. So, you know, I mean, I tend to talk to guys, but it was just like, like, you know, real short and bye, like hi bye kind of thing. Because, like I said, that just was never enforced in my family. And just never, I was never, that's never applaud. That was never applauded in when I was growing up, so I never did it, and I was scared to do it for the repercussions, getting in trouble. So.
Counselor: All right, so no dating in high school. And what type of interactions did you have in high school? You said, you said hi a few times.
Client: Yeah, just like in my science class, you know, particularly this one time, I actually sat next to this boy who was super cute, but, you know, we would say hi, and that was it. He would try to ask me stuff about classwork or the assignment, and I would not even look at him and just tell him and look at my schoolwork. And that was the extent of it, you know?
Counselor: So let's talk about your anxiety. You have anxiety and earlier, like, reaction just to thinking about it. Right. You think about dating. It's just, it's a lot for you. Do you think this anxiety comes from a fear of what might happen, or is this something more how you'll be perceived? Like, what do you think is leading to?
Client: I think it's a little bit of both. I definitely always compare myself to my sisters, and they're super pretty, and I just don't feel attractive enough to have somebody be interested in me. And if they were to be interested in me, I'm not allowed to date, you know, so the repercussion would just be, you know, I'd kind of be shunned for doing so. So it kind of just stayed with me, you know, now I'm 24 and I'm in school, and it's just so overwhelming. And I'm kind of envious of my girlfriends because they're able to do it, and I'm like, damn. Like, how did they do that? So.
Counselor: So that process is far from removed from you. You look at that and think, I don't even know how to approach it.
Client: It's like a foreign object. Like, yeah.
Counselor: So how would you say, how would you describe yourself? Like, how do you feel about yourself?
Client: I always do the right thing. I'm really studious, and I like to have fun. When I'm with my girlfriends, we have a great time, and I'm personable with them and my family, but it's just when it comes to interacting with male, it's just super difficult for me. And I can tell you why, but I can't tell you why. You know, it's kind of that, like, it's like a seesaw every time I'm with a male, you know, in a dating aspect anyway, so it's just difficult for me.
Counselor: Is there a particular outcome that you're afraid of? Like, when you're, well, you're in college now, right? So likely interact with males to some extent. Is there when an opportunity comes up when somebody's interested in you? Is there a particular fear that comes to mind?
Client: Yeah, like, I don't even know why you're talking to me. Like, why would you talk to me? I'm not pretty. I'm flipping awkward. Like, you know, why would you even be interested?
Counselor: So you think yourself as unattractive and awkward?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you question why they would be interested in you?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So have you ever had evidence presented to the contrary, like, people who thought you were attractive and not awkward?
Client: Um, well, yeah, I mean, yeah, like, people have told me that I'm pretty and, um, you know, fun and stuff like that, so, yeah, I have.
Counselor: Yeah. But there's some, so they're telling you that? But there's something else telling you that you're not?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What do you think that's coming from?
Client: I guess just from my, you know, my mom and I think just her rules that I guess I just associated, you know, me not being able to date, that I wasn't presentable enough to date. And I just got this idea that that's the reason why she just didn't want me to date.
Counselor: So you think her reasoning for not allowing you to date, I wasn't the pretty daughter? Were your sisters allowed to date?
Client: They were allowed to date, but under certain circumstances, certain rules they had to follow. But just when I would, you know, even suggest it to my mom, it was just like, no, you're not.
Counselor: So you feel like you were, of you and your sisters, you were the one treated the most strictly on that. But was it much more strictly or just a little differently?
Client: I think it was much more strictly, yeah. Because it's so much so now that I can't even talk to a guy. It's just. I mean, the anxiety and the fear is so intense. I just can't explain it. It's horrible that it's not like that for my sisters because now they're married, you know, so they have kids, and it's like, what the heck happened here? And I can recognize it, but I just can't bring myself to do it, like talk to somebody or, you know.
Counselor: So the way you perceive yourself, the self image here is part of this?
Client: Yeah. Yeah, absolutely.
Counselor: So you have evidence that says that men would be interested in going out with you, dating you, but internally, these thoughts you're having say you're just not worthy.
Client: You know what I mean?
Counselor: That's kind of the theme of it, right?
Client: Yeah, absolutely. That's it.
Counselor: And maybe this is tied to a core belief. Like we talked about core beliefs before cognitive therapy. Are there any of those core beliefs in the list I gave you a few weeks ago kind of stood out that you think might be core beliefs you have?
Client: That I'm unlovable.
Counselor: Unlovable, yeah. Any others?
Client: Fear of rejection.
Counselor: So fear of being rejected?
Client: Fear of being rejected. Yeah.
Counselor: So unlovable. And a fear of being rejected. And then when you have interactions in the moment, like, say you're in class and there's a man sitting next to you in class, and they're interested in you, he's interested in you. He says something that expresses that he's interested. You're immediately suspect.
Client: Oh, yeah.
Counselor: That's what you're.
Client: Oh, yeah. That's like. It's like, what is it? Fight or flight kind of feeling like it really is. It's like, oh, you know. Yeah. Just something comes over me where, you know, it's kind of like I'm conditioned because I don't even live with my mom and my dad now, and I'm on my own, but yet I still hold their values. And not just. All I can just think of is being in high school and having. Being told I can't do that or just the rules and having to follow it. And that's really where I feel like I'm there. If someone says something to me, it.
Counselor: Takes you right back there.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right. I. So how do your parents feel about now? Have they said anything like, your sisters are married and you're not? Have they pointed that out?
Client: No, they haven't. Not really. No. Because my mom really wants me. She. I guess. Well, maybe it has to do with that. Like, I'm smarter than my sisters, so she really wants me to be a doctor. And my sisters, they have, you know, they have great jobs, but, you know, they just stopped at a bachelor's degree, and I'm really working to be a doctor. And I always had straight a's in high school and my sisters didn't. So I think that my mom wants to hold on to that, you know, that hope that I'm going to be something great. So she doesn't really enforce the dating thing with me. I guess she's for fear that that's going to get in the way.
Counselor: That's different than being unlovable, right? Yeah. I mean, her reasoning, as you're describing her reasoning sounds more like she wants you to reach a higher educational goal.
Client: I mean, I guess. Yeah.
Counselor: What do you want?
Client: I want to be in a relationship with somebody because all of my friends are, and I'm always that. They're real and it's difficult. I mean, yeah, I want the education. Don't get me wrong, I want a great job, but I don't want to do that alone. I want to have somebody with me that I can confide in and just a confidante. And the time is now. I'm ready, you know? And maybe my mom was just protecting me, I guess. I don't know what she was doing, but I really don't care because I really want to try it. I just don't know how.
Counselor: There's opposing forces at work here, right? I mean, you're motivated to try it like it's a goal. You want to be able to date, you want to go out. It's important to you. Do you want to get married like your sisters?
Client: Yeah, I do.
Counselor: You do? So you have these clear goals, and that's one force. And then the supposing force is this. Well, one of them would be this anxiety that comes over you in the moment when a man's talking to you. Like in that way. Right. Like about going out or any topic like that. So a part of you. A part of you is saying, I really want to move forward and date different people and see if I can find a good match. And another part of you is saying I need to run away. Like you said, fight or flight, right? I want to run away and not have this awkwardness, this anxiety.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. Because it's a. I just keep thinking of the repercussions, like now as an adult, that my mom's just. I guess that she wouldn't talk to me. But I'm not in high school anymore, so I don't know. I just. I honestly don't know what the conversation would be like if I talked to a guy that I was interested in or if a guy was interested in me. I mean, because I came to the realization, and my friends have helped me with this, that I am in college, I am an adult now. And, you know, what my mom thinks is what she thinks now. It's just me peeing in front of a male that I'm attracted to, that I want to go out with.
Counselor: And what you said is you don't know what would happen, so you don't know that it would be bad. You don't know that it would be a bad experience.
Client: Right? I don't know. I don't know if it's going to be bad, but you don't know if.
Counselor: It'S going to be good either.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So there's a risk.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So in the situation you're in, if you can get through that anxiety and have a conversation, it could end up where things went very well or didn't. So what happens if it doesn't go well?
Client: Well, I mean, like I said, I think because my mom didn't let me date that it was sign that I was unattractive, so I could take it that way, that I was just unattractive, but that he wouldn't have initiated the date if I was unattractive.
Counselor: Good point.
Client: So for that, I was. It just didn't work. You know, there just wasn't anything in common with what I'm about. You know, that I have different hobbies and he has different hobbies, and maybe they just don't mesh well and I have to. That could be a reason why it didn't work. Not that I'm. I guess, nothing. I'm lovable. You know, I shouldn't take it that personal, but it's hard.
Counselor: It's difficult for you. This is painful for you.
Client: Yeah, it is.
Counselor: You're fighting through some strong feelings. If you try to look at the logical, right. If it's likely you just because of the way it works, you'd have to date several people to find somebody that was a match.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So some of those relationships you'll end, maybe some of the man will end, but eventually, one likely you would stumble on, or neither one of you would end it. So there's risk involved here. There's a risk of rejection. There's a risk of having to reject. That doesn't seem to be the risk you're most worried about, though. You're more worried about the risk of being rejected.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. Because you're questioning their intent.
Client: Yeah, yeah, yeah.
Counselor: So can you survive being rejected?
Client: I think. I think I can, you know. Yeah. I mean, because in essence, I was, you know, rejected by my mom, but I still moved forward with my life because since she didn't let me date, that's a rejection from her that I'm not worthy. So, yes, I think because my friends have helped me, so that's a step in the right direction.
Counselor: And you took that behavior from your mother as rejection. And it seems like that may not have been her reason for doing that. You don't know for sure.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But even if it was, which it seems unlikely it would have been, that's still just one person.
Client: Yeah, yeah. That is just one person.
Counselor: So if we just take it to the extreme and say for some reason.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: You know, she didn't think you were worthy. That's just one person opinion.
Client: Yeah, absolutely. Right. Because my friends think I'm worthy. Right.
Counselor: And their opinions are valid too.
Client: Right? They are.
Counselor: So if you really look at it and weigh the evidence and look at it logically, the imbalance of the evidence would say that you are worthy.
Client: Right.
Counselor: You're not unlovable. But still, in any type of relational situation, there's going to be rejection. So there's potential pain up ahead, but the reward could be you find somebody that you want to be with. And that's really your goal.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: So really part of this is pushing through a good deal of uncomfortableness, discomfort, right?
Client: Yeah, yeah, absolutely. A lot of that. A lot of it, yeah, yeah. And I think that I'm willing. I'm willing to do it because I want it so bad that, you know, I have to. You don't know until you try it, and I have to try it. I have to.
Counselor: So what, kind of a behavioral experiment. Right. So let's. Let's take it one step at a time. Let's say that back to the situation I alluded to earlier. You're in class and there's somebody that's interested in you, sitting next to you or whoever they are, and they come and initiate a conversation. What's your reaction now? What do you do now?
Client: Well, I would introduce myself because I never. I have never done that before to a guy where I introduce myself. I wouldn't even make eye contact. So I think to just look up with them and just say, you know, hi, my name is, you know, Leia, and just see what that feels like because I don't know what to do.
Counselor: You've never reached that step?
Client: No. No, I haven't, because I wouldn't even, you know, I wouldn't even look them in the eye.
Counselor:
output: Your current reaction is not look them in the eye. Not engaging in discussion.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:

Client: Feeling terrible. I had a wrestling match last night, and I lost my match again. I should just quit the team. I'm such a bad wrestler.

Client: I lost my match last week, too. I should just quit the team.

Client: Well, yes. I am clearly a bad wrestler.

Counselor: Yes, losing is unpleasant. And those two matches weren't your best. Does that mean that you're a bad wrestler?
Client: Well, I don't know. Maybe not.
Counselor: How were you doing before you lost those two matches?
Client: We've only had four matches so far, but I won my first two matches.
Counselor: Okay, so you started off the season by winning two matches in a row, which means you do know how to wrestle. You just happened to lose two matches in a row, but that's all it was?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What else are you telling yourself about wrestling?
Client: Well, I just felt terrible after I lost those two matches, and I was thinking that if I lo. That if I lose my next match, I'm never going to be able to get a scholarship to college.
Counselor: Hold on a second, Carlos. Let me stop you right there. What if you do lose your next match? What is the worst thing that could happen? Would it be the end of the world?
Client: Um, no, I guess not. The season just started.
Counselor: How much longer do you have in the season?
Client: A few more months.
Counselor: A few more months? Which means you still have plenty of matches left. So, although losing your next match would be frustrating, you would be okay. The world would not end.
Client: Yeah, I guess you're right.
Counselor: Do you enjoy wrestling?
Client: Yes. Actually, I love wrestling. I've been wrestling since my freshman year.
Counselor: You've been wrestling for three years, and it is a sport you love participating in. Does it make sense that you said you were going to quit just a few matches into the season?
Client: No, it really doesn't.
Counselor:
output: Are you starting to understand what you told yourself about the consequences of losing a few wrestling matches?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, mister Urban. It's nice to see you again. From our previous session, I know you spoke about the relationship you and your wife were going through. In the bad terms, she got left off. So I want to ask you, what would make you cheat on your wife?
Client: You know, I've been asked that question every day for the past two, three weeks. And the only thing I can respond with is what would make a wife cheat on her husband? I mean, it's petty. I know it's petty. But I loved her. And finding out that more than once she was with somebody else, that took something from me that I couldn't get back. And for months I was dealing with. What could I have done? What was it? What did I do? Because it has to have been me. She's too nice a person for that, right? She's too smart a person for that, right? And then weeks of me finally understanding that it wasn't me. A decision that you make is a decision that you make. So when Susie, my administrative assistant, came into the picture, I had a decision that I had to make. I have to take it off and spend time with Susie. Or keep it on and spend many a night alone. So why? You figure it out.
Counselor: So do you think that you did it for revenge? Were you trying to get back at your wife?
Client: I guess. I mean, what else could it be? Yeah, maybe I am that petty. But it's just. It's not love anymore.
Counselor: So why are you still in a marriage, mister Urban? If it's not love, if it's not for love, why do you feel that you must stay in America?
Client: Because that's the type of household I was brought up in.
Counselor: Explain that to me.
Client: My dad always told me that you take care of your business and your girl is your business. You never leave her. You take care of her no matter what. That's what you do. So when I got older, I asked him, what do you mean you never leave her? He said, divorce is not an option. That's pretty much how it is in my household.
Counselor: So are you saying because of how you were raised up is why you're still in the marriage?
Client: It's the only thing that makes sense.
Counselor: Are you happy?
Client: Do I seem happy?
Counselor: Have you spoken to your wife about this?
Client: No. So everything that I feel, everything that I am is stuck on the inside. This is actually the first time I've actually talked about any of her.
Counselor: Okay, mister Ermen, so let's try this exercise. I'm gonna pull out chairs, so pretend that that this is your wife here. Why are we here and express your feelings.
Client: Why do I have to do this?
Counselor: Because you never spoke about it. Right? So express your feelings. Let it out, and see how you would tell her what you're feeling inside. Do you feel uncomfortable?
Client: I felt uncomfortable since the moment I found out that you just didn't love me anymore. I felt uncomfortable every single night I've been in the guest room because I just couldn't take being with you. I felt uncomfortable since the very moment I felt like it was okay because of what you did to me. To take off my wedding band, to forget my vows, to forget you, to try and be something that I'm not. Every night that I was with Susie, I imagined that I was with you, but not who you are now. I imagine that I was with the woman that I first met, woman that I first loved. But you're not the same person anymore. I haven't been the same person over a year. Every day that I wake up and I see your face, I have to imagine that you are that same person because that's the. The only thing that keeps me around. That and the fact that I just don't think I can make. And it's not because I love you so much anymore, because it's not you that I love. It's not because of anything religious. It's because I don't want to deal with my family.
Counselor: I know that was hard to do. Mister Urban, are you doing all right? Are you feeling okay?
Client: I'm fine.
Counselor: Okay. So I want you to realize, like, can you not see that your belief is causing this pain inside your depression and your unhappiness?
Client: It makes sense, if that's what you're saying. The question is, how am I supposed to deal with, like, right now? I know I've got the option of staying with her and dealing with this every day for as long as I stay with her and deal with this or just leaving, and then I have to deal with everything else around me. How am I supposed to get past that? That's my question. And I don't know. I don't even know if that's really the right way to go.
Counselor: What is everything else?
Client: My family, the judgments. What? I'm gonna have to deal with my brother, who, by the way, is married, and he's not dealing with infidelity, but he's dealing with the same depression I am. The love isn't there anymore. We don't get divorced. Not in my household.
Counselor: So would you rather satisfy what, your family standard? Rather to be happy? Is that what you're saying?
Client: Sounds like it.
Counselor: Have you spoken to your family about this?
Client: No.
Counselor: And what do you think they would say if they were to find out.
Client: That I was thinking this way? My dad would probably disown you.
Counselor: To go that far and disown you.
Client: Especially when I seen that he dealt with the same thing. My family doesn't do well with marriages because I haven't met a single person in my lineage that has a happy marriage.
Counselor: Do you see your family often, Mister Urban?
Client: Not really.
Counselor:
output: Do you want to be happy, mister Urban?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.

Counselor: Ten minutes, yeah.
Client: So I did better. I think I ended up only doing, like, a joint a half instead of two. I was able to put it off for, I think, the ten minutes a couple times. And then I. There was, I think, one or two days where I went out for a walk because I was tired of staring at the clock, waiting for the ten minutes to pass. So I got up, went for a walk, and then I passed one of my friends, so I ended up walking with her. And I actually didn't get back to my house for, like, an hour, so I kind of put it off for, like, an hour because then I came home and took a couple hits.
Counselor: All right, so it sounds like. It sounds like you were able to maintain waiting ten minutes to smoke marijuana, at least in most cases. It was rough.
Client: It was rough, yeah.
Counselor: So it was difficult for you, but in most cases, you're able to hold off the ten minutes, and it sounds like there was a few instances where you're able to hold it off longer because something else kind of.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Came up.
Client: Yeah, I found I actually, like, talked to a couple people on the phone. Before I knew it, like, a half hour had gone by.
Counselor: So another activity presented itself. And you forgot about the marijuana?
Client: Kind of, yeah. Yeah, I guess I just wasn't thinking about it.
Counselor: So has your. Have your feelings about marijuana changed since we last talked?
Client: No, not really.
Counselor: Tell me about that.
Client: I mean, it's. I don't see it as a problem. It's legal in a lot of states now, and, I mean, it's not that bad for you. It doesn't really endanger me much.

Counselor: I know last time you were here, you were discussing some relational issues. You want to continue with that?
Client: Yeah, yeah. I mean, you know, it kind of came up again. You know, every time my wife yells at me, you know, I feel like a failure, you know, like I told you last time, I just. I just feel like I can't do anything right, you know? Like everything I try to do is met with arguing and yelling, and I just feel like there's nothing I can do right.
Counselor: So no matter what you do, it's not going to end up the way you want?
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: So it's frustrating.
Client: Yeah, it definitely is.
Counselor: How is what's going on impacted your relationship with your wife?
Client: I mean, it's rocky, you know, because I feel like I can't do anything right. She doesn't understand that. And then, you know, we don't get along ever because we're just always yelling and I'm always feeling bad, and then it just keeps going like that.
Counselor: So when you. You mentioned you feel like a failure when she. When she yells at you?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Can you think back to maybe the last time, one of the last times you guys argued and try to remember that thought? We've talked about automatic thoughts before. Remember that thought that comes in that moment when she starts. She starts yelling at you?
Client: I mean, she'll yell at me. I mean, I feel, you know, frustrated. Like, why are you yelling at me right now? And. I don't know. I mean, as I was thinking about, like we were talking about it, and as I was thinking about it more this week, kind of felt like, you know, kind of like what happened with my dad, you know? I guess I kind of felt that same way when I was younger. You know, like, if my dad would yell at me or when he would yell at me, I kind of feel that same way. And it feels like the same thing. Yeah. It's kind of the first. I guess kind of the first thought that comes to mind.
Counselor: The first thought is I've been through something like this before, I guess.
Client: Yeah. I mean, I'm not really thinking those exact words, but that's definitely what it feels like, you know? Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. Like, it's like just a sense that this isn't brand new.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And the feeling you're connecting with it is the same feeling you had when your dad. Yahweh. Yeah.
Client: Yeah, pretty much, yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. So, in a sense, these arguments are taking you back to another point in time.
Client: I guess so, in a way, that's distressing.
Counselor: Yeah, it is.
Client: I mean, it feels, you know, pretty crappy.
Counselor: Now, in these arguments, she yells at you. You mentioned before that you do some yelling of your own, you know, in the midst of all that. Right. How would you rate it in terms of, like, any physical violence? Nothing like that.
Client: No, it's just words. I mean, we're just, you know, just yelling.
Counselor: And what level, like, what level of yelling would you say? How severe compared to what you've experienced in the past?
Client: Yeah, I don't know. I mean, it's like, you know, sometimes it can get up to, like, the eight or nines, you know, but just, I guess generally it's, you know, down. Closer to a seven on scale, like one to ten. Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: So sometimes it's seven. That would be pretty bad.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor:
output: But some other times it's not.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Terry. How you doing today?
Client: I'm okay, I think.
Counselor: You okay?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I know when we talked last time, you were having a rough time dealing with the passing year, Sister Sheila.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And you're kind of a point where we were talking about emotional consequences, but also some of the thinking that's going on. Have you been processing that?
Client: Yeah, I've been thinking about some of that and, you know, trying to kind of work through it a little bit. So I think I'm kind of ready to kind of work through it and talk about it a little bit now.
Counselor: So, feeling a little less emotional and feeling a little more thinking about it. And, like, on the rational side, like we talked about rational and irrational beliefs.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: A little more focus there or more ability to focus there today.
Client: Yeah, I think I'm ready to think about it more.
Counselor: I know the emotional part was tough for you, and I'm sure it still.
Client: Is, but I think I've kind of got through some of that, and I'm ready to kind of get through the way I'm thinking about some things.
Counselor: Ready to look at through the thinking lens.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So to speak. All right. So what are some of the thoughts or beliefs that you've been having, you think maybe part of what's affecting your mood?
Client: Well, I've been. I've been thinking about it, and, you know, I just. I just feel like I don't. I don't have anybody that I can talk to. I mean, I just. I keep thinking about it. I don't have anybody to talk to. She was the only one I had to talk to.
Counselor: So in your relationship with her, you guys talked a lot. She was an important person in your life for a variety of reasons, but including that she was easy to talk to.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And that you could talk to her?
Client: I. Yes.
Counselor: So the thought is you have nobody to talk to.
Client: I just, you know, she was just everything to me. I talked to her about everything, and, you know, she was just always gave me good advice, and she could always work, you know, talk me through anything that I needed to talk about, and I just don't feel like I have that anymore. Since she's going, I don't have anybody like that anymore.
Counselor: That relationship is valuable to you, and you've lost that, and you feel like you've lost having anybody that you could talk to. Is that. Is that close?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: All right, so let's look at that thought. Let's break that down. Certainly you were able to talk to her, as you mentioned, and you have lost her.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Right. So you have lost someone that you could talk to that was very valuable to you, and that's understandably painful. The question would be, have you lost everybody that you could talk to? Is there anyone else in your life, for instance, currently, that you regularly speak with?
Client: Well, you know, since you said that, you know, maybe I do have some people that I can go to. They're not her. But, you know, you know, I have a couple of people that I can talk to that they're willing to talk to me about certain things. I guess if I give them the chance, you know, I'll be able to talk to them.
Counselor: So there are some people in your life that you can talk to. They certainly don't replace your sister, but you have people you can't communicate with, and that can be helpful for you.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So as we build kind of a rationale, self talk to replace the irrational thinking that you brought in.
Client: Right.
Counselor: Which was that you have no one to talk to. Could the replacement be something like, I had my sister to talk to, and she was really good at that, and it's painful to have lost her, but I gained something from that experience, and I do still have some people to talk to now.
Client: Yeah, that sounds about right.
Counselor:
output: Yeah.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hey, Carly. How are you doing today?
Client: I'm good. How are you?
Counselor: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. What's been going on this last week?
Client: I've just been feeling kind of in a rut. I mean, I've been looking for a job and haven't really gotten anywhere. And then I had a drink the other night, and I just felt like me not having a job and me going out and having that drink, it wasn't deserved. And I just felt like such a loser because that was the time that I should have been at work if I had a job, and instead I was at the bar drinking. So I had one drink, and then it led to another. Cause then I just felt worse and I figured I had one, so.
Counselor: All right, so how much did you drink in total?
Client: I think I lost track after four or five.
Counselor: How long had it been since you had a drink before that?
Client: I did really well. It was, I think, like three weeks.
Counselor: Three weeks?
Client: Three weeks or so.
Counselor: Oh, so you did really well and then you had one drink and that just made you feel like you weren't successful?
Client: I felt like a loser.
Counselor: Felt like a loser. And you feel that kind of led to drinking some more? So you had a rough time with things?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. How about now?
Client: I mean, now I just kind of. I don't know, I'm afraid to go back. Like, I'm afraid to go out with, like, some friends. They invite me out to dinner, but I know there's alcohol and.
Counselor: Is that where you were when you had that first drink? Was that with friends?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right, so there's a few things going on. We've talked in the past, right, about separating the behavior from the person. Right. So behavior is what we do, not who we are. You remember those discussions? And correct me if I'm wrong, but it sounds like I'm going to use some different words than you used. But it sounds like when you had that first drink, you're kind of ashamed that you had a drink and you had it during the time when you would have been working.
Client: Yeah, that's pretty accurate.
Counselor: That's pretty accurate. So, taking yourself back to that moment, right. We had that first. That first drink, like, you finished that first drink. What was your thought at that moment?
Client: Just, like, shameful. Like, I did really, really well, and then here I was, and I had just finished a drink, and I knew I wanted another one.
Counselor: Okay, so shameful is kind of like the feeling, but the thought is I did really, really well. Right. So that's what you're thinking was, I did really, really well. And what was that the end of the thought? Or was that. Was there more before you had that next drink?
Client: I guess just I was doing well, and then I had a drink, and I just felt like an awful person. So figured what was the. The hurt and having more.
Counselor: So the sequence would have been you had the drink, you felt shameful. At the same time, you're thinking that you were doing really well, and then just really, as you said before, you just felt like a loser. And then you decided, might as well just have the second drink. So another thought might be that, like, I might as well, just might as well just have a second drink.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. So you can see how there's some thoughts and some feelings at work. Right. As you finished that first drink, was it fairly quick? Were those thoughts and feelings fairly occur fairly quickly after the drink?
Client: Yeah, I would say as I was finishing and then finished.
Counselor: Right away, you regretted it. And in that regret, as you thought about it, thought, might as well just continue drinking now because you kind of blew it.
Client: Yeah, I already messed up. I might as well keep going.
Counselor: Okay. And that's a common cycle to fall into. And you had three weeks where you hadn't had a drink prior to that. So let's look at this. Let's try to separate the behavior from the self a little bit. If you had a friend who was in the same predicament, who had a history of using alcohol and then had three weeks without any alcohol use, and then their behavior was to have a drink, what would you think of them?
Client: I would think that they had a rough day or something must have happened where? I mean, it's just one drink.
Counselor: Okay. They had a rough day. One drink. And what would you think of their behavior? How would you categorize that behavior?
Client: I guess just they made a mistake.
Counselor:
output: So not ideal, depending on their point of view. Maybe a little irresponsible.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Alisa, how you doing today?
Client: Good. How are you?
Counselor: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. How has the anxiety been going since last session?
Client: It seems to be in check. Nothing really major has been going on with it. So I think I'm getting to a point where it's under control.
Counselor: It subsided a bit. That's good. That's good. How's things been going at work lately?
Client: So work's a little bit of a different story. We have our daily meetings, and. I. Actually had to pull, like, one of my coworkers aside because I feel like they undermine me all the time, and they, like, they don't give me the respect, basically, that I deserve. So I took her outside after the meeting and leaned into her about it. And afterwards, I mean, the next day, because we have these meetings every day, she, like, she came back and came at me again, but it was worse even after talking to her.
Counselor: So talking to her, that didn't improve your situation?
Client: No.
Counselor: So you have these. Someone understands. You have these daily meetings, and you mentioned that she's not showing you respect and that you deserve respect, something to that effect. So tell me about that belief. Remember we talked about ABC before, activating events and beliefs and consequences in rabt. Tell me about that belief.
Client: Well, I just feel that I do a good job and I deserve to be respected by my coworkers. Yeah, it just.
Counselor: Are there levels of respect? Is there a certain level of respect that you demand or need?
Client: I don't know if there's a certain level, but I feel just like I deserve it. Mm hmm.
Counselor: You know, and what did she do that kind of convinced you that she wasn't meeting that level of respect?
Client: Well, she was, like, shooting down my ideas and just kind of made me feel like a fool, basically. So I just. I didn't understand.
Counselor:
output: All right, so she had criticisms of your ideas, right? A few of them, it sounds like. So that would upset anybody. But were those criticisms unusual, given the tone of these meetings? Like, is this a type of meeting where people criticize each other or attempt to in a constructive way?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Gabriella. I understand that you're here today because you've been experiencing some low mood.
Client: Yeah, I just. Recently, I'm just feeling down a lot and I can't really, like, snap out of it. Like, sometimes if it's happened before, I can just, like, get myself back on track, but recently I just find it really difficult to do.
Counselor: Hey, so it sounds like you've been experiencing some low mood and you're kind of struggling to get going a bit.
Client: Yeah, yeah, definitely.
Counselor: You've had low mood in the past, but it's kind of. You've been able to pull yourself out of it before, but more recently you found that harder. Okay, so I understand that you first went to your GP. He referred you here about two months ago. Can I ask what led you to go to the GP in the first place?
Client: My long term boyfriend broke up with me and it was such a shock. Like, I really wasn't expecting it and it just got me really down and I just felt really lonely and I didn't really want to see people and just wanted to be in my own space. And my mum told me I should probably go to the doctors. Oh. And he's referred me to you.
Counselor: Okay. So it sounds then like you had that breakup and you weren't expecting it, so it kind of came out of the blue a bit and that you've been on your own quite a lot, so you've not been seeing people as much. And it sounds like your mum noticed that there's been a bit of a change in you. Okay. And how have things been then, since then, since that happened and since you went to the GP?
Client: I just. Nothing's really changed. Nothing's really improved. I just feel down, like everything's an effort and just feel distant from things. And like I said, I can't snap out of it.
Counselor: Okay. And how did you feel about coming here today?
Client: I was kind of disappointed in myself because I feel like nobody else my age is doing this. Like, I should have been able to snap out of it. Like, it's just another thing that I've not really. It's another thing that's making me stand out for the wrong reasons.
Counselor: Okay. So you feel like it's kind of odd or unusual to be coming to see a clinical psychologist? I suppose I just want to reassure you that it's absolutely normal to have feelings of depression and anxiety. It's really very common and it certainly isn't odd or strange at all. So it sounds like it was actually quite hard for you to come here today?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor:
output: So what, I guess led you to do that? Because it sounds like maybe there was a lot pushing you against coming here today, but you've managed to come anyway.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hazel, how you doing today?
Client: I'm okay.
Counselor: What's been going on?
Client: Well, last time I started to tell you a little bit about one of my friends, my best friend, actually, she had this issue. So what happened was she went to a bathroom at our local library, and she found a video camera when she was going to the bathroom.
Counselor: In the bathroom?
Client: Yeah. She actually. Yeah. And she turned it into the police, and I guess because, like, she carried it, or she had found it, her handprints were on it, and they weren't be able. They weren't able to detect who actually did it. They weren't able to catch the person.
Counselor: Oh, they didn't catch the person?
Client: No. So since then, I've been on really just high alert. Like, I'm worried that that could happen to me, to my kids, and I'm just really worried because they didn't catch the guy, that him or someone like him could be out there.
Counselor: So he's still out in the community.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So how is it affecting your. Your daily life? Can you tell me kind of what your. What you've been feeling?
Client: Um, a lot of anxiety just not knowing, maybe, you know, what if someone were to videotape me like that? I've been very aware, shall I say, of cameras.
Counselor: Okay. So anxious and aware.
Client: Right. Like, I know you have one in your office, and people on their cell phone cameras. Just all the possibilities that I could be recorded. I've just been very aware of them, which makes me not want to go anywhere. So I've been having arguments with my husband a lot because he wants to go out to restaurants, and I don't want to go because there could be cameras in the bathrooms and how I dress. Also, as you can see, I'm kind of dressed more conservatively because I remember hearing once about cameras that people use on shoes that could be used in a creepy way. And so I can't. You know, it's now almost summertime. I can't dress in skirts or be comfortable because I'm dressing like that.
Counselor: So you covered a lot of ground there. So you have the. You have the feeling of being, like, worried, nervous. Right. That's going to happen to you, but you've also had to kind of change your routine, or you feel you have to change your routine to feel safer.
Client: Right.
Counselor: Has that helped. Has changing the way you dressed or changing where you go and when you go, has that helped reduce the anxiety?
Client: Not really, no. I would say it's really starting. That's why I wanted to come in. It's really starting to affect my life.
Counselor: You mentioned specifically your husband. Like, what's been going on there?
Client: He just wants to go places with our kids, like, go out to eat. And I don't really want to go anywhere because, you know, cameras are everywhere nowadays, and I just kind of worry, like, public bathrooms, could they be there? Could someone be, you know, sometimes baby monitors are, you know, hooked up on so people can hack into that laptop, cameras. So even in my own house, I've just been really nervous, so I feel like I'm not really getting relief from that anxiety.
Counselor: Have you taken any precautions because of this persistent worry? I mean, I already mentioned, like, with the camera specifically.
Client: I mean, I've, you know, when I go into bathrooms, I've been looking for cameras to make sure they weren't there before. You know, me or my children have used the bathroom. I have tried. I read online that you can turn how to turn off the cameras on your phone and that you can close your laptop, and that way the camera will face down. And the same thing on a smart tv so it doesn't recognize your face. I've tried to turn things off. They don't need to be on as far as people being able to access my own information.
Counselor: And that seems reasonable. So you take reasonable precautions to try to avoid being video recorded against your will.
Client: Exactly.
Counselor: Okay. But still, you have this feeling of worry, anxiety, and your schedules being interfered with.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So you'd like to cope more effectively with your feelings, reduce this anxiety. So when you enter into a public bathroom. Now, we talked about automatic thoughts before.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Those thoughts just kind of pop into our head and they connect to feelings of that can be unpleasant, like anxiety and worry. So when you walk into a public restroom, what's the first thing that goes through your mind?
Client: That there might be a video camera that I don't see. That's maybe with my friend, it was big enough, but I might not catch it. And that someone's going to use that in a vulnerable way.
Counselor: Okay, so when you walk in, you're wondering if there's a camera there.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And when that automatic thought occurs, what follows that in terms of a feeling or behavior?
Client: Usually I'll try and find the camera, but it's usually anxiety, fear. My heart rate starts going up. I start getting really anxious. And then, you know, I try and either rush to use the bathroom if I really have to go, or a lot of times if I don't, I'll just leave. Sometimes I try and use the bathroom so I don't have to go out.
Counselor: So your behavior is looking for the camera or sometimes just leaving without using restroom, and you're feeling that anxiety worry that we've been talking about. Okay, so, really, if we think about. We talked before about core beliefs, intermediate beliefs, and I'm wondering if the intermediate belief isn't I'm vulnerable, or this more specifically, maybe that's more of a core belief. More specifically, I'm vulnerable in this area, like, with this guy on the loose that committed that crime, and then that's combining with situations that you encounter, and that's where you're getting those automatic thoughts. Does that sort of make sense?
Client: Exactly.
Counselor: Okay, so you remember what, in terms of cognitive therapy, we like to apply what we call the adaptive response, or self talk.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So it's that thought that you interject at that moment, you realize you're having an automatic thought that's gonna lead to, in this case, anxiety and worry and behaviors that, while looking for the camera, isn't maybe an unusual behavior, but leaving, you know, that could certainly be an unuseful behavior. So, in terms of that self talk, let's work to develop a self talk response, something you can tell yourself to that initial. I wonder if there's a camera in this bathroom. What do you think you could tell yourself that would get in between that thought and I, the feelings you're having?
Client: I could say if when I walk in the bathroom, maybe I could say, you know, while there could be a chance that there's a camera in this bathroom, the chance of it happening is not very likely. And, you know, I'm going to take steps to keep myself safe so that I won't be in a vulnerable position, such as looking for the cameras.
Counselor: Right. That's good. So you have a low probability of it happening, and you're taking useful behaviors to minimize your risk even further.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So that's a good automatic thought, I think, or good adaptive response for the automatic thought. Rather, why don't you try that one out the next time you have that automatic thought? Try out that. I think that's really logical. It's unlikely to happen. Of course there's a chance, and we acknowledge that in the self talk, there's a chance that it could happen, but there's precautions you can take, and it's a low chance sometimes as well. So keep that automatic thought. We'll review it at the end before you leave today. We'll write these down. But that's one adaptive response, rather, that I want to write down for you. I also want to talk about the worst case scenario because right now you have the anxiety and the worry about an event that while it's unlikely it could happen, it could happen. And I'm wondering how you think you would react if the worst did happen. If you used the restroom and you found out from law enforcement or by finding a camera that an offender had been watching you on a recording. I think you would react to that.
Client: I mean, I think I would be really upset. Upset. I think I would feel vulnerable probably for a while and be hesitant.
Counselor: But.
Client: I mean, I think ultimately I would be okay. My friend, this happened a while ago. She's starting to get to get over it and get back to her usual routine, although she's still hesitant. So I think I would be okay eventually, although I'd be really upset that.
Counselor: It happened and it would make sense to feel upset. That would be upsetting for anybody. But as you noted, that would probably be relatively temporary, that distress, right. Well, acute. And certainly you wouldn't be happy about it and shouldn't be happy about it. It would probably go away. You'd probably learn to adapt. How long have you been in this state of anxiety and worry?
Client: Probably it happened, like, two months ago.
Counselor: Two months. And how many days in the average week are you affected by these feelings?
Client: Usually every day.
Counselor: Every day. So if we can compare it, right, we have the chances of being recorded. Right. Illegally. That's a low probability event. It can happen. Probably not likely. The anxiety and the worry that you're having, that's a high probability event because you're suffering from it every day.
Client: Yeah, that's true. I never thought about it that way.
Counselor: So there's a point at which maybe you reach and you say, I'd rather take. I'd rather take the risk. I'd rather deal with the potential consequence of an unlikely event of being recorded and face that if it happens, than be in the state of anxiety and worry.
Client: Right. Because right now I'm suffering every day.
Counselor: Right now you're suffering, right. If you could adaptively respond effectively, you're still going to have that risk of being recorded, but, you know, you could survive that event if it happened, right?
Client: Yeah, I think I could have.
Counselor: And you're taking reasonable cautions and, you know, all the things we talked about. So as you think about this in a more general sense, is there an adaptive response you could apply to that, to that automatic thought of, I need to be worried about this, or whatever that thought looks like. Sometimes the thought's an image, right? Maybe an image of being recorded, but whatever that kind of general series of automatic thoughts are that are getting you anxious and worried before you even get out of the house. What adaptive response could you apply there?
Client: Maybe, like I said, I'm worried about all the cameras. Maybe I could say, I understand there's some cameras that, you know, used for good purposes, like security.
Counselor:
output: Probably most are right.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Okay, Marsha, so how can I help you today?
Client: Well, I'm working full time. I'm a part time student. I've just gotten engaged, and I live at home. There's just so much stress in my life. I have everything happening all at once. Just to top it all off, I failed an exam, a really big exam, and I just feel like I can't do anything anymore. I can't do anything right. I've just got so much stress, and I feel like such a disappointment, such a failure. And I've embarrassed my family by failing. I just don't know what to do anymore. I guess I've come here today to tell you, like, I want to leave uni, and I guess that's why I've come here to you today.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like a whole lot of stuff's on top of you at the moment.
Client: Yeah, just so much. Just all parting on. Yeah.
Counselor: So you're working full time, plus part time study. Part time study. And then you've got your wedding preparation.
Client: Yeah, just got engaged, and weddings just a month away now, so, yeah, so I've just got so much happening. Work is really, really demanding and. Yeah, just fail this exam. It's just. Yeah, don't know what to do all too much.
Counselor: So imagine you've been sweating on this for a while, and it's all been swirling around in your head.
Client: Just been building up and building up and so much pressure with everything. And I'm living at home, so my parents, you know, a lot of pressure, need to do everything right. And. Yeah, by failing this, I feel like I've just embarrassed and disappointed them, and I just don't feel like I'm good enough, you know, to go on studying.
Counselor: Okay. And have they said much to you about failing your exam?
Client: They haven't said much. I was really scared to tell them, actually, because I knew they'd just be so disappointed and just embarrassed by the fact that I did fail. Yeah. I've never failed anything before. And so, yeah, really hard.
Counselor: Yeah. So it's new and you don't like it at all?
Client: Not at all, no. And I think leaving uni will just be the way out, just so I don't have to go through it again.
Counselor: Right. Okay. Well, I'm glad you've come to counselling, because it's good for us to get an outsider's opinion when we've got so much on our plate and we're confused as to what to do and our emotions can get in the way. And you've just said earlier that a whole lot of stuff's on your plate at the moment. Okay. So I'm glad you've come here. Here at the clinic, we use the ABC model, which is a cognitive behavioural therapy model. So, Marsha, some counsellors have put together a list of beliefs that we often use and we don't realise that we're using those beliefs and they tend to be faulty ones. Here's the list. Here, have a look through that to see if there are any beliefs that you might be operating on at the moment.
Client: I think number two.
Counselor: Okay, read that one out for me.
Client: That it's necessary to have a high degree of order uncertainty in order to be happy and perform well.
Counselor:
output: Yeah, yeah, you mentioned that earlier.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Victoria. How you doing today?
Client: Pretty good.
Counselor: Very good. How has the anxiety been around the germs?
Client: I still catch myself, like, double, almost like double touching. Like going to touch it and then reeling back. So I'm starting to notice it, but I still, I still have that anxiety. I still don't want to touch it.
Counselor: When you pretty much touch anything you might think has germs on it.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What are some things that you've touched in the last, between the last session and this session that have distressed you?
Client: Well, I had to go to the store, which is always a nightmare for me because I don't even like touching my credit card because it's been in so many machines and there's so much dirt and junk that gets in there and then the counters and all the. I keep thinking about the food that's there, and I, you know, if I pick it up off the shelf, how many people have picked it up with their nasty hands or kids picked it up with nasty hands and then put it back, and it's like, I need to eat. But shopping's a nightmare for me.
Counselor: So really, in a, like, a supermarket, everything can be containing germs. Have germs on it?
Client: Yeah, everything does.
Counselor: Everything does. And that's what you're thinking about as you're walking through and shopping. We talked about last time, exposure and response prevention, and I explained kind of the general idea. But you remember that conversation. Yeah, I remember. I indicated that we might try some experiments right in session to see how, see if we can move kind of forward and treating your, kind of your fear and obsession with germs and really the anxiety it's causing for you, it's like getting in the way of your life.
Client: It is. It really is.
Counselor: So I was wondering, is there anything in here, in this office, as you look around, that you would look at and think, I don't want to touch that because it could have germs on it.
Client: I'm really not liking the covers on this chair because, I mean, I can't. I mean, at least what I'm sitting in now, my clothes are protecting me from the rest of the chair.
Counselor: Mm hmm.
Client: But, I mean, I have no sleeves on, so I don't like touching the armrests and the covers.
Counselor: So even thinking about, like, your arms touching the back of the chair, and.
Client: I'm not liking it, I really feel like I should probably go wash my arms.
Counselor: So what would happen if you put your hands right on the arm covers? What was your usual reaction to that?
Client: To go wash my arms until I feel like it's gone. Until all the dirt is gone.
Counselor: And how long would that take you to be sure?
Client: I mean, something like this, probably. I'd probably be in there for a good 510 minutes. Just washing.
Counselor: 510 minutes. How many times a day would you end up washing your hands?
Client: Okay. I don't. I don't keep track anymore. It makes me upset. How many?
Counselor: It says that it's that many. That is distressing. And I know that this will be uncomfortable, but I would like you to try to. If you can feel comfortable with it, put your hands on the. On the arms of the chairs. On the chair. Let's see what I'm doing. It's like. Try to stay like that. So tell me what's going through your mind?
Client: I can just. I feel the chair, and I. I don't like it. And I just. I feel almost like I can feel everybody who's ever touched it. And just what have they been doing? And what did they touch before they touched this? They probably didn't wash their hands before they touched this, and it's just really making me comfortable.
Counselor: Okay, so you're anxious now?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Is it tolerable?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So once you remember, we talked about scaling before. So, like, ten being a tremendous amount of anxiety, one being hardly any anxiety. Where. Where are you now as you sit here with your hands?
Client: What am I going to say about six or seven?
Counselor: Six or seven?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Are you feeling an urge to go wash your hands?
Client: Yes. Yes, I am.
Counselor: Yes. This is a six or seven. I want you to sit with it for a few seconds, process that, you know, feeling. Right. That you're touching everybody that's ever been in the chair. Right. So consider that thought.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: So what's the ultimate fear? Like, what's gonna happen if you don't go wash your hands now?
Client: I'm gonna get sick.
Counselor: You're gonna get sick that someone who's.
Client: Been in this chair was sick or touched something gross that can make you sick. And I'm gonna get sick, and I'm gonna die, and I don't want to die.
Counselor: Do you feel yourself getting sick?
Client: I feel like it's harder to breathe, I guess. Like, my chest is kind of just tight. Yeah.
Counselor: You can still breathe, though.
Client: I can't. I can breathe.
Counselor: Okay, so go ahead and lift your hands up. Right. And just put them where you'd normally put them. Well, now that you've touched the chair, I know that now I can still. Is that any better? Now you're touching the seat of the.
Client: Chair, but I feel like if I touch my clothes, that's even worse. Yeah. Now I will have to go home and change my clothes.
Counselor: All right, so the thought now, if I had to guess, correct me if I'm wrong, it's probably like you really would like to wash your hands.
Client: Very much so.
Counselor: And you certainly can at any time. But I'd like you to try to hold out for a little bit. So your hands where they are now, that's better than up here.
Client: At this point. I feel like they're already contaminated, so.
Counselor: They'Re at maximum contamination.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So you can't do any more damage by touching the seat.
Client: Yeah, I'm just trying to avoid touching anything else.
Counselor: So now it's not so much about getting your hands away from the arms, but getting them under the faucet. Yeah, that's the. So where's anxiety? Was a six or seven before. Where is it now?
Client: I mean, now that you mention it, it is. It is a little better. I want to say about four. About three, four. I mean, I feel better that my. My arms are off it, and I'm focusing on breathing, and, I mean, it's.
Counselor: A little easier to breathe now.
Client: A little. Yeah, it is.
Counselor:
output: So if you could go. If you could wash your hands right this second. Of course you can. But if you did, what would the anxiety move to?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: So, good morning.
Client: Good morning.
Counselor: What would you like to work on in this session?
Client: I would like to work on my avoidance behavior. I actually have an opportunity which I was looking for from a very long time to give a presentation. And now that I have this opportunity in front of me, I'm trying to avoid it.
Counselor: So you were looking forward to this opportunity for a long time?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And then now you are avoiding it. Right. And what you would like to do?
Client: I would not like to. I would not. I would like not to avoid it.
Counselor: So you would like to go ahead with the presentation?
Client: I would like to go ahead with the presentation.
Counselor: So how do you feel when you're about to avoid? In the sense, like what kind of feelings are making you avoid this?
Client: Rather whether I'll be able to do it or not, whether it will go well, like whether all the students or the people who are listening to the presentation will like it or not. What if I forget? Or what if I do a mess?
Counselor: Now, these are your thoughts. How do you feel when you think like this?
Client: I don't feel good.
Counselor: Can you label that feeling? When you. When you think like this, you don't feel good. And which is what feeling?
Client: I feel anxious.
Counselor: You feel anxious? Right. And instead of feeling anxious, how would you like to feel so that you go ahead with the presentation?
Client: Rather not anxious, but at least some little anxious.
Counselor: Little anxious. You would like to reduce your anxiety?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So you wouldn't want to get rid of the anxiety completely?
Client: Yes, I want to get rid.
Counselor: You want to get rid of the anxiety.
Client: Anxiety completely.
Counselor: So how about feeling concerned but not anxious? So you're careful about your presentation. You also work towards the presentation well and you're not ignorant or you're not indifferent towards the outcome. Would that make sense?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So you don't want to be indifferent and feel nothing about the presentation, but you would like to feel concerned and not anxious about it.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Do you also think there is a connection between your anxiety and your avoidance?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: If you were concerned and not anxious, would you continue to avoid or you would probably go ahead?
Client: I would go ahead.
Counselor: You would go ahead?
Client: I always wanted to do this, so I would go ahead.
Counselor: You would go ahead. Right. So can we set that agenda for today's session is to feel concerned and not anxious about the upcoming presentation?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Okay, fine. So now to help you reach this goal, we will have to examine one specific incident where you know you felt anxious. And then you will understand how you get anxious and how to shift your feelings from anxiety to concern. So would you mind me telling me a specific incident where you had a chance to go ahead with, you know, preparing for the presentation, but you didn't.
Client: Recently, I have a social group where there was a chance that they wanted a presentation regarding a particular topic, and they have asked me for the dates to give me my dates when I would be presenting, and I have been just postponing it. Postponing it and not giving them the dates.
Counselor: Is this the same presentation that you are postponing, or this is different one?
Client: This is, again, a different one.
Counselor: This is a different one. But this is a specific example.
Client: Yes, this is a very specific example, which I always like. On the back of my mind. This example is always disturbing me or just always coming to my mind that I did that postponing thing.
Counselor: All right, so let's take this incident where, you know, there was a social group, and they asked you about a date for presentation. And in this situation, do you remember the incident clearly?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So when you chose to avoid it, can you remember that in that moment?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: What was going through your mind that made you avoid it?
Client: Whether I will be able to do it properly or whether they will like it or not. Am I that qualified to give the presentation now?
Counselor: These are the doubts that you had in your head. Could you convert them into statements?
Client: I'm. I'm not qualified.
Counselor: I'm not qualified.
Client: I am. People will not like it.
Counselor: People will not like it, and I.
Client: Will not be able to deliver it.
Counselor: And when you thought these, how did you feel?
Client: I didn't. I was feeling nervous. Rather nervous and not happy.
Counselor: Even not happy. Nervous and anxious. Also anxious on a zero to 100, how distressing was this anxiety?
Client: It was very distressing, I think. 80.
Counselor: 80. So that was pretty intense, right?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: It is like death anxiety. Something is gonna happen to me.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: 70 rather than, I would say.
Counselor: Okay. What was your natural intention to do at that time when you felt so anxious?
Client: I just told them, I'm busy for a while, and I will just let you know the dates when I am free and when can I take up the presentation.
Counselor: So this is what you did?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Okay. Was there anything else going on in your mind? That I want to do this?
Client: No.
Counselor: And what, in this entire incident was most anxiety provoking for you?
Client: Whether I will be able to give the presentation or not. Whether the presentation would go well or not.
Counselor: So having to make a presentation was the trigger?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Your thoughts were, I won't be able to make the presentation well, I am not qualified, and these people will not like it. These were the thoughts that were going through your head. And then you felt anxious about it. You felt nervous about it. You also escaped. Or you bought time by, you know, telling them, I'll get back to you. So you postponed accepting the invitation. Is that correct?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So did I summarize that well?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So we'll go ahead with finding out where your anxiety comes from. So when you thought these three thoughts, you felt very anxious. Out of these three thoughts, which was most important thought for you, that made.
Client: You anxious whether I will be able to do it or not.
Counselor: So your prediction that you will not be able to do it well?
Client: Yes. That I will not be able to do it well.
Counselor: Do it well, right. Okay. Let's assume for the sake of therapy that you know, you do not do it well. We are trying to find out where your anxiety comes from. Are you with me?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So if you don't do it well, what does that mean to you?
Client: That I am not competent enough.
Counselor: You are not competent enough?
Client: Yes. I am incompetent.
Counselor:
output: You are incompetent and therefore you are not able to do it well.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, Miss Payne. My name is Rebecca, and I will be your therapist today. And I see on your notes that you prefer to be called Kelly. Is that correct?
Client: Yes, ma'am. My name is Kelly, but a lot of people call me Kelly Joe. They do? Yeah. My papa in particular. He likes to call me Joe. Kelly Joe. I was named after my great grandfathers.
Counselor: Okay, well, would you prefer that I call you Kelly or Kelly Joe?
Client: No, just call me Kelly. I think Kelly Joe is really country. Okay, we'll just go with Kelly.
Counselor: All right, Kelly. The first thing I want to do is I'm going to explain our roles that we have today in our session. And of course, you know, as I said, I'm your therapist, but you're also actively participating in this session. And anytime you have a question, if you have any comments, if you don't understand something, I want you to tell me so that I can make sure that you understand everything that we're doing, that we're talking about, and it will be actively. Yeah. Between both of us will be a team, if you want.
Client: Oh, I definitely ask questions. Trust me. I like to ask a lot of questions. I like to talk.
Counselor: Well, that's good. And then the other thing, we have an agenda that I'm going to try to stick by. We want to start off with a mood check. I'll just kind of see how you're feeling today. We'll talk about your presenting problems, and we'll go into making some goals, and I'll explain a little bit of the theory that I use for our sessions. Kind of do a little educational piece to make sure you understand what's going on, and we'll give a summary. And also, I may have some homework that we can talk about.
Client: Okay. Because I sure do have lots of problems. I can tell you about tons of problems.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: So I'm going to be talking your ears off.
Counselor: Well, we have approximately about 15 to 20 minutes today, and I'll let you know when the time starts to run short so you're not taken by surprise.
Client: Okay, that will be fine. But if I need more time, I'll just have to buy it, I guess.
Counselor:
output: Well, we can work something out, I'm sure.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Danielle. How are you doing today?
Client: I'm good, how are you?
Counselor: I'm good, thanks for asking. What's been going on?
Client: Well, last time we spoke, you know, I just got a promotion.
Counselor: It's great news.
Client: Yeah, great news. I'm really, really excited about the opportunity and the career advancement, but sure. I just really, it just hit me that I'm going to be having to give presentations and really kind of be a team leader and kind of be the face of a group of individuals and it's kind of making me a little shaky.
Counselor: Well, shaky. Are you a big fan of public speaking?
Client: Not. I wouldn't say a big fan, no, it's been bearable. But the thought of having to do it continuously, it's definitely a little frightening for me.
Counselor: That's frightening for you. How often would you have to, do you say continuously? How often would it be in this new job?
Client: In this new job, I would actually have to meet with them every weekly. Weekly.
Counselor: How many people on the team that you now supervise?
Client: There are ten people. Yeah.
Counselor: All right, so you have ten people that you, you're gonna have to speak to?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Right. And how long is the talk each week?
Client: Normally? Average is about like half an hour.
Counselor: Half an hour. Have you ever had to do it in the past or anything like it?
Client: I've done something like this for school, but definitely not for 30 minutes. Not for half an hour.
Counselor: Alright, so the length of time is a major stressor. How about the number of people, like ten?
Client: Is that, that's, that's a, I mean, when I did it for school, it was a group of us, so it was less anxiety. But to be doing it by myself for, you know, and all attention on me, that's. Yeah. And ten people, that's a lot of people looking up to me and, you know.
Counselor: All right, so the number of people being ten, that stresses you a bit. Little anxiety there, a good amount of anxiety and then the duration.
Client: Yeah, absolutely.
Counselor: So ten people for a minute. That wouldn't.
Client: That's not too bad.
Counselor: You can handle that?
Client: I could handle that.
Counselor: Or a half hour with like one.
Client: Person, I can definitely handle 100 one's not too bad.
Counselor: 100 one's not too bad.
Client: 100 one's not too bad. But the thought of ten people staring at me, hanging on my every word for that long, that's, that's definitely puts me out there in terms of anxiety.
Counselor: All right, so there's a lot of anxiety there and that's painful for you. Let's do this. I know that you mentioned that you're taking over for somebody but they still work there?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: How long do you have before you need to start taking over that responsibility?
Client: I have about six weeks.
Counselor: About six weeks. So you have six weeks to become reasonably comfortable with speaking in front of ten people for a half hour once a week. So what I'd like to do is I'd like to develop some steps that you can take at work. So I know you do a lot of different things at work and you mentioned that you're good with people individually, so I'm going to create some steps that you can actually conduct at work, you know, collaboratively with you. I want you to be a big part of this, and I want to rank them from the least anxiety provoking to the most anxiety provoking. And let's use about five levels. Five steps. So I'm going to develop together with you five steps. So the fifth one will be the hardest. And I'm going to take a wild guess and say that would be speaking in front of all ten people for a half hour.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So that's the most stressful it can get.
Client: Yeah, definitely.
Counselor: That's the most stressful part of your job now. Or what your job will be when you take that over. All right, so let's make that. If you agree, we'll make that kind of a five out of five. So five is the maximum level of anxiety.
Client: I can agree to that, yeah.
Counselor: So let me think of some other ways you can approach this. You said you're really good one on one. How about with two people? Like, if you're in a room with two people and talk to them, that's.
Client: Not, that's not too bad.
Counselor: That's not too bad. That's definitely not a five out of five.
Client: No, it's definitely not a five out of five.
Counselor: So let's make that one of the steps. How about speaking to two of the people for around 15 minutes? Make that one of the steps. And how about another step would be speaking to four people for 15 minutes?
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Right. Which of those two would be. Would be scarier?
Client: The four people.
Counselor: Four people.
Client: For 15 minutes.
Counselor: For 15 minutes. All right. And then if we were to say four people for a half hour, what would that rank?
Client: I would definitely say that's like a four and a half or four.
Counselor:
output: So that's. That's higher up than the. So, so far, if we rank these in terms of anxiety from the least anxiety provoking a couple people, 15 minutes, you think you could do that?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
