Client: Exactly. Exactly. And I would be devastated by that. Mister Don said that I'm right. I didn't get the job because I'm black. I'm right because I didn't. You know, my situation is what it is. Cause of racism. Mister Don. Mister Don said I wouldn't want that. It would taunt the reputation, probably hurt my employment here. So, you know, I bite my tongue.
Counselor: Is there a way to deliver your message, kind of with the same realism and heart, without including a piece that you feel like they could latch onto? It would be negative.
Client: Is there a way? Did you hear the message? Maybe if I switched it around and I put the last part first.
Counselor: I don't know.
Client: I'm just brainstorming here. Maybe I don't tell them at all. Maybe I just. I make reference and have them come to the same conclusion.
Counselor: Give them all the tools to figure it out.
Client: Figure it out for themselves. Well, if that's the case, then how did this happen? Okay, so if that's the case, if you're saying. If what you're saying is true, then how does this happen? How does this person.
Counselor: Ask them to explain your success?
Client: My success is someone else's success who came from the same neighborhood. How do you explain that same scenario? I think that might be a better way of taking this thing out of it, so to speak.
Counselor: So if that's the new message, how likely do you think you'd be able to deliver that message if somebody told you that they wanted to continue in an unproductive lifestyle?
Client: I think it would work. I think the problem for me is I gotta buy into it first.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: I think that's the issue. I really gotta buy into it because I really inundated so much negativity that I'm starting to believe the hype, so to speak. So before I can, you know how kids are, they know right away. You know, if you're bullshitting, they go right away.
Counselor: So you feel like you need to be more genuine in your acceptance of your message before you can effectively deliver that message. Because if there's a non authentic portion of that, they're gonna. They're gonna find that.
Client: They're gonna find it, and they're gonna exploit it.
Counselor: So this is really, part of this is really about you losing some hope?
Client: Yes, it is. Yeah.
Counselor: So what's your belief about their realities? Like these? Use that. You see, if you really kind of unfiltered your belief about their chances of success.
Client: I think they are very adaptable. I think their survival methods are unbelievable. But I do think they are missing some real key, just some key life skills that are going to keep them locked out and locked into their situation. One kid said to me, he said, they released me from prison, but I'm still a handcuff to the system. Oh, he's right.
Counselor: You could see his point.
Client: I can see his point. Like, yeah, you're pretty much right because it's a mindset that although you're out of prison mentally, you're still incarcerated. And I can't pull him out of that mindset. And that's so frustrating. Here's a kid that's intelligent, but he still thinks like he's in prison. He still believes that this all happens to him because he's black. And that message is reinforced by the people he's around. So it's not just him. That's the way his boys think. That's probably the way his moms think because it's easier. It's easier to think, well, it's societies. There's no personal responsibility and that's a very unpopular message to have.
Counselor: So the youth that you work with, they've been exposed to an unpopular message, a tough message, one that permeates. It's all around them. They're exposed to, it permeates them. But there's a part of you that really appreciates their adaptability and their survival skills.
Client: Yeah, yeah. I think I said to one cat that, you know, you guys remind me of like, you know, soldiers, you're like just numb to the pain. Whatever happens, you're just numb to the pain. Just keep moving forward, just keep moving it, you know? But the hardest part now is to get them to come out of that survival, and it's depressing. I don't think the other counselors at the center see it or if they're just becoming immune like me, I'm becoming more like them, you know, just becoming heartless, realizing, okay, this is just a job. So I'll come here and do my 8 hours and leave.
Counselor: Worried that exposure to this environment just makes you a certain way, makes you disconnected from really trying to find solutions or believing solutions are possible. When you say move out of survival mode, the survival characteristics, you admire that. What do they need to do? How do they need to move out of survival mode? What's the next mode?
Client: I think the next mode is accepting the reality of where they are. This is my reality and it's not going to change unless I take some accountability. It's not going to change. And I think that's the hardest transition for them to make. So these things survival, I call it the growth. Survival. There's survival and there's growth. So how do you go beyond your circumstances? You know, how do you rise above your circumstances?
Counselor: So I have to accept my reality.
Client: And move forward except it for what it is. This is real. Racism is real. Poverty is real. Yeah, my mother said, dope fiend, and she's in jail. This is real. But how do I move beyond this now? This is what it is and I'm realizing it. How do I move beyond this to the next stage of my development?
Counselor: So in a similar way, what you're dealing with from your position is the solution the same? Do you need to accept the reality of your work environment and who you're working with and what they're going through?
Client: Yeah, I think you're right. I think the same. The same solution applies to me. Probably the dose of my own medicine in that regard.
Counselor: So let's look at these thoughts. And I want to give you something to work on between the session and next session. Specifically, I want to really go after the micro level. At this moment when you're with the youth and they tell you something that's kind of triggering that automatic thought, that generally saying hope is lost. It's a kind of self defeating thought. What's something. What's a thought that you could consciously think like self talk that you could introduce at that moment and that automatic thought of it's hopeless. Just to simplify, it's hopeless. What could you say to yourself at that moment to challenge that thought?
Client: That's a good question. What could I say at that moment to alter my thinking? Talking about the kid, not me with the kid. I don't know. God makes no mistakes. God makes no mistakes. So it has to be one. There has to be redeemable quality in this human being sitting in front of it. It just has to be. I'm just not looking. Am I looking close enough? But there has to be some characteristic in this kid that I can find, that I can build on.
Counselor: So you think to yourself, you have a few things there. So you think to yourself, I can see their point of view. In a way, it's really hopeless, but there's got to be a way, something. There's got to be something in them that you can latch on to.
Client: Yeah, that may not look like what I think it should. It may not mean this kid ends up at Howard University on a full ride. Maybe it just means the kid doesn't go to jail. You know, maybe he starts smoking weed for 24 hours. So maybe I need to manage my expectations better than that happening.
Counselor: Okay, so set some goals that you feel are realistic.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So as you so think about, you have that thought. If I can see the point of view, I can see where they think it's hopeless. Maybe it's hopeless. And you have this adaptive response of, there's something in there that's redeemable. How do you think that could change your reaction to that automatic thought?
Client: I think it would. I think it would brighten my mood a little bit in terms of my disposition. I think it would brighten. I think I'd be a little bit more charismatic about the job than I have been. Because you're right. I have seen, I have noticed just a thought process that just puts me into a funk before lunchtime. So maybe this is that way of.
Counselor: Interrupting thought process, and that's exactly what you want to do. You had that automatic thought. It leads to that reaction, which in your case, is kind of not doing what you feel you should be doing and you want to disrupt that self talk. So do you think you can practice that self talk in the week between I see you again?
Client: Absolutely.
Counselor:
output: Yeah.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: So these daggy little sheets we use for cognitive behavioral therapy or strategies. And you can see at the top they talk about the situation, and down the bottom they talk about the feelings, and in between, there's a whole lot of discussion about the thoughts. Yeah. So again, it's sort of easier with a concrete example. So I might get you to write in, if you're happy, to, the situation that you mentioned, the tram situation in the little situation box there.
Client: Of course.
Counselor: Okay, so what have you written in there?
Client: Catching the tram.
Counselor: Okay, so what feelings do you have when you go to catch the tram? And just before you tell me, often it's useful to have sort of one word for a feeling, something that's really in your gut rather than a long expression. So what's your feeling?
Client: Anxious. That's the one. Anxious.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: That's the one.
Counselor: Do you want to write that in and see? Are there any other feelings that really resonate with you? I mean, that's enough. But is there anything other sort of feeling you have when you're
Client: scared?
Counselor: Okay, so pop that one in there. Anything else?
Client: Embarrassed.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: All right.
Counselor: Do you want to pop that one in there as well? This is great. You've really sort of clicked with it. All right, so now why are we doing all this? Because what I'm going to ask you now is to imagine what the little voice in your head, you know, that little self talk is saying when you're feeling anxious. So what are you feeling anxious about? What's the sort of story in your head that's going on there?
Client: All right, I'm. How's it. What happens? I'm thinking I'm gonna get lost.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Yeah. So I'm anxious because I think I'm gonna get lost.
Counselor: Okay. So do you want to write that one down?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. I'm worried I'll get lost.
Client: Yep.
Counselor: See, it's a bit artificial bringing it up, but there's sort of a point to all this.
Client: Yeah, yeah, no, I get it. It's good to actually think through what exactly.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: Happens.
Counselor: Okay, so you said you're anxious because you're worried or get lost. Any other thoughts? That sort of self talk?
Client: Um, yeah, I reckon I start blushing and, you know, going red.
Counselor: Right. Okay. It's another good one to write down. Do you want to write that one down in the thoughts as word? Brilliant. Okay, and so what have you written there?
Client: Panic that I'll go red. Blush.
Counselor: Okay. All right. Got it.
Client: I do.
Counselor: So this is sort of really useful. We've been able to sort of tease out your situation, the feelings. And really, what's that little voice in your head that's going on? Now, there's been a point to all this because what we do with this CBT approach is we try and challenge some of these thoughts. Okay.
Client: Because I know they're, you know, silly. I know that.
Counselor: Yeah. I mean, some of our thoughts are realistic, some of them are correct and. And some of them aren't realistic and not very helpful. And. And it sounds like these ones that are sort of causing problems for you. So, so what I'm going to do, let's look at this first one here. You've said, I'm worried I'll get lost. Okay? So let's just look at the evidence for that. So I'm gonna be a little bit like a lawyer here and so let's look at the evidence for that. Or not. So you say, don't worry, don't get lost. Have you ever been lost in the city?
Client: No, I don't think I have.
Counselor: Yeah. Okay. Do you usually know which tram to get on?
Client: Oh, yeah, I make sure I know because I'm so scared I'm gonna get lost. I make sure I know all the numbers of the trams, where they go. So, yeah, actually. So I've never got lost.
Counselor: Okay. All right. So in some ways, how likely do you think it really is that you're actually going to get lost? I know you're having that thought, but.
Client: Well, it's actually really unlikely.
Counselor: Fantastic. And so what I'll get you to write in this little right hand column here is it's really unlikely I'm going to get lost. Okay, so these are what we sort of call disputing thoughts or, you know, alternative ways of looking at it that a little bit fairer to ourselves and a little bit more realistic. That's fantastic.
Client: So unlikely I will get lost.
Counselor: Yeah. It's actually unlikely, isn't it? Yeah. Have a look at the next one. I'll panic and I'll blush and everyone will look at me. Okay, so let's just have a little look at that. If you did get a bit panicky, do you think people would really be noticing?
Client: Probably not. Maybe not.
Counselor: Well, let's put it another way. Do you look at other people on the tram and sort of decide whether or not they look emotionally happy or sad or panicky?
Client: Not really, no. I don't know. I look out the window or read the paper usually, yeah.
Counselor: And look. That's fantastic because do you think it's. I mean, most people are just sitting on the train doing their own thing and not that really interested in other people.
Client: Yeah, I guess.
Counselor: I mean, we've gone a long way with this today, but can you think of a more helpful thought than. I'll blush and people will look at me. Can you think of a more realistic way of thinking about that?
Client: I don't know. Look, I feel anxious sometimes. Lots of people feel anxious sometimes, and that's okay, you know. Doesn't mean I'm an idiot.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: Fantastic.
Counselor:
output: All right, so do you want to write that in here as the sort of disputing thoughts? That's really good. You've really got the hang of this. And I think you're right. I think people actually probably don't care that much. Sort of doing their own thing.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Maury. How you doing today?
Client: I'm doing all right.
Counselor: You doing all right?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I know last time you were here, you were discussing some relational issues. You want to continue with that?
Client: Yeah, yeah. I mean, you know, it kind of came up again. You know, every time my wife yells at me, you know, I feel like a failure, you know, like I told you last time, I just. I just feel like I can't do anything right, you know? Like everything I try to do is met with arguing and yelling, and I just feel like there's nothing I can do right.
Counselor: So no matter what you do, it's not going to end up the way you want?

Counselor: So it's frustrating.

Client: I mean, it's rocky, you know, because I feel like I can't do anything right. She doesn't understand that. And then, you know, we don't get along ever because we're just always yelling and I'm always feeling bad, and then it just keeps going like that.
Counselor: So when you. You mentioned you feel like a failure when she. When she yells at you?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Can you think back to maybe the last time, one of the last times you guys argued and try to remember that thought? We've talked about automatic thoughts before. Remember that thought that comes in that moment when she starts. She starts yelling at you?
Client: I mean, she'll yell at me. I mean, I feel, you know, frustrated. Like, why are you yelling at me right now? And. I don't know. I mean, as I was thinking about, like we were talking about it, and as I was thinking about it more this week, kind of felt like, you know, kind of like what happened with my dad, you know? I guess I kind of felt that same way when I was younger. You know, like, if my dad would yell at me or when he would yell at me, I kind of feel that same way. And it feels like the same thing. Yeah. It's kind of the first. I guess kind of the first thought that comes to mind.
Counselor: The first thought is I've been through something like this before, I guess.
Client: Yeah. I mean, I'm not really thinking those exact words, but that's definitely what it feels like, you know? Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. Like, it's like just a sense that this isn't brand new.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And the feeling you're connecting with it is the same feeling you had when your dad. Yahweh. Yeah.
Client: Yeah, pretty much, yeah.

Client: I guess so, in a way, that's distressing.
Counselor: Yeah, it is.
Client: I mean, it feels, you know, pretty crappy.
Counselor: Now, in these arguments, she yells at you. You mentioned before that you do some yelling of your own, you know, in the midst of all that. Right. How would you rate it in terms of, like, any physical violence? Nothing like that.

Counselor:
output: And what level, like, what level of yelling would you say? How severe compared to what you've experienced in the past?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, Jordan. How you doing today?
Client: Could have been better.
Counselor: Could be better.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What's going on?
Client: Um, well, you know, I have two jobs.
Counselor: Mm hmm.
Client: And I lost one of them.
Counselor: You lost your job? Yes. Which one did you lose?
Client: I lost one at the grocery store.
Counselor: That was your part time?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I'm sorry to hear that.
Client: Me too. And I'm just. It's all I think about now.
Counselor: And when did this happen?
Client: It happened about two, three days ago.
Counselor: Two, three days ago?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So if I remember right, you took that job not too long ago to kind of supplement your income.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So certainly that would be upsetting, but I know that's not a major part of your income.
Client: It's not, but, I mean, I'm still very worried about it.
Counselor: Tell me about the worry.
Client: I mean, I worry that, you know, I'm. Now I only had so much money, and now I have less than that. I mean, without my money, you know, God knows how many things can happen.
Counselor: So before you had the job, you were paying all your bills. You want some extra income, you've lost that extra income. And I can certainly understand how that would be disturbing. But as I understand that you were doing okay before with your full time job.
Client: I was doing okay, but, I mean, I got comfortable with that extra income, and so now my fear is that I've gotten too comfortable with it, and now that it's not there anymore, it's going to affect the fact I'm not going to be able to pay for food or my rent.
Counselor: Okay, so you adjusted to the new income level with the full time and the part time job together, and you're worried you can't adjust back?
Client: I'm worried that, I mean, things are just gonna get worse from here. I mean, it's a big deal, losing your job. Even if it was part time, I've gotten comfortable from having so much money, from the money I had to. Now that's, you know, been divided and, I mean, God knows how many things, like I said, God knows how many things can happen.
Counselor: Well, what. What can happen? So you have that income, your income is reduced now to just your full time job. What can happen from this point on?
Client: Well, I can, you know, keep. Stay in the mindset that I have that extra money and spend what I think is that extra money, digging into the money I paid for my rent, my food, my gas, my insurance, and me, who's somebody without all that.
Counselor: So you could fail to pay expenses that need to be paid.
Client: And they helped me go to my full time job that I still have. So, I mean, if I can't, if I spend the money that was from my insurance because I thought I had extra, then I'm not gonna have insurance on my cardinal. I can get pulled over, lose my license, not going to be able to get to work, and then I'll get fired there too.
Counselor: All right, so the kind of chain of causality you're seeing is that without that part time income, you might not adapt with your expense management. You might fail to pay, for example, your car insurance. You could get pulled over for something the police officer could see, don't have insurance, give you a ticket, which is just money. I don't have another expense. Right. And how would this. How would that connect to losing your job?
Client: Because I wouldn't be able to get to work.
Counselor: So it'd be. So the ticket would be so expensive, you would lose your.
Client: Well, the ticket would be expensive, so I wouldn't be able to try to pay the next month's insurance. So I just wouldn't have insurance on my car. So I.
Counselor: So you'd lose your insurance?
Client: I'd lose my insurance.
Counselor: And then by losing your insurance, you lose your transportation altogether because you can't drive that insurance. And then you lose your job.
Client: Mm hmm. I mean, it's either go to work with an uninsured car, and then I can get pulled over and go to jail for driving with no insurance multiple times.
Counselor: No, that's serious. Yeah. You wouldn't want to do that.
Client: I wouldn't go to jail.
Counselor: So there's two. You have two kind of causal change. One is losing your job. And now even just the idea you can end up incarcerated.
Client: Yes. I mean, which I definitely lose my.
Counselor: Job if I'm in jail, I would imagine.
Client: And so that would have. So then I wouldn't even have, like, any money to help me through jail. Like, to. For the commissary and stuff.
Counselor: Because you would have no income.
Client: I would have no income. And then when I get out of jail, I'm. No one's gonna hire me.
Counselor: Because you have a criminal record.
Client: Exactly.
Counselor: Which makes it challenging to find employment in some instances. So what's happened is kind of in your mind, and we've talked about how thoughts work and beliefs work, is you, in reality, you've lost this part time job. And as I said, that's certainly. That's understandable that you'd be upset about that. I doubt many people would be happy about losing additional income, but you move from there, from losing additional income, which is what has actually happened to this possibility that you could be in jail or lose your job because of this. So I remember maybe last week. Week before, you're talking about the. The letter that you received from. It was like a late notice. It wasn't. Turned out wasn't.
Client: Yeah, it was sent to me, but it was somebody else's credit card mistake. Yeah.
Counselor: Do you remember the conclusions you drew from when you believe that was actually for you, that late notice, that my.
Client: Credit score was gonna go down, that I would. I'd be stuck in that apartment, and then I'd go into depression. I wouldn't be able to do anything.
Counselor: Yeah. So you ended up in that scenario. You end up in a situation where you just couldn't function at all. And you moved there from a letter that you believe was addressed to you, saying you were one month or six days late or something on a credit card, which, of course, you don't want to be late on a credit card, but you move from there to being so depressed you couldn't work, couldn't function, I think, is how you put it. Couldn't function. Do you see, kind of, given how we've talked about cognitive behavioral strategies and concepts, do you see a pattern that's emerged over the last few times I've seen you?
Client: I mean, I've seen that, you know, sometimes I can. I can think the worst, and then. And I know it didn't happen last time, but that was, you know, a stroke of good luck.
Counselor: That it wasn't you.
Client: Yeah. That it was, you know, it wasn't me. And, you know, that was a relief. But this is something that's solid. I don't have my part time job anymore.
Counselor: You've lost real income.
Client: I mean, this isn't a mistake. This isn't a. We fired the wrong person. You know, this is real. So there's real concerns here.
Counselor: I.
Client: Unlike last time, where I was lucky.
Counselor: So this. This situation, you see, is different than the first situation because the first situation was more. You were perceiving something was wrong that wasn't wrong because you weren't the intended recipient of the letter.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But in this situation, it's different because it's real. You really lost your income.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And, of course, keeping in mind that this job, again, only a few months old, and you survived well before that, is it reason to believe you could survive well again, that you could adapt to this lost income?
Client: Well, I suppose there is, but I'm concerned about whether I'm not, whether I won't adapt.
Counselor: Well, let's look at this in terms of probabilities, right. You've had several jobs throughout your career. You've had some of them worked out. You've lost other ones. You're still paying your bills. So in terms of probabilities, how many times have you, how many times have you ended up in jail or losing your full time job?
Client: I mean, they haven't happened yet.
Counselor: It hasn't happened.
Client: Not yet. But I mean, I, I struggled a little bit when I lost a part time job or when I was younger and I had those little jobs.
Counselor: So you had to adapt.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And it was painful.
Client: I did struggle, yeah.
Counselor: You struggled.
Client: Yeah. I mean, but I'm older now. These are, you know, even though grocery stores, not a serious job. It was income.
Counselor: Sure. Yeah. And again, to lose income would be disappointing for just about anybody. Are there any upsides to not having that job?
Client: I suppose I have more time to focus on my full time job because, I mean, that is really intensive.
Counselor: Is there a possibility that you could find another part time job just as you found that one?
Client: I mean, because will somebody else take me because I was fired from that job? I mean, that's my concern, is that.
Counselor: Nobody, they're going to find out.
Client: Yeah. And then they're going to go, oh, she was fired, you know. No, we don't. We don't want her.
Counselor: But you've had other jobs that didn't work out before and that didn't affect you getting that job.
Client: That's true.
Counselor: So the worst case scenario, I guess what I'm getting at the worst case scenario is, in your case, ending up in jail or losing your full time job, which you've had for a while.
Client: Yeah, I really don't want to lose my job.
Counselor: And it seems like they like you there.
Client: I hope they do.
Counselor: Right? Yeah. So those scenarios, I guess, are possible, but they seem, based on what you're saying, is pretty unlikely. So I wonder how useful it is to invest a lot of energy in kind of tracking that causal chain to jail or prison or to unemployment when that's really not the most likely outcome. Sorry to interrupt you, but do you invest as much energy in tracking the positives or the probable outcomes?
Client: No, not even close. I know that I don't think about the positive things. I mean, I don't get fired and then go, what's good about this?
Counselor: Or get a letter in the mail and say, what's, you know, although I can see there's not much upside to that, although it turned out that was an error, so. But this has still been a theme that I've seen over the last eight to ten weeks, where you really have, you really emphasize the negative, possible, even unlikely outcomes, kind of expanding the negative as you move through. Like a causal chain.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Does that make sense? Yeah, but you don't do the same thing for the positive side. You don't look at how something could work out. Well, would you say it's fair assessment?
Client: Yeah. Yeah, no, that's. That's pretty accurate.
Counselor: But still, you're worried about this.
Client: I mean, yeah, I am worried. I'm not gonna be thrilled about it, but I suppose I don't have to go to when I'm gonna go to jail or I'm gonna lose my full time job.
Counselor: I think there's a lot of intervening factors that could occur before going to jail or losing your job. There's other things that you could do.
Client: I suppose I could get a family member to drive me or take the bus if I lost my insurance and lost my car.
Counselor: So, alternate forms of transportation. Yeah. There's adapting your spending back to where it was before.
Client: That's true.
Counselor: Part of your fear was that you wouldn't be able to adapt your spending. Right. But that's something you would have control over.
Client: I guess. I can keep, you know, better track of how much I do spend and, you know, keep track of my bank accounts and exactly how much money I have in them.
Counselor: So, having talked through this a little bit. Right. What I'm going to refer to, or is referred to as catastrophizing. Remember we talked about that when we reviewed the cognitive distortions.
Client: That sounds familiar. Yeah.
Counselor: Where a negative is taken and just making way more negative than it is at the moment. Right. Kind of knowing that, that tends to be what you do. It's what we call an error in thinking that you tend to make. Does that lower your anxiety about the situation? Does it change it in some way?
Client: I mean, knowing that I'm thinking about it wrong makes me feel a little better.

Counselor: You're investing in the negative outcomes without really looking at the positive side. Okay, so that's kind of how cognitive distortions work, right? They're consistent errors in thinking, and we'll work on the helping you to reframe circumstances like this. Granted, this is certainly more distressing than receiving that letter that you received. I'm trying to give you more options than just the catastrophic ones.

output: Sure, there's ways that are more useful to you that'll probably help you dig out of this faster and either adjust to not having the income or replace the income.

Counselor: So let's take that kind of most severe moment when you're. Let's just say we're still before the presentation.

Counselor: So you're sitting at the desk, and your heart rate's elevated, and you're not focusing on what they're doing. You're zoned out, your anxiety's high.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What thought is going through your mind right then?
Client: I think. I'm thinking, like, I'm gonna bond this anyway, so I might as well just, you know, not go through the stress of having to do it. Like, I've already. In my head, I know that it's.
Counselor: Gonna end badly, so I've already failed.
Client: Right. So there's no sense in getting up there, and maybe if I don't get up there, you know, I guess it couldn't be any worse, so I might as well just leave.
Counselor: Are you embarrassed that the professor or other students will see that you were really anxious?
Client: Yeah, I don't want. I figure if I leave, then people won't. We'll just maybe think I was sick or whatever, and it'll be a better situation if I just left than having to see me up there, you know, sweating and all this. These other symptoms that I have when I actually get up there. It would be better just to leave before that starts.
Counselor: Okay, so. So better to be thought ill that you just had to leave because you're sick.
Client: Yeah. Or have them wonder what happened than to just be up in front of.
Counselor: Everybody, you know, to have that severe anxiety in front of everybody, and then they can see.
Client: Very embarrassing.
Counselor: Yeah. That would be. That would be a very undesirable outcome for you.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So as you're debating that thought, like, if that's coming to your head and you're thinking, I just need to.
Client: Yeah, flee. I just gotta get out of here.
Counselor: What happens there? So we're maybe, what, 15 minutes before you present? So tell me about that. So you have that thought. You want to flee, right?
Client: And I'm looking at the clock and saying, you know, like, how much more time in this presentation before I have to go? Like, should I go? Should I not go? What are the consequences of running out? You know, and kind of playing out, which would be worse?
Counselor: Have you ever had to run out?
Client: Once I went to the bathroom to try to, like, calm myself down or talk to myself or, you know, like, cool off my face, but I came.
Counselor: Back and you presented.
Client: Yeah. And then I presented.
Counselor: All right, so you. You survived one of the more stressful.
Client: Yeah. I almost felt like I was gonna be ill. I was so stressed that day.
Counselor: That was very, very tough one, yet.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: That particular day, you did survive it.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. Which is very unpleasant.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So now we're. Now we're right about to where it's time to get up and present. Right. So let's say in this scenario, you haven't fled, but you had those thoughts.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So you're anxious, and you have some physical symptoms going on. You get up and it's time to present. What's the sequence from this point on?
Client: So typically, like, I go to load my presentation at this point. Like, I have my note cards or whatever in front of me. I am, like, shaking at this point. I'm so. I don't know if it's scared or worried or maybe a combination of everything. And I'm just, like, sweating. My heart is racing. Like, I almost feel dizzy. I'm just so stressed out about what's going to happen then, you know, I'm starting to speak, and then the presentations are usually, like, 20 minutes or so.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: So I have to stay up there for the duration, and I'm just, like, you know, sweating, and I'm wondering, like, are people looking at me or people. Can people see it? You know, am I gonna forget something?
Counselor: So the. So the thoughts are, I wonder if they can see how anxious I am.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: I wonder if I'm going to do poorly on the presentation.
Client: Right. Or they think I'm lazy and I didn't prepare, or are they going to think that, you know, I'm dumb or I don't know, you know, what I'm doing. What are they going to think about me?
Counselor: So they might think less of you as a person.
Client: Right. Or, like, be judging me.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So there's a number of concerns that kind of go into your mind in that moment. So when does it start to turn around? So you start presenting is 20 minutes. You initially get up there and get your presentation up on the, like, the projection monitor?
Client: Something like that, yeah.
Counselor:
output: When does it start to turn the corner?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Hazel. How you doing today?
Client: I'm okay.
Counselor: You okay?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I know when we met last time for your intake, you were concerned about some presentations that you had to give at school.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: You want to talk about that today?
Client: Yeah. So in school. I am in school for teaching, and we have to give presentations a lot, as you can imagine, on different things. And so it's something that's recurring. And what happened was I gave a really bad one one time. Yeah. I wasn't feeling very well, and I gave. I think I was just supposed tired from studying all night, and I gave a really bad presentation. And then, like, now, ever since, like, when I've tried to give subsequent presentations, I am just so nervous and I'm up there, like, sweating and, like, starting to forget what I'm gonna say. And I'm just, like, a fear of getting up there and having to get a presentation because I feel like I'm gonna bomb it.
Counselor: All right, so was there a time before, like, recently, when you had to give presentations?
Client: Yeah, I mean, like, before, earlier in my. Like, I'm towards the end of my degree, so, you know, throughout my program, I have. I have.
Counselor: And how did you do with those?
Client: Pretty well. I mean, I consider myself a pretty good student. So normally I do pretty well, it seemed, you know, come out of nowhere.
Counselor: So this presentation that you gave with the. Where you received a poor score, maybe just an isolated incident?
Client: Yeah. Like I was saying, I wasn't. I wasn't feeling very well, I don't think. And it really hasn't happened.
Counselor: But that experience has still led to a lot of anxiety with subsequent presentations.
Client: Oh, yeah. Like, I'm worried about my grades suffering as a result, and, you know, how well I'm going to do.
Counselor: All right, so would it be okay if we kind of step through the whole process of you giving a presentation? Sure. Right before I start with that, is this something that leads to anxiety, like, right now or other times or really just in that moment when you're presenting?
Client: Mostly it's most intense in that moment. And, like, maybe, like, leading up to it, like, in preparation that I know that this is gonna happen. Like, I always know when I'm gonna present. Like, it'll be like, the teacher will say, oh, well, you know, you're this Thursday, someone else is next Thursday. So the closer it gets to that event, the more anxious I am. Like, in anticipation.
Counselor: Okay, so you start feeling anxiety a few days before presentation.
Client: Yeah, I would say a few days, mostly.
Counselor: When does it start to get really distressing for you?
Client: Like, two days before or one day before? Then I'm like, oh, my gosh, like, am I ready? Like, what if I mess up? You know, what if I get a bad grade? All these, like, what ifs.
Counselor: Okay, so would you be okay if we step into this process and kind of break down the steps of the presentation? Yeah. All right, so let's say that you're taking. What's one of the classes you're taking now?
Client: Early childhood.
Counselor: Early childhood. So let's say you have a presentation in that class a few days from now. Just a normal presentation. So let's now move to two days out, where you would start to feel a little anxiety about it.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What's going through your mind at that two day out point?
Client: I would say, like, am I prepared enough? Like, did I do enough, you know, to study or to write down, did I do enough?
Counselor: All right, so your thought is, did I do enough preparation?
Client: Yeah. Which leads to maybe I did it is what I'm really thinking. Like, I'm not prepared enough as I should be.
Counselor: Okay. I'm not prepared. I'm not prepared enough.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: All right, so that's the thought you're having about 48 hours before the presentation. I'm not prepared enough.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor:
output: And kind of thinking about that thought and what happens afterward. Do you have a reaction? Like, any type of emotional. Affective. Affective reaction to that?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, Hazel. How you doing?
Client: I'm all right. I'm a little bit stressed out right now.
Counselor: A little stressed? What's going on?
Client: Well, as you know, I'm in a graduate program right now, and I'm just really coming to the. Near the end of my program, and I'm just finding it increasingly difficult. I'm just really stressed with how things have been going.
Counselor: Okay. Now, we've talked about some different struggles you've had as you balance work and school and everything. What specifically is bothering you now? It seems like you're a little more distressed today.
Client: Well, I don't really know. Just I. As I have told you before, I take school really seriously, and I really strive to do well in school and well on my assignments, and I just feel like I'm not performing as well as I need to.
Counselor: Now, what kind of grades you've been getting lately?
Client: Well, I've been getting A's, but.
Counselor: Anything else? No, just a's. Okay. That's usually considered pretty good, right?
Client: Yeah. I just feel like it's getting harder to get the a's.
Counselor: Okay. So you're working harder to get the same grade?
Client: Right. It used to be so easy for me to do what my teachers expect and to get good grades. Now I feel like it's really a struggle and I'm not doing as well as I need to. Constantly worried about not doing as well.
Counselor: Have you been getting any feedback from professors or your classmates about your performance?
Client: My teachers all seem to think I'm doing well. I seem to get good feedback on my assignments, but I feel like. I feel like I. Just to make sure I'm doing well, I really focus on, like, the details, like, making sure that the instructions are really clear, like, I'm doing everything, like, perfectly as the instructor wants, because I'm really afraid that, you know, if I'm not really clear on what the assignment is, then maybe I won't do it the right way.
Counselor: All right, so before, when you got A's, you were working hard to do a good job, but not to the level of precision in terms of, like, the detail of the assignment that you are now. You're trying to get more information about the assignments. You're working harder to get the same grade that you used to get before.
Client: Right? Like, I find myself, like, emailing the teacher, like, almost, like, obsessively, like, trying to clarify the assignment and to make sure do they think I'm doing well in class and whatnot.
Counselor:
output: So when you're having this feeling that I guess it's a feeling of anxiety or stress.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Alright. Sorry for the interruption. It's okay. You gotta do a room change. So. To pick off where to leave? To pick up where we left off. You're talking about the feeling you get when you make new friends. And you're talking about excitement. What else?
Client: And just being really nervous when I meet them because it's like, what they'll think of me.
Counselor: And has anyone ever. What makes you nervous about what they'll think of you? Because you said you were popular before, so.
Client: Yeah, just because I've always known what it feels like to be cool and to have friends and to not be in a position where I'm all alone. So I think just the thought of this being a reality, which it is, is just really scary. And I think the worst of it and.
Counselor: Yeah, so it sounds like there's a drastic change from being popular, feeling very alone and not having any friends. So it's a transition for you.
Client: Yeah. How do you.
Counselor: How are you adjusting with that? Besides going out to bars and making new friends? What are some other feelings you get with that transition?
Client: Well, just kind of. Helpless and hopeless, really. Like I said, just finding a job. I really don't know what I want to do anymore. After I graduated, I thought I was gonna get into business, but I just really don't know if that's for me. My parents always kind of gave me everything too. So the reason why I have my own apartment is because they bought it for me. But it was under the conditions of having to be in the same town as them. And so it's like I'm at a loss and I could continue just loving off my parents money, but then that kind of feels. I feel like I don't have a purpose. Like my purpose really just going to be to live off my parents money and kind of do whatever they want me to do and just to keep their money and their resources. So I'm just kind of at a loss right now in my life.
Counselor: Did you feel that way when you were in college?
Client: No. I was having time in my life. It was. I wasn't even thinking about anything like this or the next step or what's gonna happen after I graduate. And I thought I would, you know, get a really cool internship through some business company. But at the time I didn't really. I wasn't really seeking it out because I was just having fun.
Counselor: So now you're feeling like you have to actually make plans and be more self sufficient?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Do you feel like you. You mentioned being hopeless. Is that preventing you at all from taking the next step or initiating the next step in your life?
Client: I feel like I'm trying. It's just. I don't know what to do about it, though. Like, I. There's only so much you can do when you don't know what the next step is for you or what you're passionate about or. So it's hard to go in any direction when.
Counselor: You don't know what direction you want. Have you had any ideas about what you're passionate about or any.
Client: Well, I wish, like, partying was a job, but it's not. I mean, I love to have fun. And. I don't really have. I don't know.
Counselor:
output: It sounds like you may be a little confused almost because you said you didn't want the party type friends, but you're really passionate about partying.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Gabriella. I understand that you're here today because you've been experiencing some low mood.
Client: Yeah, I just. Recently, I'm just feeling down a lot and I can't really, like, snap out of it. Like, sometimes if it's happened before, I can just, like, get myself back on track, but recently I just find it really difficult to do.
Counselor: Hey, so it sounds like you've been experiencing some low mood and you're kind of struggling to get going a bit.
Client: Yeah, yeah, definitely.
Counselor: You've had low mood in the past, but it's kind of. You've been able to pull yourself out of it before, but more recently you found that harder. Okay, so I understand that you first went to your GP. He referred you here about two months ago. Can I ask what led you to go to the GP in the first place?
Client: My long term boyfriend broke up with me and it was such a shock. Like, I really wasn't expecting it and it just got me really down and I just felt really lonely and I didn't really want to see people and just wanted to be in my own space. And my mum told me I should probably go to the doctors. Oh. And he's referred me to you.
Counselor: Okay. So it sounds then like you had that breakup and you weren't expecting it, so it kind of came out of the blue a bit and that you've been on your own quite a lot, so you've not been seeing people as much. And it sounds like your mum noticed that there's been a bit of a change in you. Okay. And how have things been then, since then, since that happened and since you went to the GP?
Client: I just. Nothing's really changed. Nothing's really improved. I just feel down, like everything's an effort and just feel distant from things. And like I said, I can't snap out of it.
Counselor: Okay. And how did you feel about coming here today?
Client: I was kind of disappointed in myself because I feel like nobody else my age is doing this. Like, I should have been able to snap out of it. Like, it's just another thing that I've not really. It's another thing that's making me stand out for the wrong reasons.
Counselor: Okay. So you feel like it's kind of odd or unusual to be coming to see a clinical psychologist? I suppose I just want to reassure you that it's absolutely normal to have feelings of depression and anxiety. It's really very common and it certainly isn't odd or strange at all. So it sounds like it was actually quite hard for you to come here today?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So what, I guess led you to do that? Because it sounds like maybe there was a lot pushing you against coming here today, but you've managed to come anyway.
Client: I'm just hoping that it's gonna help, I think. I didn't really want to admit it because it's just another failure, but my mum was talking to me and I know she's not really happy with the way I'm behaving. I didn't really want to disappoint her again and so I thought there's no harm in it, so she thought it'd come.
Counselor: So it sounds like partly you're doing it then, for your mum because you're a bit worried that she isn't pleased with you at the moment.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. Well, I think it's great that you've come here and definitely there's a lot of evidence to suggest that psychological therapy can help depression and particularly the type of therapy that we're going to be doing, which is called cognitive behaviour therapy. And I'll tell you a bit more about that as we go on, but I'm just trying to find out a bit more about you today. So I saw from your notes that you're a medic student.
Client: Yeah, I'm not currently in uni at the moment, but, yeah, last year as a medic student.
Counselor: Okay. So I guess what's the reason that you're not in uni this year?
Client: It was pretty tough first year, so they then suggested that I took a year out. This is the break.
Counselor: Okay. So just thinking. So that would be about six months ago, was it that your year out started? Yeah. And it sounds then maybe like your first year was also quite tough.
Client: Yeah, it was. I thought it's tough for everyone, but obviously we all take it in different ways, don't we?
Counselor: And you're planning on. Are you planning on returning and.
Client: Yeah, I'm gonna have to. Really? So. Yeah.
Counselor: Don't sound too sure about that, though.
Client: I think returning is probably that's what's gonna make everyone happy. And I think, you know, at least I'll be able to finally achieve something and get something right, so. Yeah, like, next year I'm gonna. I'll get through it. Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. So it doesn't. It doesn't sound like you want to go back.
Client: I do. I do enjoy it. I just don't feel like me at the moment and I just. It's a lot of work and it's a lot of pressure, but that's what comes of it. And, you know, it'll work out for the best if I go.
Counselor: Okay. So I guess then there's quite a lot of thoughts and feelings about going back at the moment. I'm just wondering, in the meantime, what are you up to? What have you been doing?
Client: Well, I've not really had much on the horizon. My mum, her friend, owns a restaurant and she suggested that I did a bit of waitressing there just for a bit of money and stuff, because obviously I'm not in uni, so I've done that.
Counselor: Okay. How many shifts have you done there?
Client: I've only done one so far. Yeah. I don't know whether it's something that I'd probably go back to, but.
Counselor: Okay. When was that shift?
Client: It was last week, actually. Okay.
Counselor: And how was it? I suppose I'm intrigued. Can you tell me a bit more about that?
Client: It was different, you know, because it was like, I could. I did enjoy it because there was like. It's just different aspect and I had to, like, speak to people and, like, try to get their orders and try to remember it and stuff. Like, I wasn't very good, but I suppose, like, it was handy to have some money and, like, get out the house.
Counselor:
output: Okay, so it sounds like you quite enjoyed that, then.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Victoria. How you doing today?
Client: Doing okay.
Counselor: Been doing okay. It's been a while now. You've been practicing with the waiting after you wash your hands? Mm hmm. How's that been going for you?
Client: Well, I think it's been going pretty well. I've been able to, you know, wait pretty good. I'm gonna start it out slow like you suggested, with three minutes. Then I would wash my hands for five minutes. I would wash my hands, and I got up to about 15 minutes.
Counselor: That's great.
Client: And there were some times that I was really proud of myself that I actually forgot.
Counselor: You forgot to wash your hands entirely?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So when was the next time you washed them?
Client: When I would go to, like, eat. Dinner,
Counselor: which is when you normally wash your hands. So really, you touched something that had germs, and you had some anxiety as you had to get to that waiting period. But then the anxiety subsided to a point where I forgot about it just wasn't a priority. You just completely forgot and went on with your day?
Client: Yeah. I was really proud of myself, but I got really concerned because I got sick. I got sick recently, and I'm afraid it's from one of those times that I didn't wash my hands.
Counselor: Well, tell me about the sickness.
Client: Well, my throat started to get hurt real bad, and I was just really congested. And all I could think about was, it's because I didn't wash my hands when I went to the store or when I went to my car when I touched a jacket. That's, you know, been everywhere.
Counselor: How many times do you normally get it? Sounds like a cold.
Client: I mean, it was kind of a light cold.
Counselor: Light cold.
Client: I mean, we wouldn't wait in a.
Counselor: Few days, a couple days. So how long or how many times a year would you get something like that normally?
Client: I mean, I get sick. I mean, quite often because of my job. I'm around a lot of people, and hand sanitizer can only work so much. I do get sick.
Counselor:
output: So it's been six weeks since you started waiting? Right. I think it was around session three where we talked about putting a gap between when you touch something, when you wash your hands, like a time gap, and you got a cold once. Would that be out of the ordinary to get a cold one time in six weeks this time of year?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Lucy. Nice to meet you.
Client: Hi.
Counselor: So I understand that you were referred here by your GP because you've been feeling quite down recently.
Client: Yeah, I thought I should. I've been feeling quite bad for quite a while, so I thought maybe it's time to see someone about it because I don't want to feel like this anymore.
Counselor: Okay. So from your notes, I saw that you saw the GP about three months ago?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So how long have you been feeling down altogether?
Client: Quite a few months before that as well, actually. But it's gotten pretty bad these past few months, so that's kind of why I came.
Counselor: Okay. So has it got worse since you saw your GP?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay, so tell me, how are things at the moment?
Client: Well, it kind of started just feeling a bit low and wound up about things, but, I don't know, just recently I just can't really be bothered to do anything at all. I kind of find it hard to get motivated for things and I want to be. I really want to be better, but it's just kind of reaching the end now where I just. I want to do something about it.
Counselor: Okay, so you said that you're feeling really down, really sad?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you feel like you haven't got any motivation, but. Are you okay?
Client: Yeah, I'm fine.
Counselor: Sorry. Okay, and you haven't got any motivation, but it sounds like you've put quite a lot of pressure on yourself to try and feel a bit better.
Client: Yeah, I just. It's kind of hard as well because there's not really anyone to talk about. So I just kind of stay on my own trying to. I don't like to think about it, but I don't know.
Counselor: So you say you've been. You've been feeling quite isolated. There's not many people around.
Client: Yeah. There's no one I can talk to about it. No one would listen or understand anyway.
Counselor: Okay, so I'm just going to try and find out a little bit more about you. So I understand that you're an english student at uni.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you live away from home with some friends. Is that right?
Client: Yeah, I live here.
Counselor: Oh, okay. So you don't live far from the uni, but you say you feel like you live with your friends, but you don't feel like you can talk to them.
Client: Yeah, I mean, they're lovely. I get on really well with them, but I don't know, recently, whenever they want to go out or stuff, I just. I don't want to bring them down. I can't. They don't understand what I'm going through. They kind of. I don't know, they don't make fun of how I feel, but they don't really understand what it's like. I just. I don't want to go out with them and bring them down or stuff.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds. Do you try and hide the way you're feeling from them?
Client: I guess. I mean, it's easier to hide it than to try and explain it all the time when no one really wants to know.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like you've been feeling down, you've been feeling unmotivated, you feel like you want to be better. But actually it sounds like you feel like you can't reach out for help, you can't speak to anybody.
Client: No, I don't really talk to my parents a lot either, so that's kind of hard.
Counselor: Okay. I'm just gonna go back in time a little bit, I suppose. I'm just wondering, when did all of this start? You said it's been going on for quite a few months.
Client: Yeah, I guess it kind of started, actually, when I was revising for my exams. I guess the stress. I put a lot of stress on myself. I think I've always wanted to do well for me and I guess for my parents. So the stress of exams. And it was also kind of hard because my parents were going through a bit of a troubled time then.
Counselor: Okay, so this would be like last March, last April?
Client: Yeah, I think so.
Counselor: Around that time. So about six months ish. And it sounds like a lot was happening. So you had a lot of uni pressure on and you said that your parents were having marital problems. Okay. And it sounds like that was a real shock to you.
Client: Yeah, I guess it was hard as well because I wasn't doing well at uni. I guess I just felt a bit guilty. I know it sounds silly, but I felt like maybe if I could do better, then they would get better, but it just wasn't really happening.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like you were trying to work hard and be more successful because you thought that that would make them happier and try and fix things.
Client: Yeah, I wanted to make them feel better, but it just kind of backfired a little, I guess.
Counselor: How did it backfire?
Client: Well, it just ended up with them getting worse, and I've just been feeling worse since then.
Counselor: Okay, so after the summer, after the exam period. And how did that exam period go for you in the end?
Client: Not very well.
Counselor: Okay. That's an awful lot of pressure to put on yourself that you supposed to.
Client: Think it's just annoying because I know I should have done better and I just didn't. And I guess I beat myself up a lot about it.
Counselor: So you say. I know, I know I should have done better.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I mean, I suppose hearing it from my perspective, I'm thinking it sounds like you had an awful lot going on at the time. It would be understandable, absolutely. That you wouldn't do as well as normal. I suppose I'm just wondering if you have very high standards for yourself.
Client: Probably maybe more than other people. My parents have always kind of taught me. Not in a loving way, I guess, but that you should do your best, but also get the best. And I agree with that. I think that's the right thing to think. But when I don't do that, I don't know, it annoys me a lot and I worry that it annoys them.
Counselor: So it sounds like you feel you should always do your best. Is that the word you used? Yeah. And that there isn't any kind of exceptions for that, but no. Okay. So I can see then that was a really difficult time for you and that was when your mood started to get lower. And things are still quite bad now. I mean, what's the situation with your parents at the moment?
Client: I think it doesn't sound good. I don't really talk to them a lot, but I don't think they're going through very good. I don't like to talk to them about it because it just makes me feel worse. But I don't think it's getting any better.
Counselor: Were you home over the summer?
Client: For a little bit, yeah.
Counselor: And how was that?
Client: Not very fun? No, it was quite tense all the time. Stress me out more than relaxed me over the summer, I guess.
Counselor: Okay. Okay. So it sounds then like quite a lot has been happening. You've been feeling very low, you've had uni pressure on, and you've had problems with your parents marriage. And sounds like you feel like you can't really reach out to anyone. Like you can't understand, but you can't really reach out to your parents right now. You can't really confide in your friends. So I suppose I'm just wondering if you can tell me a bit more about how you've been feeling. I mean, say this past week.
Client: Really not good, to be honest. I actually. If I don't have to, then I don't really leave the house or get out of. But I just. I can't find the motivation for the things I used to join. I used to love doing sports or going out. And now I just prefer to lie in bed and not really do anything.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: I missed a few lectures this week that I should have gone to.
Counselor: Right. So I suppose I'm just wondering then let's see if we can think about one thing. Say a lecture. What kind of thoughts do you have about going to that lecture before it happens?
Client: I don't really see the point anymore. If I can't do as well as I should be doing, then what's the point in putting myself in those positions? I can't be bothered anymore to try. It just stresses me out more than I need to.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like the kind of thoughts you've got in your head are. It's pointless. It's not worth it.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Do you have any other thoughts in your head when you're just at that point before you go to the lecture?
Client: I feel like. I don't know. I don't really even deserve to be hear if I can't do well enough. I see all these other students who are doing well and doing better and want to be there. I don't know why I'm here, even at uni, to be honest.
Counselor:
output: So it sounds like you feel like you're not as good as other people here.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, Liz. How you doing today?
Client: I'm okay. How are you?
Counselor: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. How things been going?
Client: They've been all right.
Counselor: Last time we were talking, it sounds like you're still having some difficulty with the quizzes. Is that still the case?
Client: Yeah, I still panic when I take them.
Counselor: You still panic. Can you tell me about the process of taking the quizzes? I know we've touched on this a little bit before.
Client: Okay, so I'm going to class. I'm fine. I sit down to take the test. I'm fine. The test is in front of me. Question one. I'm not going to get that answer.
Counselor: So you're looking down. So you take these quizzes in class?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Like a paper, pencil. Okay. With other students around?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: All right. Is the. Is having other students around distracting to you?
Client: No, it's happened in previous online classes. It's the same.
Counselor: So it's. You're pretty sure it's the quiz itself and not some external. Okay. So it's paper and pencil. You're seated, you're in the room. Rooms relatively distraction free.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. Everybody's quiet.
Counselor: And you're looking down at, really the first item on the.
Client: Mm hmm.
Counselor: On the quiz. And what's happening? What's happening? Then as you look down, you read that first item. What's happening at a thought. We'll start a thought level. What's happening with your thinking?
Client: I'm thinking. I'm reading the question, and I'm thinking, oh, my God, there's. Okay, there's four. Okay. So it's got to be. It's got to be one of them. And I am not going to pick the right one. I'm going to think I picked the right one, and it's going to be the one that my second choice is, and I am not going to pick the right one.
Counselor: Okay, so your thought is that you're going to get. You're going to select the wrong response and therefore get that quiz item wrong. How about behavior? Like, do you notice anything physically going on as you're thinking about that quiz item and how you're gonna get it wrong?
Client: I'd say my palms are probably sweaty. Like, I'm probably a little tense.
Counselor: A little tense.
Client: Yeah. That's really it.
Counselor: All right. So what it could be is that this thought of I'm gonna get this item wrong is leading to these uncomfortable feelings, the physical feelings. So what happens when you answer item one like, you don't know if you have it right or wrong immediately? Right because it's a paper and pencil. So you answer item one, and you move on to item two. What happens then?
Client: It starts all over again. I'm already, like, well, I already got the first one wrong, and now I'm. My chances are higher of getting this one wrong.
Counselor: So you feel like it because you. Because you thought that you got the first one wrong, that your chances of getting the second one wrong actually increase?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Like, I get one wrong the whole test, it's all gonna be wrong.
Counselor: Have you ever had a quiz that you've taken where you were confident that you got the first item right?
Client: I'm sure I have. I can't remember any.
Counselor: But eventually you're going to come to one item that you're going to have these doubts about?
Client: Yes. Inevitably it happens.
Counselor: There's going to be one that's maybe a little more difficult or difficult for you. So it seems like what you're saying is that when you reach that item where you have that thought from that point on, the next item is. Is more difficult because you're having a similar thought. Does that pattern continue throughout the test?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So explain to me what, like, let's just go with the example of the first item, like, just to keep it more simple. So you have the first item, and that didn't work out for you, that thought? Right. The second one, your thought was, I have even a greater chance of missing a. So what happens after you respond to that second item?
Client: It just compounds. I just start. I feel worse and worse as the quiz, as I continue.
Counselor: That's awful. So it's an awful feeling for me. Right. So by the time you get to.
Client: Item five or six, I'm convinced it's over. I've gotten a zero. If it's the. Yeah, if I start at the first, I've gotten a zero. I've gotten a bad grade.
Counselor: So that's what's on your mind. And how about those physical symptoms? Are they the same, different or new symptoms?
Client: If it, like. If it's. If it, like, starts early at the beginning of the test, my heart's, like, pounding at this point, but I still have the sweaty palms. I'm still, like, tensing.
Counselor: So it really just gets mentally and physically more unpleasant for you the whole time. So when you're saying panic, the panic's really occurring a few items in after you have the first one that you thought you missed. And this has been happening for a while, as you described, right?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Well, how about your grades? How have you actually been doing on the quizzes?
Client: I've been a pretty solid b student, so. And I feel. I wish I did better. I wish I got a's, but, I mean, these are fine. But when I take those quizzes, it's not. It doesn't. I don't know how it translates.
Counselor: How about your study habits? You consider yourself effective at studying?
Client: I've tried. I've taken a workshops on studying. I've. I. I think I'm pretty effective at studying. I've found what doesn't work. So I try to study by reading the chapters, taking outlines, reviewing flashcards, which has, I think, the best results, but.
Counselor: Okay, so your study habits are good, right. And your quiz scores are good, but you're still having these distressing thoughts and these uncomfortable physical sensations when you take the quizzes.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Is that about right?
Client: Yeah, that's absolutely right.
Counselor: So really you don't necessarily need your performance to change. You just. You just need your thoughts and feelings and behaviors to change.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So how you. How you're reacting to the quizzes maybe?
Client: Yeah, because I get b is, like I said, so, yeah.
Counselor: And b is good.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So. All right, so I want to take you back to the moment when you're looking at the first item. Let's go back to that for a second. Okay. So you're taking a quiz and you're having those thoughts surrounding that first item, which I'm not mistaken, the automatic thought. We talked about this, right? With the cognitive behavioral therapy. The automatic thought is that I'm not going to get this one right or something to that effect. What does that mean to you?
Client: It means once I don't get that right, I'm not going to get anything else right.
Counselor: All right. So what that thought means to you is that you're going to miss that item and then you're going to miss all the rest of the items. So you're going to fail the whole quiz.
Client: The whole thing, yeah.
Counselor: So looking at that, let's call that an intermediate belief, right. It's more of a rule or an expectation. Right. What does that mean to you?
Client: It just gets worse. If I fail the quiz, then I'm like, oh, my God, I'm gonna fail the final, I'm gonna fail the course and that's going to affect my GPA.
Counselor: So it just keeps stacking. So other beliefs. So you're going to fail the course and we're going to fail the final rather than you can fail the course. So if you failed the course, what would that mean to you then?
Client: I'm not going to graduate.
Counselor: You're not going to graduate. So we move from fail in the quiz if we just look at the meaning, right. To fail in the final, to fail in the course, and now to not graduating. So if you didn't graduate, what would that mean to you?
Client: I can't. I can't be a teacher. I can't do what I want to do.
Counselor: So your chosen vocation to be a teacher would be not possible.
Client: Right.
Counselor: Right. So we go a step further and say, what would it mean to you if you couldn't be a teacher?
Client: I don't know who I'd be at that point. That's what I always saw as my career. So I don't know what my future would look like at that point without that.
Counselor: So if you were to phrase it and kind of think back as we to the CBT techniques and I kind of conceptualization we've covered, if you're to phrase that as an I am statement, right. What would you. What would you be if you couldn't be a teacher? What would that make you?
Client: I am a person who didn't make it. I'm a person that failed.
Counselor: Like we said earlier, I'm a person that didn't make it. I'm a person who failed. So in a way you're saying I'm a failure, right? Is that close?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So remember we talked before about core beliefs and how these core beliefs drive these intermediate beliefs which combine with situations like, in your case, taking a quiz to form these automatic thoughts. So one of your core beliefs may be that you're a failure. You may believe that. Does that seem like something that you've said to yourself before or thought before.
Client: About it like that? Until we did the step up to it now. But I can relate to that because a lot of times I do feel like, oh, I'm not going to be able to do this because it's me. I won't be able to do it.
Counselor: Not because it's challenging or difficult, but something to do with you. So that's where kind of you're personalizing.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So you're saying to yourself at a variety of levels, I'm going to be unsuccessful, I'm going to fail. Does that make sense?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you think that's what's happening?
Client: It must be because, like I said, I study, I get good grades. I've been tested years ago. I don't have ADHD. Anything intrinsic that would prohibit me.
Counselor: So you're able to focus and concentrate.
Client: Well, yes, I can do all of that, but when it comes to it, I'm like, I can't do it.
Counselor: So somewhere. Somewhere is this discord belief, and it's possible that it has something to do with you believing that you are a failure. Unsuccessful.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: How do you think your, say, friends or family would interpret that? Like, if. I'm not suggesting, telling them that, but if they were to somehow know that, that you believed you were a failure, how would they react?
Client: I don't think they would see the connection. I think they would be like, well, you do well in school. I don't understand.
Counselor: So they wouldn't believe that you're a failure?
Client: No.
Counselor: You may believe it.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: And similarly, if you had a classmate that was in the same situation and, you know, struggled with these disturbing thoughts and feelings and behaviors during quizzes, how would you evaluate them?
Client: I guess I'd say the same thing that my family would say. Like, you're look at the evidence, you're not a failure.
Counselor:
output: You'd say, look at the evidence and you'd evaluate that they weren't a failure.
