instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hazel, how you doing today?
Client: I'm okay.
Counselor: What's been going on?
Client: Well, last time I started to tell you a little bit about one of my friends, my best friend, actually, she had this issue. So what happened was she went to a bathroom at our local library, and she found a video camera when she was going to the bathroom.
Counselor: In the bathroom?
Client: Yeah. She actually. Yeah. And she turned it into the police, and I guess because, like, she carried it, or she had found it, her handprints were on it, and they weren't be able. They weren't able to detect who actually did it. They weren't able to catch the person.
Counselor: Oh, they didn't catch the person?
Client: No. So since then, I've been on really just high alert. Like, I'm worried that that could happen to me, to my kids, and I'm just really worried because they didn't catch the guy, that him or someone like him could be out there.
Counselor: So he's still out in the community.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So how is it affecting your. Your daily life? Can you tell me kind of what your. What you've been feeling?
Client: Um, a lot of anxiety just not knowing, maybe, you know, what if someone were to videotape me like that? I've been very aware, shall I say, of cameras.
Counselor: Okay. So anxious and aware.
Client: Right. Like, I know you have one in your office, and people on their cell phone cameras. Just all the possibilities that I could be recorded. I've just been very aware of them, which makes me not want to go anywhere. So I've been having arguments with my husband a lot because he wants to go out to restaurants, and I don't want to go because there could be cameras in the bathrooms and how I dress. Also, as you can see, I'm kind of dressed more conservatively because I remember hearing once about cameras that people use on shoes that could be used in a creepy way. And so I can't. You know, it's now almost summertime. I can't dress in skirts or be comfortable because I'm dressing like that.
Counselor: So you covered a lot of ground there. So you have the. You have the feeling of being, like, worried, nervous. Right. That's going to happen to you, but you've also had to kind of change your routine, or you feel you have to change your routine to feel safer.
Client: Right.
Counselor: Has that helped. Has changing the way you dressed or changing where you go and when you go, has that helped reduce the anxiety?
Client: Not really, no. I would say it's really starting. That's why I wanted to come in. It's really starting to affect my life.
Counselor: You mentioned specifically your husband. Like, what's been going on there?
Client: He just wants to go places with our kids, like, go out to eat. And I don't really want to go anywhere because, you know, cameras are everywhere nowadays, and I just kind of worry, like, public bathrooms, could they be there? Could someone be, you know, sometimes baby monitors are, you know, hooked up on so people can hack into that laptop, cameras. So even in my own house, I've just been really nervous, so I feel like I'm not really getting relief from that anxiety.
Counselor: Have you taken any precautions because of this persistent worry? I mean, I already mentioned, like, with the camera specifically.
Client: I mean, I've, you know, when I go into bathrooms, I've been looking for cameras to make sure they weren't there before. You know, me or my children have used the bathroom. I have tried. I read online that you can turn how to turn off the cameras on your phone and that you can close your laptop, and that way the camera will face down. And the same thing on a smart tv so it doesn't recognize your face. I've tried to turn things off. They don't need to be on as far as people being able to access my own information.
Counselor: And that seems reasonable. So you take reasonable precautions to try to avoid being video recorded against your will.
Client: Exactly.
Counselor: Okay. But still, you have this feeling of worry, anxiety, and your schedules being interfered with.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So you'd like to cope more effectively with your feelings, reduce this anxiety. So when you enter into a public bathroom. Now, we talked about automatic thoughts before.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor:
output: Those thoughts just kind of pop into our head and they connect to feelings of that can be unpleasant, like anxiety and worry. So when you walk into a public restroom, what's the first thing that goes through your mind?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Alisa, how are you doing today?
Client: I'm doing well, thank you.
Counselor: Doing well.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: What's going on?
Client: I have family coming into town and I have to go to the airport to pick them up.
Counselor: So you have family flying in?
Client: Yes. That's something that I get very anxious about, having to cross the bridge. I have to cross the Ben Franklin bridge and then get over the bridge that goes to the airport by the stadium. I think that's the Girard point bridge. Yeah. That's two levels there. I have to do that both ways.
Counselor: Going and coming both ways. You have to cross four times?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So what kind of feeling is this bringing up for you?
Client: I get very anxious even just thinking about it right now.
Counselor: So you're anxious right here with me?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So I want to try to scale this. We talked about this before with cognitive therapy. So let's say that ten is really the most anxious you're felt about crossing bridges, and one is no anxiety. Where would you be right now?
Client: Right now, probably an eight. Yeah.
Counselor: I don't love anxiety.
Client: Yes. It's worse when I'm at that point on that day, but right now, I think just knowing that I have to do that. Yes.
Counselor: And what's it on that day?
Client: A ten.
Counselor: It reaches a ten, definitely.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: All right. So. But even now, how far away is the. Until they.
Client: Oh, it's a week.
Counselor: So even now, a week out, it's. Nate, this is really hurting.
Client: Yes. I don't like that at all.
Counselor: So for your job and local travel, you don't really have to cross any.
Client: Ten minutes to work every day. And banks. So 20 minutes, shopping centers and everything is just within the vicinity. I don't have to cross any bridges.
Counselor: So no bridges?
Client: No, not at all. I probably planned it that way, too.
Counselor: That worked out well.
Client: That worked out very well.
Counselor: All right. But coming up, pick up the family you will be crossing. So let's look at this at each stage. So, I mean, you're clearly anxious now, as you mentioned. But let's go to, let's try to move forward a week to the day that they'll be flying, what time they fly in.
Client: It's going to be a 04:00 flight. In the afternoon.
Counselor: In the afternoon. So about what time would you have to leave to?
Client: I would have to leave probably at 03:00 because it's only about 20 minutes to the airport. Really?
Counselor: Really.
Client: But I would like to leave earlier. They'll probably take them time. By the time they land and go through, you know, getting their luggages, they probably won't even come out till maybe 430, but I'd like to make sure I'm there at around 334 o'clock.
Counselor: All right, so let's go to that day. Let's go to that day and to that afternoon. So you're still at home. And let's say we're about 15 minutes before you have to get in the car. Car. What are you thinking then?
Client: I have to do this. I have to get up and go. They need me to be there this week. It's my parents coming in and they're elderly, so I don't want them to be stuck at the airport. There's no one else that actually can go pick them up. So I have to get up and go and pick them up.
Counselor: That's what's going through your mind?
Client: That's what's going through my mind. So, you know, there's nobody else that can do this. I mean, it's cheaper than there's no. I probably can't even afford to get a taxi for them because you'd have to cross that's from Philly to. Into New Jersey. So that's going to be very expensive. I can't afford that. When all I'd have to do is pay $5 for the tow and maybe gas up my car for $10 or something. But, um, I. Yeah, I'll be thinking about, I have to do this.
Counselor: I have to do it.
Client: I can do it. Something that I can save money that way. And I don't want to leave them stranded. Definitely someone else can. I mean, they'd be lost. They're not familiar with the airport. And Philly airport is crazy to me.
Counselor: Yeah, it's a big place. A lot going on. So. So you're sitting at home in 15 minutes before getting the cardinal and you're thinking, I have to do this. But your reasons are positive. Like you save money and protect your parents from having to be there alone. So when does the anxiety come in?
Client: Just the thought of the bridge, it's just. I could drive off the bridge. I can fall off. Usually what I do is try to stay in the middle lane. I can't do more than 40 miles an hour. And I just. I'm shaking. I have the radio on and windows down because I can't swim. So if for any reason I'm to fall off, I mean, that's it for me. I even have a little metal one of those. I think it's an instrument that you use in the house for, I don't know, plier or something. Something real hard that I can hit the ground with. It sits right there on my door, on the side of my door. So I'm already, I planned, I have that. I planned ahead of time. I know what I'm going to do as soon as I approach the bridge, but I still feel anxious.
Counselor: So you're anxious before you leave and you're starting to think about the bridge at that point. You already think about it. How about when you get in your car, you start driving toward the bridge?
Client: I say a prayer. I am still anxious. I turn on the radio and the closer I get to, especially the toll point, and I know it's at me. And you see those lights flashing. Last exit before the, you know, the.
Counselor: Toll, you know you're going over once.
Client: Yeah, there's no turning back. There's no turning back.
Counselor: So before that, when you can still exit, what's your anxiety level?
Client: Before, when I can still exit?
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: It'S probably still high. It's probably at a nine or so.
Counselor: It's still high, but it's not maxed out yet. But it's pretty bad.
Client: Yeah, I think it's pretty bad at that point.
Counselor: And how about when you cross through the.
Client: That's when it's at a ten.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Yes, yes.
Counselor: So your specific fear as you start to cross, this is the Ben Franklin would be the first bridge. Right. You can go across. Is that your car will go off the bridge?
Client: Yes, definitely.
Counselor: And when does that, so that's a ten anxiety. When does that anxiety start to go away?
Client: As soon as I'm getting close to getting off the bridge, I'm now leaving a little sigh of the, there's a little release there. And I know that I've been able to manage those two, three minutes of cross. I don't know how many minutes it takes actually crossing the bridge. I start feeling a little bit of relief, but then again, I know I have to take that exit and there's another one coming right up, so starts all over again.
Counselor: All right, so then you cross the second bridge, the Gerard point bridge, you go to the airport. Does your anxiety drop, any of those points?
Client: Oh, as soon as I'm descending from the Gerard Point bridge, there's less, you know, it's almost reduced. I come, you know, really low.
Counselor: It's almost gone.
Client: Yes. It's almost gone. Yes.
Counselor: And when do you start thinking about that? You're going to have to cross them again?
Client: As soon as I'm exit, I'm getting back on 95 going north. And I know, here we go again. And cars are zooming by and you.
Counselor: Know, because you're not going very quickly.
Client: No, no, I'm that person. The middle lane doing 40 miles an hour. Yes.
Counselor: All right. So you're doing everything you can to keep your car on the bridge, but you're still feeling anxiety, like you're going to go off the bridge.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: The whole time. Until you start really descending.
Client: Exactly.
Counselor: And then you feel like you made it.
Client: Especially when there are those big trucks.
Counselor: Tractor trailers coming because the air.
Client: Yes, yes. Or if it's also in bad weather or at night, it's worst because on the bridge, especially the top one, you kind of see the sky and there's nothing else you see. So it's like you're gonna fall off. Yes.
Counselor: So in the lower level it's not as bad.
Client: On the lower, lower level, coming back it's not as bad because you're kind of like protected here and there. So it's not as bad, but going it's definitely worse. Yes.
Counselor: Are you aware of any time a car would have gone off the bridge?
Client: I hear on the news once in a while you'll hear something happen, or sometimes in movies you see things happen. I think it's possible.
Counselor: It's possible?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: You think it's a high risk?
Client: No, maybe not on that Gerard bridge. Because I noticed. I was checking it the other day, I had to go to the airport and I was trying to measure the distance between the metal poles just to see if a car could fit there. Really? And I think a car could fit there, but, you know, it just depends on the angle you were hit or something or if you flew. So, yeah.
Counselor: Done some thinking, she's done some calculations, geometry. And you've concluded that it's not really likely, but it could. It could fly off the. Alright, but either way, your anxiety is maxed out on each bridge.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Now when you get home, get your parents back to take them back to your home.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: How do you feel then?
Client: I don't even recall all the anxiety. Why it was such a big deal anyway. I don't think about it at all.
Counselor: All right, so when you arrive home, you're down to one.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: All right. So going back to the. The first stage, like when you're getting ready, you were thinking that you have to go.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And it would save your parents money?
Client: It would save me money. I would be the one calling the cat.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: But I would be the one to pick them up and save them from being stranded at the airport and being in a land that they're not familiar with an area they're not familiar with. Make sure that they're safe.
Counselor: How important is their safety to you?
Client: Oh, very important.
Counselor: Very important?
Client: Yes, very important.
Counselor: So, I mean, clearly it sounds like you picked them up before.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So picking them up is. It's worth all the anxiety?
Client: It's worth it, yes. Something that bothers me that I have to do, but, yeah, it's worth the anxiety. I would say so.
Counselor: It's worth it. But you wish that you could do it without anxiety.
Client: Yes, I wish there was another route that I could take and make it to the airport without any bridges at all, but that's not.
Counselor: There's no route without any bridges yet to find. And how long have you had the anxiety with driving fridges?
Client: As long as I can remember that. I know, maybe not when I was younger, but perhaps as a mother and, you know, as someone as I got older and had responsibilities and knew that life was important, I mean, prior to maybe marriage and kids, I didn't have that anxiety. I don't recall having that, even driving or anything like that. I don't recall that.
Counselor: All right. They developed along the way somewhere. And it's been with you ever since?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Okay, so I'd like to do what cognitive therapy, we call a reframe. And actually, you've kind of already done it, but I want to make it a little clearer. So you suffer the anxiety, and you suffer it to protect, mostly to protect your parents. So as you're going over the bridge, you're thinking about the automatic thought. We talked about these before. The thought that kind of pops in your mind is, I'm going to fly off the bridge.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So that seems pretty unlikely. Right? That's not something that maybe, as you talked about geometrically, maybe there's a way that your car could fly the bridge. With physics, maybe it could happen, but it seems like it would be. You're fairly unlikely, so you could challenge that. And this isn't the reframe part, but you could challenge that on that thought, which, with a statement and adaptive response, like, it's pretty unlikely anything's going to happen. That might help a bit. Keep applying that. The chances are vastly in your favor, considering how many cars cross that bridge. How many fly off the bridge? I don't know if I've ever heard of a car fly off one of those bridges. But the other, the reframe part is that you're doing this. You're willing to take on the bridges and have this anxiety for the betterment of your parents. For their safety.
Client: Yes, definitely.
Counselor: So in this whole equation of crossing bridges and anxiety, you're really the good guy in this, right? You're willing to suffer and overcome a fear to make sure your parents are safe.
Client: I never really thought of it like that.
Counselor: Yeah. I mean, and you've thought about it before, like, before you leave, you think, I really have to pick them up. But you've never really connected it to.
Client: No, I haven't connected it to their safety.
Counselor: Well, to be in the good guy.
Client: Well, yeah. Okay.
Counselor:
output: Does that make sense?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Victoria. How you doing today?
Client: Pretty good.
Counselor: Very good. How has the anxiety been around the germs?
Client: I still catch myself, like, double, almost like double touching. Like going to touch it and then reeling back. So I'm starting to notice it, but I still, I still have that anxiety. I still don't want to touch it.
Counselor: When you pretty much touch anything you might think has germs on it.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What are some things that you've touched in the last, between the last session and this session that have distressed you?
Client: Well, I had to go to the store, which is always a nightmare for me because I don't even like touching my credit card because it's been in so many machines and there's so much dirt and junk that gets in there and then the counters and all the. I keep thinking about the food that's there, and I, you know, if I pick it up off the shelf, how many people have picked it up with their nasty hands or kids picked it up with nasty hands and then put it back, and it's like, I need to eat. But shopping's a nightmare for me.
Counselor: So really, in a, like, a supermarket, everything can be containing germs. Have germs on it?
Client: Yeah, everything does.
Counselor: Everything does. And that's what you're thinking about as you're walking through and shopping. We talked about last time, exposure and response prevention, and I explained kind of the general idea. But you remember that conversation. Yeah, I remember. I indicated that we might try some experiments right in session to see how, see if we can move kind of forward and treating your, kind of your fear and obsession with germs and really the anxiety it's causing for you, it's like getting in the way of your life.
Client: It is. It really is.
Counselor: So I was wondering, is there anything in here, in this office, as you look around, that you would look at and think, I don't want to touch that because it could have germs on it.
Client: I'm really not liking the covers on this chair because, I mean, I can't. I mean, at least what I'm sitting in now, my clothes are protecting me from the rest of the chair.
Counselor: Mm hmm.
Client: But, I mean, I have no sleeves on, so I don't like touching the armrests and the covers.
Counselor: So even thinking about, like, your arms touching the back of the chair, and.
Client: I'm not liking it, I really feel like I should probably go wash my arms.
Counselor: So what would happen if you put your hands right on the arm covers? What was your usual reaction to that?
Client: To go wash my arms until I feel like it's gone. Until all the dirt is gone.
Counselor: And how long would that take you to be sure?
Client: I mean, something like this, probably. I'd probably be in there for a good 510 minutes. Just washing.
Counselor: 510 minutes. How many times a day would you end up washing your hands?
Client: Okay. I don't. I don't keep track anymore. It makes me upset. How many?
Counselor: It says that it's that many. That is distressing. And I know that this will be uncomfortable, but I would like you to try to. If you can feel comfortable with it, put your hands on the. On the arms of the chairs. On the chair. Let's see what I'm doing. It's like. Try to stay like that. So tell me what's going through your mind?
Client: I can just. I feel the chair, and I. I don't like it. And I just. I feel almost like I can feel everybody who's ever touched it. And just what have they been doing? And what did they touch before they touched this? They probably didn't wash their hands before they touched this, and it's just really making me comfortable.
Counselor: Okay, so you're anxious now?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor:
output: Is it tolerable?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Maury. How you doing today?
Client: I'm doing all right.
Counselor: You doing all right?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I know last time you were here, you were discussing some relational issues. You want to continue with that?
Client: Yeah, yeah. I mean, you know, it kind of came up again. You know, every time my wife yells at me, you know, I feel like a failure, you know, like I told you last time, I just. I just feel like I can't do anything right, you know? Like everything I try to do is met with arguing and yelling, and I just feel like there's nothing I can do right.
Counselor: So no matter what you do, it's not going to end up the way you want?
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: So it's frustrating.
Client: Yeah, it definitely is.
Counselor: How is what's going on impacted your relationship with your wife?
Client: I mean, it's rocky, you know, because I feel like I can't do anything right. She doesn't understand that. And then, you know, we don't get along ever because we're just always yelling and I'm always feeling bad, and then it just keeps going like that.
Counselor: So when you. You mentioned you feel like a failure when she. When she yells at you?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Can you think back to maybe the last time, one of the last times you guys argued and try to remember that thought? We've talked about automatic thoughts before. Remember that thought that comes in that moment when she starts. She starts yelling at you?
Client: I mean, she'll yell at me. I mean, I feel, you know, frustrated. Like, why are you yelling at me right now? And. I don't know. I mean, as I was thinking about, like we were talking about it, and as I was thinking about it more this week, kind of felt like, you know, kind of like what happened with my dad, you know? I guess I kind of felt that same way when I was younger. You know, like, if my dad would yell at me or when he would yell at me, I kind of feel that same way. And it feels like the same thing. Yeah. It's kind of the first. I guess kind of the first thought that comes to mind.
Counselor: The first thought is I've been through something like this before, I guess.
Client: Yeah. I mean, I'm not really thinking those exact words, but that's definitely what it feels like, you know? Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. Like, it's like just a sense that this isn't brand new.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And the feeling you're connecting with it is the same feeling you had when your dad. Yahweh. Yeah.
Client: Yeah, pretty much, yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. So, in a sense, these arguments are taking you back to another point in time.
Client: I guess so, in a way, that's distressing.
Counselor: Yeah, it is.
Client: I mean, it feels, you know, pretty crappy.
Counselor: Now, in these arguments, she yells at you. You mentioned before that you do some yelling of your own, you know, in the midst of all that. Right. How would you rate it in terms of, like, any physical violence? Nothing like that.
Client: No, it's just words. I mean, we're just, you know, just yelling.
Counselor: And what level, like, what level of yelling would you say? How severe compared to what you've experienced in the past?
Client: Yeah, I don't know. I mean, it's like, you know, sometimes it can get up to, like, the eight or nines, you know, but just, I guess generally it's, you know, down. Closer to a seven on scale, like one to ten. Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: So sometimes it's seven. That would be pretty bad.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But some other times it's not.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So do you feel like your reaction is being frustrated is disproportionate to what's really going on or you feel like it's money?
Client: I don't know what else to do. You know? I mean, it's just. It's kind of my reaction, my gut reaction to it, you know? I think I'm justified in it because, you know, she just doesn't understand how much she yells at me, you know, and how much that hurts me. You know? I do feel justified. I mean, but it just. It just keeps going, though. And I feel justified, though. I don't know.
Counselor: Let's talk for a moment about, if you're okay with it, about your father and his yelling. You've discussed this with me a little bit before. In the past few sessions. I remember you saying that most. It was in the afternoon. Most of the yelling was when you were both home.
Client: Yeah, I mean, it was. I mean, mostly when I get home from school. I mean, I wasn't, you know, I was in high school, and then after that, you know, I went to college. And so I wasn't really home much during college, but, you know, I guess it'd be after I got home from high school. You know, I'd get home and he'd get home from work and, you know, just kind of be aggravated, whatever, just start yelling and. Yeah, usually when I got back from school, yeah.
Counselor: So he would get back from work, you would get back from school. And how long would that last? How long would the period where you were kind of vulnerable to being yelled at last?
Client: I don't know. I mean, sometimes about an hour, you know, and he'd be yelling because he's, you know, frustrated from work and he's frustrated from the drive home and whatever else, you know? And at some point, he would usually start drinking, you know, so maybe about an hour or so, you know, where that was. Like, you knew you were gonna get it.
Counselor: So kind of every day you could predict that between when you. Or between when he came home after you were already home from school and when he started drinking, you were gonna. He was gonna find something to yacht you about.
Client: Yeah, yeah, yeah. And, I mean, there were some days, like, I knew when he came home, he came home the same time every day. I knew I could get out of the house, you know? Cause at some point, I had a car, my friends had cars, you know, whatever.
Counselor: You had more freedom.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. You know, at some point, I had a job, so sometimes I'd work after school and stuff, so I knew I'd be able to leave the house at times, you know, like when I knew he was gonna start yelling and stuff. But, I mean, there was a period of time probably like my senior year of high school that I just didn't, you know, I just came home and, you know, it was gonna happen, you know, that's the way it happened.
Counselor: Even though you were able to escape it.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Right. You could have stayed out long enough for him to start drinking. Yeah.
Client: Instead you stayed in the house.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: I mean, it was pretty much my whole senior year come home. I knew what was gonna happen, and I just took it. You know, I just. I knew he was gonna yell. I just took it that.
Counselor: Was there ever a period when you first got your freedom that you tried, like.
Client: Oh, yeah, yeah, I did. And. I don't know. I don't know why I didn't just keep doing that. It probably would have been easier, but. I don't know. The whole senior year, I just started. I was just back there at the house when he came home from work.
Counselor: So in that period, were you. Were you. There's times when you did leave, what did he do instead of yell at you?
Client: I guess he had to yell at somebody else. I mean, my. My sister, my brother were home. I guess he probably yelled at them. I don't know. I mean, it felt good to not be there, but I guess he probably yelled at them, which just sucks. I mean, you know, I guess somebody had. Whoever was there was gonna take it, you know?
Counselor: Somebody was gonna get you out there.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. I mean, I guess it was them when I wasn't there. I don't know.
Counselor: And how do you think you took it. When you were there, how well did you respond?
Client: I just got used to it, you know, I knew what was gonna happen. I knew he was gonna yell. I knew that it was gonna make me upset. I knew that just those repeated times, just like now, you know, I'm gonna feel like a failure, which ultimately I did. You know, maybe I probably just became numb to it, you know, it happens so often and same thing every day. Probably just became numb to it and just kind of stopped caring and kind of stopped, I don't know, believing in myself or something, you know?
Counselor: Like you've just given up.
Client: Yeah, probably. That's probably. I don't know. Probably. Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: And how many years total did this experience go on? Do you endure the yelling?
Client: I mean, it would have been while I was in middle school and most of high school. I mean, I told you at some point I was able to leave, but probably all of middle school, most of high school, and I left, and then some, you know, for the rest of the senior year, I would be there. So, I don't know, quite a few years, I guess.
Counselor:
output: A long time to suffer.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, Jordan. How you doing today?
Client: Could have been better.
Counselor: Could be better.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What's going on?
Client: Um, well, you know, I have two jobs.
Counselor: Mm hmm.
Client: And I lost one of them.
Counselor: You lost your job? Yes. Which one did you lose?
Client: I lost one at the grocery store.
Counselor: That was your part time?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I'm sorry to hear that.
Client: Me too. And I'm just. It's all I think about now.
Counselor: And when did this happen?
Client: It happened about two, three days ago.
Counselor: Two, three days ago?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So if I remember right, you took that job not too long ago to kind of supplement your income.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So certainly that would be upsetting, but I know that's not a major part of your income.
Client: It's not, but, I mean, I'm still very worried about it.
Counselor: Tell me about the worry.
Client: I mean, I worry that, you know, I'm. Now I only had so much money, and now I have less than that. I mean, without my money, you know, God knows how many things can happen.
Counselor: So before you had the job, you were paying all your bills. You want some extra income, you've lost that extra income. And I can certainly understand how that would be disturbing. But as I understand that you were doing okay before with your full time job.
Client: I was doing okay, but, I mean, I got comfortable with that extra income, and so now my fear is that I've gotten too comfortable with it, and now that it's not there anymore, it's going to affect the fact I'm not going to be able to pay for food or my rent.
Counselor: Okay, so you adjusted to the new income level with the full time and the part time job together, and you're worried you can't adjust back?
Client: I'm worried that, I mean, things are just gonna get worse from here. I mean, it's a big deal, losing your job. Even if it was part time, I've gotten comfortable from having so much money, from the money I had to. Now that's, you know, been divided and, I mean, God knows how many things, like I said, God knows how many things can happen.
Counselor: Well, what. What can happen? So you have that income, your income is reduced now to just your full time job. What can happen from this point on?
Client: Well, I can, you know, keep. Stay in the mindset that I have that extra money and spend what I think is that extra money, digging into the money I paid for my rent, my food, my gas, my insurance, and me, who's somebody without all that.
Counselor: So you could fail to pay expenses that need to be paid.
Client: And they helped me go to my full time job that I still have. So, I mean, if I can't, if I spend the money that was from my insurance because I thought I had extra, then I'm not gonna have insurance on my cardinal. I can get pulled over, lose my license, not going to be able to get to work, and then I'll get fired there too.
Counselor: All right, so the kind of chain of causality you're seeing is that without that part time income, you might not adapt with your expense management. You might fail to pay, for example, your car insurance. You could get pulled over for something the police officer could see, don't have insurance, give you a ticket, which is just money. I don't have another expense. Right. And how would this. How would that connect to losing your job?
Client: Because I wouldn't be able to get to work.
Counselor: So it'd be. So the ticket would be so expensive, you would lose your.
Client: Well, the ticket would be expensive, so I wouldn't be able to try to pay the next month's insurance. So I just wouldn't have insurance on my car. So I.
Counselor: So you'd lose your insurance?
Client: I'd lose my insurance.
Counselor: And then by losing your insurance, you lose your transportation altogether because you can't drive that insurance. And then you lose your job.
Client: Mm hmm. I mean, it's either go to work with an uninsured car, and then I can get pulled over and go to jail for driving with no insurance multiple times.
Counselor: No, that's serious. Yeah. You wouldn't want to do that.
Client: I wouldn't go to jail.
Counselor: So there's two. You have two kind of causal change. One is losing your job. And now even just the idea you can end up incarcerated.
Client: Yes. I mean, which I definitely lose my.
Counselor: Job if I'm in jail, I would imagine.
Client: And so that would have. So then I wouldn't even have, like, any money to help me through jail. Like, to. For the commissary and stuff.
Counselor: Because you would have no income.
Client: I would have no income. And then when I get out of jail, I'm. No one's gonna hire me.
Counselor: Because you have a criminal record.
Client: Exactly.
Counselor: Which makes it challenging to find employment in some instances. So what's happened is kind of in your mind, and we've talked about how thoughts work and beliefs work, is you, in reality, you've lost this part time job. And as I said, that's certainly. That's understandable that you'd be upset about that. I doubt many people would be happy about losing additional income, but you move from there, from losing additional income, which is what has actually happened to this possibility that you could be in jail or lose your job because of this. So I remember maybe last week. Week before, you're talking about the. The letter that you received from. It was like a late notice. It wasn't. Turned out wasn't.
Client: Yeah, it was sent to me, but it was somebody else's credit card mistake. Yeah.
Counselor: Do you remember the conclusions you drew from when you believe that was actually for you, that late notice, that my.
Client: Credit score was gonna go down, that I would. I'd be stuck in that apartment, and then I'd go into depression. I wouldn't be able to do anything.
Counselor: Yeah. So you ended up in that scenario. You end up in a situation where you just couldn't function at all. And you moved there from a letter that you believe was addressed to you, saying you were one month or six days late or something on a credit card, which, of course, you don't want to be late on a credit card, but you move from there to being so depressed you couldn't work, couldn't function, I think, is how you put it. Couldn't function. Do you see, kind of, given how we've talked about cognitive behavioral strategies and concepts, do you see a pattern that's emerged over the last few times I've seen you?
Client: I mean, I've seen that, you know, sometimes I can. I can think the worst, and then. And I know it didn't happen last time, but that was, you know, a stroke of good luck.
Counselor: That it wasn't you.
Client: Yeah. That it was, you know, it wasn't me. And, you know, that was a relief. But this is something that's solid. I don't have my part time job anymore.
Counselor: You've lost real income.
Client: I mean, this isn't a mistake. This isn't a. We fired the wrong person. You know, this is real. So there's real concerns here.
Counselor: I.
Client: Unlike last time, where I was lucky.
Counselor: So this. This situation, you see, is different than the first situation because the first situation was more. You were perceiving something was wrong that wasn't wrong because you weren't the intended recipient of the letter.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But in this situation, it's different because it's real. You really lost your income.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And, of course, keeping in mind that this job, again, only a few months old, and you survived well before that, is it reason to believe you could survive well again, that you could adapt to this lost income?
Client: Well, I suppose there is, but I'm concerned about whether I'm not, whether I won't adapt.
Counselor: Well, let's look at this in terms of probabilities, right. You've had several jobs throughout your career. You've had some of them worked out. You've lost other ones. You're still paying your bills. So in terms of probabilities, how many times have you, how many times have you ended up in jail or losing your full time job?
Client: I mean, they haven't happened yet.
Counselor: It hasn't happened.
Client: Not yet. But I mean, I, I struggled a little bit when I lost a part time job or when I was younger and I had those little jobs.
Counselor: So you had to adapt.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And it was painful.
Client: I did struggle, yeah.
Counselor: You struggled.
Client: Yeah. I mean, but I'm older now. These are, you know, even though grocery stores, not a serious job. It was income.
Counselor: Sure. Yeah. And again, to lose income would be disappointing for just about anybody. Are there any upsides to not having that job?
Client: I suppose I have more time to focus on my full time job because, I mean, that is really intensive.
Counselor: Is there a possibility that you could find another part time job just as you found that one?
Client: I mean, because will somebody else take me because I was fired from that job? I mean, that's my concern, is that.
Counselor: Nobody, they're going to find out.
Client: Yeah. And then they're going to go, oh, she was fired, you know. No, we don't. We don't want her.
Counselor: But you've had other jobs that didn't work out before and that didn't affect you getting that job.
Client: That's true.
Counselor: So the worst case scenario, I guess what I'm getting at the worst case scenario is, in your case, ending up in jail or losing your full time job, which you've had for a while.
Client: Yeah, I really don't want to lose my job.
Counselor: And it seems like they like you there.
Client: I hope they do.
Counselor: Right? Yeah. So those scenarios, I guess, are possible, but they seem, based on what you're saying, is pretty unlikely. So I wonder how useful it is to invest a lot of energy in kind of tracking that causal chain to jail or prison or to unemployment when that's really not the most likely outcome. Sorry to interrupt you, but do you invest as much energy in tracking the positives or the probable outcomes?
Client: No, not even close. I know that I don't think about the positive things. I mean, I don't get fired and then go, what's good about this?
Counselor: Or get a letter in the mail and say, what's, you know, although I can see there's not much upside to that, although it turned out that was an error, so. But this has still been a theme that I've seen over the last eight to ten weeks, where you really have, you really emphasize the negative, possible, even unlikely outcomes, kind of expanding the negative as you move through. Like a causal chain.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Does that make sense? Yeah, but you don't do the same thing for the positive side. You don't look at how something could work out. Well, would you say it's fair assessment?
Client: Yeah. Yeah, no, that's. That's pretty accurate.
Counselor: But still, you're worried about this.
Client: I mean, yeah, I am worried. I'm not gonna be thrilled about it, but I suppose I don't have to go to when I'm gonna go to jail or I'm gonna lose my full time job.
Counselor: I think there's a lot of intervening factors that could occur before going to jail or losing your job. There's other things that you could do.
Client: I suppose I could get a family member to drive me or take the bus if I lost my insurance and lost my car.
Counselor: So, alternate forms of transportation. Yeah. There's adapting your spending back to where it was before.
Client: That's true.
Counselor:
output: Part of your fear was that you wouldn't be able to adapt your spending. Right. But that's something you would have control over.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: So, good morning.
Client: Good morning.
Counselor: What would you like to work on in this session?
Client: I would like to work on my avoidance behavior. I actually have an opportunity which I was looking for from a very long time to give a presentation. And now that I have this opportunity in front of me, I'm trying to avoid it.
Counselor: So you were looking forward to this opportunity for a long time?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And then now you are avoiding it. Right. And what you would like to do?
Client: I would not like to. I would not. I would like not to avoid it.
Counselor: So you would like to go ahead with the presentation?
Client: I would like to go ahead with the presentation.
Counselor: So how do you feel when you're about to avoid? In the sense, like what kind of feelings are making you avoid this?
Client: Rather whether I'll be able to do it or not, whether it will go well, like whether all the students or the people who are listening to the presentation will like it or not. What if I forget? Or what if I do a mess?
Counselor: Now, these are your thoughts. How do you feel when you think like this?
Client: I don't feel good.
Counselor: Can you label that feeling? When you. When you think like this, you don't feel good. And which is what feeling?
Client: I feel anxious.
Counselor: You feel anxious? Right. And instead of feeling anxious, how would you like to feel so that you go ahead with the presentation?
Client: Rather not anxious, but at least some little anxious.
Counselor: Little anxious. You would like to reduce your anxiety?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So you wouldn't want to get rid of the anxiety completely?
Client: Yes, I want to get rid.
Counselor: You want to get rid of the anxiety.
Client: Anxiety completely.
Counselor: So how about feeling concerned but not anxious? So you're careful about your presentation. You also work towards the presentation well and you're not ignorant or you're not indifferent towards the outcome. Would that make sense?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So you don't want to be indifferent and feel nothing about the presentation, but you would like to feel concerned and not anxious about it.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Do you also think there is a connection between your anxiety and your avoidance?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: If you were concerned and not anxious, would you continue to avoid or you would probably go ahead?
Client: I would go ahead.
Counselor: You would go ahead?
Client: I always wanted to do this, so I would go ahead.
Counselor: You would go ahead. Right. So can we set that agenda for today's session is to feel concerned and not anxious about the upcoming presentation?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Okay, fine. So now to help you reach this goal, we will have to examine one specific incident where you know you felt anxious. And then you will understand how you get anxious and how to shift your feelings from anxiety to concern. So would you mind me telling me a specific incident where you had a chance to go ahead with, you know, preparing for the presentation, but you didn't.
Client: Recently, I have a social group where there was a chance that they wanted a presentation regarding a particular topic, and they have asked me for the dates to give me my dates when I would be presenting, and I have been just postponing it. Postponing it and not giving them the dates.
Counselor: Is this the same presentation that you are postponing, or this is different one?
Client: This is, again, a different one.
Counselor: This is a different one. But this is a specific example.
Client: Yes, this is a very specific example, which I always like. On the back of my mind. This example is always disturbing me or just always coming to my mind that I did that postponing thing.
Counselor: All right, so let's take this incident where, you know, there was a social group, and they asked you about a date for presentation. And in this situation, do you remember the incident clearly?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So when you chose to avoid it, can you remember that in that moment?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: What was going through your mind that made you avoid it?
Client: Whether I will be able to do it properly or whether they will like it or not. Am I that qualified to give the presentation now?
Counselor: These are the doubts that you had in your head. Could you convert them into statements?
Client: I'm. I'm not qualified.
Counselor: I'm not qualified.
Client: I am. People will not like it.
Counselor: People will not like it, and I.
Client: Will not be able to deliver it.
Counselor: And when you thought these, how did you feel?
Client: I didn't. I was feeling nervous. Rather nervous and not happy.
Counselor: Even not happy. Nervous and anxious. Also anxious on a zero to 100, how distressing was this anxiety?
Client: It was very distressing, I think. 80.
Counselor: 80. So that was pretty intense, right?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: It is like death anxiety. Something is gonna happen to me.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: 70 rather than, I would say.
Counselor: Okay. What was your natural intention to do at that time when you felt so anxious?
Client: I just told them, I'm busy for a while, and I will just let you know the dates when I am free and when can I take up the presentation.
Counselor: So this is what you did?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Okay. Was there anything else going on in your mind? That I want to do this?
Client: No.
Counselor: And what, in this entire incident was most anxiety provoking for you?
Client: Whether I will be able to give the presentation or not. Whether the presentation would go well or not.
Counselor: So having to make a presentation was the trigger?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Your thoughts were, I won't be able to make the presentation well, I am not qualified, and these people will not like it. These were the thoughts that were going through your head. And then you felt anxious about it. You felt nervous about it. You also escaped. Or you bought time by, you know, telling them, I'll get back to you. So you postponed accepting the invitation. Is that correct?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So did I summarize that well?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So we'll go ahead with finding out where your anxiety comes from. So when you thought these three thoughts, you felt very anxious. Out of these three thoughts, which was most important thought for you, that made.
Client: You anxious whether I will be able to do it or not.
Counselor: So your prediction that you will not be able to do it well?
Client: Yes. That I will not be able to do it well.
Counselor: Do it well, right. Okay. Let's assume for the sake of therapy that you know, you do not do it well. We are trying to find out where your anxiety comes from. Are you with me?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So if you don't do it well, what does that mean to you?
Client: That I am not competent enough.
Counselor:
output: You are not competent enough?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: So one of the things that we know is that sometimes people who have difficulty with anxiety and things like that have also had some bad experiences in their lives. So I'm going to ask you some questions about some of your difficult experiences that you may have had. And I'm just going to ask sort of yes or no questions. I only need sort of headlines. I don't need a lot of detail about the things that happened right now, but I'm just going to ask you those questions. And if anything about this interview starts to make you uncomfortable, you can take a break. If I ask a question you don't want to answer, you can just say, pass, and I'll just move on. So it's really up to you what you share, but I do want to ask you these questions. Is that okay?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. So have you ever been physically hurt by anyone, any. Either as a child or an adult? You know, hit.
Client: Yeah, my. I had a boyfriend a couple years ago, and he. He would hit me sometimes, but we're not together anymore, so.
Counselor: Mm hmm. Was there other kinds of physical abuse? You know, did he do more than hit you? Was there anything.
Client: No, he would just slap me sometimes. Usually when he was like, if he'd had a really hard day at work and maybe he would be drinking or something. He wouldn't slap me when he got home, but I got out of that, so that's good.
Counselor: Well, it's good that you recognize that that was really not acceptable behavior and that you didn't want that in your relationship. And it's great that you were able to get away from that. That's really good self care, that you were able to make that decision and, you know, and make a different choice and create more safety for your. Yourself. That's really good.
Client: Thanks.
Counselor: What about sexually? Has anybody ever, you know, when you were a child or as an adult, touched you against your will, anything like that?
Client: Yeah. I don't really want to talk about it, though, but, yeah, when I was. When I was little.
Counselor: How little? Just vaguely ten. Okay. Okay. And was it a family member or a stranger or.
Client: It was. It was a family member, but I don't really like talking about it.
Counselor:
output: Okay. You don't have to. Okay, great. Thank you for telling me that much. That's really all I need for right now. Although it may be important for you to talk about that later, at some point you can wait until you're ready.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Victoria. How you doing today?
Client: Pretty good.
Counselor: Very good. How has the anxiety been around the germs?
Client: I still catch myself, like, double, almost like double touching. Like going to touch it and then reeling back. So I'm starting to notice it, but I still, I still have that anxiety. I still don't want to touch it.
Counselor: When you pretty much touch anything you might think has germs on it.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What are some things that you've touched in the last, between the last session and this session that have distressed you?
Client: Well, I had to go to the store, which is always a nightmare for me because I don't even like touching my credit card because it's been in so many machines and there's so much dirt and junk that gets in there and then the counters and all the. I keep thinking about the food that's there, and I, you know, if I pick it up off the shelf, how many people have picked it up with their nasty hands or kids picked it up with nasty hands and then put it back, and it's like, I need to eat. But shopping's a nightmare for me.
Counselor: So really, in a, like, a supermarket, everything can be containing germs. Have germs on it?
Client: Yeah, everything does.
Counselor: Everything does. And that's what you're thinking about as you're walking through and shopping. We talked about last time, exposure and response prevention, and I explained kind of the general idea. But you remember that conversation. Yeah, I remember. I indicated that we might try some experiments right in session to see how, see if we can move kind of forward and treating your, kind of your fear and obsession with germs and really the anxiety it's causing for you, it's like getting in the way of your life.
Client: It is. It really is.
Counselor: So I was wondering, is there anything in here, in this office, as you look around, that you would look at and think, I don't want to touch that because it could have germs on it.
Client: I'm really not liking the covers on this chair because, I mean, I can't. I mean, at least what I'm sitting in now, my clothes are protecting me from the rest of the chair.
Counselor: Mm hmm.
Client: But, I mean, I have no sleeves on, so I don't like touching the armrests and the covers.
Counselor: So even thinking about, like, your arms touching the back of the chair, and.
Client: I'm not liking it, I really feel like I should probably go wash my arms.
Counselor: So what would happen if you put your hands right on the arm covers? What was your usual reaction to that?
Client: To go wash my arms until I feel like it's gone. Until all the dirt is gone.
Counselor: And how long would that take you to be sure?
Client: I mean, something like this, probably. I'd probably be in there for a good 510 minutes. Just washing.
Counselor: 510 minutes. How many times a day would you end up washing your hands?
Client: Okay. I don't. I don't keep track anymore. It makes me upset. How many?
Counselor:
output: It says that it's that many. That is distressing. And I know that this will be uncomfortable, but I would like you to try to. If you can feel comfortable with it, put your hands on the. On the arms of the chairs. On the chair. Let's see what I'm doing. It's like. Try to stay like that. So tell me what's going through your mind?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, misses James. How are you doing today?
Client: I'm okay.
Counselor: That's good. I just want to start out really quickly by getting a couple of the formalities out of the way. I know it's a little bit awkward coming in, you know, always the first time, but I'll just introduce myself and then you can introduce yourself and we'll just talk a little bit about you and your family and all that. So again, my name is Marisa and I just want you to know in the beginning that what I do as a counselor is more important to me than just a paycheck. I'm not in this job because it's just a source of income from. I really enjoy getting to know the clients that come through those doors and I like to help them in whatever ways I can. If it's just listening for that day and there's a burden that you have or if it's. If it's some kind of resource that you need from me and that I'm able to reach out there and get for you so that you can. You can be more successful and more fulfilled and happier than. That's what I want for you. Definitely. But why don't you tell me a little bit about yourself?
Client: Well, I don't know what to tell. I mean, they. The Medicaid office told me I had to come down and to be counseled so I can continue getting my benefits, which I need because I cancer. So that's why I'm here.
Counselor: What about your family? Tell me a little bit about them.
Client: Well, I'm married, I have three children. They're all grown. And I'm taking care of my grandson, Jason. He's seven.
Counselor: Seven, okay. And you said that you were referred here because you needed to continue benefits now that you found out you have cancer.
Client: Mm hmm.
Counselor: Okay. Do you want to tell me a little bit about that?
Client: Well, the doctors have said that I have cancer again. Had it a couple of years ago, and I beat it. And now they're saying that it's come back. It's not something I really want to talk about, but I'm still working and just trying to get through the day.
Counselor: Definitely. You are working. What is that? You know, what is it that you do?
Client: I'm a housekeeper for a hotel here.
Counselor:
output: Okay, that's wonderful. That's good. How have you been balancing that with. With getting sick? Are you feeling the effects of being sick yet? Or is it just recent that it's just.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Liz. How you doing today?
Client: I'm alright. How are you?
Counselor: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. What's been going on in the last week?
Client: It's still the same. Nothing at home is going right. It's. I'm still yelling, we're still fighting.
Counselor: Like you and your boyfriend.
Client: Yeah. He just can't get it together. He can't. He doesn't do anything right. He doesn't. And I just end up screaming every day and it takes it all out of me.
Counselor: All right, so he can't do anything right. And you're arguing, being angry every day?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So what are you taking away from this? Like, what do you think's going on?
Client: I feel like he does nothing wrong and I end up screaming at him when I come home from work, and that's a lot out of me every day, and I don't want to feel angry every single day.
Counselor: That's what's happening.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What types of things do you think are triggering your anger response?
Client: It's anything. It's. I come home, he's just sitting on the couch. I've had a long day at work. He gets homework before me, and the dishes aren't done. Nothing's, like, thawed or even started for dinner. And is that just supposed to be my, like, it's not. He could just do one thing and I just. I just lose it. I lose it and I can't. I can't control it. I just started screaming at him that he does nothing, that he could just do one thing for me. He could just have the sink clean, empty one thing, and it. Every single day. And then the next day it's something else. The trash is now, like, you name it.
Counselor: So every. Every day when you come home from work, there's something he's done or failed to do that triggers yelling?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What's his response to this? Like, what's he doing when you yell at him?
Client: He gets mad back. He just starts screaming back at me. Like, I expect too much and I get too upset and why am I always yelling at him? Why can't I give him the benefit of the doubt?
Counselor: I'm.
Client: But I don't understand it. Like, you could do one thing and then. And I just. I can't help it. I scream at him.
Counselor: Are there other things he does at other times that you feel are helpful? Or is it. Or is it always, like, when you come home, is it always something that hasn't been done right or hasn't been done?
Client: I mean, on anniversaries, whole make dinner. So that's nice.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: He makes good money. So that's. He keeps that together.
Counselor: Okay, that's about it.
Client: Yeah. The rest is just. I just get angry at him.
Counselor: So if you were to pick adjectives to describe him, what adjectives might you. Might you select?
Client: Stubborn, condescending, and intelligent.
Counselor: Intelligent, stubborn, condescending, and intelligent. Do you see him as this way kind of all the time, or is this change?
Client: I don't think it's all the time. Like, there. Like sometime, like a month ago when a friend at work died. Old age, whatever. But I had a long day. He knew it beforehand. I didn't have to say anything. When I came home, everything was good. There was no trash, no dishes. So it's not all the. All the time, but just lately, it's just. I had no words.
Counselor: So lately it's all the time. Yeah, but there's been prior occasions when this hasn't been a problem. Yeah, but there's not many of those. So after you have, you yell and argue, what's it feel like to you then? Like, what's your mood?
Client: I'm still irritable. It's like the dishes don't get done. The problem didn't go away, didn't fix itself while I was yelling. So it just sucks being that angry. Just doesn't. I hate it.
Counselor: So it's not productive for you?
Client: Right, right. It's not productive.
Counselor: But there's a part of you mentioned earlier where, like you said, you just can't help yourself.
Client: Like I said, I just lose it. And I do that because that's what it feels like.
Counselor: So it's like you just. You just see, for example, like the dishes, right? So you just see the dishes aren't done, and immediately there's the.
Client: I just. I go off. Why didn't you do the dishes? You've been home an hour and a half. You could have done one thing for me. I had a longer day, and you knew it.
Counselor: All right, so let me take an example from work, right, so you work in an office with other people. Do they ever frustrate you in a way similar to what your boyfriend does?
Client: Occasionally, yeah, on occasion. Yeah.
Counselor: So there's times where you kind of have that moment with them where you just can't believe they didn't do something.
Client: Or I. Yeah, I just can't stand them sometimes.
Counselor: What's your reaction in terms of anger and yelling to those events?
Client: I get pissed, but I just. I can't. I can't yell.
Counselor: You can't yell? No. Why is that?
Client: I get fired.
Counselor: You get fired. So in those interactions with your coworkers, would be fair to say you're in that moment just as angry as you are with your boyfriend.
Client: And, oh, if not more, because I actually choose to be with my boyfriend. I don't choose to be with those people necessarily.
Counselor: You just happen to be together. And so in those instances, because there's a consequence like being fired, you're able to control the outward expression of anger, meaning you're not yelling, but inwardly, you're still angry at them.
Client: Yeah, I guess so.
Counselor: Yeah. So they don't really know you're angry.
Client: Yeah. I just walk away. I don't think they'd be able to tell.
Counselor: And they're not being yelled at, so they're not.
Client: Right. They wouldn't react. Yeah.
Counselor: No reaction. Right. So there is a thought process that occurs between the trigger and when you act, because at work, you're thinking, you have this thought that comes up, I don't want to be fired.
Client: Yeah, I get there. Must. Yeah.
Counselor: And the consequence of that thought is I'll be angry, but I'm not going to act angry.
Client: Right. I can't act angry or I'll get fired, and I don't want to get fired, I guess.
Counselor: So knowing that there is a thought there when you come home and you see the dishes aren't done, maybe just stay with that example. What would that thought be like? Think back to the last time that happened. Do you remember what you were thinking at that moment as you saw those dishes sitting there not washed?
Client: I mean, just that he never does anything. Right.
Counselor: He never does anything. Right. So you see. So you see the dishes not washed. He never does anything. Right. That's the thought, yeah. And then the reaction, the behavior is finding him. Right. And yelling at him.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right, so you see how there is an intervening thought between the trigger, which in this case, the dishes, and the behavior, which is the yelling.
Client: Yeah. I guess there's a thought where I'm sitting there and I'm looking at him, thinking about it, saying, you never do anything. Right.
Counselor: So remember we talked a few weeks ago about cognitive distortions? We talked about, like, the errors, like, consistent. There are consistent errors in thinking. Right. And I'm wondering if that thought, he never does anything right. If that's similar to or matches up with any of the cognitive distortions we talked about. And I'm wondering if it's not. If it's not kind of blocking off your path in terms of thinking. Right. So you're saying he never does anything right.
Client: Right.
Counselor: It's kind of like maybe a kind of all or nothing thinking that we talked about that.
Client: Oh, it's absolute tunnel vision at that point.
Counselor: Tunnel vision, yeah. Okay. So a few different distortions at work. But you mentioned earlier there are times when he does do things right.
Client: Yeah. There are occasions where he must have thought about me.
Counselor: He was more thoughtful than more considerate. Okay. More considerate. So the statement he never does the thought, he never does anything right that could be challenged.
Client: Yeah, I guess technically it could.
Counselor: And what might be as an alternative to the behavior? Right. To the yelling. Instead of doing that, what might be a thought that you could kind of insert right after that he never does anything right. Thought that might change the outcome for you. That might disrupt that connection between that thought and your yelling.
Client: Maybe that he has done something right in the past.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: So it's bound to happen again. It is possible.
Counselor: All right. So an adapted response, as we call him or his self talk, that says he's not. He's not altogether bad because he has done things right in the past.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Right. Which is a little more flexible in thinking than thinking. He. Then your automatic thought.
Client: Right?
Counselor: Yeah. That's your automatic thought. Never does anything right. So a little bit more flexibility in the thinking might get you to a place where you're not yelling. And then on the other side of it, too, I'm wondering if we can't challenge the usefulness of yelling. You mentioned that you've done it quite a bit, but you're not really getting a different result.
Client: It doesn't. The dishes don't get done after that. And the next day, I might still find the dishes there. It doesn't.
Counselor: It's not working.
Client: It hasn't worked. Yeah.
Counselor: So when you're yelling, there's an expression of emotion, but there's also this hope that the yelling will change his behavior.
Client: Right.
Counselor: Something, but it's not.
Client: Yep.
Counselor: And when was the first time in terms of, like, how long ago this was a problem?
Client: I've had previous boyfriends where this was a problem, and that relationship has long gone because of it.
Counselor: So due to the yelling?
Client: Due to the yelling. So I don't. I really do like this guy who's not all bad, and I don't want my yelling to be a problem, my anger.
Counselor: But it's hard to control for you. You're struggling with the anger.
Client: Right?
Counselor: Yelling.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Rationally, you understand it doesn't work. Like, it's not getting what you want, but somehow it feels like a release it feels like justice. It feels good to be able to.
Client: It feels like that's what I'm supposed to be doing, and that's what I do.
Counselor: That's what you're supposed to be doing. Okay. So it feels like it's what you're supposed to be doing. Do you have an idea of what might be a more productive path for you as an alternative to the yelling?
Client: Protective. That's a great word. I guess walking away is what I do at the office.
Counselor: And that has worked for you.
Client: I've been able to take a minute and either remove myself or intervene my opinion more calmly because I haven't yelled at work, I guess walking away and taking a minute.
Counselor: Okay. So that would be one behavioral strategy. So you see the trigger and you have the thought. It never does anything. Right. And then you could intervene with a thought of, I need to walk away. And a behavior of walking away and taking, like, how much time?
Client: I mean, honestly, if I'm by myself, like, five minutes, ten minutes of just me time.
Counselor: So let's even say ten minutes.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor:
output: So ten minutes. And then you can respond more constructively, more usefully to what is, you know, a type of relational disagreement. Right. You have a disagreement over, it sounds like, who should be doing what.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Lisa. How you doing today?

Counselor: Sure.
Client: Well, kind of. It's kind of related to that. So I'm in school, and every few weeks we have, like, papers to write, and I know, I know it. I know I can do it. It's just actually sitting down and doing it.
Counselor: All right, well, tell me about the papers.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
