Counselor: Well, Meredith, we know each other, but the way we usually start a CBT session is to set an agenda. So we might have several ideas about what we want on the agenda. But the first thing is usually for us to make a problem list together about whatever it is that you might want to work on.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: And then we'll do the problem list, and then we'll explain, explore the thoughts and the behaviors that might be related to the problem. And hopefully, by the end of our time together, we'll have a clearer idea about what's causing the problem and some ideas about how to maybe change things.
Client: Sounds good.
Counselor: All right.
Client: So one thing that I've been noticing lately is that I have a tendency to kind of hang back in groups, and I tend to observe instead of participate.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: And a lot of times I get really nervous when I feel like I'm expected to speak up. And I want to speak up, but I kind of feel like I freeze.
Counselor: Okay. And so in particular, then, in groups, the setting is big groups, little groups. Does it matter?
Client: It doesn't matter a whole lot, but generally, I guess medium size. Like, you know, in classes that I have usually, like maybe twelve people or so. So relatively small, medium. I don't know what size that is.
Counselor: Okay. And so. But in your head, you probably would say, I would like to speak up, but for some reason, you feel inside some anxiety or nervousness about that.
Client: Definitely.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: And then sometimes when I try to force myself to speak up, when I actually don't feel ready, I get like. I feel like my throat's closing and I get a red face.
Counselor: Okay. All right. So that's sort of one possible issue for us to talk about. Could you maybe give me a specific example of a particular group situation, as recent as you can, where you had this feeling of hanging back and maybe. Maybe some fear of evaluation?
Client: So in my statistics class each week, we have a. It's called an inclusion activity. And generally, I guess it's supposed to help people feel like the group's more cohesive and included, but I usually experience it as the opposite. So there's usually a task at the beginning of each class of like, take off your shoe and talk. Talk about the most interesting place your shoe has been. Stuff like this in stats that, um, usually I get really nervous and I feel like I can't think of anything to say. And I feel like I usually end up saying something really awkward or lame, and I just don't feel good about it. Like, I feel.
Counselor: Yeah. Can you give me that specific example of the recent time when maybe. And then. And what you said, too, including sort of the beginning, what happened and then how it ended.
Client: Yeah. So when we did this activity, it's, like, a really weird example. When we did this activity, you know, probably six or seven people had gone in front of me, and I was, like, not listening to anything that anyone else was saying, just totally self absorbed in terms of, like, oh, God, what am I going to say? And not being able to think of anything. And then when it was my turn, I was wearing a pair of shoes that, like, are kind of, like, they have lace on them. And so I took it off and I said, I like these shoes because I get cool tan lines from them. So I didn't even really answer the question that was like, where have these shoes been? Or, like, the coolest place these shoes have been? Or something like that. And then after I went, I didn't really listen to anything else anyone said because I was still, like, stuck on, why didn't I answer the question and just kind of feeling awkward.
Counselor: Okay, so what I'm doing here is I've got several columns that I'm building, and the first one is, you're in the stats class, and you're going through an inclusion activity. And the second one is the thoughts that you're having. What thoughts are going through your mind? And the thoughts are, oh, God, what am I going to say? Those are the early thoughts. And then maybe the later thoughts are, why didn't I even answer the question?
Client: Yeah. And, like, why can't I ever be articulate?
Counselor: Okay. Why can't I ever be articulate? Okay. And then our third column are the emotions that you might be feeling. And so as you're in that situation and people are taking their turn, the teacher says, you're doing the inclusion activity. People are taking their turns. And what are you feeling? How would you describe your emotional state?
Client: Nervous. Yeah. Like, fearful. And, like, it's almost like I'm anticipating. Anticipating embarrassment.
Counselor: Mm hmm.
Client: So I don't know that's a feeling or not, but usually I feel embarrassed.
Counselor: I put that in the thought okay. Column just because it seems like the anticipation of it is probably a thought, but embarrassment when you're in the middle of it is probably a fear. Does that make sense? And then. So I got nervous, fearful, embarrassed as the emotions, and on a scale of zero, not at all. 100 being the most of that feeling you could ever have, how would you rate? Let's get rid of nervous because it's sort of covered by fearful. How would you rate fearful. And how would you rate embarrassed?
Client: Maybe fearful? Like a four. Okay, four or five. I don't know.
Counselor: Four out of five.
Client: Out of 140.
Counselor: Okay. I was gonna say. Oh, feeling pretty calm. So a 40 or a 50?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. And embarrassed.
Client: I'd say that's higher.
Counselor: A little higher.
Client: Yeah. Like a 70.
Counselor: So maybe a 70. And that would be at the moment that you're talking or right afterwards or right before fluctuating?
Client: Yeah, I'd say, like both during and after.
Counselor: Okay. Okay. So during and after. Alright. And so, you know, the cognitive approach to thinking about what's going on is that it's not the situation that causes the emotional reaction, but it's what you're thinking that causes the emotional reaction. And so it seems to me like one of the things that's going on. Oh, God, what am I gonna say? And why didn't I answer? Why can't I never be articulate?
Client: Why can't I never be articulate? That sounds exactly perfect.
Counselor: We might have to start rating my anxiety now, too. And then I guess there's the other thing you said that you're anticipating embarrassment. And so are those words too, also that are going through your head.
Client: Yeah. Like, I wish I could be more clever or I wish I could have just like, a funny story right now.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: Or make people laugh in a way that I want them to laugh.
Counselor: One of the things I'm doing now is a lot of times when you think about the thoughts that trigger the emotions, these are the thoughts that we would categorize as less helpful, kind of unhelpful thoughts. And then over here, what we're doing is we're coming up with some thoughts that might be more helpful. Okay. Recognizing that no thoughts are perfect, but some thoughts are more helpful. Especially some thoughts are less helpful. And you know in your SAS class, you're going to do the inclusion activity every week. Every week. And so one possibility is you could come in prepared to shift your thinking from the less helpful to the more helpful. Just an idea.
Client: It's a good idea.
Counselor: Okay, so what else besides this is silly and what I say doesn't matter all that much.
Client: I can be clever sometimes.
Counselor: I can be clever. Sometimes. Good. That's sort of a counter to the why can't I ever be articulate? Or why can't I never be articulate? Either way you say it, let's pretend for a second that you were talking to a friend who had exactly this same scenario, and she was telling you the way that she talks to herself. Oh, God. What am I going to say? And why can't I answer that? Why can't I ever be articulate? I know I'm going to embarrass myself. And so she's talking to herself that way. How would you talk to her?

Client: Um, I mean, it sounds pretty ideal, but it sounds really far away from my current experience.
Counselor: It's not what you're whispering in your own ear?
Client: No.
Counselor: What's, what would stop you from, from actually doing this, from talking to yourself? Just like you would talk to a good friend because you're talking to yourself. You're kind of talking to yourself more like somebody who wanted to pull you down. And so I just think, huh, what about that good friend? I mean, can you be a good friend to yourself in those moments and say something more supportive? You are pretty successful in a variety of different things in your life. Right. And so if you take one of those examples and you kind of break it down, are you able to, what do you do to prepare? Well, for example, even for a statistics test, I would guess that you have to go through some preparation.
Client: Mm hmm. Study.
Counselor: Study. Okay. Kind of like studying. Have you ever been in a, like a play or a dramatic performance?
Client: Oh, no, I avoid that.
Counselor: Not even, like, in grade school?
Client: No. I think I maybe was in 7th grade.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: Yeah. But I had a very small part.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: I've always, like, my whole life shied away from being the center of attention. It never feels good to me.
Counselor: No.
Client: Which is ironic since I'm going to school, become a teacher.
Counselor: Yeah. So you have taught before and spoken in front of groups. Small, medium.
Client: Yeah. But it never feels.
Counselor: It never feels comfortable.
Client: No. No. Yeah.
Counselor: So even right now, as we're, as we're talking, so I hear you say it never feels comfortable. Right. Would you put that thought in the category of helpful or unhelpful to say that to yourself?
Client: I'd say that's unhelpful.
Counselor: Unhelpful. Okay. What's unhelpful about that thought?
Client: It kind of makes me feel like no matter how much I prepare to, I still won't feel like I'm good enough or competent.
Counselor: Yeah. And just before that, you said, I always shied away from attention. It's never felt good. Okay.
Client: Pretty black and white thinking.
Counselor: Well, that is pretty. Yeah. Good job noticing that. And I hear you saying that black and white thinking is maybe too general in that it doesn't provide any real hope for it ever changing. And in that sense, it does seem like it fits in that unhelpful category.
Client: I mean, I definitely think, like, you know, if you're nervous about something, to, to a certain extent that's healthy because it makes you prepare more, but at the same time, that kind of thinking of being like, it will never get better. It'll never be okay. Probably. Isn't that helpful?
Counselor: Yeah. Yeah. So I wonder if that's maybe, as we think about the preparation stage, that's one of the things that you said for a stats test you would study. I wonder if there would be different ways you could say things to yourself.
Client: Mm hmm. For instance? For instance, there are times when I am comfortable in groups.

output: And so you hold that belief of, if I do something embarrassing, it will go down, that spiral. I'll be alone and unhappy. Counselor: So you go red, you shake. Is there anything else that you think that you do? I mean, describe yourself. How do you think you look when you're in these situations?

Client: 90.
Counselor: Okay, sorry. What was the other thing that you just said?

Client: Yeah.

Counselor: Okay. What else are you worried is going to happen when we have these conversations?

Client: 90.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: I'd say.
Counselor: What else are you worried will happen when we have this conversation. What else might you see on the camera?
Client: I think you'll probably be able to see that I'm sweating and.

Client: Again?
Counselor: 90, I think, like, visibly sweating down the face.

Client: Yeah.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Gabriella. I understand that you're here today because you've been experiencing some low mood.
Client: Yeah, I just. Recently, I'm just feeling down a lot and I can't really, like, snap out of it. Like, sometimes if it's happened before, I can just, like, get myself back on track, but recently I just find it really difficult to do.
Counselor: Hey, so it sounds like you've been experiencing some low mood and you're kind of struggling to get going a bit.
Client: Yeah, yeah, definitely.
Counselor: You've had low mood in the past, but it's kind of. You've been able to pull yourself out of it before, but more recently you found that harder. Okay, so I understand that you first went to your GP. He referred you here about two months ago. Can I ask what led you to go to the GP in the first place?
Client: My long term boyfriend broke up with me and it was such a shock. Like, I really wasn't expecting it and it just got me really down and I just felt really lonely and I didn't really want to see people and just wanted to be in my own space. And my mum told me I should probably go to the doctors. Oh. And he's referred me to you.
Counselor: Okay. So it sounds then like you had that breakup and you weren't expecting it, so it kind of came out of the blue a bit and that you've been on your own quite a lot, so you've not been seeing people as much. And it sounds like your mum noticed that there's been a bit of a change in you. Okay. And how have things been then, since then, since that happened and since you went to the GP?
Client: I just. Nothing's really changed. Nothing's really improved. I just feel down, like everything's an effort and just feel distant from things. And like I said, I can't snap out of it.
Counselor: Okay. And how did you feel about coming here today?
Client: I was kind of disappointed in myself because I feel like nobody else my age is doing this. Like, I should have been able to snap out of it. Like, it's just another thing that I've not really. It's another thing that's making me stand out for the wrong reasons.
Counselor: Okay. So you feel like it's kind of odd or unusual to be coming to see a clinical psychologist? I suppose I just want to reassure you that it's absolutely normal to have feelings of depression and anxiety. It's really very common and it certainly isn't odd or strange at all. So it sounds like it was actually quite hard for you to come here today?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So what, I guess led you to do that? Because it sounds like maybe there was a lot pushing you against coming here today, but you've managed to come anyway.
Client: I'm just hoping that it's gonna help, I think. I didn't really want to admit it because it's just another failure, but my mum was talking to me and I know she's not really happy with the way I'm behaving. I didn't really want to disappoint her again and so I thought there's no harm in it, so she thought it'd come.
Counselor: So it sounds like partly you're doing it then, for your mum because you're a bit worried that she isn't pleased with you at the moment.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. Well, I think it's great that you've come here and definitely there's a lot of evidence to suggest that psychological therapy can help depression and particularly the type of therapy that we're going to be doing, which is called cognitive behaviour therapy. And I'll tell you a bit more about that as we go on, but I'm just trying to find out a bit more about you today. So I saw from your notes that you're a medic student.
Client: Yeah, I'm not currently in uni at the moment, but, yeah, last year as a medic student.
Counselor: Okay. So I guess what's the reason that you're not in uni this year?
Client: It was pretty tough first year, so they then suggested that I took a year out. This is the break.
Counselor: Okay. So just thinking. So that would be about six months ago, was it that your year out started? Yeah. And it sounds then maybe like your first year was also quite tough.
Client: Yeah, it was. I thought it's tough for everyone, but obviously we all take it in different ways, don't we?
Counselor: And you're planning on. Are you planning on returning and.
Client: Yeah, I'm gonna have to. Really? So. Yeah.
Counselor: Don't sound too sure about that, though.
Client: I think returning is probably that's what's gonna make everyone happy. And I think, you know, at least I'll be able to finally achieve something and get something right, so. Yeah, like, next year I'm gonna. I'll get through it. Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. So it doesn't. It doesn't sound like you want to go back.
Client: I do. I do enjoy it. I just don't feel like me at the moment and I just. It's a lot of work and it's a lot of pressure, but that's what comes of it. And, you know, it'll work out for the best if I go.
Counselor: Okay. So I guess then there's quite a lot of thoughts and feelings about going back at the moment. I'm just wondering, in the meantime, what are you up to? What have you been doing?
Client: Well, I've not really had much on the horizon. My mum, her friend, owns a restaurant and she suggested that I did a bit of waitressing there just for a bit of money and stuff, because obviously I'm not in uni, so I've done that.
Counselor: Okay. How many shifts have you done there?
Client: I've only done one so far. Yeah. I don't know whether it's something that I'd probably go back to, but.
Counselor: Okay. When was that shift?
Client: It was last week, actually. Okay.
Counselor: And how was it? I suppose I'm intrigued. Can you tell me a bit more about that?
Client: It was different, you know, because it was like, I could. I did enjoy it because there was like. It's just different aspect and I had to, like, speak to people and, like, try to get their orders and try to remember it and stuff. Like, I wasn't very good, but I suppose, like, it was handy to have some money and, like, get out the house.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like you quite enjoyed that, then.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What makes you think you weren't very good?
Client: I just. I was just a bit slow and people sometimes didn't understand what I was saying, so I'd have to talk louder or quieter or slower. And I got a bit confused sometimes with the orders and I just don't really think that I'm not really, like, a friendly. Like, people don't really think that I'm a friendly person, so they didn't really want to talk to me and stuff. I felt like I was, like, inconveniencing them by, like, asking them things and getting things wrong. But, yeah, they said that apparently most people get, like, a few mistakes on their first shift. But then again, she's my mum's friend, so it's probably why she's saying it.
Counselor: So the person who owns a restaurant is your mum's friend?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. So it says you're saying that you think you weren't very good and that's because you're a bit slow and you got confused with some orders.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Is it? But you said it's common for people to do that on their first shift.
Client: That's what she said to us. But it's probably just. She's just trying to make me feel better. She probably felt sorry for me because I'm obviously not very good at it. Like, I'm not very good at any things. Recently, I think she just felt sorry for me.
Counselor: Okay. So I've just been noting down some of those thoughts that you've been having. You kind of say that you feel like you're not very good. You're slow, you're confused with the orders, and you feel like you're inconveniencing her and she feels. So for you. I suppose I'm wondering, I mean, what makes you think that she feels sorry for you?
Client: Well, like, like I said, she's my mum's friend, and she's obviously feeling sorry for my mum as well because she's got a daughter that's not like anyone else of her age, and she's just, like, all alone and she's not getting involved. So I think she just feels sorry for me and she doesn't want to say anything to upset me.
Counselor: But, yeah, when you're having these kind of thoughts, because that's quite a lot of negative thoughts you're describing, how do you feel?
Client: Empty? I don't. I'm just calling as it is. I'm just calling it as reality. And I feel like I'm being honest with myself by just voicing it and not trying to get around hiding it, because I know, like, I can say in myself.
Counselor: So it sounds like you feel like those thoughts are very true, then. I mean, if you were going to rate them, say, I'm going to pick out some of those thoughts you described. So you said I'm not very good and I'm inconveniencing them. How much would you say you believe those on a scale out of a hundred, where a hundred is like, I absolutely believe it and zero is like, I don't believe it at all.
Client: I'm about 80. Yeah.
Counselor: So you feel quite sure that you definitely believe those? Okay. And you said that when you're thinking those thoughts, you start to feel quite empty.
Client: I just feel distant. And like I said, I'm not really myself. I just. It's like I'm not really there, but when I am, I can't even do a good job.
Counselor: Are there any other emotions that you experience?
Client: I feel drained. I don't feel like I'm in touch with anything. Just. It's like everything's going on around me, but I'm just not there. I'm just. It's like I'm just watching.
Counselor: Okay, so you feel empty, distant. You feel drained. And how when you're feeling these emotions, how do you feel in your body? Kind of what sensations do you notice?
Client: I don't know how to describe it. I get, like, I have a bit of, like, you know when you kind of get, like, butterflies when you're nervous and stuff? Kind of get a bit of that.
Counselor: Do you feel some butterflies?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Did you have butterflies that night when you were at the restaurant?
Client: Yeah, I was pretty nervous then, but when I got into it, they went away and, like, it distracted me for a bit until, obviously, I realized that I wasn't doing a very good job.
Counselor: Okay. And when you have those emotions, how does it affect your energy levels? Do you feel more energetic, less energetic or about the same?
Client: When I'm feeling down, yeah.
Counselor: When you're having those emotions that you were describing, I just feel drained.
Client: Like, I didn't even have, like, the energy to wake up in the morning sometimes. Like, oh, I just feel pointless and, like, my body's heavy and I don't want to. Yeah.
Counselor: So it sounds like you feel very tired, you're struggling to wake up. You said it's pointless. And what do you do then when you feel like that? So I guess you just talked about when you wake up in the morning and you feel heavy, and I suppose you've been maybe having some of these thoughts and those emotions potentially the night before. What do you then do? How do you respond to that?
Client: I just have to get up. I suppose I don't really have a choice because my mum. I live with my mum, and I know it's hard for her, so I don't want her to be too worried. So I just. I just try to carry on as normal. I get up. It takes longer and I don't want to, but I do, and I'll get on with my routine.
Counselor: So you're a bit slower in getting up.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But you are still getting up anyway. And what about your kind of. What do you think about when you're doing that?
Client: I'm just thinking that nobody else is like me, it's my age, like, nobody should be feeling like this, and I'm the only one that does.
Counselor:
output: So it sounds like you think a bit more about the problem and you kind of spend time thinking about how.

Client: Right, right. It's not productive.
Counselor: But there's a part of you mentioned earlier where, like you said, you just can't help yourself.
Client: Like I said, I just lose it. And I do that because that's what it feels like.
Counselor: So it's like you just. You just see, for example, like the dishes, right? So you just see the dishes aren't done, and immediately there's the.
Client: I just. I go off. Why didn't you do the dishes? You've been home an hour and a half. You could have done one thing for me. I had a longer day, and you knew it.
Counselor: All right, so let me take an example from work, right, so you work in an office with other people. Do they ever frustrate you in a way similar to what your boyfriend does?
Client: Occasionally, yeah, on occasion. Yeah.
Counselor: So there's times where you kind of have that moment with them where you just can't believe they didn't do something.
Client: Or I. Yeah, I just can't stand them sometimes.
Counselor: What's your reaction in terms of anger and yelling to those events?
Client: I get pissed, but I just. I can't. I can't yell.
Counselor: You can't yell? No. Why is that?
Client: I get fired.
Counselor: You get fired. So in those interactions with your coworkers, would be fair to say you're in that moment just as angry as you are with your boyfriend.
Client: And, oh, if not more, because I actually choose to be with my boyfriend. I don't choose to be with those people necessarily.
Counselor: You just happen to be together. And so in those instances, because there's a consequence like being fired, you're able to control the outward expression of anger, meaning you're not yelling, but inwardly, you're still angry at them.
Client: Yeah, I guess so.
Counselor: Yeah. So they don't really know you're angry.
Client: Yeah. I just walk away. I don't think they'd be able to tell.
Counselor: And they're not being yelled at, so they're not.
Client: Right. They wouldn't react. Yeah.
Counselor: No reaction. Right. So there is a thought process that occurs between the trigger and when you act, because at work, you're thinking, you have this thought that comes up, I don't want to be fired.
Client: Yeah, I get there. Must. Yeah.
Counselor: And the consequence of that thought is I'll be angry, but I'm not going to act angry.
Client: Right. I can't act angry or I'll get fired, and I don't want to get fired, I guess.
Counselor: So knowing that there is a thought there when you come home and you see the dishes aren't done, maybe just stay with that example. What would that thought be like? Think back to the last time that happened. Do you remember what you were thinking at that moment as you saw those dishes sitting there not washed?
Client: I mean, just that he never does anything. Right.
Counselor: He never does anything. Right. So you see. So you see the dishes not washed. He never does anything. Right. That's the thought, yeah. And then the reaction, the behavior is finding him. Right. And yelling at him.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right, so you see how there is an intervening thought between the trigger, which in this case, the dishes, and the behavior, which is the yelling.
Client: Yeah. I guess there's a thought where I'm sitting there and I'm looking at him, thinking about it, saying, you never do anything. Right.
Counselor: So remember we talked a few weeks ago about cognitive distortions? We talked about, like, the errors, like, consistent. There are consistent errors in thinking. Right. And I'm wondering if that thought, he never does anything right. If that's similar to or matches up with any of the cognitive distortions we talked about. And I'm wondering if it's not. If it's not kind of blocking off your path in terms of thinking. Right. So you're saying he never does anything right.
Client: Right.
Counselor: It's kind of like maybe a kind of all or nothing thinking that we talked about that.
Client: Oh, it's absolute tunnel vision at that point.
Counselor: Tunnel vision, yeah. Okay. So a few different distortions at work. But you mentioned earlier there are times when he does do things right.
Client: Yeah. There are occasions where he must have thought about me.
Counselor: He was more thoughtful than more considerate. Okay. More considerate. So the statement he never does the thought, he never does anything right that could be challenged.
Client: Yeah, I guess technically it could.
Counselor: And what might be as an alternative to the behavior? Right. To the yelling. Instead of doing that, what might be a thought that you could kind of insert right after that he never does anything right. Thought that might change the outcome for you. That might disrupt that connection between that thought and your yelling.
Client: Maybe that he has done something right in the past.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: So it's bound to happen again. It is possible.
Counselor: All right. So an adapted response, as we call him or his self talk, that says he's not. He's not altogether bad because he has done things right in the past.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Right. Which is a little more flexible in thinking than thinking. He. Then your automatic thought.
Client: Right?
Counselor: Yeah. That's your automatic thought. Never does anything right. So a little bit more flexibility in the thinking might get you to a place where you're not yelling. And then on the other side of it, too, I'm wondering if we can't challenge the usefulness of yelling. You mentioned that you've done it quite a bit, but you're not really getting a different result.
Client: It doesn't. The dishes don't get done after that. And the next day, I might still find the dishes there. It doesn't.
Counselor: It's not working.
Client: It hasn't worked. Yeah.
Counselor: So when you're yelling, there's an expression of emotion, but there's also this hope that the yelling will change his behavior.
Client: Right.
Counselor: Something, but it's not.
Client: Yep.
Counselor: And when was the first time in terms of, like, how long ago this was a problem?
Client: I've had previous boyfriends where this was a problem, and that relationship has long gone because of it.
Counselor: So due to the yelling?
Client: Due to the yelling. So I don't. I really do like this guy who's not all bad, and I don't want my yelling to be a problem, my anger.
Counselor: But it's hard to control for you. You're struggling with the anger.
Client: Right?
Counselor: Yelling.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Rationally, you understand it doesn't work. Like, it's not getting what you want, but somehow it feels like a release it feels like justice. It feels good to be able to.
Client: It feels like that's what I'm supposed to be doing, and that's what I do.
Counselor: That's what you're supposed to be doing. Okay. So it feels like it's what you're supposed to be doing. Do you have an idea of what might be a more productive path for you as an alternative to the yelling?
Client: Protective. That's a great word. I guess walking away is what I do at the office.
Counselor: And that has worked for you.
Client: I've been able to take a minute and either remove myself or intervene my opinion more calmly because I haven't yelled at work, I guess walking away and taking a minute.
Counselor: Okay. So that would be one behavioral strategy. So you see the trigger and you have the thought. It never does anything. Right. And then you could intervene with a thought of, I need to walk away. And a behavior of walking away and taking, like, how much time?
Client: I mean, honestly, if I'm by myself, like, five minutes, ten minutes of just me time.
Counselor: So let's even say ten minutes.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So ten minutes. And then you can respond more constructively, more usefully to what is, you know, a type of relational disagreement. Right. You have a disagreement over, it sounds like, who should be doing what.
Client: Right. I. At what point in the day when he was working, when being considerate of the other.
Counselor: And that. That's certainly worth talking about. I mean, that makes sense that you guys would talk through that. But it seems like the yelling. I mean, you're just going right to the yelling.
Client: We're not getting anywhere.
Counselor: Right. So there's not really any time to address the issue.
Client: Right? Yeah, we have not worked out. Dad would help.
Counselor: So the yelling is really an impediment to what you want to achieve with the yelling?
Client: Yeah, I guess.
Counselor: Right. In a manner speaking. Right. It's blocking your goal. So do you kind of recognize that? Like, you seeing how I didn't think.
Client: That there was anything between me seeing the dishes and yelling at him. I knew that the anger wasn't getting me anywhere, but I didn't think I. But I guess there is a moment in between because I don't always yell. Like, I don't yell at work. So there is something else I could do.
Counselor: Right. So if I'm hearing you right, there's a sensation that it's kind of reflexive, like you see the dishes, and automatically you go right to the.
Client: Immediately it feels like I'm yelling.
Counselor: But in actuality, now you're realizing that there's a gap even if it's small, there's a gap where thinking takes place.
Client: And, yeah, there's a sliver that I must see at work that is also there at home.
Counselor: And I'm wondering, too, that there's a sense that. I mean, there's a sense that the rules, the relationship are being violated. You come home, and a part of you might know that's going to happen. Like, you. You come in, you know, you might see that this is not done or some other.
Client: Right?
Counselor: Sure. Not done. So I'm wondering, if you think about it in advance, kind of try to inoculate yourself, so to speak.
Client: Like, oh, I can definitely say it's been a thought. When I'm driving home, I'm like, it's been. Been a long day. It was a long day at the office. And I know he's not gonna have the trash taken out like I asked him or the dishes done or the chicken thought anything.
Counselor: Well, and that goes both ways. Right? The thinking about advance can be a good thing because you can prepare yourself for that moment when you're gonna apply that adaptive response. You can prepare to see something that's gonna potentially upset you. But thinking about advance can also be destructive. If you start investing in the more negative thoughts, like, if you start saying things like, I know I'm going to find something, and you already get worked.
Client: Out, you're starting to get angry.
Counselor: Right. So if you're getting angry in advance, that's not a use of the thoughts, but the thoughts you might want to consciously say to yourself, the adaptive responses would be, you know, I know I'm probably gonna find something didn't go perfectly.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: And I'm gonna be prepared to take a few minutes to. To calm down.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So that way, when you see it, it's not such a shock. It doesn't feel like such a reflex to go right to the anger. Yeah, that makes sense.
Client: It does. It does. It's like one more non productive piece of it that I could change.
Counselor: Yeah. That's within your power to change. Right. And it could be something very good for you. So now it might be working against you, the thoughts in advance of when you come home, but you could have those thoughts working for you.
Client: And just start myself off by thinking, he's not all bad. There could be something there, but it'll be okay. Like, I can just take a minute to myself.
Counselor: Right. There's good. There's useful and unuseful traits. Both. They both coexist. But I'm thinking in terms of this as the adaptive response. There's useful and unuseful traits, but I know I need to calm down if I'm going to get to the like, if I'm going to work through this matter of being considerate and this relational stressor. So adaptive responses to have to be short. They just have to be inserted at the right point, which is right after that automatic thought.
Client: Right. Okay.
Counselor: Okay. We'll work on building some adaptive responses that you can apply and we'll kind of test them and see how well they work.
Client: Yeah, that'd be great.
Counselor: It's my hope that you'll be successful at this and they'll reduce the anger, but it could take time, it could be frustrating. And these will be, we'll continue to build these skills I think will be valuable to combat the yelling reaction and the angry feelings.
Client: I bought that.
Counselor: Okay, so we'll work on that. I'm going to give you a document today called thought record where I want you to just kind of read it over this time and we'll talk about in more detail next time. But it's an opportunity to record your thoughts like a trigger and your thoughts kind of what happened. And then there's a place for adaptive responses, but we'll go through it step by step. I'm just going to give it to you today so you can look at it and familiarize yourself with the format. All fits on one page. And what I'm going to ask you to do in the future is to complete these thought records. When you have a thought that ends up with a behavior, whether it's a desirable or undesirable outcome, we're going to see what the process is and then how well the adaptive responses are working because we may have to adjust them a bit over time.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Does that more or less make sense?
Client: It does. It does.
Counselor:
output: Alright, so I'll give you that. We'll schedule another appointment and we'll pick up next week and we'll start going through the thought record for this week. I would say try the adaptive response that we worked out here and the behavioral response, which is the ten minutes walking away. Yeah, yeah. And see. And see how well that works. You know, I would expect that would have some level of success. Maybe there's certain times where you're, you're not as successful. That's okay. We want to focus on the times where you can walk away for the ten minutes and we'll see, you know.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Ashley. How you doing today?
Client: I'm doing all right.
Counselor: How you been feeling over the last few days?
Client: I'm a little bit overwhelmed with schoolwork, and my boyfriend has been getting on my nerves quite a bit, but otherwise pretty good.
Counselor: So you have a few things going on, but overall, you're feeling okay.
Client: Mm hmm.
Counselor: Yeah. I remember during the last session you had some difficulties at work.
Client: Yeah. They seem to have been getting a little bit better with the homework that you gave me. It has helped me to identify when I. I'm getting a little more overwhelmed at work, and when I'm able to identify when I'm feeling that way, it's helped me to, I guess, meet my supervisor in the middle, more or less, so I'm not as argumentative. And she seems to be a little more impressed with my work performance.
Counselor: Good.
Client: She's been good.
Counselor: So identifying the automatic thoughts has helped you kind of negotiate that relationship more productively?
Client: Yeah, absolutely. That's great.
Counselor: So you're able to complete the thought, record the homework?
Client: Yeah. And that's actually helped me a lot, not just with work, but when I'm out, say, grocery shopping, and I start feeling that way, it's helped me to bring myself back down so I don't get overwhelmed and I don't get so anxious.
Counselor: Good, good. So that's a positive result. So I want to kind of set our structure for today, like, what we'll be talking about today during this session. And I was wondering if there's a few things kind of on your mind, like what you wanted to discuss today.
Client: Oh, there's a couple things. My classwork has been really been bogging me down lately, and then while I'm still doing better at work, I'm still not where I want to be. I don't want to have to consciously think this is why I'm. I want to keep working on. And I'm not being so argumentative at work. And then my boyfriend has been, like I said earlier, really gritting on my nerves, and I don't, like, I told him the other day that I wanted to break up with him, but he told me he was going to change and that things would get better. So I'm kind of torn with whether or not to continue in their relationship or just let it go. And at the same time, I'm having a hard time keeping up with my schoolwork and getting everything done on time. And my homework isn't where I want it to be. Like, I feel like I can do better.
Counselor: So you're being pulled in a few directions here. And all of these things are important to you. Like, all these things are bothering you, the schoolwork lateness, the relationship at work. Like, you're doing better with that, but you still want some improvement there and then some relational challenges with your boyfriend. So I know it's difficult to prioritize concerns when they're all important to you. Right. But if you really only had, say, one thing to choose for today's session that you really wanted to work on as a priority, what would you choose?
Client: That's really hard. That's hard to.
Counselor: Well, tell me about your thought processes as you answer that question. As you think about that question.
Client: Well, I've been with my boyfriend for about nine months now, and I thought that we were going to go into like, marriage and children, and I thought we had a future. At the same time, my work, I need. I need my job. I need it to pay bills and basically live. And at the same time, my schoolwork is very important because as progressing in school and getting a better education, I'll be able to get a better job, which will, hopefully it'll be a job in which I don't find myself where I am right now, butting heads with my supervisor all the time and everything.
Counselor: So again, it comes down to all three goals, really are, they really are important to you. All three matter to you and you want to work on them. So I'm wondering, as we think about trying to rank them, which is what we're really doing. Right. Trying to pick one is the most important, which area you think is interfering with your functioning the most, like what's getting in the way of your mood, being good? Or are you accomplishing goals you need to accomplish to survive?
Client: Probably my, probably my schoolwork.
Counselor: How does school work? Yes, tell me about that.
Client: Well, I think it's most important because, like I said, it'll set me up later in life. So not getting a good grade on an assignment really brings me down because I view it as a threat to my future. Because if I don't get a good grade, then I could possibly fail out of school. And failing out of school means I won't have a good job job, then I won't have a good relationship and definitely top of my list.
Counselor: So that's the priority. So we'll look at that problem, the schoolwork issue. We'll make that the number one priority for today. And if we get through that and we have time, we can look at one of the other things that's going on. I want to make sure. We kind of set a structure so we know what we'll be talking about and what we want to accomplish. So what we'll do is, I'll have you tell me a little bit more about that and kind of your thoughts and feelings and behaviors surrounding that schoolwork issue. And we'll go through some techniques, and I'll assign some homework related to that, more or less like I did last time when it was the workplace challenge. The workplace relationship. That was the challenge. Does that kind of make sense?
Client: Yeah, definitely.
Counselor:
output: Does that sound like an agenda that you comfortable with for the session?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Terry. How you doing today?
Client: I'm okay, I think.
Counselor: You okay?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I know when we talked last time, you were having a rough time dealing with the passing year, Sister Sheila.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And you're kind of a point where we were talking about emotional consequences, but also some of the thinking that's going on. Have you been processing that?
Client: Yeah, I've been thinking about some of that and, you know, trying to kind of work through it a little bit. So I think I'm kind of ready to kind of work through it and talk about it a little bit now.
Counselor: So, feeling a little less emotional and feeling a little more thinking about it. And, like, on the rational side, like we talked about rational and irrational beliefs.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: A little more focus there or more ability to focus there today.
Client: Yeah, I think I'm ready to think about it more.
Counselor: I know the emotional part was tough for you, and I'm sure it still.
Client: Is, but I think I've kind of got through some of that, and I'm ready to kind of get through the way I'm thinking about some things.
Counselor: Ready to look at through the thinking lens.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So to speak. All right. So what are some of the thoughts or beliefs that you've been having, you think maybe part of what's affecting your mood?
Client: Well, I've been. I've been thinking about it, and, you know, I just. I just feel like I don't. I don't have anybody that I can talk to. I mean, I just. I keep thinking about it. I don't have anybody to talk to. She was the only one I had to talk to.
Counselor: So in your relationship with her, you guys talked a lot. She was an important person in your life for a variety of reasons, but including that she was easy to talk to.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And that you could talk to her?
Client: I. Yes.
Counselor: So the thought is you have nobody to talk to.
Client: I just, you know, she was just everything to me. I talked to her about everything, and, you know, she was just always gave me good advice, and she could always work, you know, talk me through anything that I needed to talk about, and I just don't feel like I have that anymore. Since she's going, I don't have anybody like that anymore.
Counselor: That relationship is valuable to you, and you've lost that, and you feel like you've lost having anybody that you could talk to. Is that. Is that close?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: All right, so let's look at that thought. Let's break that down. Certainly you were able to talk to her, as you mentioned, and you have lost her.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Right. So you have lost someone that you could talk to that was very valuable to you, and that's understandably painful. The question would be, have you lost everybody that you could talk to? Is there anyone else in your life, for instance, currently, that you regularly speak with?
Client: Well, you know, since you said that, you know, maybe I do have some people that I can go to. They're not her. But, you know, you know, I have a couple of people that I can talk to that they're willing to talk to me about certain things. I guess if I give them the chance, you know, I'll be able to talk to them.
Counselor: So there are some people in your life that you can talk to. They certainly don't replace your sister, but you have people you can't communicate with, and that can be helpful for you.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So as we build kind of a rationale, self talk to replace the irrational thinking that you brought in.
Client: Right.
Counselor: Which was that you have no one to talk to. Could the replacement be something like, I had my sister to talk to, and she was really good at that, and it's painful to have lost her, but I gained something from that experience, and I do still have some people to talk to now.
Client: Yeah, that sounds about right.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: Yeah, yeah. Yeah. Because nobody's gonna replace my sister. But, you know, I do think that there's other people that can. Could help me and what I need to talk. Yeah.
Counselor: And maybe one thing that you can. You can take away from this as well is that because of the way you could talk to your sister, you are a more effective communicator now, and you can make the most out of the relationships that you have now with people currently. Another rational thought kind of honors her contribution to you.
Client: Right? Yeah, because, you know, she is, like, the only one that believed in me. I mean, she just, you know, she always, you know, pushed me to go higher and, you know, on my job. She always said that, you know, that you can do it, you know, just believe in yourself. She always, you know, encouraged me to. To go back to school and, you know, I'm, you know, I have done that and, you know, continually doing that, you know, but, you know, she was a big motivator for me. And, you know, since she's gone now, you know, I don't feel like that I have anybody else that gives me that push that she did.
Counselor: So. So the thought would be, I've lost the only person that would believe in me. Yes, something like that. Okay, so she was a great positive force, great positive presence and contributor in your life, in part because she believed in you.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And now that's gone, and you feel like no one else will believe in you in that way.
Client: Not like she did.
Counselor: Not like she did.
Client: No. No.
Counselor:
output: Which could be true. Right? There may be no one else that ever believes in you that same way, but similarly, like we were doing before, can you think of some people now that believed in you, maybe in a different way that's still helpful? It doesn't replace her, but it might still be helpful to you?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Well, Meredith, we know each other, but the way we usually start a CBT session is to set an agenda. So we might have several ideas about what we want on the agenda. But the first thing is usually for us to make a problem list together about whatever it is that you might want to work on.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: And then we'll do the problem list, and then we'll explain, explore the thoughts and the behaviors that might be related to the problem. And hopefully, by the end of our time together, we'll have a clearer idea about what's causing the problem and some ideas about how to maybe change things.
Client: Sounds good.
Counselor: All right.
Client: So one thing that I've been noticing lately is that I have a tendency to kind of hang back in groups, and I tend to observe instead of participate.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: And a lot of times I get really nervous when I feel like I'm expected to speak up. And I want to speak up, but I kind of feel like I freeze.
Counselor: Okay. And so in particular, then, in groups, the setting is big groups, little groups. Does it matter?
Client: It doesn't matter a whole lot, but generally, I guess medium size. Like, you know, in classes that I have usually, like maybe twelve people or so. So relatively small, medium. I don't know what size that is.
Counselor: Okay. And so. But in your head, you probably would say, I would like to speak up, but for some reason, you feel inside some anxiety or nervousness about that.
Client: Definitely.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: And then sometimes when I try to force myself to speak up, when I actually don't feel ready, I get like. I feel like my throat's closing and I get a red face.
Counselor: Okay. All right. So that's sort of one possible issue for us to talk about. Could you maybe give me a specific example of a particular group situation, as recent as you can, where you had this feeling of hanging back and maybe. Maybe some fear of evaluation?
Client: So in my statistics class each week, we have a. It's called an inclusion activity. And generally, I guess it's supposed to help people feel like the group's more cohesive and included, but I usually experience it as the opposite. So there's usually a task at the beginning of each class of like, take off your shoe and talk. Talk about the most interesting place your shoe has been. Stuff like this in stats that, um, usually I get really nervous and I feel like I can't think of anything to say. And I feel like I usually end up saying something really awkward or lame, and I just don't feel good about it. Like, I feel.
Counselor: Yeah. Can you give me that specific example of the recent time when maybe. And then. And what you said, too, including sort of the beginning, what happened and then how it ended.
Client: Yeah. So when we did this activity, it's, like, a really weird example. When we did this activity, you know, probably six or seven people had gone in front of me, and I was, like, not listening to anything that anyone else was saying, just totally self absorbed in terms of, like, oh, God, what am I going to say? And not being able to think of anything. And then when it was my turn, I was wearing a pair of shoes that, like, are kind of, like, they have lace on them. And so I took it off and I said, I like these shoes because I get cool tan lines from them. So I didn't even really answer the question that was like, where have these shoes been? Or, like, the coolest place these shoes have been? Or something like that. And then after I went, I didn't really listen to anything else anyone said because I was still, like, stuck on, why didn't I answer the question and just kind of feeling awkward.
Counselor: Okay, so what I'm doing here is I've got several columns that I'm building, and the first one is, you're in the stats class, and you're going through an inclusion activity. And the second one is the thoughts that you're having. What thoughts are going through your mind? And the thoughts are, oh, God, what am I going to say? Those are the early thoughts. And then maybe the later thoughts are, why didn't I even answer the question?
Client: Yeah. And, like, why can't I ever be articulate?
Counselor: Okay. Why can't I ever be articulate? Okay. And then our third column are the emotions that you might be feeling. And so as you're in that situation and people are taking their turn, the teacher says, you're doing the inclusion activity. People are taking their turns. And what are you feeling? How would you describe your emotional state?
Client: Nervous. Yeah. Like, fearful. And, like, it's almost like I'm anticipating. Anticipating embarrassment.
Counselor: Mm hmm.
Client: So I don't know that's a feeling or not, but usually I feel embarrassed.
Counselor: I put that in the thought okay. Column just because it seems like the anticipation of it is probably a thought, but embarrassment when you're in the middle of it is probably a fear. Does that make sense? And then. So I got nervous, fearful, embarrassed as the emotions, and on a scale of zero, not at all. 100 being the most of that feeling you could ever have, how would you rate? Let's get rid of nervous because it's sort of covered by fearful. How would you rate fearful. And how would you rate embarrassed?
Client: Maybe fearful? Like a four. Okay, four or five. I don't know.
Counselor: Four out of five.
Client: Out of 140.
Counselor: Okay. I was gonna say. Oh, feeling pretty calm. So a 40 or a 50?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. And embarrassed.
Client: I'd say that's higher.
Counselor: A little higher.
Client: Yeah. Like a 70.
Counselor: So maybe a 70. And that would be at the moment that you're talking or right afterwards or right before fluctuating?
Client: Yeah, I'd say, like both during and after.
Counselor: Okay. Okay. So during and after. Alright. And so, you know, the cognitive approach to thinking about what's going on is that it's not the situation that causes the emotional reaction, but it's what you're thinking that causes the emotional reaction. And so it seems to me like one of the things that's going on. Oh, God, what am I gonna say? And why didn't I answer? Why can't I never be articulate?
Client: Why can't I never be articulate? That sounds exactly perfect.
Counselor: We might have to start rating my anxiety now, too. And then I guess there's the other thing you said that you're anticipating embarrassment. And so are those words too, also that are going through your head.
Client: Yeah. Like, I wish I could be more clever or I wish I could have just like, a funny story right now.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: Or make people laugh in a way that I want them to laugh.
Counselor: One of the things I'm doing now is a lot of times when you think about the thoughts that trigger the emotions, these are the thoughts that we would categorize as less helpful, kind of unhelpful thoughts. And then over here, what we're doing is we're coming up with some thoughts that might be more helpful. Okay. Recognizing that no thoughts are perfect, but some thoughts are more helpful. Especially some thoughts are less helpful. And you know in your SAS class, you're going to do the inclusion activity every week. Every week. And so one possibility is you could come in prepared to shift your thinking from the less helpful to the more helpful. Just an idea.
Client: It's a good idea.
Counselor: Okay, so what else besides this is silly and what I say doesn't matter all that much.
Client: I can be clever sometimes.
Counselor: I can be clever. Sometimes. Good. That's sort of a counter to the why can't I ever be articulate? Or why can't I never be articulate? Either way you say it, let's pretend for a second that you were talking to a friend who had exactly this same scenario, and she was telling you the way that she talks to herself. Oh, God. What am I going to say? And why can't I answer that? Why can't I ever be articulate? I know I'm going to embarrass myself. And so she's talking to herself that way. How would you talk to her?
Client: I think that I probably express surprise because I imagine that usually I don't perceive her as inarticulate or as embarrassing as she sees herself.
Counselor: Okay, so you would be surprised and kind of reassuring to her and say, oh, you don't seem that way. And if you could be on her shoulder in the situation, what would you whisper in her? Earthen, hmm, this is a good friend of yours. You want to be helpful?
Client: I would tell her that she's funny and charming and usually has really cool stories to tell because you've had lots of good experiences.
Counselor: So you'd be sitting on your shoulder saying things like, you are funny and charming and you have cool stories to tell. What's it feel like when you imagine actually even saying those words to yourself in this kind of situation?
Client: Um, I mean, it sounds pretty ideal, but it sounds really far away from my current experience.
Counselor: It's not what you're whispering in your own ear?
Client: No.
Counselor: What's, what would stop you from, from actually doing this, from talking to yourself? Just like you would talk to a good friend because you're talking to yourself. You're kind of talking to yourself more like somebody who wanted to pull you down. And so I just think, huh, what about that good friend? I mean, can you be a good friend to yourself in those moments and say something more supportive? You are pretty successful in a variety of different things in your life. Right. And so if you take one of those examples and you kind of break it down, are you able to, what do you do to prepare? Well, for example, even for a statistics test, I would guess that you have to go through some preparation.
Client: Mm hmm. Study.
Counselor: Study. Okay. Kind of like studying. Have you ever been in a, like a play or a dramatic performance?
Client: Oh, no, I avoid that.
Counselor: Not even, like, in grade school?
Client: No. I think I maybe was in 7th grade.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: Yeah. But I had a very small part.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: I've always, like, my whole life shied away from being the center of attention. It never feels good to me.
Counselor: No.
Client: Which is ironic since I'm going to school, become a teacher.
Counselor: Yeah. So you have taught before and spoken in front of groups. Small, medium.
Client: Yeah. But it never feels.
Counselor: It never feels comfortable.
Client: No. No. Yeah.
Counselor: So even right now, as we're, as we're talking, so I hear you say it never feels comfortable. Right. Would you put that thought in the category of helpful or unhelpful to say that to yourself?
Client: I'd say that's unhelpful.
Counselor: Unhelpful. Okay. What's unhelpful about that thought?
Client: It kind of makes me feel like no matter how much I prepare to, I still won't feel like I'm good enough or competent.
Counselor:
output: Yeah. And just before that, you said, I always shied away from attention. It's never felt good. Okay.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Lucy. Nice to meet you.
Client: Hi.
Counselor: So I understand that you were referred here by your GP because you've been feeling quite down recently.
Client: Yeah, I thought I should. I've been feeling quite bad for quite a while, so I thought maybe it's time to see someone about it because I don't want to feel like this anymore.
Counselor: Okay. So from your notes, I saw that you saw the GP about three months ago?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So how long have you been feeling down altogether?
Client: Quite a few months before that as well, actually. But it's gotten pretty bad these past few months, so that's kind of why I came.
Counselor: Okay. So has it got worse since you saw your GP?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay, so tell me, how are things at the moment?
Client: Well, it kind of started just feeling a bit low and wound up about things, but, I don't know, just recently I just can't really be bothered to do anything at all. I kind of find it hard to get motivated for things and I want to be. I really want to be better, but it's just kind of reaching the end now where I just. I want to do something about it.
Counselor: Okay, so you said that you're feeling really down, really sad?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you feel like you haven't got any motivation, but. Are you okay?
Client: Yeah, I'm fine.
Counselor: Sorry. Okay, and you haven't got any motivation, but it sounds like you've put quite a lot of pressure on yourself to try and feel a bit better.
Client: Yeah, I just. It's kind of hard as well because there's not really anyone to talk about. So I just kind of stay on my own trying to. I don't like to think about it, but I don't know.
Counselor: So you say you've been. You've been feeling quite isolated. There's not many people around.
Client: Yeah. There's no one I can talk to about it. No one would listen or understand anyway.
Counselor: Okay, so I'm just going to try and find out a little bit more about you. So I understand that you're an english student at uni.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you live away from home with some friends. Is that right?
Client: Yeah, I live here.
Counselor: Oh, okay. So you don't live far from the uni, but you say you feel like you live with your friends, but you don't feel like you can talk to them.
Client: Yeah, I mean, they're lovely. I get on really well with them, but I don't know, recently, whenever they want to go out or stuff, I just. I don't want to bring them down. I can't. They don't understand what I'm going through. They kind of. I don't know, they don't make fun of how I feel, but they don't really understand what it's like. I just. I don't want to go out with them and bring them down or stuff.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds. Do you try and hide the way you're feeling from them?
Client: I guess. I mean, it's easier to hide it than to try and explain it all the time when no one really wants to know.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like you've been feeling down, you've been feeling unmotivated, you feel like you want to be better. But actually it sounds like you feel like you can't reach out for help, you can't speak to anybody.
Client: No, I don't really talk to my parents a lot either, so that's kind of hard.
Counselor: Okay. I'm just gonna go back in time a little bit, I suppose. I'm just wondering, when did all of this start? You said it's been going on for quite a few months.
Client: Yeah, I guess it kind of started, actually, when I was revising for my exams. I guess the stress. I put a lot of stress on myself. I think I've always wanted to do well for me and I guess for my parents. So the stress of exams. And it was also kind of hard because my parents were going through a bit of a troubled time then.
Counselor: Okay, so this would be like last March, last April?
Client: Yeah, I think so.
Counselor: Around that time. So about six months ish. And it sounds like a lot was happening. So you had a lot of uni pressure on and you said that your parents were having marital problems. Okay. And it sounds like that was a real shock to you.
Client: Yeah, I guess it was hard as well because I wasn't doing well at uni. I guess I just felt a bit guilty. I know it sounds silly, but I felt like maybe if I could do better, then they would get better, but it just wasn't really happening.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like you were trying to work hard and be more successful because you thought that that would make them happier and try and fix things.
Client: Yeah, I wanted to make them feel better, but it just kind of backfired a little, I guess.
Counselor: How did it backfire?
Client: Well, it just ended up with them getting worse, and I've just been feeling worse since then.
Counselor: Okay, so after the summer, after the exam period. And how did that exam period go for you in the end?
Client: Not very well.
Counselor: Okay. That's an awful lot of pressure to put on yourself that you supposed to.
Client: Think it's just annoying because I know I should have done better and I just didn't. And I guess I beat myself up a lot about it.
Counselor: So you say. I know, I know I should have done better.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I mean, I suppose hearing it from my perspective, I'm thinking it sounds like you had an awful lot going on at the time. It would be understandable, absolutely. That you wouldn't do as well as normal. I suppose I'm just wondering if you have very high standards for yourself.
Client: Probably maybe more than other people. My parents have always kind of taught me. Not in a loving way, I guess, but that you should do your best, but also get the best. And I agree with that. I think that's the right thing to think. But when I don't do that, I don't know, it annoys me a lot and I worry that it annoys them.
Counselor: So it sounds like you feel you should always do your best. Is that the word you used? Yeah. And that there isn't any kind of exceptions for that, but no. Okay. So I can see then that was a really difficult time for you and that was when your mood started to get lower. And things are still quite bad now. I mean, what's the situation with your parents at the moment?
Client: I think it doesn't sound good. I don't really talk to them a lot, but I don't think they're going through very good. I don't like to talk to them about it because it just makes me feel worse. But I don't think it's getting any better.
Counselor: Were you home over the summer?
Client: For a little bit, yeah.
Counselor: And how was that?
Client: Not very fun? No, it was quite tense all the time. Stress me out more than relaxed me over the summer, I guess.
Counselor: Okay. Okay. So it sounds then like quite a lot has been happening. You've been feeling very low, you've had uni pressure on, and you've had problems with your parents marriage. And sounds like you feel like you can't really reach out to anyone. Like you can't understand, but you can't really reach out to your parents right now. You can't really confide in your friends. So I suppose I'm just wondering if you can tell me a bit more about how you've been feeling. I mean, say this past week.
Client: Really not good, to be honest. I actually. If I don't have to, then I don't really leave the house or get out of. But I just. I can't find the motivation for the things I used to join. I used to love doing sports or going out. And now I just prefer to lie in bed and not really do anything.
Counselor:
output: Okay.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hazel, how you doing today?
Client: I'm okay.
Counselor: What's been going on?
Client: Well, last time I started to tell you a little bit about one of my friends, my best friend, actually, she had this issue. So what happened was she went to a bathroom at our local library, and she found a video camera when she was going to the bathroom.
Counselor: In the bathroom?
Client: Yeah. She actually. Yeah. And she turned it into the police, and I guess because, like, she carried it, or she had found it, her handprints were on it, and they weren't be able. They weren't able to detect who actually did it. They weren't able to catch the person.
Counselor: Oh, they didn't catch the person?
Client: No. So since then, I've been on really just high alert. Like, I'm worried that that could happen to me, to my kids, and I'm just really worried because they didn't catch the guy, that him or someone like him could be out there.
Counselor: So he's still out in the community.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So how is it affecting your. Your daily life? Can you tell me kind of what your. What you've been feeling?
Client: Um, a lot of anxiety just not knowing, maybe, you know, what if someone were to videotape me like that? I've been very aware, shall I say, of cameras.
Counselor: Okay. So anxious and aware.
Client: Right. Like, I know you have one in your office, and people on their cell phone cameras. Just all the possibilities that I could be recorded. I've just been very aware of them, which makes me not want to go anywhere. So I've been having arguments with my husband a lot because he wants to go out to restaurants, and I don't want to go because there could be cameras in the bathrooms and how I dress. Also, as you can see, I'm kind of dressed more conservatively because I remember hearing once about cameras that people use on shoes that could be used in a creepy way. And so I can't. You know, it's now almost summertime. I can't dress in skirts or be comfortable because I'm dressing like that.
Counselor: So you covered a lot of ground there. So you have the. You have the feeling of being, like, worried, nervous. Right. That's going to happen to you, but you've also had to kind of change your routine, or you feel you have to change your routine to feel safer.
Client: Right.
Counselor: Has that helped. Has changing the way you dressed or changing where you go and when you go, has that helped reduce the anxiety?
Client: Not really, no. I would say it's really starting. That's why I wanted to come in. It's really starting to affect my life.
Counselor: You mentioned specifically your husband. Like, what's been going on there?
Client: He just wants to go places with our kids, like, go out to eat. And I don't really want to go anywhere because, you know, cameras are everywhere nowadays, and I just kind of worry, like, public bathrooms, could they be there? Could someone be, you know, sometimes baby monitors are, you know, hooked up on so people can hack into that laptop, cameras. So even in my own house, I've just been really nervous, so I feel like I'm not really getting relief from that anxiety.
Counselor: Have you taken any precautions because of this persistent worry? I mean, I already mentioned, like, with the camera specifically.
Client: I mean, I've, you know, when I go into bathrooms, I've been looking for cameras to make sure they weren't there before. You know, me or my children have used the bathroom. I have tried. I read online that you can turn how to turn off the cameras on your phone and that you can close your laptop, and that way the camera will face down. And the same thing on a smart tv so it doesn't recognize your face. I've tried to turn things off. They don't need to be on as far as people being able to access my own information.
Counselor: And that seems reasonable. So you take reasonable precautions to try to avoid being video recorded against your will.
Client: Exactly.
Counselor: Okay. But still, you have this feeling of worry, anxiety, and your schedules being interfered with.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So you'd like to cope more effectively with your feelings, reduce this anxiety. So when you enter into a public bathroom. Now, we talked about automatic thoughts before.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Those thoughts just kind of pop into our head and they connect to feelings of that can be unpleasant, like anxiety and worry. So when you walk into a public restroom, what's the first thing that goes through your mind?
Client: That there might be a video camera that I don't see. That's maybe with my friend, it was big enough, but I might not catch it. And that someone's going to use that in a vulnerable way.
Counselor: Okay, so when you walk in, you're wondering if there's a camera there.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And when that automatic thought occurs, what follows that in terms of a feeling or behavior?
Client: Usually I'll try and find the camera, but it's usually anxiety, fear. My heart rate starts going up. I start getting really anxious. And then, you know, I try and either rush to use the bathroom if I really have to go, or a lot of times if I don't, I'll just leave. Sometimes I try and use the bathroom so I don't have to go out.
Counselor: So your behavior is looking for the camera or sometimes just leaving without using restroom, and you're feeling that anxiety worry that we've been talking about. Okay, so, really, if we think about. We talked before about core beliefs, intermediate beliefs, and I'm wondering if the intermediate belief isn't I'm vulnerable, or this more specifically, maybe that's more of a core belief. More specifically, I'm vulnerable in this area, like, with this guy on the loose that committed that crime, and then that's combining with situations that you encounter, and that's where you're getting those automatic thoughts. Does that sort of make sense?
Client: Exactly.
Counselor: Okay, so you remember what, in terms of cognitive therapy, we like to apply what we call the adaptive response, or self talk.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So it's that thought that you interject at that moment, you realize you're having an automatic thought that's gonna lead to, in this case, anxiety and worry and behaviors that, while looking for the camera, isn't maybe an unusual behavior, but leaving, you know, that could certainly be an unuseful behavior. So, in terms of that self talk, let's work to develop a self talk response, something you can tell yourself to that initial. I wonder if there's a camera in this bathroom. What do you think you could tell yourself that would get in between that thought and I, the feelings you're having?
Client: I could say if when I walk in the bathroom, maybe I could say, you know, while there could be a chance that there's a camera in this bathroom, the chance of it happening is not very likely. And, you know, I'm going to take steps to keep myself safe so that I won't be in a vulnerable position, such as looking for the cameras.
Counselor: Right. That's good. So you have a low probability of it happening, and you're taking useful behaviors to minimize your risk even further.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So that's a good automatic thought, I think, or good adaptive response for the automatic thought. Rather, why don't you try that one out the next time you have that automatic thought? Try out that. I think that's really logical. It's unlikely to happen. Of course there's a chance, and we acknowledge that in the self talk, there's a chance that it could happen, but there's precautions you can take, and it's a low chance sometimes as well. So keep that automatic thought. We'll review it at the end before you leave today. We'll write these down. But that's one adaptive response, rather, that I want to write down for you. I also want to talk about the worst case scenario because right now you have the anxiety and the worry about an event that while it's unlikely it could happen, it could happen. And I'm wondering how you think you would react if the worst did happen. If you used the restroom and you found out from law enforcement or by finding a camera that an offender had been watching you on a recording. I think you would react to that.
Client: I mean, I think I would be really upset. Upset. I think I would feel vulnerable probably for a while and be hesitant.
Counselor: But.
Client: I mean, I think ultimately I would be okay. My friend, this happened a while ago. She's starting to get to get over it and get back to her usual routine, although she's still hesitant. So I think I would be okay eventually, although I'd be really upset that.
Counselor: It happened and it would make sense to feel upset. That would be upsetting for anybody. But as you noted, that would probably be relatively temporary, that distress, right. Well, acute. And certainly you wouldn't be happy about it and shouldn't be happy about it. It would probably go away. You'd probably learn to adapt. How long have you been in this state of anxiety and worry?
Client: Probably it happened, like, two months ago.
Counselor: Two months. And how many days in the average week are you affected by these feelings?
Client: Usually every day.
Counselor: Every day. So if we can compare it, right, we have the chances of being recorded. Right. Illegally. That's a low probability event. It can happen. Probably not likely. The anxiety and the worry that you're having, that's a high probability event because you're suffering from it every day.
Client: Yeah, that's true. I never thought about it that way.
Counselor: So there's a point at which maybe you reach and you say, I'd rather take. I'd rather take the risk. I'd rather deal with the potential consequence of an unlikely event of being recorded and face that if it happens, than be in the state of anxiety and worry.
Client: Right. Because right now I'm suffering every day.
Counselor: Right now you're suffering, right. If you could adaptively respond effectively, you're still going to have that risk of being recorded, but, you know, you could survive that event if it happened, right?
Client: Yeah, I think I could have.
Counselor: And you're taking reasonable cautions and, you know, all the things we talked about. So as you think about this in a more general sense, is there an adaptive response you could apply to that, to that automatic thought of, I need to be worried about this, or whatever that thought looks like. Sometimes the thought's an image, right? Maybe an image of being recorded, but whatever that kind of general series of automatic thoughts are that are getting you anxious and worried before you even get out of the house. What adaptive response could you apply there?
