Client: Maybe, like I said, I'm worried about all the cameras. Maybe I could say, I understand there's some cameras that, you know, used for good purposes, like security.
Counselor: Probably most are right.
Client: And the chances of being recorded illegally are not likely. And I'm taking precautions to, you know, go to the right places, the good area, good areas. So it's not likely to happen overall. And me going outside the house is worth the risk, you know, the minimal risk that it would happen. And if it did happen, I could survive.
Counselor: That's great. That's a great adaptive response. Yeah. And actually, that's kind of a few adaptive responses, but that's good. And you can apply them, and we'll kind of break them down. Like I said before you leave today, we'll break those down so you can hammer it down as you go out. And I think it's important because the automatic thoughts tend to spring on us quickly. It's important to rehearse these adaptive responses so we're ready to go and kind of, we're preparing ourselves to apply that adaptive response. And in order to be prepared, you have to know what it is. So it's good to have it written down and kind of more or less commit to memory.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Does that kind of make sense?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right, so before you leave today, I'll take care of that, and I want you to use those adaptive responses for this week. I'll see you next week and record what the outcome was every time you're able to apply the adaptive response. And that includes what you felt and what you actually did.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: And, of course, as you mentioned, any physiological reactions like your heart racing or anything like that. So that's really. That's a behavior. But note both physiological behaviors and other behaviors. Once you're consciously controlling. And then any feelings. And we'll go through them. We'll go through each time you use it one by one, depending how many there are. I and kind of see if we need to adjust the adaptive response and see how well it's working.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Does that sound like the plan?
Client: Yeah, I think that would be really helpful.
Counselor:
output: So we'll go from there. And I appreciate you coming in today.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: So one of the things that we know is that sometimes people who have difficulty with anxiety and things like that have also had some bad experiences in their lives. So I'm going to ask you some questions about some of your difficult experiences that you may have had. And I'm just going to ask sort of yes or no questions. I only need sort of headlines. I don't need a lot of detail about the things that happened right now, but I'm just going to ask you those questions. And if anything about this interview starts to make you uncomfortable, you can take a break. If I ask a question you don't want to answer, you can just say, pass, and I'll just move on. So it's really up to you what you share, but I do want to ask you these questions. Is that okay?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. So have you ever been physically hurt by anyone, any. Either as a child or an adult? You know, hit.
Client: Yeah, my. I had a boyfriend a couple years ago, and he. He would hit me sometimes, but we're not together anymore, so.
Counselor: Mm hmm. Was there other kinds of physical abuse? You know, did he do more than hit you? Was there anything.
Client: No, he would just slap me sometimes. Usually when he was like, if he'd had a really hard day at work and maybe he would be drinking or something. He wouldn't slap me when he got home, but I got out of that, so that's good.
Counselor: Well, it's good that you recognize that that was really not acceptable behavior and that you didn't want that in your relationship. And it's great that you were able to get away from that. That's really good self care, that you were able to make that decision and, you know, and make a different choice and create more safety for your. Yourself. That's really good.
Client: Thanks.
Counselor: What about sexually? Has anybody ever, you know, when you were a child or as an adult, touched you against your will, anything like that?
Client: Yeah. I don't really want to talk about it, though, but, yeah, when I was. When I was little.
Counselor: How little? Just vaguely ten. Okay. Okay. And was it a family member or a stranger or.
Client: It was. It was a family member, but I don't really like talking about it.
Counselor: Okay. You don't have to. Okay, great. Thank you for telling me that much. That's really all I need for right now. Although it may be important for you to talk about that later, at some point you can wait until you're ready.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Okay. As a child, you know, sometimes parents aren't very available, don't provide basic food, clothing, shelter, that kind of thing. Did you ever have that experience of being neglected? Hmm? What's going on, Tricia?
Client: I don't like all these questions.
Counselor: Yeah? Starting to get uncomfortable, huh? You feel that somewhere in your body, you're feeling that in your. Your body? Yeah. Sometimes these questions can bring up very difficult things. I know. Sorry. When you're feeling like this, what helps you?
Client: My cat.
Counselor: Hmm. Tell me about your cat.
Client: She's a jerk. She's a jerk? Yeah. She's not very friendly. Um, she's friendly to me, though, when I'm really upset. She, uh, she'll, like, cuddle with me on the bed and stuff, so she knows when I'm really upset. But it's great that she knows. Yeah.
Counselor: That's pretty amazing.
Client: She's just kind of a jerk. She'll bite and scratch it, whoever she wants to. She wants to be snuggled until she doesn't want to be snuggled.
Counselor: What's her name?
Client: Persephone.
Counselor: Persephone. That's a great name for a cat.
Client: She came with it, and I decided to just leave it.
Counselor: Wow. I like it a lot.
Client: Great.
Counselor: It's wonderful to have a cat named Persephone who's good at helping you when your feelings are difficult. That's really good. That's, you know, that's a blessing there. Can we go on with the interview now?
Client: Yeah, I guess.
Counselor: Okay. About continuing. Okay. I'm going to ask you some different questions. I want to ask you a little bit about your living situation. So what kind of housing do you live in?
Client: I have an apartment.
Counselor: Mm hmm. And how long have you lived there?
Client: Almost a year.
Counselor: So not that long. And who do you live with?
Client: Just the cat.
Counselor: Just per second. Okay. Do you feel safe where you live?
Client: Safer than when I was homeless.
Counselor: Mm hmm. Safer, but maybe not entirely safe.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. What makes you not feel that safe where you live?
Client: I've kind of a. Have a landlord situation. Mm.
Counselor: Difficult relationship with your landlord?
Client: You could say that.
Counselor: Can you tell me about it?
Client: I don't. I don't make a lot of money, and my hours got cut at work recently, and he said he was going to evict me, and I really didn't want to be homeless again, so he said if I had sex with him that I wouldn't have to pay my rent.
Counselor: Wow. That's really hard. It makes sense. So you agreed to that I didn't.
Client: Want to be homeless again.
Counselor: That's right. And in order to survive, anyone is going to do what they have to do. Right.
Client: But it sounds like that's what I keep telling myself.
Counselor: Mm hmm. But it's also upsetting you a lot.
Client: I just keep thinking, like, what if somebody finds out? And now I told you so, obviously people are gonna find out.
Counselor: Well, what do you mean people?
Client: Well, I mean, don't you have to tell people when stuff like that happens?
Counselor: No, actually, what you and I discuss is between us, and you'll get to decide what you want to do about that situation so we can talk about it. But you get to decide. I only have to disclose if you're going to kill yourself or someone else to somebody else. Those are, you know, or if you're abusing an elder. Those are the circumstances under which I have to let other people know. So this is something that's just for you and I to talk about. And as part of, you know, our work together, we can decide what's the best way to take care of yourself going forward. So it's entirely up to you what we do from here. And I totally appreciate the courage it took to let me know that that was happening. And I'm happy to be with you as you sort out what's really the best path for you going forward for your own well being. We'll work on that together. Does that make sense to you?
Client: Kind of. No one's ever said it to me like that before, so I thought you had to tell people. But no. If not, but no.
Counselor: And I should tell you that. Remember how I said earlier in the interview that people who've had adverse experiences like sexual abuse in their past or physical abuse in their past, that sometimes that's connected to what happens going forward?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Well, it's not. It's really common for girls who've experienced sexual abuse later in life to end up using or being in a position where they end up using that for survival purposes. So what you're experiencing is actually probably a lot more common than you think. But just like you didn't want to talk about it, you know, the reason you don't know that other people are doing that is because they don't have often talk about it. So that way you think you're the only one in the world who ever ended up in this position. But in reality, lots of girls who've experienced sexual abuse grow up and it changes something that then they end up putting themselves, they end up in situations. Now, obviously you didn't create this situation. Your landlord is the one who is proposing to use his position of power to get you to do something that isn't what you want to do. And you're not responsible for his doing that. You're not. You're just doing what you've learned to do to help you survive. And we can work together for you to figure out what other options you have and what else you can do. Do.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Does that make sense?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Good. Thanks. Thanks for being so open. So are you ready to continue with the rest of the interview?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. You're doing a really good job. A really good job, a lot of hard stuff. And you're letting me in and that'll help us to be able to, you know, figure out together what you need to do to, you know, help with your anxiety and to make your life work better for you.
Client: Okay?
Counselor: Okay. So now I'm going to ask you some questions about your. So we've come to the end of all the questions and thanks for hanging in with me. I know it was a lot of questions, but I feel like, you know, I've gotten to know you a lot by asking these questions. So actually you've done a really good job of helping me to sort of begin to piece together the puzzle of what we're going to work on together. So that's really good. So now that the interview is over, the next step will be we'll make an appointment before you go, you know, for you to come back. But I just want to ask you now, how are you doing? How are you feeling?
Client: Well, I'm not shaking anymore, so that's good. I think I'll be okay.
Counselor: All right. So if after this interview you go about your life and you start to have difficult feelings, what are some things that you already know that you can do to help yourself with those feelings?
Client: Well, I. I play the guitar, so I think sometimes that helps a little bit. And, you know, and then there's Persephone, the mean cat. Yeah.
Counselor:
output: Yes. Uh huh.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Jeff. How you doing today?
Client: I'm alright. Thanks for actually seeing me today. Sure.
Counselor: How have you been? I know last time I spoke with you, you were having some difficulties at work.
Client: I'm still having difficulties at work and that's why I'm glad I have a session today because it hasn't stopped. The frustration and anger is just, it's there ten times more than normal.
Counselor: You're really frustrated. Way more than normal, way more angry.
Client: Yes, it's, there seems to be a lot that's going on and I continually don't get the help that I need, not only not from my coworker, but also my supervisor. So it just feels so that everything is my responsibility and I have to make it happen. And if I don't make it happen, it's not going to happen. And then it's just, it's all on me and I don't feel as though that it's fair. But I also don't want us to not succeed. So I don't know how to navigate those two field.
Counselor: So the weight of the work assignments is really on you. You're feeling that pressure. You want to do right by your employer and there's an emotional toll this is taken on you. Has it reached a point where you've talked to your, it's a coworker supervisor you mentioned?
Client: Yes. So I talked to my supervisor about my coworker actually assisting me with some of the projects that we have going on. And my supervisor keeps on saying, oh, they're helping out and they're doing what they're supposed to do, but they're not doing what they're supposed to do because I end up doing their work. Because, say, for example, last week we actually had to turn in this huge report that we were working on for over a month. Literally, my coworker came to me on Monday and said I didn't do my portion of the report. And I was just like, we had a month to work on a lot of time. And so I spent the next three days doing everything for their part of the report. Luckily, I had already finished my part of the report and then combined it and actually turned it into my supervisor. Of course we get the, oh, this is a wonderful, great job that you guys did. And I'm just like you guys, as.
Counselor: If you both contributed equally.
Client: Correct? Correct.
Counselor: So in three days, you made up for a month's worth of work.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So I could see how that could be. It's very stressful.
Client: Very, very taxing. Very, very taxing.
Counselor: And this wasn't an isolated incident?
Client: Oh, no. This has been going on for probably three or four months now.
Counselor: So this is almost the expectation when you get to work.
Client: Correct? Correct. I think that you hit the nail on the head. It's expected of me and nobody actually sees it as an expectation anymore.
Counselor: It's just what you do. It's just what I do. So you can know that going into work the next day, you go in, whenever that is, that there's always this probability, this chance that you could have work just thrown on you that wasn't budgeted for, you weren't planning on.
Client: Correct. And sometimes that work actually comes out from my supervisor, but it's mostly coming from my coworker. Like, I know they're not going to do their portion, so I just automatically start doing it anyway because, you know.
Counselor: You kind of have to.
Client: I know it's going to fall on my lap either today, tomorrow, next week. So I would rather be preemptive and actually start it then so that I'm not rushing like I was, like last week to finish a month's worth of work and three days worth of time. So I'm not as stressed.
Counselor: So you've tried to address this in the framework, in the context of your work. You've talked to the supervisor, to the co worker?
Client: I talked to the supervisor, I'm afraid. Well, I can't really talk to the coworker because I don't feel as though that's my position. However, I have expressed my frustration, my anger, my disappointment with my supervisor. And my supervisor keeps on saying, oh, I'll fix it, or, oh, it doesn't seem as though that they haven't done their piece of the work because I do all of it and it's turned in. So I have. But there doesn't seem to be anything happening outside of that.
Counselor: What kind of options, in terms of your job do you feel like you have now?
Client: I don't feel as though that I have any options. That's the thing. I think that either if I can, if I don't do the work and we fail, we're going to lose some of these big projects that we're working with, which then is going to impact our entire office. And if it impacts our entire office, like somebody might be let go. And because I am the newest person in our office, I feel as though that's going to be me. So I need to protect my job by doing not only my work, but my coworkers work and sometimes my supervisors work.
Counselor: So you're really figuratively fighting for survival?
Client: Correct.
Counselor: Do you think your coworker is aware that if there is a failure with getting projects done, that you would be the one that would be let go?
Client: I think, yes. I think that they understand that since they are the senior member on team, it would be most likely that the junior member myself would possibly be let go if a budget cut were to happen.
Counselor: So you're really largely stuck.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: With having to do the work.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: How about the emotions involved? You mentioned before, the frustration? Anger. Anger directed at.
Client: I think most of my anger is directed at my supervisor for not doing something because they can clearly see that something's wrong or that I'm handling a lot more, but they're not willing to step in. And I think a little bit of that anger is also at myself, because I haven't just said to my coworker, like, you need to step up and you need to do this. So I'm a little disappointed and angry at myself as well.
Counselor: You're angry at yourself, so you feel like you don't have the ability or courage to make that confrontation?
Client: I don't have the confidence to. The confidence to actually confront my coworker.
Counselor: All right, so before we dig into that too much, is it a good idea to confront the coworker?
Client: I think it would be good for them to understand how their lack of participation in our projects is impacting me and could also possibly impact our entire department. However, I don't know exactly how to say that and not come off as I'm. I know more than you, even though that you've been here longer than me.
Counselor: So you're searching for a friendly, understanding way to convey a tough subject matter.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: To someone who may or may not be receptive.
Client: Correct.
Counselor: But you may presume that they're more likely to not be receptive.
Client: I can 100%. I don't want to say 100%. I will say 99.9% say that they will not probably be receptive if I said that.
Counselor: So you're in for a bit of a battle.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And that was started.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So one option is to avoid it and continue do the work. And that's unpleasant, but you survived. Another option is to, in the gentlest way possible, introduce that confrontation to the relationship and then deal with the fallout of that.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Any potential benefit?
Client: Yes.
Counselor:
output: So let's look at that. What's the worst that can happen from making that, confronting that cohort.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Samantha. How you doing today?
Client: Good, how are you?
Counselor: I'm doing all right. How have things been since last week?
Client: Things? You know, I've been really sort of preoccupied and anxious a lot this weekend. My daughter got sick, so I had to take three days off of work to take care of her. And I'm starting to worry. She's been sick a lot since I've gone back to work, and she's in daycare, and I've had to take a lot of time off work, and I'm getting close to going over my allotted amount of days. And so I'm finding myself being very anxious about that and then feeling guilty because when I'm trying to take care of her, I'm always worrying about work. So.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like a couple things may be going on. Child. Child's been sick, so you're taking off days. So you're a little worried about your relationship with your employer. At the same time, you want to make sure you're taking good care of your child, so you're having trouble reconciling those two.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right. What was the last time it happened? Can you describe what happened the last.
Client: Time I had to take off work? It was just this week. She woke up one morning with a really high fever, so I had to call out that day, and then she still had a fever the next day, and then I had to take a third day because she has to be fever free before she can go back to daycare. So the first day was, I was okay with that. But then, like, the second. And then when I started realizing that I was going to have to take a third day, then I really start to get kind of panicky and worried about it.
Counselor: All right, so let me see. Let's go through each day. So the first day when you discovered that she was sick, right. What were you thinking then when you had to call out of work?
Client: Well, because she's been sort of sick a lot lately, I was a little bit worried, and I was sort of, you know, I have this number, ten, because I only have ten days for the whole year. So I have this number in my head, and I just thought, well, there's one more day I gotta take away from that ten that I have. And. But I was able to sort of think about. I was a little worried about any work that I would miss, you know, keeping up with my caseload and stuff at work, so. But I was able to kind of figure out that I would be okay for a day. And I can kind of make up for that when I get back.
Counselor: Okay, so your thinking was, this isn't ideal, but I can live with it.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Just one day, right? How about on day two when you realize that you're going to have to take a second day?
Client: Then I got a little bit more worried. And then I did start to also, you know, add the worry of I was going to start to get behind at work. Not only was I missing more time, but I was also going to be behind on my work. So then I started thinking, when I go back, it's going to be a mad scramble to kind of catch up and keep up with everything and, you know, so then it became worrying about my workload and worrying about taking more time.
Counselor: Okay, so a little more stressful version of what happened on day one. And then how about when you discovered that you had to take a third day off?
Client: I was. Then it was just more amplified, you know, amplified worry. And it was a lot harder for me to let it go. I just kept thinking. I kept going back to it. And then I started feeling guilty because I was so preoccupied, worried about that. And I was trying to answer emails and do some stuff and send out some emails to people that I work with to try to help me out with things at work since I wasn't there. And then I felt guilty because I wasn't really caring for my child as best as I felt I should have been. You know, I started feeling kind of like a bad mom.
Counselor: So, so guilty and a bad mom. And that was mostly on the third day? That was the worst of it, yes. Now, did this go up against the weekend? It was the third day, Friday. So then you kind of knew that by Monday things would be able to return to work. So tell me what happened when you returned to work on Monday.
Client: Well, I checked in with the main office and, you know, I just said, I'm really, you know, I'm starting to worry. I'm getting. I know I had to take a lot of time, but you. I've done the best I can to try to make other arrangements, but just starting back in, starting in daycare, she's just been sick a lot and I can't control it. I'm doing the best I can. I asked them if there was anything I needed to do as far as providing doctor's notes and stuff, and they said, no, they don't need a doctor's note since it was my daughter that was sick. They said there's nothing, nothing that I really can do and just try to not have it happen much more if I can just do what I can to not miss more.
Counselor: So they said that to you?
Client: Yeah, but. Yeah.
Counselor: How did they frame that?
Client: They kind of just said, you know, do what you can to not have it happen, but if it, you know, if it has to happen, you know, what can I do about it? It's kind of. They were saying.
Counselor: So they were understanding.
Client: I didn't feel like they were that understanding, but I also didn't feel like they were gonna take any punitive action against me. Right. Right then and there or anything.
Counselor: Did you anticipate a worse reaction than you experienced?
Client: Yeah, I did. And I also anticipated that they would maybe have more of a procedure for how to handle it, and they didn't have a procedure, which also made me feel a little worried. I can't imagine I'm the first mom that has had to deal with this. And they kind of talked like it's never happened before, so I kind of felt anxious because I thought, am I really the first mom that's had to take a lot of time off because their child's sick? They didn't give me the impression that they had sort of a protocol or like they had dealt with this before.
Counselor: Right. So sort of like it took them by surprise.
Client: Yeah. Or they just didn't have a plan for what to do about it.
Counselor: They weren't investing a lot of energy in thinking about that?
Client: No. No, I guess nothing.
Counselor: And when was this again? How long ago?
Client: Just this past week.
Counselor: So how has this week been? Bag of work?
Client: Oh, it's been very busy because I'm trying to catch up and get everything handled, but that's the way it always is. So nobody has said anything to me or anything about the absences other than that first, yeah.
Counselor: And there have been no more absences. Okay. Earlier you mentioned being a good mom. What does a good mom look like?
Client: Somebody who takes care of their child and puts them. Makes them a priority, like their first priority, and, you know, does the things that they need to do to make sure they're child is taken care of.
Counselor: And you're a little worried through this last experience you were telling me about that you didn't rise to the level of good mom.
Client: Yeah, I felt like I wasn't being a good mom because I was preoccupied and making work a bit of a bigger priority than taking care of my kidney.
Counselor: Okay. So good mom's more about. More than just rather your behavior, what you're doing. It's about what you're also thinking. So you took care of your child.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But your mind, your thoughts were somewhere else some of the time, and that's where you feel like you've wandered out of the good mom area. Okay, how about on the other side? How about a good employee? Did you mention that you want to be a good employee?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. What's that look like?
Client: Well, somebody that, you know, takes care of all of their workload and handles all of the tasks that they have each day, and someone that's consistent and reliable and, you know, puts effort into what they're doing and gets their job done, really, you know, reliably.
Counselor: And that's where you feel like with this. So the last eight work days you missed. You missed three. Okay, how about in the last year, how many days have you missed?
Client: Well, I missed a lot for maternity leave, certainly.
Counselor: Understandable.
Client: But excluding that I've missed since the school year started, I've missed. If you include the three, I've missed nine days. But some of those were half days. They add up to nine days.
Counselor: Okay, total nine days?
Client: Yeah. And you're allowed ten per school year? For school year, it's only January and I'm already at nine.
Counselor: I can see where that would cause worry. What happens if you go over the.
Client: I don't know. I mean, I think that they would dock my pay for those. If I was there a day and I didn't have any more sick days left, they would just dock my pay for that day. But outside of that, I don't know what else would happen.
Counselor: Is there anybody that you work with that you could ask that question to, like an HR department?
Client: Yeah, I guess I could contact the HR department.
Counselor: I'm just thinking. Cause you're just one day away from being at that number, might be prudent just to talk with them and see. So you know what to expect.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So this is this whole thing, though, the missing days cause you anxiety, frustration?
Client: Yeah, a little bit, yeah.
Counselor: How about any type of feeling down at all?
Client: A little bit. Sometimes when I start feeling like I'm a bad mom.
Counselor: Okay, so as far as your child is concerned, your relationship with your child, you have some anxiety, relationship at work, some anxiety. But the sadness mostly surrounds how you feel you're treating your child. Of all the emotions, frustration, anxiety, what I'll refer to as depression, let's just say sadness. What's bothering you the most? What emotional response does bother you most?
Client: Probably sort of the guilt and the feelings of not being able to be the best mom.
Counselor: How would you rate yourself right now as a mother if, say, ten was the best mother you could imagine. Right. And one was the absolute worst.
Client: Probably like, I don't know, an eight.
Counselor: An eight? Okay. That's pretty good, right?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What would be the cutoff to where. What's the cutoff score in that little scale I just gave you for good mother and not good mother?
Client: I guess, like halfway, like.
Counselor: So five is good enough?
Client: Yeah, I don't feel like it's good enough for me.
Counselor: Okay. Okay.
Client: I wouldn't be okay with that.
Counselor: So if you looked at somebody else, another person in a similar situation, a five would be acceptable, right?
Client: Probably, yeah.
Counselor: But how about for you specifically?
Client: Yeah, that's not.
Counselor: That's not gonna cut it. What would cut it?
Client: Um. I don't know. At least a seven.
Counselor: At least a seven, yeah. And you're an eight?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Sure.
Client: No, not sure.
Counselor: Okay. So you're close to the border. I feel like you're close to the border and you're.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Out of your value system of being not a good mother.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: What happens if you.
Client: Well, as good a mother as I want to be.
Counselor: Okay. How good do you want to be?
Client: Yeah, I want to be like an eight or higher.
Counselor: Eight or higher. Well, you are an eight, you said.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay, so you want to be a ten, sounds like.
Client: Well, yeah. Doesn't everybody want to be the best at what they do?
Counselor: I mean, I think people are driven to do their best, but is it crucial to be perfect? Is it crucial to be a tendency.
Client: No, there's some leeway. I guess you have to allow for that.
Counselor: Remember before, in other sessions, for other situations you've brought in here, we talked about dysfunctional thinking, irrational thinking. How does when you reflect on that, like, the usefulness of these thoughts, that other mothers can be a five and be. And that's good, right. You need to be an eight or higher. Eight, nine or ten. Does this seem useful, like a useful way of thinking?
Client: In some ways it's useful because it keeps me. It keeps me on track, if that makes sense. It keeps me pushing to keep doing the best I can. Driven.
Counselor: Motivated.
Client: Yeah, motivated.
Counselor: So it does have a useful side. Does it have an unuseful side, a less than useful side?
Client: Well, yeah, I guess it does. In the sense that if I become too worried about it, then I'm wasting energy on worry instead of being able to put that energy into being a good mom.
Counselor:
output: Yeah. So I guess one of the things I'm getting at here is has the worry. Has the anxiety and the worry paid off for you?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Does the feeling itself, the worry about not being prepared, interfere with preparing?
Client: Yes, it's really hard. So, like, when I'm in the middle of being worried, it's really hard for me to focus. So I can't focus on what I need to do because I feel like my mind is on a lot of different things and I can't focus on, you know, exactly what I should be doing. It's just like I'm worried about, you know, all the different aspects.
Counselor: All right, so your ability to concentrate through the hard work of preparing.
Client: Yeah. To, like, focus my energy on the right things. I'm just, like, wasting time worrying.
Counselor: All right, so this, this excessive worrying and all this interfering and preparing, all this goes on right up until you're getting ready to present.
Client: Yeah. And then, like, while I'm presenting.
Counselor: So let's talk about that. Let's go into the actual day of presenting. So we have the success of work coming in. It's interfered with your ability to prepare. It's distressing for you.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Now it's what in class presentations are in class.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So you're in the classroom. Do you, are you the only one to present during that class, or does it rotate through several people?
Client: It depends on the presentation. Sometimes there's, like, one or two other people that have to present that night, depending on, like, how long the topic is.
Counselor: All right, let's use the last time you present that classes as a tempo. What was the order? Like, what order did you go in there?
Client: The one. Well, the one that I really messed up. I think I was first, but usually I'm second, maybe.
Counselor: Okay, so for this example, let's say you do the second. Okay, so you're sitting in the classroom and another student is presenting.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What's going through your mind then?
Client: I feel like I am totally zoned out. Like, I'm not even paying attention to what that person is saying because I'm so worried about how I'm gonna mess it up. You know, I'm. I'm starting to, like, be sweaty, like, my hands are clammy, my heart starting to race a little bit, and I'm just totally zoned out on what they're doing. I'm just, you know, worrying about what's going to happen when I get up there.
Counselor: All right, so in that moment as you're seated, you're not really watching their presentation. As much because you have these strong or somewhat strong physical symptoms. You have your heart racing a bit. You said sweaty palms. You're zoned out.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Have you ever felt the. The need, desire to run out of the room?
Client: Yes. It's funny you should say that. I was a little bit hesitant to mention that, but I kind of. I do. I feel like I need to find an excuse to, like, use the bathroom or I just need to get out of there.
Counselor: Yeah. So what do you feel is most pressuring you to leave the room? Like, what symptom?
Client: Um, I would say that just, like, my anxiety and my heart rate are starting to increase, and I feel like I just need to get out of there and what.
Counselor: What thoughts going through your mind right then?
Client: Like.
Counselor: So let's take that kind of most severe moment when you're. Let's just say we're still before the presentation.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: So you're sitting at the desk, and your heart rate's elevated, and you're not focusing on what they're doing. You're zoned out, your anxiety's high.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What thought is going through your mind right then?
Client: I think. I'm thinking, like, I'm gonna bond this anyway, so I might as well just, you know, not go through the stress of having to do it. Like, I've already. In my head, I know that it's.
Counselor: Gonna end badly, so I've already failed.
Client: Right. So there's no sense in getting up there, and maybe if I don't get up there, you know, I guess it couldn't be any worse, so I might as well just leave.
Counselor: Are you embarrassed that the professor or other students will see that you were really anxious?
Client: Yeah, I don't want. I figure if I leave, then people won't. We'll just maybe think I was sick or whatever, and it'll be a better situation if I just left than having to see me up there, you know, sweating and all this. These other symptoms that I have when I actually get up there. It would be better just to leave before that starts.
Counselor: Okay, so. So better to be thought ill that you just had to leave because you're sick.
Client: Yeah. Or have them wonder what happened than to just be up in front of.
Counselor: Everybody, you know, to have that severe anxiety in front of everybody, and then they can see.
Client: Very embarrassing.
Counselor: Yeah. That would be. That would be a very undesirable outcome for you.
Client: Right.
Counselor: So as you're debating that thought, like, if that's coming to your head and you're thinking, I just need to.
Client: Yeah, flee. I just gotta get out of here.
Counselor:
output: What happens there? So we're maybe, what, 15 minutes before you present? So tell me about that. So you have that thought. You want to flee, right?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Carly. How you doing today?
Client: I'm good. How about you?
Counselor: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. How did you do this week?
Client: Better. Well, last time we talked about that postpone gratification. Yeah, that, and I think you wanted ten minutes for me to put it off.
Counselor: Ten minutes, yeah.

Client: It was rough, yeah.
Counselor: So it was difficult for you, but in most cases, you're able to hold off the ten minutes, and it sounds like there was a few instances where you're able to hold it off longer because something else kind of.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Came up.

Counselor: So another activity presented itself. And you forgot about the marijuana?
Client: Kind of, yeah. Yeah, I guess I just wasn't thinking about it.
Counselor: So has your. Have your feelings about marijuana changed since we last talked?
Client: No, not really.
Counselor: Tell me about that.
Client: I mean, it's. I don't see it as a problem. It's legal in a lot of states now, and, I mean, it's not that bad for you. It doesn't really endanger me much.
Counselor: So you still. You still believe you should have the right to smoke marijuana?
Client: Yeah, I mean, I'm not hurting anybody.
Counselor: Else, but at the same time, you want to go back to work, and if I remember right, you're the person that you could go work for. I guess you know them, right?
Client: Yeah, it's my uncle.
Counselor: Your uncle. And you need to be clean for, what was it, about two months?
Client: Yeah, I think two to three months.
Counselor: So you have kind of opposing forces here, right? You have your enjoyment of marijuana, and then you. That's something you, like. You don't want to give up, and you believe you should have a right to do that, but then there's that job.
Client: Yeah. I mean, my parents are pretty cool with it. Like, they know, but, I mean, I'm at the point now where they kind of want me to move on and move out. But I don't know. I mean, I just. It'd be nice to have that job. Like, it's a really good job, but at the same time, like, I don't see why I have to sacrifice something that I like.
Counselor: So it doesn't seem fair to you, but she recognizes the reality of your situation. Yeah, it really does come down, in your instance, to marijuana use or employment.
Client: Yeah, it's pretty accurate.
Counselor: Okay, so you're not happy about that choice?
Client: Not at all.
Counselor: Yeah. And kind of what we did with the postponed gratification was just. I mean, I really just ask you to wait ten minutes, and you were able to do that and more. Although it was difficult.
Client: It was difficult.
Counselor: It was difficult for you. So I asked you to track the number of times you smoked marijuana. Did you. Were you able to track that over the last week?
Client: Yeah, for the most part.
Counselor: Do you remember how many times that was?
Client: I think. I think I did, like, 15.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Between 15 and 20.
Counselor: Between 15 and 20. And how many times did something kind of get in the way? Did something else come up in that ten minute span that distracted you or that you enjoyed?
Client: Like, almost closer to 20 times, I guess. Otherwise I probably would have kept going, smoked more. I mean, there were a couple times where, like, somebody would call me or somebody would text me, and that kind of distracted me, so I was able to put it off for a little bit.
Counselor: So you can see in that ten minutes, things can happen. Things can happen that can help you to avoid the marijuana. Sometimes nothing does, and after the ten minutes you use it, and sometimes something does kind of get in the way with the marijuana, like, distract you or you have another activity that you enjoy and then you didn't use. So with that in mind, you found the experience rough. But was it tolerable?
Client: Yeah, it wasn't bad.
Counselor: Was it bad? Do you think for this next week we could try postponing that gratification from ten minutes to 20 minutes?
Client: I don't know. That seems kinda. Yeah, that seems like a longer time.
Counselor: That is definitely. That is a longer time.
Client: I don't know about that.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: Maybe like 15 minutes.
Counselor:
output: No, a compromise. Is 15 okay. Yeah. Do you think you could maintain 15 minutes weighing 15?

Client: Well, I just felt terrible after I lost those two matches, and I was thinking that if I lo. That if I lose my next match, I'm never going to be able to get a scholarship to college.

Client: Yeah.

Client: It happened about two, three days ago.

Client: Yeah.

Client: Yeah.

Client: Well, I can, you know, keep. Stay in the mindset that I have that extra money and spend what I think is that extra money, digging into the money I paid for my rent, my food, my gas, my insurance, and me, who's somebody without all that.
Counselor: So you could fail to pay expenses that need to be paid.
Client: And they helped me go to my full time job that I still have. So, I mean, if I can't, if I spend the money that was from my insurance because I thought I had extra, then I'm not gonna have insurance on my cardinal. I can get pulled over, lose my license, not going to be able to get to work, and then I'll get fired there too.
Counselor: All right, so the kind of chain of causality you're seeing is that without that part time income, you might not adapt with your expense management. You might fail to pay, for example, your car insurance. You could get pulled over for something the police officer could see, don't have insurance, give you a ticket, which is just money. I don't have another expense. Right. And how would this. How would that connect to losing your job?
Client: Because I wouldn't be able to get to work.
Counselor: So it'd be. So the ticket would be so expensive, you would lose your.
Client: Well, the ticket would be expensive, so I wouldn't be able to try to pay the next month's insurance. So I just wouldn't have insurance on my car. So I.
Counselor: So you'd lose your insurance?
Client: I'd lose my insurance.
Counselor: And then by losing your insurance, you lose your transportation altogether because you can't drive that insurance. And then you lose your job.
Client: Mm hmm. I mean, it's either go to work with an uninsured car, and then I can get pulled over and go to jail for driving with no insurance multiple times.
Counselor: No, that's serious. Yeah. You wouldn't want to do that.
Client: I wouldn't go to jail.
Counselor: So there's two. You have two kind of causal change. One is losing your job. And now even just the idea you can end up incarcerated.
Client: Yes. I mean, which I definitely lose my.
Counselor: Job if I'm in jail, I would imagine.
Client: And so that would have. So then I wouldn't even have, like, any money to help me through jail. Like, to. For the commissary and stuff.
Counselor: Because you would have no income.
Client: I would have no income. And then when I get out of jail, I'm. No one's gonna hire me.
Counselor: Because you have a criminal record.
Client: Exactly.
Counselor: Which makes it challenging to find employment in some instances. So what's happened is kind of in your mind, and we've talked about how thoughts work and beliefs work, is you, in reality, you've lost this part time job. And as I said, that's certainly. That's understandable that you'd be upset about that. I doubt many people would be happy about losing additional income, but you move from there, from losing additional income, which is what has actually happened to this possibility that you could be in jail or lose your job because of this. So I remember maybe last week. Week before, you're talking about the. The letter that you received from. It was like a late notice. It wasn't. Turned out wasn't.
Client: Yeah, it was sent to me, but it was somebody else's credit card mistake. Yeah.
Counselor: Do you remember the conclusions you drew from when you believe that was actually for you, that late notice, that my.
Client: Credit score was gonna go down, that I would. I'd be stuck in that apartment, and then I'd go into depression. I wouldn't be able to do anything.
Counselor: Yeah. So you ended up in that scenario. You end up in a situation where you just couldn't function at all. And you moved there from a letter that you believe was addressed to you, saying you were one month or six days late or something on a credit card, which, of course, you don't want to be late on a credit card, but you move from there to being so depressed you couldn't work, couldn't function, I think, is how you put it. Couldn't function. Do you see, kind of, given how we've talked about cognitive behavioral strategies and concepts, do you see a pattern that's emerged over the last few times I've seen you?
Client: I mean, I've seen that, you know, sometimes I can. I can think the worst, and then. And I know it didn't happen last time, but that was, you know, a stroke of good luck.
Counselor: That it wasn't you.
Client: Yeah. That it was, you know, it wasn't me. And, you know, that was a relief. But this is something that's solid. I don't have my part time job anymore.
Counselor: You've lost real income.
Client: I mean, this isn't a mistake. This isn't a. We fired the wrong person. You know, this is real. So there's real concerns here.
Counselor: I.
Client: Unlike last time, where I was lucky.
Counselor: So this. This situation, you see, is different than the first situation because the first situation was more. You were perceiving something was wrong that wasn't wrong because you weren't the intended recipient of the letter.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But in this situation, it's different because it's real. You really lost your income.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And, of course, keeping in mind that this job, again, only a few months old, and you survived well before that, is it reason to believe you could survive well again, that you could adapt to this lost income?
Client: Well, I suppose there is, but I'm concerned about whether I'm not, whether I won't adapt.
Counselor: Well, let's look at this in terms of probabilities, right. You've had several jobs throughout your career. You've had some of them worked out. You've lost other ones. You're still paying your bills. So in terms of probabilities, how many times have you, how many times have you ended up in jail or losing your full time job?
Client: I mean, they haven't happened yet.
Counselor: It hasn't happened.
Client: Not yet. But I mean, I, I struggled a little bit when I lost a part time job or when I was younger and I had those little jobs.
Counselor: So you had to adapt.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And it was painful.
Client: I did struggle, yeah.
Counselor: You struggled.
Client: Yeah. I mean, but I'm older now. These are, you know, even though grocery stores, not a serious job. It was income.
Counselor: Sure. Yeah. And again, to lose income would be disappointing for just about anybody. Are there any upsides to not having that job?
Client: I suppose I have more time to focus on my full time job because, I mean, that is really intensive.
Counselor: Is there a possibility that you could find another part time job just as you found that one?
Client: I mean, because will somebody else take me because I was fired from that job? I mean, that's my concern, is that.
Counselor: Nobody, they're going to find out.
Client: Yeah. And then they're going to go, oh, she was fired, you know. No, we don't. We don't want her.
Counselor: But you've had other jobs that didn't work out before and that didn't affect you getting that job.
Client: That's true.
Counselor: So the worst case scenario, I guess what I'm getting at the worst case scenario is, in your case, ending up in jail or losing your full time job, which you've had for a while.
Client: Yeah, I really don't want to lose my job.
Counselor: And it seems like they like you there.
Client: I hope they do.
Counselor:
output: Right? Yeah. So those scenarios, I guess, are possible, but they seem, based on what you're saying, is pretty unlikely. So I wonder how useful it is to invest a lot of energy in kind of tracking that causal chain to jail or prison or to unemployment when that's really not the most likely outcome. Sorry to interrupt you, but do you invest as much energy in tracking the positives or the probable outcomes?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Kelsey. It's so good to see you again.
Client: Thanks.
Counselor: Okay, so for today, is there anything that you really want to talk about that's really just on your mind that you want to share today?
Client: Yeah. I was at a party, and I was kind of hesitant about going, and then I went and I realized, like, I just can't talk. Like, I don't like meeting new people. I never know what to say. And then it's, like, an awkward silence, and then I just feel like I don't want to be there anymore.
Counselor: So has this been something that you've struggled with for a long time, or are you just noticing this recently?
Client: A long time, but I kind of avoided social situations where I had to.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: So it was just, like, a reminder that I'm just a super awkward person.
Counselor: Okay, so what are some of the feelings that are associated with that feeling super awkward?
Client: I think, like, embarrassment and just, like, weird. Like, I feel like people are just, like, not wanting to be my friend.
Counselor: So you almost feel, like, what sounds like possibly not being accepted?
Client: Mm hmm.
Counselor: Okay. Has anyone ever made you feel that way before?
Client: Um, I can't remember a time. No. I think I just, like, feel I'm so embarrassed and made such a fool in myself that I don't, like, pursue that friendship as much. Okay.
Counselor: You feel like you're going to make a fool of yourself, or you felt.
Client: Like, when I first meet them, if I was, like, a super awkward silence, I feel so embarrassed, I don't want to talk to them again.
Counselor: So awkward silences, that's one that really causes some anxiety for you. Anything else that makes you really anxious before talking to them? Some of those fears you have?
Client: I think I'm very self conscious about maybe how I look. I think I'm very concerned about, like, how I present myself to people, that I'm always trying to figure out what to say, if that makes sense.
Counselor: And how do you think you look from your perspective?
Client: I don't know. I think I'm just. I think it's more of how I want, like, how I think other people do. Like, I feel like I'm fine, but I feel like other people may not think I'm attractive, and so I feel like they don't want to be friends, but, like, an unattractive person.
Counselor: So you think that other people think that you're unattractive, but you feel fine about yourself.
Client: Mm hmm.
Counselor: So can you kind of tell me what you think is fine? What do you mean by that?
Client: Like, my appearance. I mean, I think I'm like, a cute person. But I also know, like, everyone has a type and, like, a certain group of friends they want. Maybe I don't fit into that. Mm, tight.
Counselor: Okay, so when you said that, that you think you're a cute person, you gave a smile. So it seems like you really believe in that, which is great. So can you give me a number from zero to ten? What you think about yourself? That you're fine, that you're kind of cute. Zero being not at all pretty ugly, or I don't really believe in that. And ten being I'm certain I'm confident in this. And I think I'm pretty cute.
Client: Maybe like, a seven and a half.
Counselor: Seven.
Client: Five.
Counselor: That's really good.
Client: Eight. Seven and a half. Okay.
Counselor: Either one. That's a pretty good number. A pretty strong number. So it seems like you have pretty good self esteem on your end as far as how you value yourself, but it's the fear of how other people value and think about you. Okay. And so is the only concern of people thinking that you're not good looking, unattractive, or is there other concerns too?
Client: I think just the attraction thing is just always in the back of my mind and kind of affects how people talk to you. So I feel like I have to cater around their judgment. Yeah. So it's just hard for me to initiate conversation without knowing, like, what they think about me. Okay.
Counselor: So you're just what? Sounds like you're just kind of thinking what they might be thinking of you, but you don't know. But with you not knowing, that causes.
Client: That anxiety, and it would just be awkward for me to ask them directly, like, what do you think about me? Okay.
Counselor: Now when you can, you kind of guide me on a typical conversation. So say we're in a bar right now, or where do you typically meet people or try to make conversation?
Client: Well, like, the party was one example, and I was just meeting new people, and so let's go with the party.
Counselor: Okay. So we're at a party right now, and I sitting next to you, and you kind of feel like talking to me. How would you approach me?
Client: I probably wouldn't. Okay.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: I, like, wait for. I just, like, hang out with my friends, and then if a new person approaches us in a group, then I'll do it, but I don't venture out by myself.
Counselor: And do you like it that way?
Client: Yes. Okay.
Counselor: So when you came in here, the kind of issue is not making friends and not being able to talk to people. Is it more just not being able.
Client: To talk to people? Just not knowing what to say and just not the anxiety around meeting new people.
Counselor: Okay, but then you're fine with not.
Client: Meeting new people, just in, like, the way. It's just very anxiety, like, causes a lot of anxiety in me. Yeah.
Counselor:
output: Like, I want to meet new people.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Victoria. How you doing today?
Client: Pretty good.
Counselor: Very good. How has the anxiety been around the germs?
Client: I still catch myself, like, double, almost like double touching. Like going to touch it and then reeling back. So I'm starting to notice it, but I still, I still have that anxiety. I still don't want to touch it.
Counselor: When you pretty much touch anything you might think has germs on it.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What are some things that you've touched in the last, between the last session and this session that have distressed you?
Client: Well, I had to go to the store, which is always a nightmare for me because I don't even like touching my credit card because it's been in so many machines and there's so much dirt and junk that gets in there and then the counters and all the. I keep thinking about the food that's there, and I, you know, if I pick it up off the shelf, how many people have picked it up with their nasty hands or kids picked it up with nasty hands and then put it back, and it's like, I need to eat. But shopping's a nightmare for me.
Counselor: So really, in a, like, a supermarket, everything can be containing germs. Have germs on it?
Client: Yeah, everything does.
Counselor: Everything does. And that's what you're thinking about as you're walking through and shopping. We talked about last time, exposure and response prevention, and I explained kind of the general idea. But you remember that conversation. Yeah, I remember. I indicated that we might try some experiments right in session to see how, see if we can move kind of forward and treating your, kind of your fear and obsession with germs and really the anxiety it's causing for you, it's like getting in the way of your life.
Client: It is. It really is.
Counselor: So I was wondering, is there anything in here, in this office, as you look around, that you would look at and think, I don't want to touch that because it could have germs on it.
Client: I'm really not liking the covers on this chair because, I mean, I can't. I mean, at least what I'm sitting in now, my clothes are protecting me from the rest of the chair.
Counselor: Mm hmm.
Client: But, I mean, I have no sleeves on, so I don't like touching the armrests and the covers.
Counselor: So even thinking about, like, your arms touching the back of the chair, and.
Client: I'm not liking it, I really feel like I should probably go wash my arms.
Counselor: So what would happen if you put your hands right on the arm covers? What was your usual reaction to that?
Client: To go wash my arms until I feel like it's gone. Until all the dirt is gone.
Counselor: And how long would that take you to be sure?
Client: I mean, something like this, probably. I'd probably be in there for a good 510 minutes. Just washing.
Counselor: 510 minutes. How many times a day would you end up washing your hands?
Client: Okay. I don't. I don't keep track anymore. It makes me upset. How many?
Counselor: It says that it's that many. That is distressing. And I know that this will be uncomfortable, but I would like you to try to. If you can feel comfortable with it, put your hands on the. On the arms of the chairs. On the chair. Let's see what I'm doing. It's like. Try to stay like that. So tell me what's going through your mind?
Client: I can just. I feel the chair, and I. I don't like it. And I just. I feel almost like I can feel everybody who's ever touched it. And just what have they been doing? And what did they touch before they touched this? They probably didn't wash their hands before they touched this, and it's just really making me comfortable.
Counselor: Okay, so you're anxious now?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Is it tolerable?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So once you remember, we talked about scaling before. So, like, ten being a tremendous amount of anxiety, one being hardly any anxiety. Where. Where are you now as you sit here with your hands?
Client: What am I going to say about six or seven?
Counselor: Six or seven?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Are you feeling an urge to go wash your hands?
Client: Yes. Yes, I am.
Counselor: Yes. This is a six or seven. I want you to sit with it for a few seconds, process that, you know, feeling. Right. That you're touching everybody that's ever been in the chair. Right. So consider that thought.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: So what's the ultimate fear? Like, what's gonna happen if you don't go wash your hands now?
Client: I'm gonna get sick.
Counselor: You're gonna get sick that someone who's.
Client: Been in this chair was sick or touched something gross that can make you sick. And I'm gonna get sick, and I'm gonna die, and I don't want to die.
Counselor: Do you feel yourself getting sick?
Client: I feel like it's harder to breathe, I guess. Like, my chest is kind of just tight. Yeah.
Counselor: You can still breathe, though.
Client: I can't. I can breathe.
Counselor: Okay, so go ahead and lift your hands up. Right. And just put them where you'd normally put them. Well, now that you've touched the chair, I know that now I can still. Is that any better? Now you're touching the seat of the.
Client: Chair, but I feel like if I touch my clothes, that's even worse. Yeah. Now I will have to go home and change my clothes.
Counselor: All right, so the thought now, if I had to guess, correct me if I'm wrong, it's probably like you really would like to wash your hands.
Client: Very much so.
Counselor: And you certainly can at any time. But I'd like you to try to hold out for a little bit. So your hands where they are now, that's better than up here.
Client: At this point. I feel like they're already contaminated, so.
Counselor: They'Re at maximum contamination.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So you can't do any more damage by touching the seat.
Client: Yeah, I'm just trying to avoid touching anything else.
Counselor: So now it's not so much about getting your hands away from the arms, but getting them under the faucet. Yeah, that's the. So where's anxiety? Was a six or seven before. Where is it now?
Client: I mean, now that you mention it, it is. It is a little better. I want to say about four. About three, four. I mean, I feel better that my. My arms are off it, and I'm focusing on breathing, and, I mean, it's.
Counselor: A little easier to breathe now.
Client: A little. Yeah, it is.
Counselor: So if you could go. If you could wash your hands right this second. Of course you can. But if you did, what would the anxiety move to?
Client: A one.
Counselor: A one.
Client: I mean, it would take a little bit to get to a one. A little bit actually washing, but then it'll get to a one. Then I'll feel okay.
Counselor: All right, so you move from just in a short time, from a six or seven to a three or four for anxiety, when, of course, the goal was one. Right. So you could say roughly halfway. Roughly halfway down toward your goal without washing your hands at all.
Client: Oh, wow. I didn't consider that.
Counselor: So are you doing okay? You're holding up okay. All right, so this is what I want you to do. Before you go wash your hands, I want to use this moment to give you some ideas for the next few weeks. When you touch something that causes you to feel like the germs are on your hands. Chairs, whatever it is, I want you to try progressively to wait more and more time between that event. Like when you feel that urge when you actually wash your hands.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: I mean, you have to wash your hands at some point, right. You're gonna wash them at some point. That's normal. I'm asking, try to delay that.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: I try to try to stall and not wash them immediately.
Client: Okay.
Counselor:
output: Okay. Kind of, you know, eventually, when you get to the point where you can. You can wash them when you choose to. Cause right now, like, the germs are kind of dictating when I wash them, right? I mean, the way you're thinking about the germs is really laying down the rules, and I want to give you some more control over it. So where's the anxiety right now?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: You've said that when you're in work, you worry a lot about how you come across in social situations.
Client: Yeah, it really makes me feel really anxious, like what I look like and what people are thinking.
Counselor: Yeah. You said that you worry that you visibly shake.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Are there any other things that you worry that people will notice?
Client: I think obviously, the shaking. I think my hands and legs shaking and going really red and sweating and just looking really weird.
Counselor: So it sounds like you have quite a strong mental image of how you see yourself when you're in these social situations.
Client: Yeah, definitely.
Counselor: So you go red, you shake. Is there anything else that you think that you do? I mean, describe yourself. How do you think you look when you're in these situations?
Client: Just like, I think I just look really obviously weird and out of place and, like, really red and just visibly shaking and sweating and kind of not being able to communicate properly with people.
Counselor: Is there anything that you do to try and kind of defend against these things, to manage these problems?
Client: I guess, like, when I'm holding the camera, I just grip onto it really, really tight, or I kind of clench all my muscles and just find something that I can focus on and to kind of try and make myself shake less and not go as red and stuff.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.

We hope that by doing this, it's going to help lessen those nightmares and flashbacks and other upsetting memories of the attack that are bothering you quite a bit at the moment. output: Yeah. Look, I think we do know that this is difficult right now. But what I also expect is that it's going to get easier and easier for you to talk about this memory the more often you do. And I'm going to ask you to start at the bit where you are waiting for the tramdhead and end it at the part where your mum is there or your mum arrives.
