instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Elizabeth. How you doing today?
Client: I'm all right.
Counselor: How things been going since the last time I met?
Client: It's about the same. I'm still feeling pretty down. I mean, I just. I feel really stuck and not happy, and I just don't know why.
Counselor: Okay, so there's a few things going on there. You said you're feeling stuck, not happy, and sound like you're a little confused as to what's going on, what's causing it. Do you have any suspicions about what might be causing it?
Client: I mean, I've been feeling, like, really isolated lately, you know, because I'm a stay at home mom. It's hard. There's not a lot of people, you know, right at my fingertips to spend my time with, you know, obviously my family, but. So I guess, you know, I kind of. I had some friends in the neighborhood, but, like, our friendships just kind of fizzled out, and I. Ever since then, it's just like, I don't really feel like doing much. I just kind of feel like, what's the point? And let my husband take care of a lot of stuff. You know, I used to, you know, shop for the groceries all the time and make sure the house is always stocked and make dinner every night and get the kids ready for school in the morning. And I still do that stuff. But a lot of times, you know, I let it slide. Sometimes I won't make dinner or whatever. And when I do do it, I just feel like I'm forcing myself to do it. The passion is gone.
Counselor: And how long have you been. You say housewife, right? How long have you been housewife?
Client: For a long time. I have two boys. They're eight and ten. And I've been staying home since my first one was born, so ten years. And, you know, it's been really rewarding for me. I'm not really interested in going back to work or anything like that because I know people always say you're feeling unfulfilled, like you should go back to work, but it's not, you know, I felt happy with it for so long. I don't think that it's being home. I think it's something inside of me.
Counselor: Something's changed. So for a long time, you were satisfied being a housewife. You enjoyed that life or found satisfaction in that life. And somewhere along the line, something changed in you and now you're not happy with it. So what it represents in terms of activities like caring for your children and shopping, now, that's what changed.
Client: Yeah, exactly. Well, I guess, you know, my youngest is eight, so he's only been in school for a couple of years. So I guess, like, it's not super recent, but recently I finally have no children in the home, so it's more. It's more time to myself, and I kind of filled that gap a little bit with other things. Like, I did Cub scouts with the boys for a while, and like I said, I had some friends around the neighborhood, so that kind of, like, filled that time. But now that stuff, it's just not really happening anymore. So now I kind of feel like it's not boredom. You know, it's not like I don't have enough to do. It's like I don't want to do anything, but then at the same time, I feel frustrated because there's nothing to do.
Counselor: All right, so you're frustrated with your situation, maybe with yourself a little bit?
Client: Yeah, I think a lot more with myself because I know that I would feel better if I had, you know, maybe found more friends or found something to do with my time, but I don't want to at the same time. So I'm frustrated with myself because I kind of know what would help, but then I don't really have the, like, the volition to do it.
Counselor: You're not motivated?
Client: Yeah, I'm not motivated.
Counselor: Have you received any feedback from other people about this meeting? Has anyone else noticed that you're down?
Client: Yeah, I mean, obviously my husband has noticed because he has to get the boys ready in the morning. He's really supportive. I know he can tell that I'm not feeling the same, but, you know, he works, and then he has to come home and pick up my slack. So he is getting frustrated, which I understand. And, you know, my mom has said to me that, you know, she thinks I'm not doing as much, and so it kind of hurts. It feels like everybody's trying to tell me I'm lazy and that I'm not doing enough. And it's always that, like, feeling, you know, like nobody really understands how much work goes into being a mother. But then, at the same time, now that I'm doing less and less, I feel like they're all right, you know? I am lazy. I'm not doing anything.
Counselor: They use the word lazy?
Client: No, not that I can remember. You know, I think my mom said, like, you're not doing as much as you used to. And I kind of took offense to that, even though it's kind of true. It's like. I don't know. It hurt.
Counselor: Okay. That was painful for you what about what your husband said? What's he been saying?
Client: You know, I think at first we didn't really acknowledge it. It was like, you know, I took a break here. He picked up the slack, and it was fine. But now that it's been more and more, he's kind of getting frustrated. And, you know, he's been asking me about how I feel and why I'm not doing as much. But at the same time, like, even though he knows that, not motivated, it's still frustrating because it's my responsibility. So I think he's. You know, he's been saying, like, I need you to do more around the house, pretty much is what he said. I need you to do more.
Counselor: What was your response to that? When he said, I need you to.
Client: Do more, I started crying because I know he's right. And that's what I tell myself every day. I need to do more, but I don't have the motivation to do it. And so I'm so frustrated with myself, and, you know, I know that he needs that from me, and I don't know why I'm not motivated to do it.
Counselor: Okay, so you're frustrated for feeling down.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you're frustrated for lacking motivation, and just as little as a few years ago, you didn't feel it this way at all.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. I actually think, you know, I've been feeling this way more, like, in the past, like, six months or something like that. Like, I. It was hard for me when my youngest son went to school, but more in, like, the natural way that it is hard, but this is something else. This is more consuming. It's, you know, like, the difficulty of him going away to school almost was motivating. Like, it was hard, but at the same time, it was freeing because I had other opportunities to do stuff. This is just, like, stunting.
Counselor: Okay, so let me shift gears a little bit. Can you tell me about your. Well, a recent day. It's kind of typical of what you're telling me now. Meaning not motivated. Down.
Client: Sure. On Wednesday, I was having a really hard time getting out of bed, so my husband just got the kids ready in the morning, and I felt really bad about that. So I just stayed in bed for a couple more hours, probably until, like, 1030, and I got up, you know, and made myself something to eat. And then I thought, you know, I should probably go to the store because we're almost out of milk and, you know, and I think the boys need shampoo. But I just. I just sat down and I just sat there, and I think I sat for. I don't even know how long the boys came home from school. It was like, you know, 330, and I hadn't even gotten up. And so then I said, okay, the boys are home. I should probably get started on dinner soon because my husband will be home soon. And I. I found something in the fridge to make, and I made dinner. And, you know, after that, everybody, you know, just sat down. We just watched tv, and I just sat there until it was time to go to bed.
Counselor: You said this was recently, right? What would the ideal day have looked like? Take that same day and do what you wish you could have done.
Client: I wish that I would wake up and, you know, I would want to wake up when it was time for the kids to get ready to go to school. You know, I could make sure that everything that they had, everything they needed, I could pack their lunches and get the boys dressed and, you know, check if they needed any permission slip sign, that kind of thing, send them out the door, and then I would see if we needed anything from the store. I probably do a little bit of cleaning around the house. I used to, like, have a list of chores that I would do different things on different days and different days of the month and stuff. So bedding would get washed one day of the week and that kind of thing. Probably, like, follow that list. Nowadays, I just, you know, if it gets done, it gets done. And usually my husband helps me with some of the stuff. And, you know, I would do the bathrooms one day a week. That probably gets done, like, once a month now, but I would do that. So do the cleaning. If we. If I needed to go to the store, I would do that. I'd get ready for the boys to come home. I'd probably make them a snack and figure out what was going to be for dinner. I would go ahead and do that, and then probably, you know, sometimes we would watch tv after my husband got home after dinner, or I would figure out something for us to do. We could play a board game, or I'll watch a movie as a family or something like that. But that would be after the kids did their homework and everything like that. And then after we spent some time together, I'd put them to bed.
Counselor: All right, so there's a fairly wide discrepancy between where you are in terms of behavior and where you want to be. So let me ask you a very specific question about one of the first things in the day. You had mentioned that when it was time to get up you didn't. So you were awake and aware of it, but you went back to sleep, I presume. And of course, your husband got up and he took care of things. How did you feel allowing that to happen? Because clearly that's not what you wanted to happen. How did you feel about that? Oversleeping?
Client: It's just like, you know, the alarm goes off and I know it's time to get up, and my husband's getting out of bed, and I just look at the clock and I think, what's the point? And, you know, it's just this instant feeling of. I can't even describe it, like pointlessness of getting up. And so I go back to sleep, but I feel worse for doing it, you know, like it's a catch 22. Like, I don't want to wake up. I just don't want to. But then when I go back to sleep, I feel bad. I feel guilty.
Counselor: Okay, so by not getting up in the time you wanted, you feel guilty. But you also mentioned something that you thought, which was, if I'm not mistaken, you said, what's the point? Can you expand on that?
Client: It just. It's just like, you know, when I'm sleeping, I don't realize how sad I am, and I don't realize how hard it is to function when I'm sleeping. I'm not aware of that. And as soon as I wake up, I am. And so I just have this feeling of, like, what's the point of getting up and experiencing these feelings when I could go back to sleep and not have to?
Counselor: What's the point of getting up when sleeping will keep the pain at bay?
Client: Yes. Yeah.
Counselor: But then when you do get up, you feel sad and guilty about having overslept.
Client: Yeah. Yeah, definitely. Definitely.
Counselor: So really, functionally, what you're doing is you're delaying experiencing the pain. And then in terms of how it affects your relationships and your family, you're not getting your kids off to school, your husband's getting real frustrated, and all you've really bought yourself is a couple extra hours of sleep and presumably without pain because you're sleeping but you're not really escaping it. Does that make sense?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Before, when you felt more satisfaction and purpose, did you get up and help the kids off to school?
Client: Yeah, it was so easy. I would just like, you know, I would wake up and I would be like, okay, it's time to get up and get out of bed and get ready to go. I mean, you know, sometimes if I was a little bit tired, it would be a little bit hard, but, you know, it's nothing. You know, as a stay at home mom, I usually get enough sleep for the most part, now that the kids are older and everything. So it's not usually too hard to get up. And I would, you know, it would be another good day. You know, I would be glad to get up and take care of the things that I needed to take care of, and I felt accomplished.
Counselor: So maybe what's going on here? Or maybe we could help remember, you know, over the last few sessions, we talked about. About cognitive behavioral therapy and the different techniques that I'll be using and different things we'll be talking about. Sometimes with behavior, the behavior that's useful, which in this case, I'm assuming we can agree, is the getting up one time behavior that's useful has to come first, even if the feeling doesn't match. So sleeping those extra, I presume, a couple hours, delays you from feeling sad, but it causes other problems. If you were to get up one time, you might still feel sad, right? Because that's why you're oversleeping, because you're sleeping longer, to avoid that. But the functional part of being a housewife, as you identify, would be completed. So maybe some of those feelings of sadness and guilt would, over time, abate, because, functionally speaking, you're completing the task that you want. What's tough about that is that in the moment, it's easy for me to say this now, but in the moment, like, for instance, when you have to get up out of bed tomorrow, you're going to be facing that same challenge, which is, I can get up now and feel depressed or I can wait and feel depressed later. So in that moment, it's hard to act on the behavior that you kind of know you want to move towards. I mean, it sounds like you want to get up and see if the kids are.
Client: Yeah, I mean, I want everything to be normal again. And I guess I never really thought of it like that. Like, I just thought, well, if I'm waking up at the right time and I'm just feeling bad, then, like I said, what's the point? But I guess it makes sense. Like, even if I don't feel like doing it, maybe it'll make me feel better if I do do it, even if it's hard, because nothing's really harder than what I'm already going through.
Counselor: Well, it seems like you're more or less making things worse in an effort to avoid the pain that you're going to suffer anyway. You're making the pain worse. Just delaying it a little bit. Right. What thought? We talked before about automatic thoughts, these thoughts that come up kind of when your belief system meets, these different situations that occur when you have that thought that this is pointless. And I'm going to expand on that thought a little. That what that thought's really getting at is I can avoid this pain if I sleep a little while longer. That's a version of the thought. Does that make sense?
Client: Yeah. And also, I guess I thought that, no, it wouldn't really be that beneficial to get up.
Counselor: Okay, so you're also minimizing the benefit.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So there's a couple things going on. Right. I can avoid the pain by sipping in, and there's really no point to getting out because I won't do any good anyway.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: What adaptive response, that self talk. We talked about those things we consciously think to ourselves, could you apply in that moment when you're, you know, whatever time you get up in the morning when you're thinking about this and that thought comes in that it doesn't really matter if I get up anyway.
Client: I mean, I guess I could tell myself, like, I can do this. Like, instead of, you know, when I say to myself, what's the point? Instead I can say, I can do this. I can get out of bed. It'll be okay. I can. I'm strong enough. Even though it's hard to push through the pain and get up now, even though I don't want to, I can say, I can do this.
Counselor: Okay, so that would be your adaptive response. I'm strong enough. I can get through this, but it will be difficult. How about the value of getting up early and seeing the kids off to school? The automatic thought right now is telling you that's not valuable, but I think that you believe it is valuable.
Client: Yeah, I mean, I know it's valuable. I guess what my frustration is is that I know it's valuable. And it used to give me, like, an emotional payoff of, like, pride and satisfaction, and now I'm not getting that anymore. So I guess I need to realize that even though I'm not getting it right now, if I keep trying, maybe it will happen again. Because it did happen before.
Counselor: Well, it seemed logical that you have a higher probability of getting that back. If you do get up, then if you.
Client: I guess that's true. You'll never get the satisfaction of sending my kids off to school. If I never send my kids off to school.
Counselor: So you have a 0% chance of successful successfully moving past this with a sleeping in and you have some other probability greater than zero if you do.
Client: I never thought about it like that.
Counselor: Does that kind of make sense?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor:
output: So even though getting up early is going to be painful and going to seem like not a practical move, logically, you know that it has a better chance of paying off for you. And I think that with these type of, what you're going through is probably depression. I'd like to talk to you further to make sure that's what's going on, but it seems like you're depressed and sometimes with depression you just have to get one thing going your way each day. Right. So I'm not saying necessarily tomorrow you have to get up on time and then go make new friends and then go find social activities. You don't have to build Rome in a day here. It's more like, can I do this one thing? Can I prove to myself just what I'm saying, which is I'm strong enough to get up, see the kids off and have that one victory for tomorrow and build on that?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Maury. How you doing today?
Client: I'm doing all right.
Counselor: You doing all right?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I know last time you were here, you were discussing some relational issues. You want to continue with that?
Client: Yeah, yeah. I mean, you know, it kind of came up again. You know, every time my wife yells at me, you know, I feel like a failure, you know, like I told you last time, I just. I just feel like I can't do anything right, you know? Like everything I try to do is met with arguing and yelling, and I just feel like there's nothing I can do right.
Counselor: So no matter what you do, it's not going to end up the way you want?
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: So it's frustrating.
Client: Yeah, it definitely is.
Counselor: How is what's going on impacted your relationship with your wife?
Client: I mean, it's rocky, you know, because I feel like I can't do anything right. She doesn't understand that. And then, you know, we don't get along ever because we're just always yelling and I'm always feeling bad, and then it just keeps going like that.
Counselor: So when you. You mentioned you feel like a failure when she. When she yells at you?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Can you think back to maybe the last time, one of the last times you guys argued and try to remember that thought? We've talked about automatic thoughts before. Remember that thought that comes in that moment when she starts. She starts yelling at you?
Client: I mean, she'll yell at me. I mean, I feel, you know, frustrated. Like, why are you yelling at me right now? And. I don't know. I mean, as I was thinking about, like we were talking about it, and as I was thinking about it more this week, kind of felt like, you know, kind of like what happened with my dad, you know? I guess I kind of felt that same way when I was younger. You know, like, if my dad would yell at me or when he would yell at me, I kind of feel that same way. And it feels like the same thing. Yeah. It's kind of the first. I guess kind of the first thought that comes to mind.
Counselor: The first thought is I've been through something like this before, I guess.
Client: Yeah. I mean, I'm not really thinking those exact words, but that's definitely what it feels like, you know? Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. Like, it's like just a sense that this isn't brand new.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And the feeling you're connecting with it is the same feeling you had when your dad. Yahweh. Yeah.
Client: Yeah, pretty much, yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. So, in a sense, these arguments are taking you back to another point in time.
Client: I guess so, in a way, that's distressing.
Counselor: Yeah, it is.
Client: I mean, it feels, you know, pretty crappy.
Counselor: Now, in these arguments, she yells at you. You mentioned before that you do some yelling of your own, you know, in the midst of all that. Right. How would you rate it in terms of, like, any physical violence? Nothing like that.
Client: No, it's just words. I mean, we're just, you know, just yelling.
Counselor: And what level, like, what level of yelling would you say? How severe compared to what you've experienced in the past?
Client: Yeah, I don't know. I mean, it's like, you know, sometimes it can get up to, like, the eight or nines, you know, but just, I guess generally it's, you know, down. Closer to a seven on scale, like one to ten. Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: So sometimes it's seven. That would be pretty bad.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But some other times it's not.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So do you feel like your reaction is being frustrated is disproportionate to what's really going on or you feel like it's money?
Client: I don't know what else to do. You know? I mean, it's just. It's kind of my reaction, my gut reaction to it, you know? I think I'm justified in it because, you know, she just doesn't understand how much she yells at me, you know, and how much that hurts me. You know? I do feel justified. I mean, but it just. It just keeps going, though. And I feel justified, though. I don't know.
Counselor: Let's talk for a moment about, if you're okay with it, about your father and his yelling. You've discussed this with me a little bit before. In the past few sessions. I remember you saying that most. It was in the afternoon. Most of the yelling was when you were both home.
Client: Yeah, I mean, it was. I mean, mostly when I get home from school. I mean, I wasn't, you know, I was in high school, and then after that, you know, I went to college. And so I wasn't really home much during college, but, you know, I guess it'd be after I got home from high school. You know, I'd get home and he'd get home from work and, you know, just kind of be aggravated, whatever, just start yelling and. Yeah, usually when I got back from school, yeah.
Counselor: So he would get back from work, you would get back from school. And how long would that last? How long would the period where you were kind of vulnerable to being yelled at last?
Client: I don't know. I mean, sometimes about an hour, you know, and he'd be yelling because he's, you know, frustrated from work and he's frustrated from the drive home and whatever else, you know? And at some point, he would usually start drinking, you know, so maybe about an hour or so, you know, where that was. Like, you knew you were gonna get it.
Counselor: So kind of every day you could predict that between when you. Or between when he came home after you were already home from school and when he started drinking, you were gonna. He was gonna find something to yacht you about.
Client: Yeah, yeah, yeah. And, I mean, there were some days, like, I knew when he came home, he came home the same time every day. I knew I could get out of the house, you know? Cause at some point, I had a car, my friends had cars, you know, whatever.
Counselor: You had more freedom.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. You know, at some point, I had a job, so sometimes I'd work after school and stuff, so I knew I'd be able to leave the house at times, you know, like when I knew he was gonna start yelling and stuff. But, I mean, there was a period of time probably like my senior year of high school that I just didn't, you know, I just came home and, you know, it was gonna happen, you know, that's the way it happened.
Counselor: Even though you were able to escape it.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Right. You could have stayed out long enough for him to start drinking. Yeah.
Client: Instead you stayed in the house.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: I mean, it was pretty much my whole senior year come home. I knew what was gonna happen, and I just took it. You know, I just. I knew he was gonna yell. I just took it that.
Counselor: Was there ever a period when you first got your freedom that you tried, like.
Client: Oh, yeah, yeah, I did. And. I don't know. I don't know why I didn't just keep doing that. It probably would have been easier, but. I don't know. The whole senior year, I just started. I was just back there at the house when he came home from work.
Counselor: So in that period, were you. Were you. There's times when you did leave, what did he do instead of yell at you?
Client: I guess he had to yell at somebody else. I mean, my. My sister, my brother were home. I guess he probably yelled at them. I don't know. I mean, it felt good to not be there, but I guess he probably yelled at them, which just sucks. I mean, you know, I guess somebody had. Whoever was there was gonna take it, you know?
Counselor: Somebody was gonna get you out there.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. I mean, I guess it was them when I wasn't there. I don't know.
Counselor: And how do you think you took it. When you were there, how well did you respond?
Client: I just got used to it, you know, I knew what was gonna happen. I knew he was gonna yell. I knew that it was gonna make me upset. I knew that just those repeated times, just like now, you know, I'm gonna feel like a failure, which ultimately I did. You know, maybe I probably just became numb to it, you know, it happens so often and same thing every day. Probably just became numb to it and just kind of stopped caring and kind of stopped, I don't know, believing in myself or something, you know?
Counselor: Like you've just given up.
Client: Yeah, probably. That's probably. I don't know. Probably. Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: And how many years total did this experience go on? Do you endure the yelling?
Client: I mean, it would have been while I was in middle school and most of high school. I mean, I told you at some point I was able to leave, but probably all of middle school, most of high school, and I left, and then some, you know, for the rest of the senior year, I would be there. So, I don't know, quite a few years, I guess.
Counselor: A long time to suffer.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: And now if we move back forward in time, you're in a relationship where you're getting yelled at a bit. Right. And that's sometimes quite a bit, and that's causing you distress.
Client: It's like the same thing. You're yelling a little bit and. Yeah.
Counselor: So you feel like you're back in the same place.
Client: Yeah, I mean, it does. Yeah. I mean, obviously, you know, she's. She's not doing anything like he was, you know, like drinking or anything like that, but it does. I mean, it's like the same thing that happened is happening again.
Counselor: So that's. In your opinion, that's the consequence of what happened to you. Like, all this yelling that you endured before in some way is significantly contributing to what you're going through now.
Client: Maybe. I mean, I guess it could, you know, because it is the same thing. So maybe it's.
Counselor: There could be some connection.
Client: Maybe. Yeah.
Counselor:
output: I mean, maybe not 100% explain it, but it explains part of it.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Sarah. How are you doing today?
Client: Good.
Counselor: Doing well.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Yeah. A little better than last time. Worse?
Client: Kind of. No change.
Counselor: No change?
Client: Mm hmm.
Counselor: So you're still having sadness?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. And frustrated.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So tell me what's been going on this last week.
Client: Well, Mary's been crying a lot and I'm really tired, so I've needed extra help, you know, with her because I'm so tired and I just can't get out of bed.
Counselor: How much have you been sleeping each night? Like, on average?
Client: I don't know. Maybe 810, maybe more.
Counselor: Maybe more? Yeah. And how long did you sleep each night before you had Mary?
Client: I don't know. Maybe six, eight at the most.
Counselor: So your sleep habits have changed a bit?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you talked last time about feeling sad. What else has changed?
Client: I'm kind of feeling, you know, like I'm not doing good with Mary, that maybe I should think about getting a job again.
Counselor: And when you say not doing good with Mary, what specifically is going on that's contributing to that thought?
Client: I just remember with George, you know, he would cry in the middle of the night and I would hop right up. And with Mary, when she cries, I just want to roll over.
Counselor: So you're less enthusiastic about caring for her than were as compared to George?
Client: That's a good way of putting it, yeah.
Counselor: You still do care for her though.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Anything else has changed?
Client: I can't think of anything, but I'm sure there is.
Counselor: Well, tell me more about the sadness. Where do you think that's coming from?
Client: Um, I'm not really sure. Maybe just because she's crying all the time and I don't feel like I did with George. You know, everyone said I did such a good job with him and I was a fantastic mother and I was doing such a great job. And, you know, and I just. People are saying it, but I just don't feel like I'm doing as good a job as I did with him.
Counselor: All right, so people are giving the same input. They're saying that you're. You're a great mother in regard to Mary, like you were with George, but you're feeling differently about it.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So their piece really hasn't changed. Like, they're still giving you the same feedback, but your feelings definitely have changed.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: To the point where you feel like you should just get a full time job. And I guess Mary go to daycare.
Client: Yeah. Because she's, you know, little. She's only six weeks now, so, yeah, she would go to daycare.
Counselor: So what comes to mind when you consider doing that, like, working full time.
Client: Um, kind of mixed feelings. Like, I was home with George until he went to school, so I feel like Mary wouldn't be getting the same thing that George got, but I feel like she's not getting the same thing right now.
Counselor: Like, you're just, you're just not doing the same quality job.
Client: Right.
Counselor: What kind of things did you do with George that you look forward to? Like, when he was that age, I.
Client: Would sing to him a lot and we would read books. You know, I started reading to him when he was still in my belly. And then when he came out, everyone's like, oh, it's too soon. But we would read all the time. I would take him to the playground quite often.
Counselor: Like, most days, pretty much, yeah. And that was something you really look forward to.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Have you done those same things with Mary?
Client: I try to, but maybe it's because she's a little fussier. You know, I try singing to her, and with George, it would be like one or two songs, maybe even just one song, and he'd calm down. And Mary's just not the same. It takes longer. Or she just doesn't respond to singing or reading books like he did.
Counselor: All right, so each infant or baby is going to be a little different.
Client: Right.
Counselor: But that feedback is still important to you. You'd prefer if her temperament was more in line with how George's was?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: If it were, do you think that would make enough of a difference to kind of break you out of this, these feelings of sadness?
Client: I would like to hope so.
Counselor: Mm hmm. So part of this could be just adapting to her personality?
Client: Maybe.
Counselor: Maybe. What else could be a part of it?
Client: Um, I don't know. I mean, you know, some of my girlfriends have kids the same age, or I babies the same age, and they're going back to work now, or they have been working for a while. And I kind of feel like now that they're working and have two kids, they kind of look down on me.
Counselor: So they look upon you negatively because you don't work.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Now you say you get that feeling. Is there evidence that you talked about cognitive behavioral therapy and evaluating evidence? Do you have evidence that that's the way they feel?
Client: It's kind of just a feeling. And I forget exactly what she said, but one of my friends was like, oh, you have so much time to do all this? And I'm always working. And it just, the way she worded it kind of made it feel like, you know, I have so much to do. What are you doing?
Counselor: Kind of minimized your place. Well, I can see how that would hurt. And there's always going to be people that say things that we prefer they not say or feel a way that we perceive negatively as a negative effect. But this sadness, I mean, as we've been talking about it in weeks prior, is really markedly worse than what you've experienced ever before.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So after you had. How old is George now?
Client: Six.
Counselor: Six. So after you had George, there was really no period of sadness from what you reported?
Client: No, it was just not sadness. It was just having to get used to having a baby around, but adjustment. Yeah. He was my first, and I was so ecstatic to have him. And my husband and I were so happy. You know, he was our first baby. We were really happy with it. With him.
Counselor: Mm hmm. And you don't have that same. That same feeling now?
Client: It's not that I'm not happy to have Maryland. It's just. I don't know, I feel like things are so different. You know, I have George to take care of. He's running around. I can't give him my full attention anymore. Mary's constantly crying, and I can't seem to soothe her, and I just get frustrated with her.
Counselor: So there's adapting to her needs and personality. But also George's role has to change.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Because he has to fit into it a family with a new member. So there's a lot going on in your mind and a lot of different feelings, but still, the sadness is when you first came in, this was really what was on your mind, sleeping more than you wanted, not really experiencing enjoyment with Mary the way you'd hoped.
Client: Right.
Counselor: And then I think too, kind of a negativistic view of your situation that we talked about. You're seeing things from a negative point of view when before you reported you had not.
Client: Right. You know, with George, he would start to fuss and cry, and I could get him calmed down fairly quickly. Well, with Mary, you know, she starts crying and fussing, and I feel like it may only take, like, 15 or 20 minutes, but to me, it just feels so much longer. And I give up at a certain point, and I just hand her off to whoever's closest, and they seem to get her soothed right away, which may.
Counselor: Be all the more frustrating.
Client: Cause you couldn't exactly.
Counselor: So have any feelings of, like, guilt or anything like that.
Client: Yeah, I mean, when I can't soothe her and I just hand her off, I feel like I'm not a good mom to her. Like, I was with George.
Counselor: So it comes back to, like, you just feel like you're not, you're not given the same quality care, right? Yeah. All right, well, there's a lot of thoughts going on, a lot of feelings going on, and I want to get to those and talk about those and work through them, but in the immediate, I want to look at some of the behaviors. So thoughts, obviously, what you're thinking, behavior is what you're doing. Like, in terms of, like, you mentioned reading when you used to read with George, something you enjoyed. And sometimes when a person has kind of depressive feelings, it's important to engage in activities that would normally bring enjoyment. Even if you don't get the enjoyment, which at the time doesn't feel comfortable, it actually can be a little frustrating.
Client: Right.
Counselor: But the alternative is an avoidance. Oftentimes there's an avoidance of those activities, which can make things even worse.
Client: Makes sense.
Counselor: That makes sense. So in this particular case, what's going on with your family having to adjust to a new member? What activities were you really looking forward to when you're pregnant? What things are you looking forward to? Doing it maryland that we could kind of schedule like, that we could kind of plan for you to do.
Client: I would definitely say reading and singing to her and just, you know, being able to hold her when she was calm.
Counselor: Okay. Okay. So reading to her, singing to her. Anything else? Anything else that you were, like back when you're pregnant, you're thinking, all that would be really fun if I could do that with my child.
Client: I guess just thinking back to what I used to do with George was taking him to the park, and I was really looking forward to that with Mary, but it just didn't happen.
Counselor: It's not been happening. Huh. Have you tried before to go to the park? Like, have you started, like, packing or getting your car keys and getting things ready?
Client: We went once so far with some of my girlfriends, and then it was okay. And then she got fussy towards the end. And the next time, you know, I said I would go, and I just didn't.
Counselor: So what happened at that moment when you were, when you said you were going to go and it was getting close to the time you wanted to go, what happened then that led to you not going?
Client: I just kind of, I guess I got sad thinking about what happened last time, so it just frustrated me, and I didn't want to end up, you know, unhappy.
Counselor: So feelings of sadness and thoughts that you would be unhappy. Mm hmm. Okay. So that's one of the obstacles that we'll have to look at with that particular behavior. So I like to. I like to plan these things out. Let's go with those three things that you have. You have the. You have the reading. Right. And singing. And I presume both of those you just do in your home.
Client: Right.
Counselor: And then the going to the park. Okay. Which, this time of year, I imagine you could go almost every day.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Was that. Would that something you would done?
Client: Yes.
Counselor:
output: With George? Yeah, I did do. All right, so maybe we can schedule this, the reading. How many times a day did you do that with George on, say, average?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Lucy. Nice to meet you.
Client: Hi.
Counselor: So I understand that you were referred here by your GP because you've been feeling quite down recently.
Client: Yeah, I thought I should. I've been feeling quite bad for quite a while, so I thought maybe it's time to see someone about it because I don't want to feel like this anymore.
Counselor: Okay. So from your notes, I saw that you saw the GP about three months ago?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So how long have you been feeling down altogether?
Client: Quite a few months before that as well, actually. But it's gotten pretty bad these past few months, so that's kind of why I came.
Counselor: Okay. So has it got worse since you saw your GP?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay, so tell me, how are things at the moment?
Client: Well, it kind of started just feeling a bit low and wound up about things, but, I don't know, just recently I just can't really be bothered to do anything at all. I kind of find it hard to get motivated for things and I want to be. I really want to be better, but it's just kind of reaching the end now where I just. I want to do something about it.
Counselor: Okay, so you said that you're feeling really down, really sad?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you feel like you haven't got any motivation, but. Are you okay?
Client: Yeah, I'm fine.
Counselor: Sorry. Okay, and you haven't got any motivation, but it sounds like you've put quite a lot of pressure on yourself to try and feel a bit better.
Client: Yeah, I just. It's kind of hard as well because there's not really anyone to talk about. So I just kind of stay on my own trying to. I don't like to think about it, but I don't know.
Counselor: So you say you've been. You've been feeling quite isolated. There's not many people around.
Client: Yeah. There's no one I can talk to about it. No one would listen or understand anyway.
Counselor: Okay, so I'm just going to try and find out a little bit more about you. So I understand that you're an english student at uni.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you live away from home with some friends. Is that right?
Client: Yeah, I live here.
Counselor: Oh, okay. So you don't live far from the uni, but you say you feel like you live with your friends, but you don't feel like you can talk to them.
Client: Yeah, I mean, they're lovely. I get on really well with them, but I don't know, recently, whenever they want to go out or stuff, I just. I don't want to bring them down. I can't. They don't understand what I'm going through. They kind of. I don't know, they don't make fun of how I feel, but they don't really understand what it's like. I just. I don't want to go out with them and bring them down or stuff.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds. Do you try and hide the way you're feeling from them?
Client: I guess. I mean, it's easier to hide it than to try and explain it all the time when no one really wants to know.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like you've been feeling down, you've been feeling unmotivated, you feel like you want to be better. But actually it sounds like you feel like you can't reach out for help, you can't speak to anybody.
Client: No, I don't really talk to my parents a lot either, so that's kind of hard.
Counselor: Okay. I'm just gonna go back in time a little bit, I suppose. I'm just wondering, when did all of this start? You said it's been going on for quite a few months.
Client: Yeah, I guess it kind of started, actually, when I was revising for my exams. I guess the stress. I put a lot of stress on myself. I think I've always wanted to do well for me and I guess for my parents. So the stress of exams. And it was also kind of hard because my parents were going through a bit of a troubled time then.
Counselor: Okay, so this would be like last March, last April?
Client: Yeah, I think so.
Counselor: Around that time. So about six months ish. And it sounds like a lot was happening. So you had a lot of uni pressure on and you said that your parents were having marital problems. Okay. And it sounds like that was a real shock to you.
Client: Yeah, I guess it was hard as well because I wasn't doing well at uni. I guess I just felt a bit guilty. I know it sounds silly, but I felt like maybe if I could do better, then they would get better, but it just wasn't really happening.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like you were trying to work hard and be more successful because you thought that that would make them happier and try and fix things.
Client: Yeah, I wanted to make them feel better, but it just kind of backfired a little, I guess.
Counselor:
output: How did it backfire?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: So, good morning.
Client: Good morning.
Counselor: What would you like to work on in this session?
Client: I would like to work on my avoidance behavior. I actually have an opportunity which I was looking for from a very long time to give a presentation. And now that I have this opportunity in front of me, I'm trying to avoid it.
Counselor: So you were looking forward to this opportunity for a long time?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And then now you are avoiding it. Right. And what you would like to do?
Client: I would not like to. I would not. I would like not to avoid it.
Counselor: So you would like to go ahead with the presentation?
Client: I would like to go ahead with the presentation.
Counselor: So how do you feel when you're about to avoid? In the sense, like what kind of feelings are making you avoid this?
Client: Rather whether I'll be able to do it or not, whether it will go well, like whether all the students or the people who are listening to the presentation will like it or not. What if I forget? Or what if I do a mess?
Counselor: Now, these are your thoughts. How do you feel when you think like this?
Client: I don't feel good.
Counselor: Can you label that feeling? When you. When you think like this, you don't feel good. And which is what feeling?
Client: I feel anxious.
Counselor: You feel anxious? Right. And instead of feeling anxious, how would you like to feel so that you go ahead with the presentation?
Client: Rather not anxious, but at least some little anxious.
Counselor: Little anxious. You would like to reduce your anxiety?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So you wouldn't want to get rid of the anxiety completely?
Client: Yes, I want to get rid.
Counselor: You want to get rid of the anxiety.
Client: Anxiety completely.
Counselor: So how about feeling concerned but not anxious? So you're careful about your presentation. You also work towards the presentation well and you're not ignorant or you're not indifferent towards the outcome. Would that make sense?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So you don't want to be indifferent and feel nothing about the presentation, but you would like to feel concerned and not anxious about it.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Do you also think there is a connection between your anxiety and your avoidance?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: If you were concerned and not anxious, would you continue to avoid or you would probably go ahead?
Client: I would go ahead.
Counselor: You would go ahead?
Client: I always wanted to do this, so I would go ahead.
Counselor: You would go ahead. Right. So can we set that agenda for today's session is to feel concerned and not anxious about the upcoming presentation?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Okay, fine. So now to help you reach this goal, we will have to examine one specific incident where you know you felt anxious. And then you will understand how you get anxious and how to shift your feelings from anxiety to concern. So would you mind me telling me a specific incident where you had a chance to go ahead with, you know, preparing for the presentation, but you didn't.
Client: Recently, I have a social group where there was a chance that they wanted a presentation regarding a particular topic, and they have asked me for the dates to give me my dates when I would be presenting, and I have been just postponing it. Postponing it and not giving them the dates.
Counselor: Is this the same presentation that you are postponing, or this is different one?
Client: This is, again, a different one.
Counselor: This is a different one. But this is a specific example.
Client: Yes, this is a very specific example, which I always like. On the back of my mind. This example is always disturbing me or just always coming to my mind that I did that postponing thing.
Counselor: All right, so let's take this incident where, you know, there was a social group, and they asked you about a date for presentation. And in this situation, do you remember the incident clearly?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So when you chose to avoid it, can you remember that in that moment?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: What was going through your mind that made you avoid it?
Client: Whether I will be able to do it properly or whether they will like it or not. Am I that qualified to give the presentation now?
Counselor: These are the doubts that you had in your head. Could you convert them into statements?
Client: I'm. I'm not qualified.
Counselor: I'm not qualified.
Client: I am. People will not like it.
Counselor: People will not like it, and I.
Client: Will not be able to deliver it.
Counselor: And when you thought these, how did you feel?
Client: I didn't. I was feeling nervous. Rather nervous and not happy.
Counselor: Even not happy. Nervous and anxious. Also anxious on a zero to 100, how distressing was this anxiety?
Client: It was very distressing, I think. 80.
Counselor: 80. So that was pretty intense, right?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: It is like death anxiety. Something is gonna happen to me.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: 70 rather than, I would say.
Counselor: Okay. What was your natural intention to do at that time when you felt so anxious?
Client: I just told them, I'm busy for a while, and I will just let you know the dates when I am free and when can I take up the presentation.
Counselor: So this is what you did?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Okay. Was there anything else going on in your mind? That I want to do this?
Client: No.
Counselor: And what, in this entire incident was most anxiety provoking for you?
Client: Whether I will be able to give the presentation or not. Whether the presentation would go well or not.
Counselor: So having to make a presentation was the trigger?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Your thoughts were, I won't be able to make the presentation well, I am not qualified, and these people will not like it. These were the thoughts that were going through your head. And then you felt anxious about it. You felt nervous about it. You also escaped. Or you bought time by, you know, telling them, I'll get back to you. So you postponed accepting the invitation. Is that correct?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So did I summarize that well?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So we'll go ahead with finding out where your anxiety comes from. So when you thought these three thoughts, you felt very anxious. Out of these three thoughts, which was most important thought for you, that made.
Client: You anxious whether I will be able to do it or not.
Counselor: So your prediction that you will not be able to do it well?
Client: Yes. That I will not be able to do it well.
Counselor: Do it well, right. Okay. Let's assume for the sake of therapy that you know, you do not do it well. We are trying to find out where your anxiety comes from. Are you with me?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So if you don't do it well, what does that mean to you?
Client: That I am not competent enough.
Counselor: You are not competent enough?
Client: Yes. I am incompetent.
Counselor: You are incompetent and therefore you are not able to do it well.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Right. So do you think that this label and the rating you have attached to it has something to do with your anxiety? I am incompetent. How?
Client: When I say I am incompetent, how.
Counselor: Do you feel then?
Client: I feel anxious as well as I feel very disappointed.
Counselor: So it's usually self doubting when you say that I am incompetent. You might feel depressed or ashamed when you say this. Depressed. And when you have to present a presentation, you will feel anxious because the underlying thought is I am incompetent. Do you see the connection between your depression and your anxiety? Let's double check it. Right. Let's assume that you do make a very bad presentation. You do not live up to the mark or you do not. Your presentation is not up to the mark. In spite of this, you don't believe that you are incompetent. Let's say in spite of this, you don't believe that you are incompetent. You say that just my presentation was bad, but you don't believe that you are incompleted. Would you be anxious in the first place before the presentation began?
Client: Can we do that?
Counselor: Let's assume, hypothetically, that you make a very bad presentation. And even in this situation, you don't call yourself incompetent. You are a person. You are a kind of a person who does not call herself incompetent. Even in case of a bad presentation. Imagine yourself a person who does not label herself as incompetent even if things go wrong. And still then would you be anxious about a presentation?
Client: No. Then why?
Counselor: That's what I'm saying. So if you were not to label yourself as impedance, you would not be anxious in case of a presentation where there are chances that it may go wrong?
Client: Yes. If I am. If I do not label myself incompetent, then I would not be anxious.
Counselor: You would not be anxious. So the possibility of a presentation going wrong, does that make you anxious or your own belief that you are incompetent in such a case makes you anxious?
Client: I am incompetent. The possibility of presentation going wrong would make me incompetent.
Counselor: That would only make you.
Client: Not a good presenter.
Counselor: This is what you think. My point is, does this possibility lead to your feelings or your own? Labelling leads to your feelings.
Client: Labelling.
Counselor: Labelling leads to feelings. Is that good news?
Client: I dont know.
Counselor: I think thats the good news. You tell me how?
Client: So that if I do not label myself, then I will not be anxious.
Counselor: Right. And at the same time the possibility can never be zero. You know you can always goof up in a presentation, right? But if you are anxious, the chances of making a bad presentation are more so. Worst case scenario, presentation goes wrong if you are prepared for it and you do not beat yourself up. You do not label yourself as incompetent. You are probably going to be little more confident in that case. And if you are more confident, your thought clarity would be better. So you will be most likely be able to present better if you are concerned and not anxious. So I want you to examine this belief of yours that you are incompetent if you don't make a presentation well. How convinced are you that you are an incompetent person if you do not present well?
Client: Yeah. If the presentation doesn't go well, it does not make me incompetent.
Counselor: It does not?
Client: No.
Counselor: Why?
Client: Because I am a different person and a presentation is a different thing. Just one presentation will not make me incompetent.
Counselor: This is what you are thinking now. But that time when you were anxious, you had a different conviction, right?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: What were you convinced of that time? That if my presentation goes wrong, it means I am inconvenient. And now you are thinking differently. Are you anxious now?
Client: If I think this way, you are not anxious.
Counselor: So what does this suggest? The chances of presentation going wrong are equal. Even if you make a presentation now, there are chances that it will go wrong. But you are not anxious now?
Client: No. But there are chances that it might go well also.
Counselor: But you were not focusing on those chances that time. Right?
Client: Right.
Counselor: So when your belief is triggered that I am incompetent, you also overlook the chances that it might go well. We'll come to that later. But we're just assuming the worst case scenario that let's assume that the presentation goes wrong. The point I'm trying to make is that time you were thinking differently. Now you're thinking differently and your feelings are different, which means that what you think about the presentation going wrong has a huge role to play in your anxiety.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: What you think is you are incompetent in case the presentation goes wrong.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And I want you to check if this belief of yours is valid or not. Would you like to check?
Client: Yes, I would like to.
Counselor: So I do understand, I am with you that if a presentation doesn't go well, as per your standards or somebody else's standards, and if it goes wrong, for instance, you do make some mistakes. So it might mean various things. For instance, you do not have the knowledge that is required. You do not have the skills that are required. You do not have the competencies that are required. Right. So it might suggest that you have or you lack certain attributes. And I am with you on that. So let's say that you know you lack certain competencies. That is proven beyond doubt. Right. But how does that mean that you are an incompetent person?
Client: If I don't have the knowledge, if I don't have the skills, if I don't have the competencies, it will make me.
Counselor: That means you are a person who lacks these competencies.
Client: Yes. That means I am a person who lacks these competencies.
Counselor: Right. But how does that mean that you are an incompetent person?
Client: Yes. It does not mean that I am an incompetent person, but I am a person who lacks these competencies, the knowledge, the skill and the competencies which are required.
Counselor: So, competencies is not you. For instance, if you have a competency, it doesn't mean you are competent. Let me give an example. I have ring. I am not ring.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: All right. I have a phone. I am not phone. I have it or I don't. In a similar way, you have a competency, but you are not competent. So you lack or have an ability. You lack or have a skill. You lack or have a competency. Fine. I am with you on that.
Client: But that does not make me an incompetent person.
Counselor: It does not define you fully and accurately.
Client: My skills are different from a person.
Counselor: Absolutely. Absolutely. You are not your skill.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Skill is just a small part of the whole human being. You know, we are made up of so many complex attributes. Skill is just one of them.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And it would be a little too much to label a person based on their skill or behavior or knowledge or their finances or their looks or their materialistic possessions or, you know, their social status. I mean, like, these are few things that we define human beings on, but they are pretty inaccurate to label anyone as good or bad based on these things. So coming back to the point, how much are you convinced that lacking a competency does not make you incompetent?
Client: Yes, I am convinced that my skills and me is a. We are different. Skills can be learned and they can be learned over time. They can be mastered over time.
Counselor: Mastered over time?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And you will have to do what to master them?
Client: I'll have to study more, practice more.
Counselor: To do that, and fail more, goof up with presentations more. So, you know, when you make mistakes, you learn best. So this is your conviction now. But as human beings, you know, conviction is very unstable. It goes up and down with adversities. So why don't you prepare yourself for an adversity and convince yourself in case of an adversity? Because right now there is no adversity. Right.
Client: Right.
Counselor: If you are able to convince yourself in adversities. Excuse me. I think you will be able to manage your feelings better next time. Then when you are able to manage your feelings, you will also be able to get over the avoidance that you were talking about.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Right. Okay. Would you mind practicing this, what you have learned in this session in a real life situation?
Client: Yes, I would like to.
Counselor: So how about getting yourself invited for a presentation or making a presentation and actually making a mistake that only you know?
Client: Yes, I can.
Counselor: You can? Right.
Client: There is a presentation coming up.
Counselor: Okay. And how likely are you to avoid this presentation?
Client: No, now I am not likely to avoid it.
Counselor: In fact. Okay, great. Wonderful.
Client: In fact, I would just call them and tell them that.
Counselor: So why don't you call them right now? Do you have a phone?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Okay, so why don't you make a call right now?
Client: I make a call right now. Okay.
Counselor: Okay. Take your phone and.
Client: Hi. You were talking about the dates, so, yes, we can do it. Okay. Next week would be fine with me. Yeah. Yes. Yes. Okay. Thank you.
Counselor: Hey, that was quick. So did she give you a date or. It's gonna be decided.
Client: It's gonna be decided within a day. She'll just let me know.
Counselor: So she's going to let you know. I thought like.
Client: No, she was just going to tell me, like, my tentative dates were. Would be so.
Counselor: And then you're going to confirm it, right?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Did you feel anxious before making the call?
Client: No.
Counselor: No, not really.
Client: No, not really.
Counselor: That's cool. Interesting. Okay. So now I would want you to actually prepare for the presentation in this week and have a slide that has one mistake in it.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: And then you would know that you have made a mistake in the presentation and I want you to feel anxious about it.
Client: But when I know that I have made a mistake, then how would I feel anxious about it?
Counselor: You never know.
Client: Let me try.
Counselor: When you know that you have made a mistake, you will know that it is not up to the mark. You might feel anxious about it. No.
Client: No.
Counselor: What can trigger anxiety in you about a presentation?
Client: My predictions that it might go wrong.
Counselor: Okay. And how can we actually bring on this anxiety in real life? What can actually make you anxious?
Client: The predictions. The future predictions.
Counselor:
output: Correct. And how can we experimentally. Experimentally make you anxious?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Any other evidence that points toward you being an imposter
Client: besides my bad grade that I got that? Yeah. Not a whole lot.
Counselor: All right, so it would be safe to say that a lot of that thought of I'm not good enough is kind of based on this, on these feelings of anxiety.
Client: Yeah. Which are really intense. Like panic almost in the moment.
Counselor: Yes. So in a way, you're believing what the anxiety would lead you to believe.
Client: Yeah, definitely.
Counselor: But in the bright light of scrutiny, there aren't a lot of facts to support the worst case, which is you don't deserve it.
Client: Right?
Counselor: Right. How about evidence that refutes that you're not good enough?
Client: I would say that, you know, I was accepted into the program. Like, there's kind of like a pretty rigorous sort of testing and stuff, which I passed to get interviews and such, to get into the program. So I did that. Like I said, I'm a pretty good student, all considering, you know, before this kind of like what's happening.
Counselor: Okay, so you got through a rigorous process to become a student. You're doing well.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: You mentioned before just the one bad grade. Right. Okay, so if, you know, you have friends in this program. Right. If one of them came to you with this balance of one bad grade and some anxiety versus passing rigorous standards and doing well, otherwise, what advice would you give them?
Client: I mean, now that you're kind of, like, talking about it like this or that sort of thing, it makes sense. I would probably say that, well, you seem to be doing pretty well so far. You know, that anyone evaluating would look at all of cumulative, how you're doing, your performance, rather than that of weight.
Counselor: Would you feel comfortable giving that advice to yourself?
Client: I think I try to sometimes, but my anxiety symptoms kind of, like, really, like you were saying, your anxiety tells you sort of. I think I can think that, but I think my anxiety symptoms are such in the moment that it's really hard, you know, and I'm replaying what happened before in my head, anticipation, predicting that it'll happen again.
Counselor: All right, so let's look at. Let's look at the thought and the feeling. If you had to rate the percent that you believed this thought, this belief that you are not good enough to be in the program, like right now.
Client: Right now, yeah.
Counselor: But here with me, how much of your mind believes that that's true?
Client: I would say, like, you know, a two or a three? Like, not very. I don't believe it very much right now because, you know, I'm not presenting and it's just you and I, not like a group full of people. So that's, that pressure is not there here.
Counselor: So right now, you're really not buying the idea that you're not good enough.
Client: Yeah. Correct.
Counselor:
output: So now let's move to, let's say right in the. Near the end of, like, presentation, when that anxiety is there. And the classmates, they could be looking at you, they could be negatively evaluating you. That's what you're worried about. How much do you believe that thought then?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: You've said that when you're in work, you worry a lot about how you come across in social situations.
Client: Yeah, it really makes me feel really anxious, like what I look like and what people are thinking.
Counselor: Yeah. You said that you worry that you visibly shake.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Are there any other things that you worry that people will notice?
Client: I think obviously, the shaking. I think my hands and legs shaking and going really red and sweating and just looking really weird.
Counselor: So it sounds like you have quite a strong mental image of how you see yourself when you're in these social situations.
Client: Yeah, definitely.
Counselor: So you go red, you shake. Is there anything else that you think that you do? I mean, describe yourself. How do you think you look when you're in these situations?
Client: Just like, I think I just look really obviously weird and out of place and, like, really red and just visibly shaking and sweating and kind of not being able to communicate properly with people.
Counselor: Is there anything that you do to try and kind of defend against these things, to manage these problems?
Client: I guess, like, when I'm holding the camera, I just grip onto it really, really tight, or I kind of clench all my muscles and just find something that I can focus on and to kind of try and make myself shake less and not go as red and stuff.
Counselor: So you focus on something, you grip onto the camera. Do you make eye contact with people?
Client: No, I just tend to just look down.
Counselor: Okay. So you also avoid eye contact. Is there anything else that you do to manage the sweating, for example?
Client: I just, as I kind of looking down and wearing all black, so it's less obvious or kind of wearing just more layers and all black, so you just can't tell.
Counselor: Okay. What do you think would happen if you stopped doing these things? If you stopped gripping onto the camera or you started making eye contact and not looking down, what do you think could happen?
Client: I think it would be so much worse. Yeah. I think I just would just shake even more and be more anxious and look more obviously kind of weird and out of place.
Counselor: What I'm thinking now is, how would you feel about if we did an experiment to test out your thoughts on what would happen if you stopped doing these things? If we did a bit of a role play where we pretended to enact a situation at work.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: And if you did this maybe twice in the first time, you do all the things that you normally do. Grip onto something, look down. Is there anything else that you do when you're in these situations, these work conversations to try and cope?
Client: I just kind of all just, like, fumble and kind of just clench whatever it is I'm holding just really tight. And just make sure I don't make any eye contact at all. Just kind of get through it.
Counselor: Okay. So in the first time, I want you to do those things as much as you normally would. In fact, maybe even slightly more than you normally would. And then the second time, I want you to drop doing those things altogether. How does that sound?
Client: Try my best.
Counselor: And how would you feel about if we filmed this so you could actually see what you looked like?
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Do you have a camera with you that we could video on?
Client: Yeah. Is my phone okay?
Counselor: Yeah, yeah, we'll use that in just a sec.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Before we do this, then we're just going to fill out this form, because what we're doing now is an experiment. We call it a behavioral experiment to see what happens when you change the way that you're behaving.
Client: Right. Okay.
Counselor: Okay. So the first column says, I need to fill out an experiment to test this thought that you have so that our experiment is going to be that we do a conversation at work. Who should I play? If you're playing yourself in this role play, who should I be?
Client: Maybe like a client at work, I always have to sit down with clients before we do the shoot and kind of get to know a little bit more about what they want.
Counselor:
output: Okay, so would it work if I was maybe having a wedding and I was hiring you to be a wedding photographer?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Alisa, how are you doing today?
Client: I'm doing well, thank you.
Counselor: Doing well.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: What's going on?
Client: I have family coming into town and I have to go to the airport to pick them up.
Counselor: So you have family flying in?
Client: Yes. That's something that I get very anxious about, having to cross the bridge. I have to cross the Ben Franklin bridge and then get over the bridge that goes to the airport by the stadium. I think that's the Girard point bridge. Yeah. That's two levels there. I have to do that both ways.
Counselor: Going and coming both ways. You have to cross four times?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So what kind of feeling is this bringing up for you?
Client: I get very anxious even just thinking about it right now.
Counselor: So you're anxious right here with me?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So I want to try to scale this. We talked about this before with cognitive therapy. So let's say that ten is really the most anxious you're felt about crossing bridges, and one is no anxiety. Where would you be right now?
Client: Right now, probably an eight. Yeah.
Counselor: I don't love anxiety.
Client: Yes. It's worse when I'm at that point on that day, but right now, I think just knowing that I have to do that. Yes.
Counselor: And what's it on that day?
Client: A ten.
Counselor: It reaches a ten, definitely.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: All right. So. But even now, how far away is the. Until they.
Client: Oh, it's a week.
Counselor: So even now, a week out, it's. Nate, this is really hurting.
Client: Yes. I don't like that at all.
Counselor: So for your job and local travel, you don't really have to cross any.
Client: Ten minutes to work every day. And banks. So 20 minutes, shopping centers and everything is just within the vicinity. I don't have to cross any bridges.
Counselor: So no bridges?
Client: No, not at all. I probably planned it that way, too.
Counselor: That worked out well.
Client: That worked out very well.
Counselor: All right. But coming up, pick up the family you will be crossing. So let's look at this at each stage. So, I mean, you're clearly anxious now, as you mentioned. But let's go to, let's try to move forward a week to the day that they'll be flying, what time they fly in.
Client: It's going to be a 04:00 flight. In the afternoon.
Counselor: In the afternoon. So about what time would you have to leave to?
Client: I would have to leave probably at 03:00 because it's only about 20 minutes to the airport. Really?
Counselor: Really.
Client: But I would like to leave earlier. They'll probably take them time. By the time they land and go through, you know, getting their luggages, they probably won't even come out till maybe 430, but I'd like to make sure I'm there at around 334 o'clock.

Client: I have to do this. I have to get up and go. They need me to be there this week. It's my parents coming in and they're elderly, so I don't want them to be stuck at the airport. There's no one else that actually can go pick them up. So I have to get up and go and pick them up.
Counselor: That's what's going through your mind?
Client: That's what's going through my mind. So, you know, there's nobody else that can do this. I mean, it's cheaper than there's no. I probably can't even afford to get a taxi for them because you'd have to cross that's from Philly to. Into New Jersey. So that's going to be very expensive. I can't afford that. When all I'd have to do is pay $5 for the tow and maybe gas up my car for $10 or something. But, um, I. Yeah, I'll be thinking about, I have to do this.
Counselor: I have to do it.
Client: I can do it. Something that I can save money that way. And I don't want to leave them stranded. Definitely someone else can. I mean, they'd be lost. They're not familiar with the airport. And Philly airport is crazy to me.
Counselor: Yeah, it's a big place. A lot going on. So. So you're sitting at home in 15 minutes before getting the cardinal and you're thinking, I have to do this. But your reasons are positive. Like you save money and protect your parents from having to be there alone. So when does the anxiety come in?
Client: Just the thought of the bridge, it's just. I could drive off the bridge. I can fall off. Usually what I do is try to stay in the middle lane. I can't do more than 40 miles an hour. And I just. I'm shaking. I have the radio on and windows down because I can't swim. So if for any reason I'm to fall off, I mean, that's it for me. I even have a little metal one of those. I think it's an instrument that you use in the house for, I don't know, plier or something. Something real hard that I can hit the ground with. It sits right there on my door, on the side of my door. So I'm already, I planned, I have that. I planned ahead of time. I know what I'm going to do as soon as I approach the bridge, but I still feel anxious.
Counselor: So you're anxious before you leave and you're starting to think about the bridge at that point. You already think about it. How about when you get in your car, you start driving toward the bridge?
Client: I say a prayer. I am still anxious. I turn on the radio and the closer I get to, especially the toll point, and I know it's at me. And you see those lights flashing. Last exit before the, you know, the.
Counselor: Toll, you know you're going over once.
Client: Yeah, there's no turning back. There's no turning back.
Counselor: So before that, when you can still exit, what's your anxiety level?
Client: Before, when I can still exit?
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: It'S probably still high. It's probably at a nine or so.
Counselor: It's still high, but it's not maxed out yet. But it's pretty bad.
Client: Yeah, I think it's pretty bad at that point.
Counselor: And how about when you cross through the.

Counselor: Okay.
Client: Yes, yes.
Counselor: So your specific fear as you start to cross, this is the Ben Franklin would be the first bridge. Right. You can go across. Is that your car will go off the bridge?
Client: Yes, definitely.
Counselor: And when does that, so that's a ten anxiety. When does that anxiety start to go away?
Client: As soon as I'm getting close to getting off the bridge, I'm now leaving a little sigh of the, there's a little release there. And I know that I've been able to manage those two, three minutes of cross. I don't know how many minutes it takes actually crossing the bridge. I start feeling a little bit of relief, but then again, I know I have to take that exit and there's another one coming right up, so starts all over again.
Counselor: All right, so then you cross the second bridge, the Gerard point bridge, you go to the airport. Does your anxiety drop, any of those points?
Client: Oh, as soon as I'm descending from the Gerard Point bridge, there's less, you know, it's almost reduced. I come, you know, really low.
Counselor: It's almost gone.
Client: Yes. It's almost gone. Yes.
Counselor: And when do you start thinking about that? You're going to have to cross them again?
Client: As soon as I'm exit, I'm getting back on 95 going north. And I know, here we go again. And cars are zooming by and you.
Counselor: Know, because you're not going very quickly.
Client: No, no, I'm that person. The middle lane doing 40 miles an hour. Yes.
Counselor: All right. So you're doing everything you can to keep your car on the bridge, but you're still feeling anxiety, like you're going to go off the bridge.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: The whole time. Until you start really descending.
Client: Exactly.
Counselor: And then you feel like you made it.
Client: Especially when there are those big trucks.
Counselor: Tractor trailers coming because the air.
Client: Yes, yes. Or if it's also in bad weather or at night, it's worst because on the bridge, especially the top one, you kind of see the sky and there's nothing else you see. So it's like you're gonna fall off. Yes.
Counselor: So in the lower level it's not as bad.
Client: On the lower, lower level, coming back it's not as bad because you're kind of like protected here and there. So it's not as bad, but going it's definitely worse. Yes.
Counselor: Are you aware of any time a car would have gone off the bridge?

Counselor: It's possible?

Counselor: You think it's a high risk?

I was checking it the other day, I had to go to the airport and I was trying to measure the distance between the metal poles just to see if a car could fit there. Really?
