Counselor: Done some thinking, she's done some calculations, geometry. And you've concluded that it's not really likely, but it could. It could fly off the. Alright, but either way, your anxiety is maxed out on each bridge.

Counselor: All right, so when you arrive home, you're down to one.

Counselor: All right. So going back to the. The first stage, like when you're getting ready, you were thinking that you have to go.

output: So, I mean, clearly it sounds like you picked them up before.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Jeff. How you doing today?
Client: I'm alright. Thanks for actually seeing me today. Sure.
Counselor: How have you been? I know last time I spoke with you, you were having some difficulties at work.
Client: I'm still having difficulties at work and that's why I'm glad I have a session today because it hasn't stopped. The frustration and anger is just, it's there ten times more than normal.
Counselor: You're really frustrated. Way more than normal, way more angry.
Client: Yes, it's, there seems to be a lot that's going on and I continually don't get the help that I need, not only not from my coworker, but also my supervisor. So it just feels so that everything is my responsibility and I have to make it happen. And if I don't make it happen, it's not going to happen. And then it's just, it's all on me and I don't feel as though that it's fair. But I also don't want us to not succeed. So I don't know how to navigate those two field.
Counselor: So the weight of the work assignments is really on you. You're feeling that pressure. You want to do right by your employer and there's an emotional toll this is taken on you. Has it reached a point where you've talked to your, it's a coworker supervisor you mentioned?
Client: Yes. So I talked to my supervisor about my coworker actually assisting me with some of the projects that we have going on. And my supervisor keeps on saying, oh, they're helping out and they're doing what they're supposed to do, but they're not doing what they're supposed to do because I end up doing their work. Because, say, for example, last week we actually had to turn in this huge report that we were working on for over a month. Literally, my coworker came to me on Monday and said I didn't do my portion of the report. And I was just like, we had a month to work on a lot of time. And so I spent the next three days doing everything for their part of the report. Luckily, I had already finished my part of the report and then combined it and actually turned it into my supervisor. Of course we get the, oh, this is a wonderful, great job that you guys did. And I'm just like you guys, as.
Counselor: If you both contributed equally.
Client: Correct? Correct.
Counselor: So in three days, you made up for a month's worth of work.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So I could see how that could be. It's very stressful.
Client: Very, very taxing. Very, very taxing.
Counselor: And this wasn't an isolated incident?
Client: Oh, no. This has been going on for probably three or four months now.
Counselor: So this is almost the expectation when you get to work.
Client: Correct? Correct. I think that you hit the nail on the head. It's expected of me and nobody actually sees it as an expectation anymore.
Counselor: It's just what you do. It's just what I do. So you can know that going into work the next day, you go in, whenever that is, that there's always this probability, this chance that you could have work just thrown on you that wasn't budgeted for, you weren't planning on.
Client: Correct. And sometimes that work actually comes out from my supervisor, but it's mostly coming from my coworker. Like, I know they're not going to do their portion, so I just automatically start doing it anyway because, you know.
Counselor: You kind of have to.
Client: I know it's going to fall on my lap either today, tomorrow, next week. So I would rather be preemptive and actually start it then so that I'm not rushing like I was, like last week to finish a month's worth of work and three days worth of time. So I'm not as stressed.
Counselor: So you've tried to address this in the framework, in the context of your work. You've talked to the supervisor, to the co worker?
Client: I talked to the supervisor, I'm afraid. Well, I can't really talk to the coworker because I don't feel as though that's my position. However, I have expressed my frustration, my anger, my disappointment with my supervisor. And my supervisor keeps on saying, oh, I'll fix it, or, oh, it doesn't seem as though that they haven't done their piece of the work because I do all of it and it's turned in. So I have. But there doesn't seem to be anything happening outside of that.
Counselor: What kind of options, in terms of your job do you feel like you have now?
Client: I don't feel as though that I have any options. That's the thing. I think that either if I can, if I don't do the work and we fail, we're going to lose some of these big projects that we're working with, which then is going to impact our entire office. And if it impacts our entire office, like somebody might be let go. And because I am the newest person in our office, I feel as though that's going to be me. So I need to protect my job by doing not only my work, but my coworkers work and sometimes my supervisors work.
Counselor: So you're really figuratively fighting for survival?
Client: Correct.
Counselor: Do you think your coworker is aware that if there is a failure with getting projects done, that you would be the one that would be let go?
Client: I think, yes. I think that they understand that since they are the senior member on team, it would be most likely that the junior member myself would possibly be let go if a budget cut were to happen.
Counselor: So you're really largely stuck.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: With having to do the work.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: How about the emotions involved? You mentioned before, the frustration? Anger. Anger directed at.
Client: I think most of my anger is directed at my supervisor for not doing something because they can clearly see that something's wrong or that I'm handling a lot more, but they're not willing to step in. And I think a little bit of that anger is also at myself, because I haven't just said to my coworker, like, you need to step up and you need to do this. So I'm a little disappointed and angry at myself as well.
Counselor: You're angry at yourself, so you feel like you don't have the ability or courage to make that confrontation?
Client: I don't have the confidence to. The confidence to actually confront my coworker.
Counselor: All right, so before we dig into that too much, is it a good idea to confront the coworker?
Client: I think it would be good for them to understand how their lack of participation in our projects is impacting me and could also possibly impact our entire department. However, I don't know exactly how to say that and not come off as I'm. I know more than you, even though that you've been here longer than me.
Counselor: So you're searching for a friendly, understanding way to convey a tough subject matter.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: To someone who may or may not be receptive.
Client: Correct.
Counselor: But you may presume that they're more likely to not be receptive.
Client: I can 100%. I don't want to say 100%. I will say 99.9% say that they will not probably be receptive if I said that.
Counselor: So you're in for a bit of a battle.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And that was started.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So one option is to avoid it and continue do the work. And that's unpleasant, but you survived. Another option is to, in the gentlest way possible, introduce that confrontation to the relationship and then deal with the fallout of that.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: Any potential benefit?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So let's look at that. What's the worst that can happen from making that, confronting that cohort.
Client: It could make things in the office be a little bit more tense. It could possibly put an additional spotlight on what I am doing, or rather not doing, which I'm doing everything. So what I'm doing, it could cause friction between my coworker and my supervisor. It could just cause this unwarranted or unnecessary stress for me to actually just go and say something to them.
Counselor: Could you lose your job or anything like that?
Client: No, I don't think that I could lose my job. I don't think that. If I said something to my coworker, I hope that they wouldn't go to, like, our human resources department, but I don't know if that's something that they would do.
Counselor: So really, you're just talking about going to them and saying, hey, things feel a bit imbalanced. Is there anything maybe we could do to level out the work across us a little better?
Client: When you say it like that, that sounds really easy and non confrontational. So, yeah.
Counselor: Were you thinking of. Did you have another narrative in mind?
Client: Well, I was actually thinking about going to them and saying, hey, you remember this report? You remember this report? You remember this report? You didn't do this, this, this. And I had to pick up your slack on all of that. Can we not make that happen again in the past?
Counselor: Okay, so maybe a little more direct than what I was.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Which is, in part an expression of the way you feel.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: You have feelings that match that pretty well.
Client: Very much so.
Counselor: Do you feel. I know you mentioned a lack of confidence in this area, but do you feel like you could approach it with them or they have a potential win in the end? So before you answer that, let me explain that a little. When we confront people, if we don't leave them an avenue to kind of protect their position in the relationship a bit, it's more of a trapping or cornering. But if we leave an avenue where they can make changes without really having to take full responsibility or blame, sometimes that's more productive, especially for the first introduction of a subject matter, like the first time you confront them. Clearly, if that doesn't work, there's other avenues, different types of confrontation. But I'm wondering if there's a way. So back to my original question. If there's a way that they can be confronted, that leaves them a win in the whole process?
Client: There might be one of the things for each of our projects, we have a timeline, but we don't have a set timeline within the office space to actually say, I'm going to have this done by this date. And you're going to have this done by this date. That's something that I could suggest so that we can hold each other accountable for the work that we have to do. So that might be a way that I could start to broach the subject. So that's one way, but that's the only thing that I can think off the top of my head.
Counselor: And that way may not be really consistent with the way you feel.
Client: It's definitely not consistent with the way I feel.
Counselor: What method? And I don't, you know, this isn't a question where I presume know the answer. What method do you think could lead to a better outcome? Has a better chance of leading to a better outcome?
Client: I believe if I was able to have a conversation where we didn't necessarily talk about the distribution of work, but if we had a conversation on what we're both good at and how we can actually complement each other with doing our work, I think that that would be a better conversation so that they could easily, they could take what I had to say a lot easier, so I could go to them and say, hey, I understand that you're not good at doing this type of report. However, I'm really good at doing this. However, I see that you have excellent skills when it comes to formatting and getting everything together and actually submitting it to whom it needs to get to. Can we actually start to distribute the work that way so that they can do what's. I don't want to say easy, but what's going to be productive for them? And I can do what's going to be productive for me.
Counselor: So really what you're suggesting is not even confrontational. It's just going in and saying, you have some strengths. They have some strengths. Wouldn't it be great if we could explore those strengths and the way we divide up those.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: If you went and said that, would there be a part of you that is kind of stuffing down those emotions of frustration during that talk?
Client: Yeah, but I think that if I do have that conversation that way, I think that that frustration and anger that I. That I have had, I think it would slowly disappear because then I know that they would still be doing something for the projects that we have to complete. So I think that my past feelings, they would slowly diminish because I know that we would be doing equal work moving forward.
Counselor: Okay, so you may have some feelings at that moment, but looking at the outcome, as you think about the outcome, you could think, well, this is tough right now, but I feel hopeful that it's going to work out in the future.
Client: Yes. Correct.
Counselor: And that could give you the confidence, ability to kind of push through that exercise, that discussion.
Client: Correct? Yep.
Counselor: Is there a certain time of the day where you feel less frustrated?
Client: It's probably around 03:00 generally, there's a 03:00 slump where everybody goes out and grabs coffee or something. And I think that during that time, that might be a good time to possibly bring up that conversation or at least brooch the subject. I can actually probably broach that subject with my supervisor at that time to see if they think that that might be a good idea.
Counselor: Okay. To get some buy in at that level. So maybe a little bit in the afternoon. 03:00 is there a particular day of the week that's better for discussion like that? There's less stress, less going on?
Client: No, there's not. Basically our weeks, or it all depends on what projects we have coming in, so I can't give a specific day. I know Monday's not a good day just because. And Friday, it's probably not a good day because everybody's just like, I just want to go home and have fun the weekend. So it's probably Tuesday, Wednesday, or Thursday. That's probably the best time to have that conversation.
Counselor: Now, this is a topic you certainly thought about. You've had feelings about. What do you think you could do to prepare for that talk? What could you rehearse?
Client: For one thing, I think that I need to look at what I'm good at or what I think I'm good at, and then also compare that to what I believe my coworker is good at, so I can figure out what duties can be split up. So that's one thing.
Counselor: So maybe writing that down.
Client: Yep, writing that down. Also, I think that me going into the situation because I don't have the confidence, I think that if I write down what I think I want to say or need to say, I think that might be a way for me to keep the conversation on track and not letting it go off into left field somewhere.
Counselor:
output: You don't want it to go off in left field. That's a goal. That's something you want to avoid. Is there a specific trigger or event that when it comes along, that conversation, that you may see that and say, I need to just break off this conversation, or else I'm risking going off in the left field?

Client: Not really. I mean, it's pretty much the same pace. I'm very frustrated with the whole system. I'm working with inner city kids, african american kids, males in particular. Counselor: All right, so as you're working with these use, you're looking at their circumstances and you're saying the odds just don't look good for major improvement. That's leading you to lose hope in your ability to help them into different circumstances.
Client: Absolutely, yeah. I mean, it's just their reality. A kid comes in and mom is either dad's incarcerated, rotted, a picture. Mom is either on drugs or not fully engaged. Counselor: All right, so can you think of a particular case, particular youth that you're working with that, where you're finding the struggle. I just think of one particular individual where you're frustrated, you're making these statements that kind of. This is the way it is. They don't seem like they have much hope. You don't seem like they have much hope for them. Right. So you have one in mind.
Client: Yes, they do.
Counselor: Okay, so what's his self statement? What's he saying to you that you think is getting a reaction from you?
Client: That he's a drug dealer. He's going to continue to be a drug dealer. He's not going to stop. And that he's involved with gang activity, and that's his family. It's the only family he's ever known, and he's loyal to them. And that loyalty is deep. And he has absolutely no. Even the thought of going back to prison doesn't shape this kid.
Counselor:
output: Not afraid of that.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.

Client: Not too good. Doctor Grande?
Counselor: Not so good.
Client: Nah. I just got into a. I got into a fight with my parents.
Counselor: What's been going on?

output: So the weight of the work assignments is really on you. You're feeling that pressure. You want to do right by your employer and there's an emotional toll this is taken on you. Has it reached a point where you've talked to your, it's a coworker supervisor you mentioned?

Counselor: What I'm thinking now is, how would you feel about if we did an experiment to test out your thoughts on what would happen if you stopped doing these things? If we did a bit of a role play where we pretended to enact a situation at work.
Client: Okay.

Counselor: And how would you feel about if we filmed this so you could actually see what you looked like?

Counselor: Do you have a camera with you that we could video on?
Client: Yeah. Is my phone okay?
Counselor: Yeah, yeah, we'll use that in just a sec.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Before we do this, then we're just going to fill out this form, because what we're doing now is an experiment. We call it a behavioral experiment to see what happens when you change the way that you're behaving.

Counselor: Okay. So the first column says, I need to fill out an experiment to test this thought that you have so that our experiment is going to be that we do a conversation at work. Who should I play? If you're playing yourself in this role play, who should I be?

Counselor: What kind of problems do you see coming up in this conversation that we have? Like, what we see yourself doing on camera?
Client: Shaking. Like, being really obviously shaking and. Okay, bright red and.
Counselor: Okay, so visibly shaking. So how. How much will you be shaking? If a hundred is, like, shaking uncontrollably and zero is not shaking at all, how visibly shaking will you be?
Client: 90.
Counselor: Okay, sorry. What was the other thing that you just said?
Client: Like, I go really red.
Counselor: Okay, so you're gonna go red?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: How red will you go? I mean, if we look around this room.

Counselor: Okay, so you're going to be as kind of brightly pink as these chairs are.

Counselor: Okay, so out of 100, then how pink would you say these chairs are?

Counselor: Okay. What else are you worried is going to happen when we have these conversations?
Client: Just worried I'll be like, say something stupid and not be able to kind of get what I'm trying to say across properly.
Counselor: Okay, and how stupid out of 100? If 100 is ridiculously stupid, probably like, similar.
Client: 90.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: I'd say.
Counselor: What else are you worried will happen when we have this conversation. What else might you see on the camera?
Client: I think you'll probably be able to see that I'm sweating and.
Counselor: Okay, and how much will you be sweating.
Client: Again?
Counselor: 90, I think, like, visibly sweating down the face.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Okay. And what do you think will happen the second time around when you stop kind of doing the things you normally do to cope? When you maybe start to make eye contact and you're not gripping onto something?
Client: I think it'll be even worse. I think it'll. Yeah.
Counselor: How much worse? Slightly worse. Like, twice as bad.
Client: Twice as bad.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. Right. Can you give me your phone and we'll.
Client: Yeah. Okay.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Should I just use this?
Counselor: Yeah. Yeah.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Probably best. Okay.

Counselor: I suppose I'd like lots of shots of our family and our friends. Quite a lot of natural shots. You know, people talking when they're having drinks. Yeah.

Client: Yeah, I recently did some shoots outside, kind of in, like, a wood environment, so that I could show you that maybe it would kind of help with some ideas.
Counselor: Okay, great. Right, let's do the second one now.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Okay. You ready to put down a bottle and just to make eye contact.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Okay.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Michelle. How you doing today?
Client: Um, I'm kind of doing. I'm feeling a little bit stressed out.
Counselor: Stressed?
Client: Yeah. I feel like I have a lot on my plate. I have this test that I have to take for work.
Counselor: What kind of test?
Client: It's like an aptitude test. It has, like, math problems on it and, like, scenarios in order for me to move up to the assistant manager. Precision.
Counselor: That's a job that you've been interested in for a while?
Client: Yes, it is. Yes. So I've been just feeling a lot of anxiety about taking the test, and then they actually scheduled for me to take the test, and I went and I just got really overwhelmed, and I started, like, I felt my heart was racing. I felt like I wish my hands were shaking. And I just really couldn't concentrate on the test, even though the night before, me and my friend did practice problems and I knew all the answers with no problem, like, I didn't miss any of the questions.
Counselor: So you know the material on this test pretty well.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: But the feelings and that physiological response to heart rate and sweating, that the feelings of anxiety plus those physiological responses, they got in the way of you completing it. Like, you weren't able to complete it?
Client: No, I wasn't able to complete it. And thankfully, they gave me a chance to come back. I just told them I didn't feel well, so they rescheduled. So now I'm feeling a lot of anxiety because I'm scared the same thing's gonna happen when I go back.
Counselor: All right, so you weren't. You weren't feeling great about taking the test in the first place?
Client: The day, the night before, I felt like, I know all the answers, but the minute I walked into the room, all of a sudden, all these fears kind of took over.
Counselor: But did you know that was coming?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: You did? Okay.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So you had some anxiety in advance. Yes or not? You did? Okay.
Client: I had some anxiety the day before, but when I reviewed it with my friend, I'm like, oh, I know the answer. So I thought that would kind of push it down. But I think once I got there, it all came back up to the surface.
Counselor: It erupted in that moment. And that prevented you. What do you think is leading to this?
Client: Well, I've always kind of struggled with tests. Like, I can remember when I was in third grade, I had to take this test because I was really struggling in math, and I had to pass this test in order to move to the next grade. And I thought, just like this test, that I was ready for it. I had a tutor, and I felt really prepared for it. And then when I took it, I failed and I was held back. And I feel like, you know, that was so. It was. It was really embarrassing for me to be held back. And I felt like. I don't want to say, but I did feel like a failure at the time because I felt like I really did know this. So I don't know why I couldn't pass the test.
Counselor: And since that you said this was third grade?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And since that bad testing experience, have you had trouble with tests since?
Client: Yes, I always feel really anxious. I mean, I'm able to pass tests, obviously, because I graduated from grade school and went on to high school. But it's so hard for me because of this anxiety that I feel that even though I may think I know it, I may still fail the test anyway. Maybe like a repeat of what happened.
Counselor: All right, so in third grade, you had a really bad testing experience, and as you moved forward from there, you've never really been thrilled about taking tests.
Client: No.
Counselor: But you've been able to adapt. You've been able to take them and still, like, pass them.
Client: Yeah. I mean, sometimes I get an a. So that's.
Counselor: That's good, right? Yeah.
Client: I mean, yeah, it is good. Yeah, it's good.
Counselor: But with this particular test, which is not for school, which is for work.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: This one. This is more of a stomach block for you.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: You have any ideas as to what may be making this test such a point of anxiety for you?
Client: I think it's just the fact that it's this promotion, it's almost like the same thing. Like, if I fail, I'm being held back, and I feel like it's reliving that moment of being held back. And that's like, a fear that I have, that by not being able to pass these tests, they're holding me back.
Counselor: So, really, that same feeling you had in third grade that's coming up with this test now, right?
Client: Yeah. I mean, I didn't put them together until now, but, yeah.
Counselor: And the other tests you've taken throughout the rest of grade school and high school, they didn't have that same value attached to them?
Client: No, because they didn't have all that pressure that it was either win or lose.
Counselor: Basically, you could take them again or take that course again, or I could.
Client: Take another test to raise the grade if I didn't do good on that test.
Counselor: So you maybe had more options in school.
Client: Yes. It wasn't fail, pass or fail.
Counselor: It's the pressure. It's the pressure of you need to get through this. And you don't have the safety nets that you had in school.
Client: Yeah. If I fail it, then I'm not going to be able to get the promotion. I would have to wait just like I did. I'm going to have to wait a certain amount of time, I think, an ear before I could take it again.
Counselor: So that is a lot of pressure.
Client: Yeah, it is.
Counselor: So is there any time limit to this tests for work?
Client: No, there isn't.
Counselor: There's no time?
Client: No.
Counselor: How many? Is it like a. Like a multiple choice?
Client: Yes, it is.
Counselor: Okay. And you seem like. Like you said you study the night before with your friend.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: You're really well prepared for it.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So I have a few thoughts about this.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: One is I'm wondering, you know, we've talked before about cognitive therapy, about the core beliefs. So I'm curious as to what you think about, like, what core belief may be operating for you now with this.
Client: Test, this work test that I could fail, and then if I fail, I could end up being a failure at all, you know, the things that I try.
Counselor: So something like I am a failure, or I'm. I'm bound to be a failure. I'm destined to be a failure.
Client: I would say, like, I'm destined to be a failure.
Counselor: Okay, so I'm destined to be a failure. So that. So that potentially is a core belief, right? That's operating?
Client: Yeah. I mean, that's what scares me. That's exactly the thought that I'm thinking when I'm about to take the test. And if I don't pass it, it's just going to have, like, this dominant effect of failure.
Counselor: Okay. So it could be a core belief, but it also seems like it's the automatic thought. Like, as you get ready to take that test, you're thinking I'm destined to be a failure.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: And you're having what sounds like a panic response with the heart racing.
Client: Yeah. My hands.
Counselor: My hands shaking. Are you in the room alone when you're taking the test? Yes, you are. So no one's really seeing you have this? I wouldn't want to call it a panic attack yet. We haven't really gotten that far into it. But it sounds like a. It has some panic like features. Yeah, because it's not. It's interfering with you thinking clearly enough to get through the items. So. Okay, so one thought I have is you've. Have you ever had panic attacks in the past or anything like this? The third grade thing?
Client: No. Not really. I mean, sometimes I get worked up when I'm about to take a test, but it's only around tests.
Counselor: And what happens once you get worked up? Like, once your heart rate increases and you have the other physiological symptoms?
Client: When I actually do take the test, I kind of try to work through it and start trying to answer one question at a time to get to the last question.
Counselor: So, one possible strategy here is we talked about the adaptive response. Right. So which is that thought that you say to yourself, that self talk. I wonder if your adaptive response couldn't be, I can ride this out. Like, you have no time limit test.
Client: Yeah, that's true.
Counselor: I mean, the panic responses only maintained for so long.
Client: And I could also choose, like, maybe questions that I know the answer to automatically. So that could help maybe relieve some.
Counselor: Of that stress to get some, in a sense, to get some minor victories under your belt by, like, answering those. Right. You know you're closer to achieving your goal.
Client: Yes. And then I feel like I know. At least I know that. Like, they'll validate the feeling that I. Maybe I can pass this test.
Counselor: Mm hmm. So the more items you. You answer correctly, the less anxious you're gonna feel because you're closer to the end of.
Client: Yeah, definitely. Because then I start to feel more calm because I know that. I know these questions are definitely going to be right.
Counselor: So that's. So that's one. Well, that's a cognitive and behavioral strategy. Right? Like, you can. You can wait out the. The panic. I mean, you're in the room alone.
Client: Yeah, that's true. Nobody's there. Nobody's gonna see me. I'm kind of trying to get myself together.
Counselor: Yeah. Now, the panic's painful. Right? The panic symptoms are painful. So what you could tell yourself is, yeah, this is unpleasant, but I can ride out these symptoms because they only last so long.
Client: Okay. I could use, like, self talk.
Counselor:
output: Exactly.

And I am not going to pick the right one. I'm going to think I picked the right one, and it's going to be the one that my second choice is, and I am not going to pick the right one.
Counselor: Okay, so your thought is that you're going to get. You're going to select the wrong response and therefore get that quiz item wrong. How about behavior? Like, do you notice anything physically going on as you're thinking about that quiz item and how you're gonna get it wrong?
Client: I'd say my palms are probably sweaty. Like, I'm probably a little tense.

What happens then?

Client: Like, I get one wrong the whole test, it's all gonna be wrong.

Does that pattern continue throughout the test?
Client: Yes.
Counselor:
output: So explain to me what, like, let's just go with the example of the first item, like, just to keep it more simple. So you have the first item, and that didn't work out for you, that thought? instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Elizabeth. How you doing today?
Client: I'm all right.
Counselor: How things been going since the last time I met?
Client: It's about the same. I'm still feeling pretty down. I mean, I just. I feel really stuck and not happy, and I just don't know why.
Counselor: Okay, so there's a few things going on there. You said you're feeling stuck, not happy, and sound like you're a little confused as to what's going on, what's causing it. Do you have any suspicions about what might be causing it?
Client: I mean, I've been feeling, like, really isolated lately, you know, because I'm a stay at home mom. It's hard. There's not a lot of people, you know, right at my fingertips to spend my time with, you know, obviously my family, but. So I guess, you know, I kind of. I had some friends in the neighborhood, but, like, our friendships just kind of fizzled out, and I. Ever since then, it's just like, I don't really feel like doing much. I just kind of feel like, what's the point? And let my husband take care of a lot of stuff. You know, I used to, you know, shop for the groceries all the time and make sure the house is always stocked and make dinner every night and get the kids ready for school in the morning. And I still do that stuff. But a lot of times, you know, I let it slide. Sometimes I won't make dinner or whatever. And when I do do it, I just feel like I'm forcing myself to do it. The passion is gone.
Counselor: And how long have you been. You say housewife, right? How long have you been housewife?
Client: For a long time. I have two boys. They're eight and ten. And I've been staying home since my first one was born, so ten years. And, you know, it's been really rewarding for me. I'm not really interested in going back to work or anything like that because I know people always say you're feeling unfulfilled, like you should go back to work, but it's not, you know, I felt happy with it for so long. I don't think that it's being home. I think it's something inside of me.
Counselor: Something's changed. So for a long time, you were satisfied being a housewife. You enjoyed that life or found satisfaction in that life. And somewhere along the line, something changed in you and now you're not happy with it. So what it represents in terms of activities like caring for your children and shopping, now, that's what changed.
Client: Yeah, exactly. Well, I guess, you know, my youngest is eight, so he's only been in school for a couple of years. So I guess, like, it's not super recent, but recently I finally have no children in the home, so it's more. It's more time to myself, and I kind of filled that gap a little bit with other things. Like, I did Cub scouts with the boys for a while, and like I said, I had some friends around the neighborhood, so that kind of, like, filled that time. But now that stuff, it's just not really happening anymore. So now I kind of feel like it's not boredom. You know, it's not like I don't have enough to do. It's like I don't want to do anything, but then at the same time, I feel frustrated because there's nothing to do.
Counselor: All right, so you're frustrated with your situation, maybe with yourself a little bit?
Client: Yeah, I think a lot more with myself because I know that I would feel better if I had, you know, maybe found more friends or found something to do with my time, but I don't want to at the same time. So I'm frustrated with myself because I kind of know what would help, but then I don't really have the, like, the volition to do it.
Counselor: You're not motivated?
Client: Yeah, I'm not motivated.
Counselor: Have you received any feedback from other people about this meeting? Has anyone else noticed that you're down?
Client: Yeah, I mean, obviously my husband has noticed because he has to get the boys ready in the morning. He's really supportive. I know he can tell that I'm not feeling the same, but, you know, he works, and then he has to come home and pick up my slack. So he is getting frustrated, which I understand. And, you know, my mom has said to me that, you know, she thinks I'm not doing as much, and so it kind of hurts. It feels like everybody's trying to tell me I'm lazy and that I'm not doing enough. And it's always that, like, feeling, you know, like nobody really understands how much work goes into being a mother. But then, at the same time, now that I'm doing less and less, I feel like they're all right, you know? I am lazy. I'm not doing anything.
Counselor: They use the word lazy?
Client: No, not that I can remember. You know, I think my mom said, like, you're not doing as much as you used to. And I kind of took offense to that, even though it's kind of true. It's like. I don't know. It hurt.
Counselor: Okay. That was painful for you what about what your husband said? What's he been saying?
Client: You know, I think at first we didn't really acknowledge it. It was like, you know, I took a break here. He picked up the slack, and it was fine. But now that it's been more and more, he's kind of getting frustrated. And, you know, he's been asking me about how I feel and why I'm not doing as much. But at the same time, like, even though he knows that, not motivated, it's still frustrating because it's my responsibility. So I think he's. You know, he's been saying, like, I need you to do more around the house, pretty much is what he said. I need you to do more.
Counselor: What was your response to that? When he said, I need you to.
Client: Do more, I started crying because I know he's right. And that's what I tell myself every day. I need to do more, but I don't have the motivation to do it. And so I'm so frustrated with myself, and, you know, I know that he needs that from me, and I don't know why I'm not motivated to do it.
Counselor: Okay, so you're frustrated for feeling down.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And you're frustrated for lacking motivation, and just as little as a few years ago, you didn't feel it this way at all.
Client: Yeah. Yeah. I actually think, you know, I've been feeling this way more, like, in the past, like, six months or something like that. Like, I. It was hard for me when my youngest son went to school, but more in, like, the natural way that it is hard, but this is something else. This is more consuming. It's, you know, like, the difficulty of him going away to school almost was motivating. Like, it was hard, but at the same time, it was freeing because I had other opportunities to do stuff. This is just, like, stunting.
Counselor: Okay, so let me shift gears a little bit. Can you tell me about your. Well, a recent day. It's kind of typical of what you're telling me now. Meaning not motivated. Down.
Client: Sure. On Wednesday, I was having a really hard time getting out of bed, so my husband just got the kids ready in the morning, and I felt really bad about that. So I just stayed in bed for a couple more hours, probably until, like, 1030, and I got up, you know, and made myself something to eat. And then I thought, you know, I should probably go to the store because we're almost out of milk and, you know, and I think the boys need shampoo. But I just. I just sat down and I just sat there, and I think I sat for. I don't even know how long the boys came home from school. It was like, you know, 330, and I hadn't even gotten up. And so then I said, okay, the boys are home. I should probably get started on dinner soon because my husband will be home soon. And I. I found something in the fridge to make, and I made dinner. And, you know, after that, everybody, you know, just sat down. We just watched tv, and I just sat there until it was time to go to bed.
Counselor:
output: You said this was recently, right? What would the ideal day have looked like? Take that same day and do what you wish you could have done.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, Jordan. How you doing today?
Client: Could have been better.
Counselor: Could be better.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What's going on?
Client: Um, well, you know, I have two jobs.
Counselor: Mm hmm.
Client: And I lost one of them.
Counselor: You lost your job? Yes. Which one did you lose?
Client: I lost one at the grocery store.
Counselor: That was your part time?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I'm sorry to hear that.
Client: Me too. And I'm just. It's all I think about now.
Counselor: And when did this happen?
Client: It happened about two, three days ago.
Counselor: Two, three days ago?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So if I remember right, you took that job not too long ago to kind of supplement your income.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So certainly that would be upsetting, but I know that's not a major part of your income.
Client: It's not, but, I mean, I'm still very worried about it.
Counselor: Tell me about the worry.
Client: I mean, I worry that, you know, I'm. Now I only had so much money, and now I have less than that. I mean, without my money, you know, God knows how many things can happen.
Counselor: So before you had the job, you were paying all your bills. You want some extra income, you've lost that extra income. And I can certainly understand how that would be disturbing. But as I understand that you were doing okay before with your full time job.
Client: I was doing okay, but, I mean, I got comfortable with that extra income, and so now my fear is that I've gotten too comfortable with it, and now that it's not there anymore, it's going to affect the fact I'm not going to be able to pay for food or my rent.
Counselor: Okay, so you adjusted to the new income level with the full time and the part time job together, and you're worried you can't adjust back?
Client: I'm worried that, I mean, things are just gonna get worse from here. I mean, it's a big deal, losing your job. Even if it was part time, I've gotten comfortable from having so much money, from the money I had to. Now that's, you know, been divided and, I mean, God knows how many things, like I said, God knows how many things can happen.
Counselor: Well, what. What can happen? So you have that income, your income is reduced now to just your full time job. What can happen from this point on?
Client: Well, I can, you know, keep. Stay in the mindset that I have that extra money and spend what I think is that extra money, digging into the money I paid for my rent, my food, my gas, my insurance, and me, who's somebody without all that.
Counselor: So you could fail to pay expenses that need to be paid.
Client: And they helped me go to my full time job that I still have. So, I mean, if I can't, if I spend the money that was from my insurance because I thought I had extra, then I'm not gonna have insurance on my cardinal. I can get pulled over, lose my license, not going to be able to get to work, and then I'll get fired there too.
Counselor: All right, so the kind of chain of causality you're seeing is that without that part time income, you might not adapt with your expense management. You might fail to pay, for example, your car insurance. You could get pulled over for something the police officer could see, don't have insurance, give you a ticket, which is just money. I don't have another expense. Right. And how would this. How would that connect to losing your job?
Client: Because I wouldn't be able to get to work.
Counselor: So it'd be. So the ticket would be so expensive, you would lose your.
Client: Well, the ticket would be expensive, so I wouldn't be able to try to pay the next month's insurance. So I just wouldn't have insurance on my car. So I.
Counselor: So you'd lose your insurance?
Client: I'd lose my insurance.
Counselor: And then by losing your insurance, you lose your transportation altogether because you can't drive that insurance. And then you lose your job.
Client: Mm hmm. I mean, it's either go to work with an uninsured car, and then I can get pulled over and go to jail for driving with no insurance multiple times.
Counselor: No, that's serious. Yeah. You wouldn't want to do that.
Client: I wouldn't go to jail.
Counselor: So there's two. You have two kind of causal change. One is losing your job. And now even just the idea you can end up incarcerated.
Client: Yes. I mean, which I definitely lose my.
Counselor: Job if I'm in jail, I would imagine.
Client: And so that would have. So then I wouldn't even have, like, any money to help me through jail. Like, to. For the commissary and stuff.
Counselor: Because you would have no income.
Client: I would have no income. And then when I get out of jail, I'm. No one's gonna hire me.
Counselor: Because you have a criminal record.
Client: Exactly.
Counselor: Which makes it challenging to find employment in some instances. So what's happened is kind of in your mind, and we've talked about how thoughts work and beliefs work, is you, in reality, you've lost this part time job. And as I said, that's certainly. That's understandable that you'd be upset about that. I doubt many people would be happy about losing additional income, but you move from there, from losing additional income, which is what has actually happened to this possibility that you could be in jail or lose your job because of this. So I remember maybe last week. Week before, you're talking about the. The letter that you received from. It was like a late notice. It wasn't. Turned out wasn't.
Client: Yeah, it was sent to me, but it was somebody else's credit card mistake. Yeah.
Counselor: Do you remember the conclusions you drew from when you believe that was actually for you, that late notice, that my.
Client: Credit score was gonna go down, that I would. I'd be stuck in that apartment, and then I'd go into depression. I wouldn't be able to do anything.
Counselor: Yeah. So you ended up in that scenario. You end up in a situation where you just couldn't function at all. And you moved there from a letter that you believe was addressed to you, saying you were one month or six days late or something on a credit card, which, of course, you don't want to be late on a credit card, but you move from there to being so depressed you couldn't work, couldn't function, I think, is how you put it. Couldn't function. Do you see, kind of, given how we've talked about cognitive behavioral strategies and concepts, do you see a pattern that's emerged over the last few times I've seen you?
Client: I mean, I've seen that, you know, sometimes I can. I can think the worst, and then. And I know it didn't happen last time, but that was, you know, a stroke of good luck.
Counselor: That it wasn't you.
Client: Yeah. That it was, you know, it wasn't me. And, you know, that was a relief. But this is something that's solid. I don't have my part time job anymore.
Counselor: You've lost real income.
Client: I mean, this isn't a mistake. This isn't a. We fired the wrong person. You know, this is real. So there's real concerns here.
Counselor: I.
Client: Unlike last time, where I was lucky.
Counselor: So this. This situation, you see, is different than the first situation because the first situation was more. You were perceiving something was wrong that wasn't wrong because you weren't the intended recipient of the letter.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But in this situation, it's different because it's real. You really lost your income.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And, of course, keeping in mind that this job, again, only a few months old, and you survived well before that, is it reason to believe you could survive well again, that you could adapt to this lost income?
Client: Well, I suppose there is, but I'm concerned about whether I'm not, whether I won't adapt.
Counselor: Well, let's look at this in terms of probabilities, right. You've had several jobs throughout your career. You've had some of them worked out. You've lost other ones. You're still paying your bills. So in terms of probabilities, how many times have you, how many times have you ended up in jail or losing your full time job?
Client: I mean, they haven't happened yet.
Counselor: It hasn't happened.
Client: Not yet. But I mean, I, I struggled a little bit when I lost a part time job or when I was younger and I had those little jobs.
Counselor: So you had to adapt.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And it was painful.
Client: I did struggle, yeah.
Counselor: You struggled.
Client: Yeah. I mean, but I'm older now. These are, you know, even though grocery stores, not a serious job. It was income.
Counselor: Sure. Yeah. And again, to lose income would be disappointing for just about anybody. Are there any upsides to not having that job?
Client: I suppose I have more time to focus on my full time job because, I mean, that is really intensive.
Counselor: Is there a possibility that you could find another part time job just as you found that one?
Client: I mean, because will somebody else take me because I was fired from that job? I mean, that's my concern, is that.
Counselor: Nobody, they're going to find out.
Client: Yeah. And then they're going to go, oh, she was fired, you know. No, we don't. We don't want her.
Counselor: But you've had other jobs that didn't work out before and that didn't affect you getting that job.
Client: That's true.
Counselor: So the worst case scenario, I guess what I'm getting at the worst case scenario is, in your case, ending up in jail or losing your full time job, which you've had for a while.
Client: Yeah, I really don't want to lose my job.
Counselor: And it seems like they like you there.
Client: I hope they do.
Counselor: Right? Yeah. So those scenarios, I guess, are possible, but they seem, based on what you're saying, is pretty unlikely. So I wonder how useful it is to invest a lot of energy in kind of tracking that causal chain to jail or prison or to unemployment when that's really not the most likely outcome. Sorry to interrupt you, but do you invest as much energy in tracking the positives or the probable outcomes?
Client: No, not even close. I know that I don't think about the positive things. I mean, I don't get fired and then go, what's good about this?
Counselor: Or get a letter in the mail and say, what's, you know, although I can see there's not much upside to that, although it turned out that was an error, so. But this has still been a theme that I've seen over the last eight to ten weeks, where you really have, you really emphasize the negative, possible, even unlikely outcomes, kind of expanding the negative as you move through. Like a causal chain.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Does that make sense? Yeah, but you don't do the same thing for the positive side. You don't look at how something could work out. Well, would you say it's fair assessment?
Client: Yeah. Yeah, no, that's. That's pretty accurate.
Counselor: But still, you're worried about this.
Client: I mean, yeah, I am worried. I'm not gonna be thrilled about it, but I suppose I don't have to go to when I'm gonna go to jail or I'm gonna lose my full time job.
Counselor: I think there's a lot of intervening factors that could occur before going to jail or losing your job. There's other things that you could do.
Client: I suppose I could get a family member to drive me or take the bus if I lost my insurance and lost my car.
Counselor: So, alternate forms of transportation. Yeah. There's adapting your spending back to where it was before.
Client: That's true.
Counselor: Part of your fear was that you wouldn't be able to adapt your spending. Right. But that's something you would have control over.
Client: I guess. I can keep, you know, better track of how much I do spend and, you know, keep track of my bank accounts and exactly how much money I have in them.
Counselor: So, having talked through this a little bit. Right. What I'm going to refer to, or is referred to as catastrophizing. Remember we talked about that when we reviewed the cognitive distortions.
Client: That sounds familiar. Yeah.
Counselor: Where a negative is taken and just making way more negative than it is at the moment. Right. Kind of knowing that, that tends to be what you do. It's what we call an error in thinking that you tend to make. Does that lower your anxiety about the situation? Does it change it in some way?
Client: I mean, knowing that I'm thinking about it wrong makes me feel a little better.
Counselor: I would say you're thinking about it in a way that's less than useful.
Client: Okay. That actually makes me feel better. Knowing that, you know, these things can happen, but it might not. There's other things that can happen before them.
Counselor: Yeah. I mean, I would even say probably not.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So one way, potentially, and there's a few things we can review over the next few sessions. One way to address catastrophizing, in addition to the adaptive responses which we've talked about before, would be to find some sort of peace with the worst outcome, meaning you kind of take away the power of that anxiety over you. When you can accept worst possible outcomes doesn't mean you look forward to them or you think they're likely, or you dwell on them and ponder them. But I mean, obviously, being in jail, even though it's an extremely low probability event in your circumstance, being in jail would be survivable. Being unemployed would be survivable.
Client: People weaker than me have gone through jail.
Counselor: I guess a lot of people have been to jail. A lot of people lost their jobs. And while it's certainly a struggle, to use your word, right, I mean, that would be more than a struggle. It'd be quite unpleasant. It's at the point where you can accept that that could happen and that you would survive, that you could find some peace with the catastrophizing. Again, we'll have other routes. We'll attack these cognitive distortions from a few different angles. But one of the angles is reaching a point where you could accept that those things could happen. They're unlikely. They could happen, and you would survive.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: I mean, one thing you've shown throughout your. I mean, based on what you described to me, is that you're a survivor. You find a way to make it work.
Client: That makes me feel better. They're thinking about me as a survivor.
Counselor:
output: Right. So in a sense, kind of reframing. We talked about that before, too. Right. Your circumstances as you're somebody that's surviving adversely losing a job is. We talk about negative things.

Client: Well, I had to go to the store, which is always a nightmare for me because I don't even like touching my credit card because it's been in so many machines and there's so much dirt and junk that gets in there and then the counters and all the. But shopping's a nightmare for me.
Counselor: So really, in a, like, a supermarket, everything can be containing germs. Have germs on it?
Client: Yeah, everything does.
Counselor: Everything does. And that's what you're thinking about as you're walking through and shopping. We talked about last time, exposure and response prevention, and I explained kind of the general idea. But you remember that conversation. Yeah, I remember. I indicated that we might try some experiments right in session to see how, see if we can move kind of forward and treating your, kind of your fear and obsession with germs and really the anxiety it's causing for you, it's like getting in the way of your life.
Client: It is. It really is.
Counselor: So I was wondering, is there anything in here, in this office, as you look around, that you would look at and think, I don't want to touch that because it could have germs on it.
Client: I'm really not liking the covers on this chair because, I mean, I can't. I mean, at least what I'm sitting in now, my clothes are protecting me from the rest of the chair.
Counselor: Mm hmm.
Client: But, I mean, I have no sleeves on, so I don't like touching the armrests and the covers.
Counselor: So even thinking about, like, your arms touching the back of the chair, and.
Client: I'm not liking it, I really feel like I should probably go wash my arms.
Counselor: So what would happen if you put your hands right on the arm covers? What was your usual reaction to that?
Client: To go wash my arms until I feel like it's gone. Until all the dirt is gone.
Counselor: And how long would that take you to be sure?
Client: I mean, something like this, probably. I'd probably be in there for a good 510 minutes. Just washing.
Counselor: 510 minutes. How many times a day would you end up washing your hands?
Client: Okay. I don't. I don't keep track anymore. It makes me upset. How many?
Counselor: It says that it's that many. That is distressing. And I know that this will be uncomfortable, but I would like you to try to. If you can feel comfortable with it, put your hands on the. On the arms of the chairs. On the chair. Let's see what I'm doing. It's like. Try to stay like that. So tell me what's going through your mind?
Client: I can just. I feel the chair, and I. I don't like it. And I just. I feel almost like I can feel everybody who's ever touched it. And just what have they been doing? And what did they touch before they touched this? They probably didn't wash their hands before they touched this, and it's just really making me comfortable.
Counselor: Okay, so you're anxious now?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Is it tolerable?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So once you remember, we talked about scaling before. So, like, ten being a tremendous amount of anxiety, one being hardly any anxiety. Where. Where are you now as you sit here with your hands?
Client: What am I going to say about six or seven?
Counselor: Six or seven?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Are you feeling an urge to go wash your hands?
Client: Yes. Yes, I am.
Counselor: Yes. This is a six or seven. I want you to sit with it for a few seconds, process that, you know, feeling. Right. That you're touching everybody that's ever been in the chair. Right. So consider that thought.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: So what's the ultimate fear? Like, what's gonna happen if you don't go wash your hands now?
Client: I'm gonna get sick.
Counselor: You're gonna get sick that someone who's.
Client: Been in this chair was sick or touched something gross that can make you sick. And I'm gonna get sick, and I'm gonna die, and I don't want to die.
Counselor: Do you feel yourself getting sick?
Client: I feel like it's harder to breathe, I guess. Like, my chest is kind of just tight. Yeah.
Counselor: You can still breathe, though.
Client: I can't. I can breathe.
Counselor: Okay, so go ahead and lift your hands up. Right. And just put them where you'd normally put them. Well, now that you've touched the chair, I know that now I can still. Is that any better? Now you're touching the seat of the.
Client: Chair, but I feel like if I touch my clothes, that's even worse. Yeah. Now I will have to go home and change my clothes.
Counselor: All right, so the thought now, if I had to guess, correct me if I'm wrong, it's probably like you really would like to wash your hands.
Client: Very much so.
Counselor: And you certainly can at any time. But I'd like you to try to hold out for a little bit. So your hands where they are now, that's better than up here.
Client: At this point. I feel like they're already contaminated, so.
Counselor: They'Re at maximum contamination.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So you can't do any more damage by touching the seat.
Client: Yeah, I'm just trying to avoid touching anything else.
Counselor: So now it's not so much about getting your hands away from the arms, but getting them under the faucet. Yeah, that's the. So where's anxiety? Was a six or seven before. Where is it now?
Client: I mean, now that you mention it, it is. It is a little better. I want to say about four. About three, four. I mean, I feel better that my. My arms are off it, and I'm focusing on breathing, and, I mean, it's.
Counselor: A little easier to breathe now.
Client: A little. Yeah, it is.
Counselor: So if you could go. If you could wash your hands right this second. Of course you can. But if you did, what would the anxiety move to?
Client: A one.
Counselor: A one.
Client: I mean, it would take a little bit to get to a one. A little bit actually washing, but then it'll get to a one. Then I'll feel okay.
Counselor:
output: All right, so you move from just in a short time, from a six or seven to a three or four for anxiety, when, of course, the goal was one. Right. So you could say roughly halfway. Roughly halfway down toward your goal without washing your hands at all.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi. Thank you for being here today. I just wanted to start off by asking how your homework was from last week and if it was helpful.
Client: Well, I think it was a little helpful. I did try the breathing exercises, but sometimes I don't think to do them right away. But I did try it a little bit and it did help. Good.
Counselor: So you said you wanted to work on the problem with your anxiety when you leave your son for therapy.
Client: Yes, that's what.
Counselor: Yeah. So we've been working on your breathing like you've been talking about, and if we work on this, then maybe we can move into other things, you know, like in addressing your anxiety elsewhere. But. So why don't you tell me about how you feel when he is in therapy or getting occupational therapy?

Client: I mean, that's not my job. You know, you're the counsellor, but I'd like to be able to let them know that there's help for them.
Counselor: Sure.
Client: And guide them towards you. Maybe not do it all myself, but, you know, I don't like to think that I just send them on their way, not caring about them.
Counselor: But you. You know yourself that you do care about them. Yeah. And, you know, building a relationship with students does take time. So, you know, in the situation with you and Vince, you know that that wasn't going to happen when he needed it because he barely knew you. And his structures around the school where you only see him three times a week, you know, that doesn't support. That doesn't support a relationship building approach either. So how can you blame yourself for not having that opportunity to build that relationship, to let them know that you are there, to listen, you know, lots of other factors in play here, Liz.
Client: Yeah. Yeah.
Counselor: So, you know, let's think about what you were talking about before, you know, how you led this to happen. Do you still think you. You led this to happen?
Client: Well, no. I mean, I still kind of feel like I should have done something and maybe he still would have tried to kill himself, but, you know, I just feel that, you know, what if I had taken a moment to talk to him, okay? You know, just to let one. Him know that one person noticed, and it might not have changed anything, but it might have.
Counselor: And it might have. You're absolutely right. It might have. But we'll never know that. And there's your shoulds and what ifs. We can't change the past, but we can use the past to help us in the future. All right?
Client: Yeah. And.
Counselor: But I know. I'm still really concerned that you might think that you had at least something to do with this. But when you first came in here, you were really distressed. All right? Like, so on a scale of one to five, you were a five.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Now, how are you feeling now?
Client: I don't know. I mean, you know, talking about it does sort of put things into perspective. I mean, that. That's been great, you know?
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: I am just one person. I mean, I don't know, somewhere between a two and a three. I suppose. I do still worry that I didn't do enough. But as you say, I'm just one person in his life and I hardly know him. But, you know, that doesn't stop me from caring. But, yeah. Yeah, I feel better. You know, what can we do to.
Counselor: Make it a one or a one? What can we do?
Client: I don't know. I don't know. I guess make him come back to school healthy and happy. But, yeah, I suppose. I mean, knowing that he didn't succeed is a good thing, at least, you know? And now he's gonna get more help. That's right. To help him. So maybe, you know, it's. It's been taken out of my hands. That's good, too, knowing that, you know, ultimately, he's not my responsibility.
Counselor: Not alone, anyway.
Client: Exactly. Yeah. And that's good, because yesterday when I first heard it, I just really felt like it was all my fault. So. Yeah, you've helped me see and realize it's. Yeah. And I guess maybe in the future. Yeah, I'll feel better knowing that if I just have a quick word to students who, you know, display that kind of behavior and sentiments. So, I guess, you know, I'm better equipped to deal with the warning signs.
Counselor:
output: Sure, sure. That's good. They can take that with you.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Alisa, how are you doing today?
Client: I'm doing well, thank you.
Counselor: Doing well.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: What's going on?
Client: I have family coming into town and I have to go to the airport to pick them up.
Counselor: So you have family flying in?
Client: Yes. That's something that I get very anxious about, having to cross the bridge. I have to cross the Ben Franklin bridge and then get over the bridge that goes to the airport by the stadium. I think that's the Girard point bridge. Yeah. That's two levels there. I have to do that both ways.
Counselor: Going and coming both ways. You have to cross four times?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So what kind of feeling is this bringing up for you?
Client: I get very anxious even just thinking about it right now.
Counselor: So you're anxious right here with me?
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So I want to try to scale this. We talked about this before with cognitive therapy. So let's say that ten is really the most anxious you're felt about crossing bridges, and one is no anxiety. Where would you be right now?
Client: Right now, probably an eight. Yeah.
Counselor: I don't love anxiety.
Client: Yes. It's worse when I'm at that point on that day, but right now, I think just knowing that I have to do that. Yes.
Counselor: And what's it on that day?
Client: A ten.
Counselor: It reaches a ten, definitely.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: All right. So. But even now, how far away is the. Until they.
Client: Oh, it's a week.
Counselor: So even now, a week out, it's. Nate, this is really hurting.
Client: Yes. I don't like that at all.
Counselor: So for your job and local travel, you don't really have to cross any.
Client: Ten minutes to work every day. And banks. So 20 minutes, shopping centers and everything is just within the vicinity. I don't have to cross any bridges.
Counselor: So no bridges?
Client: No, not at all. I probably planned it that way, too.
Counselor: That worked out well.
Client: That worked out very well.
Counselor: All right. But coming up, pick up the family you will be crossing. So let's look at this at each stage. So, I mean, you're clearly anxious now, as you mentioned. But let's go to, let's try to move forward a week to the day that they'll be flying, what time they fly in.
Client: It's going to be a 04:00 flight. In the afternoon.
Counselor: In the afternoon. So about what time would you have to leave to?
Client: I would have to leave probably at 03:00 because it's only about 20 minutes to the airport. Really?
Counselor: Really.
Client: But I would like to leave earlier. They'll probably take them time. By the time they land and go through, you know, getting their luggages, they probably won't even come out till maybe 430, but I'd like to make sure I'm there at around 334 o'clock.
Counselor: All right, so let's go to that day. Let's go to that day and to that afternoon. So you're still at home. And let's say we're about 15 minutes before you have to get in the car. Car. What are you thinking then?
Client: I have to do this. I have to get up and go. They need me to be there this week. It's my parents coming in and they're elderly, so I don't want them to be stuck at the airport. There's no one else that actually can go pick them up. So I have to get up and go and pick them up.
Counselor:
output: That's what's going through your mind?

Client: Yes, it is. Yes. instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: So these daggy little sheets we use for cognitive behavioral therapy or strategies. And you can see at the top they talk about the situation, and down the bottom they talk about the feelings, and in between, there's a whole lot of discussion about the thoughts. Yeah. So again, it's sort of easier with a concrete example. So I might get you to write in, if you're happy, to, the situation that you mentioned, the tram situation in the little situation box there.
Client: Of course.
Counselor: Okay, so what have you written in there?
Client: Catching the tram.
Counselor: Okay, so what feelings do you have when you go to catch the tram? And just before you tell me, often it's useful to have sort of one word for a feeling, something that's really in your gut rather than a long expression. So what's your feeling?
Client: Anxious. That's the one. Anxious.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: That's the one.
Counselor: Do you want to write that in and see? Are there any other feelings that really resonate with you? I mean, that's enough. But is there anything other sort of feeling you have when you're
Client: scared?
Counselor: Okay, so pop that one in there. Anything else?
Client: Embarrassed.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: All right.
Counselor: Do you want to pop that one in there as well? This is great. You've really sort of clicked with it. All right, so now why are we doing all this? Because what I'm going to ask you now is to imagine what the little voice in your head, you know, that little self talk is saying when you're feeling anxious. So what are you feeling anxious about? What's the sort of story in your head that's going on there?
Client: All right, I'm. How's it. What happens? I'm thinking I'm gonna get lost.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: Yeah. So I'm anxious because I think I'm gonna get lost.
Counselor: Okay. So do you want to write that one down?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Yeah. I'm worried I'll get lost.
Client: Yep.
Counselor: See, it's a bit artificial bringing it up, but there's sort of a point to all this.
Client: Yeah, yeah, no, I get it. It's good to actually think through what exactly.
Counselor: Yeah.
Client: Happens.
Counselor: Okay, so you said you're anxious because you're worried or get lost. Any other thoughts? That sort of self talk?
Client: Um, yeah, I reckon I start blushing and, you know, going red.
Counselor: Right. Okay. It's another good one to write down. Do you want to write that one down in the thoughts as word? Brilliant. Okay, and so what have you written there?
Client: Panic that I'll go red. Blush.
Counselor: Okay. All right. Got it.
Client: I do.
Counselor: So this is sort of really useful. We've been able to sort of tease out your situation, the feelings. And really, what's that little voice in your head that's going on? Now, there's been a point to all this because what we do with this CBT approach is we try and challenge some of these thoughts. Okay.
Client: Because I know they're, you know, silly. I know that.
Counselor: Yeah. I mean, some of our thoughts are realistic, some of them are correct and. And some of them aren't realistic and not very helpful. And. And it sounds like these ones that are sort of causing problems for you. So, so what I'm going to do, let's look at this first one here. You've said, I'm worried I'll get lost. Okay? So let's just look at the evidence for that. So I'm gonna be a little bit like a lawyer here and so let's look at the evidence for that. Or not. So you say, don't worry, don't get lost. Have you ever been lost in the city?
Client: No, I don't think I have.
Counselor: Yeah. Okay. Do you usually know which tram to get on?
Client: Oh, yeah, I make sure I know because I'm so scared I'm gonna get lost. I make sure I know all the numbers of the trams, where they go. So, yeah, actually. So I've never got lost.
Counselor: Okay. All right. So in some ways, how likely do you think it really is that you're actually going to get lost? I know you're having that thought, but.
Client: Well, it's actually really unlikely.
Counselor: Fantastic. And so what I'll get you to write in this little right hand column here is it's really unlikely I'm going to get lost. Okay, so these are what we sort of call disputing thoughts or, you know, alternative ways of looking at it that a little bit fairer to ourselves and a little bit more realistic. That's fantastic.
Client: So unlikely I will get lost.
Counselor: Yeah. It's actually unlikely, isn't it? Yeah. Have a look at the next one. I'll panic and I'll blush and everyone will look at me. Okay, so let's just have a little look at that. If you did get a bit panicky, do you think people would really be noticing?
Client: Probably not. Maybe not.
Counselor: Well, let's put it another way. Do you look at other people on the tram and sort of decide whether or not they look emotionally happy or sad or panicky?
Client: Not really, no. I don't know. I look out the window or read the paper usually, yeah.
Counselor:
output: And look. That's fantastic because do you think it's. I mean, most people are just sitting on the train doing their own thing and not that really interested in other people.
