instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Samantha. How you doing today?
Client: Good, how are you?
Counselor: I'm doing all right. How have things been since last week?
Client: Things? You know, I've been really sort of preoccupied and anxious a lot this weekend. My daughter got sick, so I had to take three days off of work to take care of her. And I'm starting to worry. She's been sick a lot since I've gone back to work, and she's in daycare, and I've had to take a lot of time off work, and I'm getting close to going over my allotted amount of days. And so I'm finding myself being very anxious about that and then feeling guilty because when I'm trying to take care of her, I'm always worrying about work. So.
Counselor: Okay, so it sounds like a couple things may be going on. Child. Child's been sick, so you're taking off days. So you're a little worried about your relationship with your employer. At the same time, you want to make sure you're taking good care of your child, so you're having trouble reconciling those two.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right. What was the last time it happened? Can you describe what happened the last.
Client: Time I had to take off work? It was just this week. She woke up one morning with a really high fever, so I had to call out that day, and then she still had a fever the next day, and then I had to take a third day because she has to be fever free before she can go back to daycare. So the first day was, I was okay with that. But then, like, the second. And then when I started realizing that I was going to have to take a third day, then I really start to get kind of panicky and worried about it.
Counselor: All right, so let me see. Let's go through each day. So the first day when you discovered that she was sick, right. What were you thinking then when you had to call out of work?
Client: Well, because she's been sort of sick a lot lately, I was a little bit worried, and I was sort of, you know, I have this number, ten, because I only have ten days for the whole year. So I have this number in my head, and I just thought, well, there's one more day I gotta take away from that ten that I have. And. But I was able to sort of think about. I was a little worried about any work that I would miss, you know, keeping up with my caseload and stuff at work, so. But I was able to kind of figure out that I would be okay for a day. And I can kind of make up for that when I get back.
Counselor: Okay, so your thinking was, this isn't ideal, but I can live with it.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Just one day, right? How about on day two when you realize that you're going to have to take a second day?
Client: Then I got a little bit more worried. And then I did start to also, you know, add the worry of I was going to start to get behind at work. Not only was I missing more time, but I was also going to be behind on my work. So then I started thinking, when I go back, it's going to be a mad scramble to kind of catch up and keep up with everything and, you know, so then it became worrying about my workload and worrying about taking more time.
Counselor: Okay, so a little more stressful version of what happened on day one. And then how about when you discovered that you had to take a third day off?
Client: I was. Then it was just more amplified, you know, amplified worry. And it was a lot harder for me to let it go. I just kept thinking. I kept going back to it. And then I started feeling guilty because I was so preoccupied, worried about that. And I was trying to answer emails and do some stuff and send out some emails to people that I work with to try to help me out with things at work since I wasn't there. And then I felt guilty because I wasn't really caring for my child as best as I felt I should have been. You know, I started feeling kind of like a bad mom.
Counselor: So, so guilty and a bad mom. And that was mostly on the third day? That was the worst of it, yes. Now, did this go up against the weekend? It was the third day, Friday. So then you kind of knew that by Monday things would be able to return to work. So tell me what happened when you returned to work on Monday.
Client: Well, I checked in with the main office and, you know, I just said, I'm really, you know, I'm starting to worry. I'm getting. I know I had to take a lot of time, but you. I've done the best I can to try to make other arrangements, but just starting back in, starting in daycare, she's just been sick a lot and I can't control it. I'm doing the best I can. I asked them if there was anything I needed to do as far as providing doctor's notes and stuff, and they said, no, they don't need a doctor's note since it was my daughter that was sick. They said there's nothing, nothing that I really can do and just try to not have it happen much more if I can just do what I can to not miss more.
Counselor: So they said that to you?
Client: Yeah, but. Yeah.
Counselor: How did they frame that?
Client: They kind of just said, you know, do what you can to not have it happen, but if it, you know, if it has to happen, you know, what can I do about it? It's kind of. They were saying.
Counselor: So they were understanding.
Client: I didn't feel like they were that understanding, but I also didn't feel like they were gonna take any punitive action against me. Right. Right then and there or anything.
Counselor: Did you anticipate a worse reaction than you experienced?
Client: Yeah, I did. And I also anticipated that they would maybe have more of a procedure for how to handle it, and they didn't have a procedure, which also made me feel a little worried. I can't imagine I'm the first mom that has had to deal with this. And they kind of talked like it's never happened before, so I kind of felt anxious because I thought, am I really the first mom that's had to take a lot of time off because their child's sick? They didn't give me the impression that they had sort of a protocol or like they had dealt with this before.
Counselor: Right. So sort of like it took them by surprise.
Client: Yeah. Or they just didn't have a plan for what to do about it.
Counselor: They weren't investing a lot of energy in thinking about that?
Client: No. No, I guess nothing.
Counselor: And when was this again? How long ago?
Client: Just this past week.
Counselor: So how has this week been? Bag of work?
Client: Oh, it's been very busy because I'm trying to catch up and get everything handled, but that's the way it always is. So nobody has said anything to me or anything about the absences other than that first, yeah.
Counselor: And there have been no more absences. Okay. Earlier you mentioned being a good mom. What does a good mom look like?
Client: Somebody who takes care of their child and puts them. Makes them a priority, like their first priority, and, you know, does the things that they need to do to make sure they're child is taken care of.
Counselor: And you're a little worried through this last experience you were telling me about that you didn't rise to the level of good mom.
Client: Yeah, I felt like I wasn't being a good mom because I was preoccupied and making work a bit of a bigger priority than taking care of my kidney.
Counselor: Okay. So good mom's more about. More than just rather your behavior, what you're doing. It's about what you're also thinking. So you took care of your child.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But your mind, your thoughts were somewhere else some of the time, and that's where you feel like you've wandered out of the good mom area. Okay, how about on the other side? How about a good employee? Did you mention that you want to be a good employee?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor:
output: Yeah. What's that look like?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Alex, we're going to continue today with the trauma memory task like last time. So this is, of course, you talking about your memory of the attack from beginning to end in as much detail as you can. Just to remind you, we've said that we are doing this to help put this memory sort of back into the past, I guess, where it belongs. We hope that by doing this, it's going to help lessen those nightmares and flashbacks and other upsetting memories of the attack that are bothering you quite a bit at the moment. So how do you feel about that? About going through the memory again together today?
Client: Can't say I'm excited about it, but I'll give it another shot.
Counselor: Yeah. Look, I think we do know that this is difficult right now. But what I also expect is that it's going to get easier and easier for you to talk about this memory the more often you do. And I'll be right here with you to support you with that. So, same as last time, I'm going to ask you to talk about the memory as if it were happening now. So in the present tense. And I'm going to ask you to start at the bit where you are waiting for the tramdhead and end it at the part where your mum is there or your mum arrives. And I'll be checking in with you about where you are on the thermometer again. So before you begin, where are you in terms of your distress on that zero to ten thermometer?
Client: I'm about a five.
Counselor: About a five?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay, well, let's go through that memory again, starting whenever you're ready.
Client: So I'm sitting playing with my phone at the tram stop. I see them out of the corner of my eye. Two guys wearing jeans, hoodies and sneakers. I don't think much of it. Then they come up behind me, grab my arms and put them behind my back. My phone smashes to the ground. I can feel my heart pounding. I'm thinking, oh, God, what are they gonna do to me?
Counselor: Okay, you're doing well. Where are you on that thermometer?
Client: About a seven.
Counselor: Okay, stick with it.
Client: Then. I feel something cold metal on my neck. I realize it's a knife. I think, oh, shit. Then one of them whispers into my ear, give us your watch or I'll stab you. I can smell booze on his breath.
Counselor: You're doing well. Where are you now?
Client: Eight.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: I'm too paralyzed to speak. I just try and nod. They let go of my arms, but the knife is still there. One of them takes the watch off my arm. Then they start going through my pockets. I guess they're looking for cards or money. He finally puts the knife away. Then they pull me onto my feet and one of them knees me so hard in the stomach that I fall back down. Then they start kicking me in the stomach and just run off.
Counselor: Ok, you're doing well. Where are you on that thermometer now?
Client: About a seven.
Counselor: Keep going if you can.
Client: I'm lying on the ground in pretty bad shape. I can't breathe properly. I'm thinking, I don't have my phone. How is anyone gonna find me? Are they gonna come back for me?
Counselor: Okay, doing well. Where are you on that thermometer?
Client: I'm about an eight.
Counselor: Okay, keep going.
Client: I feel like I'm there forever, but finally I hear a guy calling out. He's asking him if I'm okay. I couldn't get any words out, so I just make a weird sound. He comes over. He's an older guy, about 50. He says everything's gonna be okay. And I'm so relieved I start crying.
Counselor: Where are you on that scale now?
Client: About six?
Counselor: Yeah, yeah, keep going.
Client: I don't remember telling him my mum's number, but I must have. Cause the next thing I know, she's there next to me. She looks like she's been crying. She holds me in her arms and says, I'm safe now.
Counselor:
output: Okay, and where are you on the thermometer now?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, Jordan. How you doing today?
Client: Could have been better.
Counselor: Could be better.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What's going on?
Client: Um, well, you know, I have two jobs.
Counselor: Mm hmm.
Client: And I lost one of them.
Counselor: You lost your job? Yes. Which one did you lose?
Client: I lost one at the grocery store.
Counselor: That was your part time?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I'm sorry to hear that.
Client: Me too. And I'm just. It's all I think about now.
Counselor: And when did this happen?
Client: It happened about two, three days ago.
Counselor: Two, three days ago?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So if I remember right, you took that job not too long ago to kind of supplement your income.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So certainly that would be upsetting, but I know that's not a major part of your income.
Client: It's not, but, I mean, I'm still very worried about it.
Counselor: Tell me about the worry.
Client: I mean, I worry that, you know, I'm. Now I only had so much money, and now I have less than that. I mean, without my money, you know, God knows how many things can happen.
Counselor: So before you had the job, you were paying all your bills. You want some extra income, you've lost that extra income. And I can certainly understand how that would be disturbing. But as I understand that you were doing okay before with your full time job.
Client: I was doing okay, but, I mean, I got comfortable with that extra income, and so now my fear is that I've gotten too comfortable with it, and now that it's not there anymore, it's going to affect the fact I'm not going to be able to pay for food or my rent.
Counselor: Okay, so you adjusted to the new income level with the full time and the part time job together, and you're worried you can't adjust back?
Client: I'm worried that, I mean, things are just gonna get worse from here. I mean, it's a big deal, losing your job. Even if it was part time, I've gotten comfortable from having so much money, from the money I had to. Now that's, you know, been divided and, I mean, God knows how many things, like I said, God knows how many things can happen.
Counselor: Well, what. What can happen? So you have that income, your income is reduced now to just your full time job. What can happen from this point on?
Client: Well, I can, you know, keep. Stay in the mindset that I have that extra money and spend what I think is that extra money, digging into the money I paid for my rent, my food, my gas, my insurance, and me, who's somebody without all that.
Counselor: So you could fail to pay expenses that need to be paid.
Client: And they helped me go to my full time job that I still have. So, I mean, if I can't, if I spend the money that was from my insurance because I thought I had extra, then I'm not gonna have insurance on my cardinal. I can get pulled over, lose my license, not going to be able to get to work, and then I'll get fired there too.
Counselor: All right, so the kind of chain of causality you're seeing is that without that part time income, you might not adapt with your expense management. You might fail to pay, for example, your car insurance. You could get pulled over for something the police officer could see, don't have insurance, give you a ticket, which is just money. I don't have another expense. Right. And how would this. How would that connect to losing your job?

Client: I guess, like, when I'm holding the camera, I just grip onto it really, really tight, or I kind of clench all my muscles and just find something that I can focus on and to kind of try and make myself shake less and not go as red and stuff.
Counselor: So you focus on something, you grip onto the camera. Do you make eye contact with people?
Client: No, I just tend to just look down.
Counselor: Okay. So you also avoid eye contact. Is there anything else that you do to manage the sweating, for example?
Client: I just, as I kind of looking down and wearing all black, so it's less obvious or kind of wearing just more layers and all black, so you just can't tell.
Counselor: Okay. What do you think would happen if you stopped doing these things? If you stopped gripping onto the camera or you started making eye contact and not looking down, what do you think could happen?
Client: I think it would be so much worse. Yeah. I think I just would just shake even more and be more anxious and look more obviously kind of weird and out of place.
Counselor: What I'm thinking now is, how would you feel about if we did an experiment to test out your thoughts on what would happen if you stopped doing these things? If we did a bit of a role play where we pretended to enact a situation at work.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: And if you did this maybe twice in the first time, you do all the things that you normally do. Grip onto something, look down. Is there anything else that you do when you're in these situations, these work conversations to try and cope?
Client: I just kind of all just, like, fumble and kind of just clench whatever it is I'm holding just really tight. And just make sure I don't make any eye contact at all. Just kind of get through it.
Counselor: Okay. So in the first time, I want you to do those things as much as you normally would. In fact, maybe even slightly more than you normally would. And then the second time, I want you to drop doing those things altogether. How does that sound?
Client: Try my best.
Counselor: And how would you feel about if we filmed this so you could actually see what you looked like?
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Do you have a camera with you that we could video on?
Client: Yeah. Is my phone okay?
Counselor: Yeah, yeah, we'll use that in just a sec.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: Before we do this, then we're just going to fill out this form, because what we're doing now is an experiment. We call it a behavioral experiment to see what happens when you change the way that you're behaving.
Client: Right. Okay.
Counselor: Okay. So the first column says, I need to fill out an experiment to test this thought that you have so that our experiment is going to be that we do a conversation at work. Who should I play? If you're playing yourself in this role play, who should I be?
Client: Maybe like a client at work, I always have to sit down with clients before we do the shoot and kind of get to know a little bit more about what they want.
Counselor: Okay, so would it work if I was maybe having a wedding and I was hiring you to be a wedding photographer?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What kind of problems do you see coming up in this conversation that we have? Like, what we see yourself doing on camera?
Client: Shaking. Like, being really obviously shaking and. Okay, bright red and.
Counselor: Okay, so visibly shaking. So how. How much will you be shaking? If a hundred is, like, shaking uncontrollably and zero is not shaking at all, how visibly shaking will you be?
Client: 90.
Counselor: Okay, sorry. What was the other thing that you just said?
Client: Like, I go really red.
Counselor:
output: Okay, so you're gonna go red?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Ashley. How you doing today?
Client: I'm doing all right.
Counselor: How you been feeling over the last few days?
Client: I'm a little bit overwhelmed with schoolwork, and my boyfriend has been getting on my nerves quite a bit, but otherwise pretty good.
Counselor: So you have a few things going on, but overall, you're feeling okay.
Client: Mm hmm.
Counselor: Yeah. I remember during the last session you had some difficulties at work.
Client: Yeah. They seem to have been getting a little bit better with the homework that you gave me. It has helped me to identify when I. I'm getting a little more overwhelmed at work, and when I'm able to identify when I'm feeling that way, it's helped me to, I guess, meet my supervisor in the middle, more or less, so I'm not as argumentative. And she seems to be a little more impressed with my work performance.
Counselor: Good.
Client: She's been good.
Counselor: So identifying the automatic thoughts has helped you kind of negotiate that relationship more productively?
Client: Yeah, absolutely. That's great.
Counselor: So you're able to complete the thought, record the homework?
Client: Yeah. And that's actually helped me a lot, not just with work, but when I'm out, say, grocery shopping, and I start feeling that way, it's helped me to bring myself back down so I don't get overwhelmed and I don't get so anxious.
Counselor: Good, good. So that's a positive result. So I want to kind of set our structure for today, like, what we'll be talking about today during this session. And I was wondering if there's a few things kind of on your mind, like what you wanted to discuss today.
Client: Oh, there's a couple things. My classwork has been really been bogging me down lately, and then while I'm still doing better at work, I'm still not where I want to be. I don't want to have to consciously think this is why I'm. I want to keep working on. And I'm not being so argumentative at work. And then my boyfriend has been, like I said earlier, really gritting on my nerves, and I don't, like, I told him the other day that I wanted to break up with him, but he told me he was going to change and that things would get better. So I'm kind of torn with whether or not to continue in their relationship or just let it go. And at the same time, I'm having a hard time keeping up with my schoolwork and getting everything done on time. And my homework isn't where I want it to be. Like, I feel like I can do better.
Counselor: So you're being pulled in a few directions here. And all of these things are important to you. Like, all these things are bothering you, the schoolwork lateness, the relationship at work. Like, you're doing better with that, but you still want some improvement there and then some relational challenges with your boyfriend. So I know it's difficult to prioritize concerns when they're all important to you. Right. But if you really only had, say, one thing to choose for today's session that you really wanted to work on as a priority, what would you choose?
Client: That's really hard. That's hard to.
Counselor: Well, tell me about your thought processes as you answer that question. As you think about that question.
Client: Well, I've been with my boyfriend for about nine months now, and I thought that we were going to go into like, marriage and children, and I thought we had a future. At the same time, my work, I need. I need my job. I need it to pay bills and basically live. And at the same time, my schoolwork is very important because as progressing in school and getting a better education, I'll be able to get a better job, which will, hopefully it'll be a job in which I don't find myself where I am right now, butting heads with my supervisor all the time and everything.
Counselor: So again, it comes down to all three goals, really are, they really are important to you. All three matter to you and you want to work on them. So I'm wondering, as we think about trying to rank them, which is what we're really doing. Right. Trying to pick one is the most important, which area you think is interfering with your functioning the most, like what's getting in the way of your mood, being good? Or are you accomplishing goals you need to accomplish to survive?
Client: Probably my, probably my schoolwork.
Counselor: How does school work? Yes, tell me about that.
Client: Well, I think it's most important because, like I said, it'll set me up later in life. So not getting a good grade on an assignment really brings me down because I view it as a threat to my future. Because if I don't get a good grade, then I could possibly fail out of school. And failing out of school means I won't have a good job job, then I won't have a good relationship and definitely top of my list.
Counselor:
output: So that's the priority. So we'll look at that problem, the schoolwork issue. We'll make that the number one priority for today. And if we get through that and we have time, we can look at one of the other things that's going on. I want to make sure. We kind of set a structure so we know what we'll be talking about and what we want to accomplish. So what we'll do is, I'll have you tell me a little bit more about that and kind of your thoughts and feelings and behaviors surrounding that schoolwork issue. And we'll go through some techniques, and I'll assign some homework related to that, more or less like I did last time when it was the workplace challenge. The workplace relationship. That was the challenge. Does that kind of make sense?

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Victoria. How you doing today?
Client: Doing okay.
Counselor: Been doing okay. It's been a while now. You've been practicing with the waiting after you wash your hands? Mm hmm. How's that been going for you?
Client: Well, I think it's been going pretty well. I've been able to, you know, wait pretty good. I'm gonna start it out slow like you suggested, with three minutes. Then I would wash my hands for five minutes. I would wash my hands, and I got up to about 15 minutes.
Counselor: That's great.
Client: And there were some times that I was really proud of myself that I actually forgot.
Counselor: You forgot to wash your hands entirely?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So when was the next time you washed them?
Client: When I would go to, like, eat. Dinner,
Counselor: which is when you normally wash your hands. So really, you touched something that had germs, and you had some anxiety as you had to get to that waiting period. But then the anxiety subsided to a point where I forgot about it just wasn't a priority. You just completely forgot and went on with your day?
Client: Yeah. I was really proud of myself, but I got really concerned because I got sick. I got sick recently, and I'm afraid it's from one of those times that I didn't wash my hands.
Counselor: Well, tell me about the sickness.
Client: Well, my throat started to get hurt real bad, and I was just really congested. And all I could think about was, it's because I didn't wash my hands when I went to the store or when I went to my car when I touched a jacket. That's, you know, been everywhere.
Counselor: How many times do you normally get it? Sounds like a cold.
Client: I mean, it was kind of a light cold.
Counselor: Light cold.
Client: I mean, we wouldn't wait in a.
Counselor: Few days, a couple days. So how long or how many times a year would you get something like that normally?
Client: I mean, I get sick. I mean, quite often because of my job. I'm around a lot of people, and hand sanitizer can only work so much. I do get sick.
Counselor: So it's been six weeks since you started waiting? Right. I think it was around session three where we talked about putting a gap between when you touch something, when you wash your hands, like a time gap, and you got a cold once. Would that be out of the ordinary to get a cold one time in six weeks this time of year?
Client: I suppose not. I mean, the rational part of me knows that I get sick, but just because I'm trying something new with the, you know, and then the waiting and then the not washing, I'm just afraid that there was, you know, you're afraid.
Counselor: They were linked at one cause the other that waiting to wash your hands got you sick. And that could have happened. I don't know. But let's talk about the cold. You said it was a couple days.
Client: It wasn't severe. I mean, I took some, you know, over the counter medicine, slept it off.
Counselor: So wasn't a catastrophe.
Client: No, I've definitely been sicker in my life. And I mean, it did seem like one of those ones that I get every now and then.
Counselor: So when we spoke, I remember before you had said that the kind of worst case scenario, the reason that you're thinking so much about the germs on your hands is that it could make you sick. But you did get sick and you were able to tolerated.
Client: Yeah, I was. Which I found kind of odd because I was. I was panicked at the beginning when I started to feel those first, you know, the itchy throat, the headaches.
Counselor: Sure, it's miserable, right? Nobody wants to get sick.
Client: And I got concerned, you know, that it was because of that. Then it just kind of subsided. I guess I felt a little better, you know, as the days went on, I felt better about it happening, about.
Counselor: The whole getting sick and you started to recover. So kind of the worst case scenario occurred and you survived. And again, we don't know if the, the amount of hand washing you were doing before the ERP exposure and response prevention, we don't know if that would have prevented the cold or not. Yeah, because you do get sick several times, several times a year, in a year. So there's a lot we don't know. But we do know that you survived it and it wasn't as bad looking back at it.
Client: I mean, in my head, not washing my hands and the sick that I would get is a lot worse. It's like hospital worthy. And this was, you know, like I said over the counter, you know, relax a little bit.
Counselor: So not pleasant, but survivable.
Client: It definitely wasn't pleasant, but it wasn't as bad as it could have gone in my mind.
Counselor: So presume for a moment that it was a consequence of not immediately rushing over and washing your hands. What would you rather have? The occasional cold like that or the excessive hand washing and anxiety?
Client: I mean, I definitely don't like the excessive hand washing. I don't. I mean, it ruins my skin and I. It's expensive and it makes me feel bad about myself. And I mean, I guess the trade off is if I get a little sick and that would be okay.
Counselor: Again, that's presuming that it did cause you to get sick, which it may not have.
Client: I suppose that's true.
Counselor:
output: So I wanted to point out, too, that I remember when we, we first started the exposure response prevention exercise, we did it right here in session by touching the arms of the chair. And I can see now your arms are.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Victoria. How you doing today?
Client: Pretty good.
Counselor: Very good. How has the anxiety been around the germs?
Client: I still catch myself, like, double, almost like double touching. Like going to touch it and then reeling back. So I'm starting to notice it, but I still, I still have that anxiety. I still don't want to touch it.
Counselor: When you pretty much touch anything you might think has germs on it.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What are some things that you've touched in the last, between the last session and this session that have distressed you?
Client: Well, I had to go to the store, which is always a nightmare for me because I don't even like touching my credit card because it's been in so many machines and there's so much dirt and junk that gets in there and then the counters and all the. I keep thinking about the food that's there, and I, you know, if I pick it up off the shelf, how many people have picked it up with their nasty hands or kids picked it up with nasty hands and then put it back, and it's like, I need to eat. But shopping's a nightmare for me.
Counselor: So really, in a, like, a supermarket, everything can be containing germs. Have germs on it?
Client: Yeah, everything does.
Counselor: Everything does. And that's what you're thinking about as you're walking through and shopping. We talked about last time, exposure and response prevention, and I explained kind of the general idea. But you remember that conversation. Yeah, I remember. I indicated that we might try some experiments right in session to see how, see if we can move kind of forward and treating your, kind of your fear and obsession with germs and really the anxiety it's causing for you, it's like getting in the way of your life.
Client: It is. It really is.
Counselor: So I was wondering, is there anything in here, in this office, as you look around, that you would look at and think, I don't want to touch that because it could have germs on it.
Client: I'm really not liking the covers on this chair because, I mean, I can't. I mean, at least what I'm sitting in now, my clothes are protecting me from the rest of the chair.
Counselor: Mm hmm.
Client: But, I mean, I have no sleeves on, so I don't like touching the armrests and the covers.
Counselor: So even thinking about, like, your arms touching the back of the chair, and.
Client: I'm not liking it, I really feel like I should probably go wash my arms.
Counselor: So what would happen if you put your hands right on the arm covers? What was your usual reaction to that?
Client: To go wash my arms until I feel like it's gone. Until all the dirt is gone.
Counselor: And how long would that take you to be sure?
Client: I mean, something like this, probably. I'd probably be in there for a good 510 minutes. Just washing.
Counselor: 510 minutes. How many times a day would you end up washing your hands?
Client: Okay. I don't. I don't keep track anymore. It makes me upset. How many?
Counselor: It says that it's that many. That is distressing. And I know that this will be uncomfortable, but I would like you to try to. If you can feel comfortable with it, put your hands on the. On the arms of the chairs. On the chair. Let's see what I'm doing. It's like. Try to stay like that. So tell me what's going through your mind?
Client: I can just. I feel the chair, and I. I don't like it. And I just. I feel almost like I can feel everybody who's ever touched it. And just what have they been doing? And what did they touch before they touched this? They probably didn't wash their hands before they touched this, and it's just really making me comfortable.
Counselor: Okay, so you're anxious now?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Is it tolerable?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So once you remember, we talked about scaling before. So, like, ten being a tremendous amount of anxiety, one being hardly any anxiety. Where. Where are you now as you sit here with your hands?
Client: What am I going to say about six or seven?
Counselor: Six or seven?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Are you feeling an urge to go wash your hands?
Client: Yes. Yes, I am.
Counselor: Yes. This is a six or seven. I want you to sit with it for a few seconds, process that, you know, feeling. Right. That you're touching everybody that's ever been in the chair. Right. So consider that thought.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: So what's the ultimate fear? Like, what's gonna happen if you don't go wash your hands now?
Client: I'm gonna get sick.
Counselor: You're gonna get sick that someone who's.
Client: Been in this chair was sick or touched something gross that can make you sick. And I'm gonna get sick, and I'm gonna die, and I don't want to die.
Counselor: Do you feel yourself getting sick?
Client: I feel like it's harder to breathe, I guess. Like, my chest is kind of just tight. Yeah.
Counselor: You can still breathe, though.
Client: I can't. I can breathe.
Counselor: Okay, so go ahead and lift your hands up. Right. And just put them where you'd normally put them. Well, now that you've touched the chair, I know that now I can still. Is that any better? Now you're touching the seat of the.
Client: Chair, but I feel like if I touch my clothes, that's even worse. Yeah. Now I will have to go home and change my clothes.
Counselor: All right, so the thought now, if I had to guess, correct me if I'm wrong, it's probably like you really would like to wash your hands.
Client: Very much so.
Counselor: And you certainly can at any time. But I'd like you to try to hold out for a little bit. So your hands where they are now, that's better than up here.
Client: At this point. I feel like they're already contaminated, so.
Counselor: They'Re at maximum contamination.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So you can't do any more damage by touching the seat.
Client: Yeah, I'm just trying to avoid touching anything else.
Counselor: So now it's not so much about getting your hands away from the arms, but getting them under the faucet. Yeah, that's the. So where's anxiety? Was a six or seven before. Where is it now?
Client: I mean, now that you mention it, it is. It is a little better. I want to say about four. About three, four. I mean, I feel better that my. My arms are off it, and I'm focusing on breathing, and, I mean, it's.
Counselor: A little easier to breathe now.
Client: A little. Yeah, it is.
Counselor: So if you could go. If you could wash your hands right this second. Of course you can. But if you did, what would the anxiety move to?
Client: A one.
Counselor: A one.
Client: I mean, it would take a little bit to get to a one. A little bit actually washing, but then it'll get to a one. Then I'll feel okay.
Counselor: All right, so you move from just in a short time, from a six or seven to a three or four for anxiety, when, of course, the goal was one. Right. So you could say roughly halfway. Roughly halfway down toward your goal without washing your hands at all.
Client: Oh, wow. I didn't consider that.
Counselor: So are you doing okay? You're holding up okay. All right, so this is what I want you to do. Before you go wash your hands, I want to use this moment to give you some ideas for the next few weeks. When you touch something that causes you to feel like the germs are on your hands. Chairs, whatever it is, I want you to try progressively to wait more and more time between that event. Like when you feel that urge when you actually wash your hands.
Client: Okay.
Counselor: I mean, you have to wash your hands at some point, right. You're gonna wash them at some point. That's normal. I'm asking, try to delay that.
Client: Okay.
Counselor:
output: I try to try to stall and not wash them immediately.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Liz. How you doing today?
Client: I'm alright. How are you?
Counselor: I'm doing well, thanks for asking. What's been going on in the last week?
Client: It's still the same. Nothing at home is going right. It's. I'm still yelling, we're still fighting.
Counselor: Like you and your boyfriend.
Client: Yeah. He just can't get it together. He can't. He doesn't do anything right. He doesn't. And I just end up screaming every day and it takes it all out of me.
Counselor: All right, so he can't do anything right. And you're arguing, being angry every day?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So what are you taking away from this? Like, what do you think's going on?
Client: I feel like he does nothing wrong and I end up screaming at him when I come home from work, and that's a lot out of me every day, and I don't want to feel angry every single day.
Counselor: That's what's happening.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What types of things do you think are triggering your anger response?
Client: It's anything. It's. I come home, he's just sitting on the couch. I've had a long day at work. He gets homework before me, and the dishes aren't done. Nothing's, like, thawed or even started for dinner. And is that just supposed to be my, like, it's not. He could just do one thing and I just. I just lose it. I lose it and I can't. I can't control it. I just started screaming at him that he does nothing, that he could just do one thing for me. He could just have the sink clean, empty one thing, and it. Every single day. And then the next day it's something else. The trash is now, like, you name it.
Counselor: So every. Every day when you come home from work, there's something he's done or failed to do that triggers yelling?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What's his response to this? Like, what's he doing when you yell at him?
Client: He gets mad back. He just starts screaming back at me. Like, I expect too much and I get too upset and why am I always yelling at him? Why can't I give him the benefit of the doubt?
Counselor: I'm.
Client: But I don't understand it. Like, you could do one thing and then. And I just. I can't help it. I scream at him.
Counselor: Are there other things he does at other times that you feel are helpful? Or is it. Or is it always, like, when you come home, is it always something that hasn't been done right or hasn't been done?
Client: I mean, on anniversaries, whole make dinner. So that's nice.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: He makes good money. So that's. He keeps that together.
Counselor: Okay, that's about it.
Client: Yeah. The rest is just. I just get angry at him.
Counselor: So if you were to pick adjectives to describe him, what adjectives might you. Might you select?
Client: Stubborn, condescending, and intelligent.
Counselor: Intelligent, stubborn, condescending, and intelligent. Do you see him as this way kind of all the time, or is this change?
Client: I don't think it's all the time. Like, there. Like sometime, like a month ago when a friend at work died. Old age, whatever. But I had a long day. He knew it beforehand. I didn't have to say anything. When I came home, everything was good. There was no trash, no dishes. So it's not all the. All the time, but just lately, it's just. I had no words.
Counselor: So lately it's all the time. Yeah, but there's been prior occasions when this hasn't been a problem. Yeah, but there's not many of those. So after you have, you yell and argue, what's it feel like to you then? Like, what's your mood?
Client: I'm still irritable. It's like the dishes don't get done. The problem didn't go away, didn't fix itself while I was yelling. So it just sucks being that angry. Just doesn't. I hate it.
Counselor: So it's not productive for you?
Client: Right, right. It's not productive.
Counselor: But there's a part of you mentioned earlier where, like you said, you just can't help yourself.
Client: Like I said, I just lose it. And I do that because that's what it feels like.
Counselor: So it's like you just. You just see, for example, like the dishes, right? So you just see the dishes aren't done, and immediately there's the.
Client: I just. I go off. Why didn't you do the dishes? You've been home an hour and a half. You could have done one thing for me. I had a longer day, and you knew it.
Counselor: All right, so let me take an example from work, right, so you work in an office with other people. Do they ever frustrate you in a way similar to what your boyfriend does?
Client: Occasionally, yeah, on occasion. Yeah.
Counselor: So there's times where you kind of have that moment with them where you just can't believe they didn't do something.
Client: Or I. Yeah, I just can't stand them sometimes.
Counselor: What's your reaction in terms of anger and yelling to those events?
Client: I get pissed, but I just. I can't. I can't yell.
Counselor: You can't yell? No. Why is that?
Client: I get fired.
Counselor: You get fired. So in those interactions with your coworkers, would be fair to say you're in that moment just as angry as you are with your boyfriend.
Client: And, oh, if not more, because I actually choose to be with my boyfriend. I don't choose to be with those people necessarily.
Counselor: You just happen to be together. And so in those instances, because there's a consequence like being fired, you're able to control the outward expression of anger, meaning you're not yelling, but inwardly, you're still angry at them.
Client: Yeah, I guess so.
Counselor: Yeah. So they don't really know you're angry.
Client: Yeah. I just walk away. I don't think they'd be able to tell.
Counselor: And they're not being yelled at, so they're not.
Client: Right. They wouldn't react. Yeah.
Counselor: No reaction. Right. So there is a thought process that occurs between the trigger and when you act, because at work, you're thinking, you have this thought that comes up, I don't want to be fired.
Client: Yeah, I get there. Must. Yeah.
Counselor: And the consequence of that thought is I'll be angry, but I'm not going to act angry.
Client: Right. I can't act angry or I'll get fired, and I don't want to get fired, I guess.
Counselor: So knowing that there is a thought there when you come home and you see the dishes aren't done, maybe just stay with that example. What would that thought be like? Think back to the last time that happened. Do you remember what you were thinking at that moment as you saw those dishes sitting there not washed?
Client: I mean, just that he never does anything. Right.
Counselor: He never does anything. Right. So you see. So you see the dishes not washed. He never does anything. Right. That's the thought, yeah. And then the reaction, the behavior is finding him. Right. And yelling at him.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right, so you see how there is an intervening thought between the trigger, which in this case, the dishes, and the behavior, which is the yelling.
Client: Yeah. I guess there's a thought where I'm sitting there and I'm looking at him, thinking about it, saying, you never do anything. Right.
Counselor: So remember we talked a few weeks ago about cognitive distortions? We talked about, like, the errors, like, consistent. There are consistent errors in thinking. Right. And I'm wondering if that thought, he never does anything right. If that's similar to or matches up with any of the cognitive distortions we talked about. And I'm wondering if it's not. If it's not kind of blocking off your path in terms of thinking. Right. So you're saying he never does anything right.
Client: Right.
Counselor: It's kind of like maybe a kind of all or nothing thinking that we talked about that.
Client: Oh, it's absolute tunnel vision at that point.
Counselor: Tunnel vision, yeah. Okay. So a few different distortions at work. But you mentioned earlier there are times when he does do things right.
Client: Yeah. There are occasions where he must have thought about me.
Counselor: He was more thoughtful than more considerate. Okay. More considerate. So the statement he never does the thought, he never does anything right that could be challenged.
Client: Yeah, I guess technically it could.
Counselor: And what might be as an alternative to the behavior? Right. To the yelling. Instead of doing that, what might be a thought that you could kind of insert right after that he never does anything right. Thought that might change the outcome for you. That might disrupt that connection between that thought and your yelling.
Client: Maybe that he has done something right in the past.
Counselor: Okay.
Client: So it's bound to happen again. It is possible.
Counselor: All right. So an adapted response, as we call him or his self talk, that says he's not. He's not altogether bad because he has done things right in the past.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Right. Which is a little more flexible in thinking than thinking. He. Then your automatic thought.
Client: Right?
Counselor: Yeah. That's your automatic thought. Never does anything right. So a little bit more flexibility in the thinking might get you to a place where you're not yelling. And then on the other side of it, too, I'm wondering if we can't challenge the usefulness of yelling. You mentioned that you've done it quite a bit, but you're not really getting a different result.
Client: It doesn't. The dishes don't get done after that. And the next day, I might still find the dishes there. It doesn't.
Counselor: It's not working.
Client: It hasn't worked. Yeah.
Counselor: So when you're yelling, there's an expression of emotion, but there's also this hope that the yelling will change his behavior.
Client: Right.
Counselor: Something, but it's not.
Client: Yep.
Counselor: And when was the first time in terms of, like, how long ago this was a problem?
Client: I've had previous boyfriends where this was a problem, and that relationship has long gone because of it.
Counselor: So due to the yelling?
Client: Due to the yelling. So I don't. I really do like this guy who's not all bad, and I don't want my yelling to be a problem, my anger.
Counselor: But it's hard to control for you. You're struggling with the anger.
Client: Right?
Counselor: Yelling.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Rationally, you understand it doesn't work. Like, it's not getting what you want, but somehow it feels like a release it feels like justice. It feels good to be able to.
Client: It feels like that's what I'm supposed to be doing, and that's what I do.
Counselor: That's what you're supposed to be doing. Okay. So it feels like it's what you're supposed to be doing. Do you have an idea of what might be a more productive path for you as an alternative to the yelling?
Client: Protective. That's a great word. I guess walking away is what I do at the office.
Counselor: And that has worked for you.
Client: I've been able to take a minute and either remove myself or intervene my opinion more calmly because I haven't yelled at work, I guess walking away and taking a minute.
Counselor: Okay. So that would be one behavioral strategy. So you see the trigger and you have the thought. It never does anything. Right. And then you could intervene with a thought of, I need to walk away. And a behavior of walking away and taking, like, how much time?
Client: I mean, honestly, if I'm by myself, like, five minutes, ten minutes of just me time.
Counselor: So let's even say ten minutes.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So ten minutes. And then you can respond more constructively, more usefully to what is, you know, a type of relational disagreement. Right. You have a disagreement over, it sounds like, who should be doing what.
Client: Right. I. At what point in the day when he was working, when being considerate of the other.
Counselor: And that. That's certainly worth talking about. I mean, that makes sense that you guys would talk through that. But it seems like the yelling. I mean, you're just going right to the yelling.
Client: We're not getting anywhere.
Counselor: Right. So there's not really any time to address the issue.
Client: Right? Yeah, we have not worked out. Dad would help.
Counselor: So the yelling is really an impediment to what you want to achieve with the yelling?
Client: Yeah, I guess.
Counselor: Right. In a manner speaking. Right. It's blocking your goal. So do you kind of recognize that? Like, you seeing how I didn't think.
Client: That there was anything between me seeing the dishes and yelling at him. I knew that the anger wasn't getting me anywhere, but I didn't think I. But I guess there is a moment in between because I don't always yell. Like, I don't yell at work. So there is something else I could do.
Counselor: Right. So if I'm hearing you right, there's a sensation that it's kind of reflexive, like you see the dishes, and automatically you go right to the.
Client: Immediately it feels like I'm yelling.
Counselor: But in actuality, now you're realizing that there's a gap even if it's small, there's a gap where thinking takes place.
Client: And, yeah, there's a sliver that I must see at work that is also there at home.
Counselor: And I'm wondering, too, that there's a sense that. I mean, there's a sense that the rules, the relationship are being violated. You come home, and a part of you might know that's going to happen. Like, you. You come in, you know, you might see that this is not done or some other.
Client: Right?
Counselor: Sure. Not done. So I'm wondering, if you think about it in advance, kind of try to inoculate yourself, so to speak.
Client: Like, oh, I can definitely say it's been a thought. When I'm driving home, I'm like, it's been. Been a long day. It was a long day at the office. And I know he's not gonna have the trash taken out like I asked him or the dishes done or the chicken thought anything.
Counselor:
output: Well, and that goes both ways. Right? The thinking about advance can be a good thing because you can prepare yourself for that moment when you're gonna apply that adaptive response. You can prepare to see something that's gonna potentially upset you. But thinking about advance can also be destructive. If you start investing in the more negative thoughts, like, if you start saying things like, I know I'm going to find something, and you already get worked.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, Jordan. How you doing today?
Client: Could have been better.
Counselor: Could be better.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What's going on?
Client: Um, well, you know, I have two jobs.
Counselor: Mm hmm.
Client: And I lost one of them.
Counselor: You lost your job? Yes. Which one did you lose?
Client: I lost one at the grocery store.
Counselor: That was your part time?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: I'm sorry to hear that.
Client: Me too. And I'm just. It's all I think about now.
Counselor: And when did this happen?
Client: It happened about two, three days ago.
Counselor: Two, three days ago?
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So if I remember right, you took that job not too long ago to kind of supplement your income.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So certainly that would be upsetting, but I know that's not a major part of your income.
Client: It's not, but, I mean, I'm still very worried about it.
Counselor: Tell me about the worry.
Client: I mean, I worry that, you know, I'm. Now I only had so much money, and now I have less than that. I mean, without my money, you know, God knows how many things can happen.
Counselor: So before you had the job, you were paying all your bills. You want some extra income, you've lost that extra income. And I can certainly understand how that would be disturbing. But as I understand that you were doing okay before with your full time job.
Client: I was doing okay, but, I mean, I got comfortable with that extra income, and so now my fear is that I've gotten too comfortable with it, and now that it's not there anymore, it's going to affect the fact I'm not going to be able to pay for food or my rent.
Counselor: Okay, so you adjusted to the new income level with the full time and the part time job together, and you're worried you can't adjust back?
Client: I'm worried that, I mean, things are just gonna get worse from here. I mean, it's a big deal, losing your job. Even if it was part time, I've gotten comfortable from having so much money, from the money I had to. Now that's, you know, been divided and, I mean, God knows how many things, like I said, God knows how many things can happen.
Counselor: Well, what. What can happen? So you have that income, your income is reduced now to just your full time job. What can happen from this point on?
Client: Well, I can, you know, keep. Stay in the mindset that I have that extra money and spend what I think is that extra money, digging into the money I paid for my rent, my food, my gas, my insurance, and me, who's somebody without all that.
Counselor: So you could fail to pay expenses that need to be paid.
Client: And they helped me go to my full time job that I still have. So, I mean, if I can't, if I spend the money that was from my insurance because I thought I had extra, then I'm not gonna have insurance on my cardinal. I can get pulled over, lose my license, not going to be able to get to work, and then I'll get fired there too.
Counselor: All right, so the kind of chain of causality you're seeing is that without that part time income, you might not adapt with your expense management. You might fail to pay, for example, your car insurance. You could get pulled over for something the police officer could see, don't have insurance, give you a ticket, which is just money. I don't have another expense. Right. And how would this. How would that connect to losing your job?
Client: Because I wouldn't be able to get to work.
Counselor: So it'd be. So the ticket would be so expensive, you would lose your.
Client: Well, the ticket would be expensive, so I wouldn't be able to try to pay the next month's insurance. So I just wouldn't have insurance on my car. So I.
Counselor: So you'd lose your insurance?
Client: I'd lose my insurance.
Counselor: And then by losing your insurance, you lose your transportation altogether because you can't drive that insurance. And then you lose your job.
Client: Mm hmm. I mean, it's either go to work with an uninsured car, and then I can get pulled over and go to jail for driving with no insurance multiple times.
Counselor: No, that's serious. Yeah. You wouldn't want to do that.
Client: I wouldn't go to jail.
Counselor: So there's two. You have two kind of causal change. One is losing your job. And now even just the idea you can end up incarcerated.
Client: Yes. I mean, which I definitely lose my.
Counselor: Job if I'm in jail, I would imagine.
Client: And so that would have. So then I wouldn't even have, like, any money to help me through jail. Like, to. For the commissary and stuff.
Counselor: Because you would have no income.
Client: I would have no income. And then when I get out of jail, I'm. No one's gonna hire me.
Counselor: Because you have a criminal record.
Client: Exactly.
Counselor: Which makes it challenging to find employment in some instances. So what's happened is kind of in your mind, and we've talked about how thoughts work and beliefs work, is you, in reality, you've lost this part time job. And as I said, that's certainly. That's understandable that you'd be upset about that. I doubt many people would be happy about losing additional income, but you move from there, from losing additional income, which is what has actually happened to this possibility that you could be in jail or lose your job because of this. So I remember maybe last week. Week before, you're talking about the. The letter that you received from. It was like a late notice. It wasn't. Turned out wasn't.
Client: Yeah, it was sent to me, but it was somebody else's credit card mistake. Yeah.
Counselor: Do you remember the conclusions you drew from when you believe that was actually for you, that late notice, that my.
Client: Credit score was gonna go down, that I would. I'd be stuck in that apartment, and then I'd go into depression. I wouldn't be able to do anything.
Counselor: Yeah. So you ended up in that scenario. You end up in a situation where you just couldn't function at all. And you moved there from a letter that you believe was addressed to you, saying you were one month or six days late or something on a credit card, which, of course, you don't want to be late on a credit card, but you move from there to being so depressed you couldn't work, couldn't function, I think, is how you put it. Couldn't function. Do you see, kind of, given how we've talked about cognitive behavioral strategies and concepts, do you see a pattern that's emerged over the last few times I've seen you?
Client: I mean, I've seen that, you know, sometimes I can. I can think the worst, and then. And I know it didn't happen last time, but that was, you know, a stroke of good luck.
Counselor: That it wasn't you.
Client: Yeah. That it was, you know, it wasn't me. And, you know, that was a relief. But this is something that's solid. I don't have my part time job anymore.
Counselor: You've lost real income.
Client: I mean, this isn't a mistake. This isn't a. We fired the wrong person. You know, this is real. So there's real concerns here.
Counselor: I.
Client: Unlike last time, where I was lucky.
Counselor: So this. This situation, you see, is different than the first situation because the first situation was more. You were perceiving something was wrong that wasn't wrong because you weren't the intended recipient of the letter.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: But in this situation, it's different because it's real. You really lost your income.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And, of course, keeping in mind that this job, again, only a few months old, and you survived well before that, is it reason to believe you could survive well again, that you could adapt to this lost income?
Client: Well, I suppose there is, but I'm concerned about whether I'm not, whether I won't adapt.
Counselor: Well, let's look at this in terms of probabilities, right. You've had several jobs throughout your career. You've had some of them worked out. You've lost other ones. You're still paying your bills. So in terms of probabilities, how many times have you, how many times have you ended up in jail or losing your full time job?
Client: I mean, they haven't happened yet.
Counselor: It hasn't happened.
Client: Not yet. But I mean, I, I struggled a little bit when I lost a part time job or when I was younger and I had those little jobs.
Counselor: So you had to adapt.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And it was painful.
Client: I did struggle, yeah.
Counselor: You struggled.
Client: Yeah. I mean, but I'm older now. These are, you know, even though grocery stores, not a serious job. It was income.
Counselor: Sure. Yeah. And again, to lose income would be disappointing for just about anybody. Are there any upsides to not having that job?
Client: I suppose I have more time to focus on my full time job because, I mean, that is really intensive.
Counselor: Is there a possibility that you could find another part time job just as you found that one?
Client: I mean, because will somebody else take me because I was fired from that job? I mean, that's my concern, is that.
Counselor: Nobody, they're going to find out.
Client: Yeah. And then they're going to go, oh, she was fired, you know. No, we don't. We don't want her.
Counselor: But you've had other jobs that didn't work out before and that didn't affect you getting that job.
Client: That's true.
Counselor: So the worst case scenario, I guess what I'm getting at the worst case scenario is, in your case, ending up in jail or losing your full time job, which you've had for a while.
Client: Yeah, I really don't want to lose my job.
Counselor: And it seems like they like you there.
Client: I hope they do.
Counselor: Right? Yeah. So those scenarios, I guess, are possible, but they seem, based on what you're saying, is pretty unlikely. So I wonder how useful it is to invest a lot of energy in kind of tracking that causal chain to jail or prison or to unemployment when that's really not the most likely outcome. Sorry to interrupt you, but do you invest as much energy in tracking the positives or the probable outcomes?
Client: No, not even close. I know that I don't think about the positive things. I mean, I don't get fired and then go, what's good about this?
Counselor: Or get a letter in the mail and say, what's, you know, although I can see there's not much upside to that, although it turned out that was an error, so. But this has still been a theme that I've seen over the last eight to ten weeks, where you really have, you really emphasize the negative, possible, even unlikely outcomes, kind of expanding the negative as you move through. Like a causal chain.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Does that make sense? Yeah, but you don't do the same thing for the positive side. You don't look at how something could work out. Well, would you say it's fair assessment?
Client: Yeah. Yeah, no, that's. That's pretty accurate.
Counselor: But still, you're worried about this.
Client: I mean, yeah, I am worried. I'm not gonna be thrilled about it, but I suppose I don't have to go to when I'm gonna go to jail or I'm gonna lose my full time job.
Counselor: I think there's a lot of intervening factors that could occur before going to jail or losing your job. There's other things that you could do.
Client: I suppose I could get a family member to drive me or take the bus if I lost my insurance and lost my car.
Counselor: So, alternate forms of transportation. Yeah. There's adapting your spending back to where it was before.
Client: That's true.
Counselor: Part of your fear was that you wouldn't be able to adapt your spending. Right. But that's something you would have control over.
Client: I guess. I can keep, you know, better track of how much I do spend and, you know, keep track of my bank accounts and exactly how much money I have in them.
Counselor: So, having talked through this a little bit. Right. What I'm going to refer to, or is referred to as catastrophizing. Remember we talked about that when we reviewed the cognitive distortions.
Client: That sounds familiar. Yeah.
Counselor: Where a negative is taken and just making way more negative than it is at the moment. Right. Kind of knowing that, that tends to be what you do. It's what we call an error in thinking that you tend to make. Does that lower your anxiety about the situation? Does it change it in some way?
Client: I mean, knowing that I'm thinking about it wrong makes me feel a little better.
Counselor: I would say you're thinking about it in a way that's less than useful.
Client: Okay. That actually makes me feel better. Knowing that, you know, these things can happen, but it might not. There's other things that can happen before them.
Counselor:
output: Yeah. I mean, I would even say probably not.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hi, Jeff. How you doing today?
Client: I'm alright. Thanks for actually seeing me today. Sure.
Counselor: How have you been? I know last time I spoke with you, you were having some difficulties at work.
Client: I'm still having difficulties at work and that's why I'm glad I have a session today because it hasn't stopped. The frustration and anger is just, it's there ten times more than normal.
Counselor: You're really frustrated. Way more than normal, way more angry.
Client: Yes, it's, there seems to be a lot that's going on and I continually don't get the help that I need, not only not from my coworker, but also my supervisor. So it just feels so that everything is my responsibility and I have to make it happen. And if I don't make it happen, it's not going to happen. And then it's just, it's all on me and I don't feel as though that it's fair. But I also don't want us to not succeed. So I don't know how to navigate those two field.
Counselor: So the weight of the work assignments is really on you. You're feeling that pressure. You want to do right by your employer and there's an emotional toll this is taken on you. Has it reached a point where you've talked to your, it's a coworker supervisor you mentioned?
Client: Yes. So I talked to my supervisor about my coworker actually assisting me with some of the projects that we have going on. And my supervisor keeps on saying, oh, they're helping out and they're doing what they're supposed to do, but they're not doing what they're supposed to do because I end up doing their work. Because, say, for example, last week we actually had to turn in this huge report that we were working on for over a month. Literally, my coworker came to me on Monday and said I didn't do my portion of the report. And I was just like, we had a month to work on a lot of time. And so I spent the next three days doing everything for their part of the report. Luckily, I had already finished my part of the report and then combined it and actually turned it into my supervisor. Of course we get the, oh, this is a wonderful, great job that you guys did. And I'm just like you guys, as.
Counselor: If you both contributed equally.
Client: Correct? Correct.
Counselor: So in three days, you made up for a month's worth of work.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: So I could see how that could be. It's very stressful.
Client: Very, very taxing. Very, very taxing.
Counselor: And this wasn't an isolated incident?
Client: Oh, no. This has been going on for probably three or four months now.
Counselor: So this is almost the expectation when you get to work.
Client: Correct? Correct. I think that you hit the nail on the head. It's expected of me and nobody actually sees it as an expectation anymore.
Counselor: It's just what you do. It's just what I do. So you can know that going into work the next day, you go in, whenever that is, that there's always this probability, this chance that you could have work just thrown on you that wasn't budgeted for, you weren't planning on.
Client: Correct. And sometimes that work actually comes out from my supervisor, but it's mostly coming from my coworker. Like, I know they're not going to do their portion, so I just automatically start doing it anyway because, you know.
Counselor: You kind of have to.
Client: I know it's going to fall on my lap either today, tomorrow, next week. So I would rather be preemptive and actually start it then so that I'm not rushing like I was, like last week to finish a month's worth of work and three days worth of time. So I'm not as stressed.
Counselor: So you've tried to address this in the framework, in the context of your work. You've talked to the supervisor, to the co worker?
Client: I talked to the supervisor, I'm afraid. Well, I can't really talk to the coworker because I don't feel as though that's my position. However, I have expressed my frustration, my anger, my disappointment with my supervisor. And my supervisor keeps on saying, oh, I'll fix it, or, oh, it doesn't seem as though that they haven't done their piece of the work because I do all of it and it's turned in. So I have. But there doesn't seem to be anything happening outside of that.
Counselor: What kind of options, in terms of your job do you feel like you have now?
Client: I don't feel as though that I have any options. That's the thing. I think that either if I can, if I don't do the work and we fail, we're going to lose some of these big projects that we're working with, which then is going to impact our entire office. And if it impacts our entire office, like somebody might be let go. And because I am the newest person in our office, I feel as though that's going to be me. So I need to protect my job by doing not only my work, but my coworkers work and sometimes my supervisors work.
Counselor: So you're really figuratively fighting for survival?
Client: Correct.
Counselor: Do you think your coworker is aware that if there is a failure with getting projects done, that you would be the one that would be let go?
Client: I think, yes. I think that they understand that since they are the senior member on team, it would be most likely that the junior member myself would possibly be let go if a budget cut were to happen.
Counselor: So you're really largely stuck.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: With having to do the work.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: How about the emotions involved? You mentioned before, the frustration? Anger. Anger directed at.
Client: I think most of my anger is directed at my supervisor for not doing something because they can clearly see that something's wrong or that I'm handling a lot more, but they're not willing to step in. And I think a little bit of that anger is also at myself, because I haven't just said to my coworker, like, you need to step up and you need to do this. So I'm a little disappointed and angry at myself as well.
Counselor: You're angry at yourself, so you feel like you don't have the ability or courage to make that confrontation?
Client: I don't have the confidence to. The confidence to actually confront my coworker.
Counselor: All right, so before we dig into that too much, is it a good idea to confront the coworker?
Client: I think it would be good for them to understand how their lack of participation in our projects is impacting me and could also possibly impact our entire department. However, I don't know exactly how to say that and not come off as I'm. I know more than you, even though that you've been here longer than me.
Counselor: So you're searching for a friendly, understanding way to convey a tough subject matter.
Client: Yes.
Counselor: To someone who may or may not be receptive.
Client: Correct.
Counselor: But you may presume that they're more likely to not be receptive.
Client: I can 100%. I don't want to say 100%. I will say 99.9% say that they will not probably be receptive if I said that.
Counselor: So you're in for a bit of a battle.
Client: Yes.
Counselor:
output: And that was started.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: All right, so let's. If we could, let's rank those two things, right. So one is everyone's judging me, that they saw how I was.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: And the other is a poor grade. Which one is a larger fear for you?
Client: I would say maybe like judging.
Counselor: Okay, so the grade's a concern.
Client: Yeah. But I figure I could do better on a subsequent one. But when people have this opinion of you, I feel like that doesn't go away as quickly.
Counselor: All right, and what would it mean if they. They thought you were anxious during that presentation?
Client: I guess I worry that they would think I'm anxious because I don't know what I'm doing or I don't belong there.
Counselor: Okay. I don't belong there.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: All right, so if they notice your anxiety, then they think you don't belong at that level.
Client: Yeah. Like, I don't deserve to be in that program.
Counselor: I don't deserve to be in that program.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: Okay. If they don't recognize those symptoms, they wouldn't think that. But if they do, that's what they might think, right?
Client: Like that. Maybe they think that's why I'm anxious or that's why I'm not doing well.
Counselor: Well, how do you feel about your abilities and status in the program you're in?
Client: I think, you know, typically I'm one of the top students in my program, and I seem to get the concepts pretty well. It's just when I have to demonstrate those concepts or demonstrate via, like, a presentation or something that I'm worried that, you know, maybe I'm an imposter or something. But. So I start to question myself. But I think in general that, you know, I'm a pretty good student before this and I'm doing pretty well in the program.
Counselor: All right, so you're. You're a good student. You recognize that you have this one area where you don't feel like you do a great job. Presentations. Yeah, but in terms of grade, you really only had one bad presentation. Yeah, but grades aside, you're anxious and you're worried your classmates can pick up on that.
Client: Yeah, exactly.
Counselor: Okay, so if they thought you were. Used the word impostor.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: So if they thought you were an imposter, let's just say that that was something they actually believed because of what's been happening.
Client: Yeah.
Counselor: What would that mean? What would it mean to you if your classmates thought you were an imposter.
Client: Um, I don't know. Maybe I am. Maybe I don't deserve to be there.
Counselor: I don't deserve to be there.
Client: Yeah. Like, maybe I shouldn't be in this program. Like, maybe I should just drop out.
Counselor:
output: All right, so if they believe. If they believe you're an imposter based on these physical symptoms and anxiety, maybe that means to you anyway, that means you shouldn't, or you are an imposter, you shouldn't be there.

instruction: You are playing the role of a counselor in a psychological counseling session. Your task is to generate the next counselor utterance in the dialogue. The goal is to create a natural and engaging response that builds on the previous conversation.
input:
Counselor: Hello, Carlos. How are you feeling today?
Client: Feeling terrible. I had a wrestling match last night, and I lost my match again. I should just quit the team. I'm such a bad wrestler.
Counselor: What do you mean by again?
Client: I lost my match last week, too. I should just quit the team.
